10025-gaslight-sonatas:
Fannie Hurst's 1918 story collection takes its title from the gaslit city, and its tales are set among modern women making their way. The contents run from Bitter-Sweet and Sieve of Fulfilment to Ice-Water, Hers Not to Reason Why, Golden Fleece, and Nightshade.

Hurst writes about love, work, and ambition with warmth and a sharp eye for detail, and her heroines refuse easy endings. The final story, Get Ready the Wreaths, closes the set on a note of earned hope. Readers get early twentieth-century New York in story form, told by one of its most popular writers.
10045-dave-darrin-s-second-year-at-annap:
H. Irving Hancock's 1911 school story follows Dave Darrin through his second year at the Naval Academy at Annapolis, when he and his classmates are still youngsters. The book opens on a question of midshipman honor, with advice on pap-sheets and a Pennington who goes too far.

Later chapters bring a meeting ashore, trouble on foreign soil, the tragedy of a gale, the despair of a recall, and a grim watch from the waves. Hancock writes brisk, patriotic adventure for boys. Readers get academy life, friendship, and the discipline that turns schoolboys into officers.
10930-the-buccaneer-farmer-published-in-:
Harold Bindloss set this 1918 novel between an English estate and the Caribbean. Kit Askew, a young farmer, fights a landlord's pressure at home in the Lake District, then sails to a Spanish-American coast where an old buccaneer's gold, a prison. The book appeared in England as Askew's Victory.

Three parts carry the story: trouble at Ashness, adventure abroad, and Kit's return to settle accounts. Grace, Janet, and the proud Osborn shape the home plot, while Kit's courage and loyalty drive the sea plot. Readers get a fast-moving tale of land, money, and honour, told with the outdoor detail Bindloss favoured.
11400-mystic-isles-of-the-south-seas:
Frederick O'Brien's Mystic Isles of the South Seas records his days and nights, thoughts and dreams in Tahiti and Moorea, written without authority of science or exactitude, as vivid impressions. O'Brien went below the equator with one thought, to play, and offers his chronicle as an anodyne. transporting readers to sapphire lagoons, silver beaches, songs, dances, and the merriest, most fascinating world of the cosmos. The book precedes White Shadows in the South Seas in experience.

A promised sequel, Atolls of the Sun, would cover the Dangerous Archipelago. O'Brien's tone is romantic and unapologetic, celebrating island life against the machine age's afflictions. Travel readers will find the book a period escape, beautiful in description and frank about its lack of science.
11897-on-the-indian-sect-of-the-jainas:
Johann Georg Bühler's essay On the Indian Sect of the Jainas was read at the anniversary meeting of Vienna's Imperial Academy of Sciences. It was translated from German and edited by James Burgess, with an outline of Jaina mythology. The 1903 edition presents a European scholar's systematic account of a religion little known to English readers.

Bühler, a member of the Imperial Academy, draws on Sanskrit and Prakrit sources to describe Jaina doctrine, community, and history. Burgess's outline helps readers place gods, teachers, and myths. The book remains a landmark of early Indology: a careful, source-based introduction to Jainism, written before the field had the translations and fieldwork it later gained.
11906-four-dimensional-vistas:
Claude Bragdon's Four-Dimensional Vistas argues that human perception can be enlarged beyond ordinary three-dimensional space. Chapters move from the quest for freedom and the failure of common sense to a dimensional ladder. They teach readers to think in terms of spaces, and to grasp the subjectivity of space itself.

Bragdon draws on mathematics, science, and intuition, and even suggests that sleep may involve a higher-dimensional existence, answering a longing that waking life cannot satisfy. Written in a speculative, earnest style, the book belongs to the early twentieth-century fashion for a fourth dimension, treating it less as a puzzle than as a path to freedom.
11938-folklore-of-the-santal-parganas:
Folklore of the Santal Parganas, translated by Cecil Henry Bompas of the Indian Civil Service and published in 1909, gathers tales from the Santal people of eastern India. Part 1 opens with Bajun and Jhore, Anuwa and his mother, Ledha and the leopard, and the cruel stepmother, followed by Karmu and Dharmu and the jealous stepmother.

Later tales include the pious woman, the wise daughter-in-law, the oilman and his sons, the girl who found helpers, and how to grow rich. Bompas's translations preserve the stories' plain, oral shape, with stepmothers, leopards, helpers. Moral turns that will feel familiar to readers of European folktales, yet rooted in Santal village life.
1291-herodias:
Gustave Flaubert tells the tale of Herodias, wife of Herod Antipas, whose daughter Salome dances for the king and asks for the head of John the Baptist. The short novel follows the feast, the dance, and the execution in the desert fortress of Machaerus, with Roman, Jewish, and Arab powers circling.

Flaubert writes the East in jeweled, exact prose, and his Salome is cool, political, and deadly. The tale, third of his Three Tales, inspired Wilde's play and Strauss's opera. It stands as a masterclass in short, rich historical fiction.
13508-weird-tales-from-northern-seas:
Jonas Lie's weird tales from northern seas, translated from Danish by R. Nisbet Bain in 1893 with twelve illustrations by Laurence Housman, open with a fisherman and a draug on Kvalholm in Helgeland. Elias, a poor fisherman, lives with his wife Karen, once in service at the parson's house at Alstad, and meets the dead at sea.

Jack of Sjöholm and the Gan-Finn, Tug of War, The Earth Draws, the Cormorants of Andvaer, Isaac and the Parson of Brönö, the Wind-Gnome, the Huldrefish, and Finn Blood follow. A boatman, uneasy about a new sekstring, tests its keel by club light and hears a gulping sound and a stench of rottenness from the sea. Lie writes northern folk horror with salt, cold, and dread.
14323-la-bas:
J. K. Huysmans's Là-Bas, translated by Keene Wallace and privately published in English in 1928, follows Durtal, a writer abandoning modern novel subjects to study Gilles de Rais. Des Hermies, his friend, accepts naturalist vocabulary for latrines, hospitals, and workshops, since Zola proved heavy-handed words can carry power. He objects instead to naturalism's earthy ideas, which flatten human mystery into mere appetite.

Medicine supplies a strange debate. Doctors, one speaker complains, poison bodies with pilocarpine, drive eczema inward until old men grow childish or dangerous, and chase drugs they barely understand. Antipyrine, applied with iodide and cold Bondonneau water, supposedly combats cancer, yet no doctor knows the cure. Old-time doctors, Durtal wonders, came nearer healing. Decadent, learned, and unsettling, Là-Bas pairs medieval Satanism with modern Paris talk, and finds both haunted by the same hunger for more.
14384-white-shadows-in-the-south-seas:
Frederick O'Brien sailed to the Marquesas Islands in the early 1900s and stayed on, living at Atuona among islanders whose world was changing fast. His 1919 travel book records that stay in vivid, firsthand prose.

O'Brien describes traders, missionaries, and French officials, the decline of old customs, and the lure of copra and pearl shell. He also writes about Paul Gauguin, who had died at Atuona years before and whose house and pictures lingered in local memory. The book helped shape Western images of the South Seas, for better and for worse.
14552-a-catechism-of-christian-doctrine-:
This Baltimore Catechism No. 2, prepared by order of the Third Plenary Council of Baltimore and approved in 1885, served confirmation classes in American Catholic schools. Cardinal McCloskey and Archbishop Gibbons gave its imprimatur.

Questions and answers in numbered form cover the Creed, the commandments, prayer, and the sacraments, with prayers and hymns appended. One section sets out the five steps for a good confession, from sorrow to penance. The book shaped Catholic teaching for generations, and its crisp question-and-answer form remains instantly recognizable. Millions of American schoolchildren learned their faith from its pages.
14572-the-spirit-of-christmas:
Henry Van Dyke's Spirit of Christmas, copyrighted in 1905 and issued by Scribner in 1911, gathers a dream story, an essay, a sermon, and two prayers for the season. Van Dyke was a Princeton professor and popular preacher.

The Christmas Angel dreams of a country beyond the stars, where silver bells chime over golden ways and meadows of asphodel. An essay on Christmas giving and living, a sermon on keeping Christmas, and prayers for home and lonely folks follow. The book is warm, literary, and devout, a classic American Christmas keepsake. Van Dyke's Christmas writings stayed in print for decades.
14629-a-wonderful-night-an-interpretatio:
James H. Snowden wrote A Wonderful Night, an interpretation of Christmas, published by Macmillan with decorations by Maud and Miska Petersham. The dust jacket calls the nativity night crowned with supreme distinction.

Snowden traces the steps leading to Bethlehem, from angels singing to the inn with no room. He reads that exclusion as prophetic of Christ's later reception, when Herod and others left no room for him. The book invests the story with poetic light for modern readers. It is a devotional Christmas interpretation, earnest and lyrical. Snowden was a Presbyterian minister and seminary professor.
14782-england-over-seas:
Lloyd Roberts's 1914 poems, dedicated to Hope, sing England and the lands beyond it in short lyrics. England's fields are green and cliffs white like milk. Grey fogs creep across moors, warm suns stand between, summer winds sing in the wheat and poppies burn red along the hedges.

Later poems follow a homesteader and husbands over seas. The trail from Napoli, runners of the rain and spring madness follow, with a morning when rain birds call, flutes of frogs, berry pickers and a fruit rancher from exile. August on the river, musk rats, the kill on the marshes and winter winds close the year. Roberts writes with a light, musical touch, and his England is felt as much as described.
15229-a-review-of-the-resources-and-indu:
Issued by Washington's Bureau of Statistics, Agriculture and Immigration in 1909, this review surveys the state's resources and industries for free distribution. A frontispiece shows the new capitol to rise at Olympia, authorized by the 1909 legislature. A transmittal letter to Governor Hay fronts the report.

Chapters, in biennial report form, cover farms, forests, mines, fisheries, and manufactures, with figures for growth and trade. The tone is boosterish and official, aimed at settlers and investors. Historians of the Pacific Northwest will find the review a detailed snapshot of Washington on the verge of modern growth.
15343-a-little-book-for-christmas:
Cyrus Townsend Brady's Little Book for Christmas, published by Putnam in 1917, contains a greeting, advice, personal adventures, a carol, a meditation, and three Christmas stories for all ages. Will Crawford drew pictures and decorations, including the author making his book. Brady dedicates it to Mrs. Leonard Hill and her Criterion Society companions.

Brady, chaplain to that society, writes with warmth for friends at Christmas, mixing memory, faith, and cheer. His stories suit reading by the fire. Readers who love old Christmas books will find this one gentle, nostalgic, and full of holiday spirit.
15532-novelas-cortas:
Pedro A. de Alarcón, member of the Spanish Academy, wrote these short novels, edited with notes and vocabulary by W. F. Giese of the University of Wisconsin, published by Ginn and Company. The edition is made for American students of Spanish, with idiomatic commentary, notes, exercises for translation into Spanish, and a full vocabulary.

Contents include La Buenaventura, La Corneta de Llaves, Las Dos Glorias, El Afrancesado, Viva el Papa, El Extranjero, El Libro Talonario, Moros y Cristianos, and El Año en Spitzberg. The first tale opens in August 1816, when a ragged gypsy shearer named Heredia rides a thin donkey to the captain general's doors at Granada and asks to see him. Alarcón's tales mix humor, history, and Spanish custom, in clear prose suited to learners.
1571-critias:
Plato's Critias is a fragment that breaks off in mid-sentence, meant as the second part of a trilogy with the Timaeus. In it Critias tells of ancient Athens and of Atlantis, a great island empire of wealth and power that grew proud, warred against Athens. Sank beneath the sea in a single day and night.

Translated by Benjamin Jowett, the dialogue gives the fullest ancient account of Atlantis, with its rings of land and water, its temples, and its kings. Its unfinished state adds to its mystery. The fragment has haunted later ages, and it remains the source of every Atlantis tale since.
1591-protagoras:
Plato's Protagoras, translated by Benjamin Jowett, stages a conversation at the house of Callias. Socrates meets the great Sophist Protagoras, a man said to have spent more on sophists than all the rest of the world. Their talk asks whether virtue can be taught, and what a teacher of virtue truly sells.

Socrates and Protagoras argue by myth, by logic, and by a poem, and the dialogue ends with roles reversed and questions open. Its portrait of Athenian intellectual life is vivid. The Protagoras is a lively, witty introduction to Plato's contest with the Sophists.
16012-the-ned-m-keown-stories-traits-and:
A volume of Irish peasant tales by William Carleton, volume three of his works, issued in 1881. Traits and Stories of the Irish Peasantry gathers Ned M'Keown, The Three Tasks, Shane Fadh's Wedding, Larry M'Farland's Wake, and The Battle of the Factions. Carleton's introduction prepares English and Scotch readers for a people who form an important part of the empire.

Ned M'Keown leads with humour and shrewdness, while weddings, wakes, and faction fights show peasant life in full. Carleton writes from inside the cabins he knew. His tales mix laughter with sorrow, never scorning his folk. The volume stands as a classic of Irish letters: a peasantry, drawn true, in stories that still live.
1608-camille-la-dame-aux-camilias:
Alexandre Dumas fils's Camille, La Dame aux Camelias, follows Marguerite Gautier, a Paris courtesan known for her camellias, who falls truly in love with the young Armand Duval. Their happiness in the country is broken by Armand's father, who begs Marguerite to give Armand up for his family's sake.

Marguerite's sacrifice, her return to Paris, and her death from consumption close a tale that made its author famous and inspired Verdi's Traviata. Dumas writes with sentiment and moral force. Camille is a classic of French romantic literature, and a tearful favourite ever since.
16241-barbara-s-heritage-young-americans:
Deristhe L. Hoyt's Barbara's Heritage, or Young Americans Among the Old Italian Masters, reached a third edition in Boston and Chicago in 1899 with W. A. Wilde. Hoyt, author of The World's Painters, dedicates the book to the brother and sister who shared many happy sojourns in Italy. A frontispiece shows Titian's Assumption of the Virgin in the Venice Academy.

Chapters carry young Americans across two oceans to beautiful Florence, where a new friend appears, straws show the wind, and a startling disclosure unfolds. Rome, a coming-out party, a mystery for Howard, and Cupid laughing follow. The book mixes travel, art history, and romance for young readers. Art lovers will enjoy its Italian gallery tour.
16431-richard-wagner-composer-of-operas:
John F. Runciman traces Wagner's life from his 1813 Leipzig birth to his death in Venice in 1883. Early boyhood, Paris years, Dresden, and exile lead into the great operas: Rienzi, The Flying Dutchman, Tannhauser, Lohengrin, Tristan, the Mastersingers, and the Ring cycle, closing with Parsifal. King Ludwig of Bavaria plays a key role.

Runciman writes as an admirer who still notes flaws, and the chapters move opera by opera. Plates show Wagner, his birthplace, and the Bayreuth theater. The book suits readers who want one clear life of the composer, tied at each step to the music he was making.
16458-the-princess-pocahontas:
Virginia Watson retells the Pocahontas story for young readers in this illustrated volume. Chapters follow the return of warriors, midnight in the forest, running the gauntlet, a fight in the swamp, and Pocahontas defying Powhatan. Later chapters bring Jamestown, a baptism, John Rolfe, a wedding, and Pocahontas in England.

Watson writes in the earnest, adventurous style of early children's history, with drawings by George Wharton Edwards. The tale follows the familiar Smith and Rolfe episodes as they were told in her day. Young readers meeting Pocahontas for the first time will find a clear, stirring version of the legend.
16601-the-death-wake-or-lunacy-a-necroma:
Thomas T. Stoddart wrote this long poem in three linked parts, first put out in London in 1895 with a short lead-in by Andrew Lang. It tells of a monk driven mad by love who sails with the dead bride he calls the Bride of Heaven. Sea, sky, and grave images run through the whole work.

Lang praises the poem for its clear peace in sea and sky, set against its wild and grim tale. Readers get a strange, dream-like voyage where love, death, and faith mix with sharp sights of the shore. The verse is best read slowly, for its force lies in mood and image more than in plain plot.
1672-gorgias:
Athens loved a good speech, and Gorgias of Leontini was the most famous speech-teacher in Greece when Socrates met him and asked what his art was actually good for. Gorgias claims that rhetoric, the art of persuasion, is the greatest power a man can hold.

Socrates answers that persuasion without knowledge of right and wrong is mere flattery, and that it is better to suffer injustice than to do it. The dialogue turns fierce as Callicles defends the strong man's right to take what he wants. It remains the classic attack on the idea that winning an argument is the same as being right.
1673-lesser-hippias:
Plato's Lesser Hippias, translated by Benjamin Jowett, asks whether the man who does wrong knowingly is better than the man who does wrong unknowingly. Socrates argues, against Hippias the Sophist, that the skilled liar and the skilled truth-teller share one art, and the dialogue ends in the usual Socratic puzzle.

An appendix on genuine and spurious Platonic works frames the text, noting that Aristotle's evidence is the most valuable for sorting them. The dialogue is short and provocative. It is a challenging early Plato work, best read as a paradox about skill, knowledge, and moral choice.
1681-eryxias:
Eryxias, another dialogue by a Platonic imitator translated by Benjamin Jowett, asks a question friends can quarrel over for a lifetime: is wealth a good thing or a bad one. Socrates, Eryxias, and Erasistratus start as dear friends and soon fall to disputing, because wealth seems good when it buys comfort and evil when it feeds greed.

The talk moves through examples of what money can and cannot do, and it ends without a tidy verdict, which is the point. Like the other dialogues in the appendix, this one is not Plato's own work. It keeps his method alive: take a word everyone uses, press it hard, and watch certainty thin out.
17135-twas-the-night-before-christmas-a-:
Clement C. Moore's Visit from St. Nicholas, pictured by Jessie Willcox Smith in this Houghton Mifflin edition, is the poem most of us call 'Twas the Night Before Christmas. An introduction tells how friends once gathered at Moore's tomb on Christmas Eve to recite it together. Moore, born near Chelsea Square in 1781, wrote it as a gift for his own children, never expecting fame from verse.

He thought his Hebrew dictionary would be his mark, yet the poem outlived all his learned work. Smith's pictures add warmth to the sleigh, the stockings, and the happy Christmas to all. Families will find here the classic text in a handsome, gift-ready form for reading aloud each Eve.
17382-a-visit-from-saint-nicholas:
Clement C. Moore's beloved Christmas poem appears here in an illustrated edition from James G. Gregory of New York, entered in 1862, with drawings by F. O. C. Darley. The poem tells of a household asleep on Christmas Eve, stockings hung by the chimney, and a sudden visit from Saint Nicholas with his sleigh and reindeer. Its opening lines are among the best known in American verse.

Readers get the poem in a handsome period setting, with Darley's pictures beside Moore's text. The edition suits families reading aloud at Christmas and collectors of the poem's publishing history. Its charm lies in the match of simple verse and Victorian illustration.
17733-the-black-douglas:
S. R. Crockett wrote The Black Douglas in 1899, a Scottish romance set in the days of the great Douglas lords. The hero rides home to a land of castles, feuds, and hard men, and soon meets a fair lady, a witch woman, and foes who would see his house fall.

Chapters carry the tale from the Douglas muster to a rose-red pavilion, the jailing of Malise the Smith, and rides across wild hills. Crockett, famed for The Raiders, writes in a rich Scots voice, with sword play, love, and old border pride. Readers who like bold, old-style Scottish tales will find this one full of color, clash, and loyal hearts.
1841-z-marcas:
Z. Marcas was, the narrator insists, a political genius without a party, a man who did other men's work and watched lesser men take the credit. Marcas, a political genius without a party, does the work of others and watches lesser men take the credit, while he labors on in a garret.

Balzac dedicates the tale to Count William of Württemberg. Its bitterness is personal: Marcas is Balzac's portrait of talent wasted by a system that rewards connections over merit. The novella is short and fierce, and its hero's obscurity — a name reduced to an initial — is the whole point.
1850-old-christmas:
Is old, good old Christmas gone, with nothing left but the hair of his gray head and beard. Irving answers by gathering sketches of an English country Christmas. The contents run from the stage-coach to Christmas Day itself, with a squire's hall, a manor house in the French taste of Charles II's time, and moonbeams on old rooms.

Irving writes as an American visitor charmed by English custom. The sketches helped fix the modern image of Christmas: feasting, games, and a great house open to neighbors. Readers who love A Christmas Carol's world will find its source here, in prose that is warm, nostalgic, and fond of every rite it describes.
18908-christmas:
Robert Haven Schauffler edited this Christmas anthology for the Our American Holidays series, a set of school and college collections of verse, plays, stories, addresses, articles, and orations suited to each holiday. The Christmas volume gathers the best seasonal writing for students and teachers, chosen for classroom use and for reading aloud.

Inside are poems, stories, and speeches that mark December 25th, from religious verse to fireside tales. The series aimed to give young readers good writing tied to the year's festivals. Readers get a varied, old-fashioned Christmas reader, useful for holiday programs, family reading, and anyone who enjoys seasonal literature in its traditional forms.
1900-typee-a-romance-of-the-south-seas:
Herman Melville's Typee, a romance of the South Seas, records his months among the Typee people of the Marquesas after deserting a whaling ship. The preface notes that more than three years have passed since the events, most of them spent by the author tossing about on the wide ocean.

Melville and his companion Toby, sharing a small morsel of refreshment from a sacred package, enter a valley that is both paradise and prison. Melville writes its customs, feasts, and taboos with wonder. The book made his name, and it remains a vivid early account of Polynesian life, told by a sailor who loved what he found and feared what it cost.
19014-nibsy-s-christmas:
Jacob August Riis published this Christmas story in 1893, reprinted in 1969 in the Short Story Index Reprint Series. Riis, the Danish-American reformer known for exposing New York's slums, dedicated the story to Queen Louise of Denmark, friend of the afflicted and mother of the motherless in his childhood home. An illustration shows Nibsy as Santa Claus.

The tale opens on Christmas Eve on the East Side, in cold and darkness, with light struggling through frozen windows of a delicatessen and a corner saloon. From that hard setting grows a story of charity and childhood hope. Readers get a short, humane Christmas tale from the reform era, written by a man who knew the streets he described.
19649-the-captain-of-the-kansas:
Louis Tracy was a British writer of popular adventure and mystery novels. His 1906 novel The Captain of the Kansas is a sea story built around shipboard life and romance. A sampler of its pages shows bright drawing-room talk at sea. One young woman jokes that she makes a most fascinating invalid. Banter like that carries much of the book's charm.

Tracy sold stories on pace, charm, and cliff-edge turns. A liner setting let him mix social comedy with danger at sea. Edwardian readers bought his novels in large numbers. This one shows why: light dialogue on deck, trouble never far off. It is a clean sample of the popular sea romance of its time.
19757-return-loads-to-increase-transport:
Trucks that haul goods one way often return empty. Return Loads addresses that waste in wartime America. The Council of National Defense, through its Highways Transport Committee, built a system against empty running. State councils of defense, chambers of commerce, and war boards cooperated. Their aim was to use highways to strengthen the nation's transport resources.

Rail lines were strained during the First World War. Loaded returns could free rail capacity and save fuel, tires, and labor. The plan linked local groups into one working network. Pamphlets like this show home-front logistics in detail. Moving food and materiel was a weapon of war too. This is the paperwork of that effort, preserved.
20218-history-of-the-incas:
Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa wrote History of the Incas for King Philip II of Spain. His contents list opens with a dedicatory letter to that king. Early chapters divide the history and describe the ancient land. One chapter tells of a lost Atlantic island and its first peoples.

Later chapters give the fable of Peru's first peoples in their own telling. Sarmiento wrote from Quechua accounts gathered in Peru itself. His work is a key early source on Inca kings and myths. Readers get Inca history as a Spanish captain recorded it in the 1570s.
20979-brother-copas:
The master of St. Hospital-by-Merton sharpens his Trinity Gaudy sermon in Brother Copas. Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch gives Eustace Blanchminster a quick, fastidious sense of style. Pains over each phrase mark the cleric's care as the tale opens.

Copas, a lay brother of the hospital, stands at the tale's warm heart. Q sets cloister calm against the claims of love and the world. His prose, rich yet clear, dignifies small lives and old stones. Brother Copas shows Quiller-Couch in his tender vein, a tale of faith, duty, and a heart that outgrows its walls.
21356-nat-the-naturalist-a-boy-s-adventu:
Nat is an orphan raised by an aunt who dislikes boys and an uncle who loves him. He already collects specimens when his aunt's brother, a famous naturalist back from South America, comes home. George Manville Fenn lets the boy help stuff and catalogue the new specimens and beg his way onto the next expedition. Shooting and sailing lessons follow.

They sail by P and O liner from Marseilles to the Java Seas and buy a small boat. There they spend years collecting birds, beetles, and whatever else the islands offer, helped by a local assistant. When a hostile tribe steals their boat and the assistant vanishes, the collectors must build their way home.
21375-the-weathercock-being-the-adventur:
Vane Lee, sixteen, lives with his doctor uncle in a Lincolnshire village and invents things, not always safely. George Manville Fenn gave the book a second title, The Boy Inventor. He shows Vane taking the church clock apart, cleaning it, and rebuilding it without two vital wheels. At midnight the bell strikes without stopping, the village fire signal.

Fire hoses turn out for a fire that never existed. Later, two gipsy boys beat Vane nearly to death, and for long he cannot say who did it. A naturalist like his creator, Vane makes friends among the rector's pupils while the village sorts out his accident and his attackers.
21387-in-the-eastern-seas:
Walter Heathfield and his sister Emily are pulled from a sinking ship at the start of W. H. G. Kingston's In the Eastern Seas. Their father dies, kin in London show no care, and a kind uncle soon dies too. The captain who saved them takes the pair into his own family.

He then carries them on his next voyage, bound for the East Indies on the Bussorah Merchant. A fellow guest, Mr Nicholas Hooker, is a keen student of nature. He points out the plants and beasts they meet on the way. Storms, strange coasts, and sea perils fill this long, warm tale.
21504-my-first-voyage-to-southern-seas:
A London merchant's sudden death opens W. H. G. Kingston's My First Voyage to Southern Seas. The family lived near Blackheath, above Greenwich and the Thames. The eldest son had gone to sea and vanished; some thought him dead.

The second son, our hero, ships as a midshipman in the 1850s, the age of sail. Rumour and chance lead him toward his lost brother, held captive far away. Pirates, drunken captains, and wrecks crowd the long tale, with fine views of Ceylon. Kingston's seamanship, as ever, is exact, and the action never drags.
21784-the-goblins-christmas:
Goblins hold a wild Christmas frolic in this rhymed picture book by Elizabeth Anderson, published at Los Angeles in 1908. A big bright moon hangs over tall pines as the Man in the Moon calls the spooks out for a merry dance. A witch and a goblin lead the sprites down the Milky Way. A black caldron boils high enough to light the sky.

Alexander Sharp's pictures follow the fun: a fairy queen, sprites and toadstools, a boy and a rabbit, an elf and a spider. Anderson wrote the book for two children, Earl and Georgia, who loved fairies in the grass. The verse is spooky without real fright. It is a playful American fairy book from the age of color picture books.
22033-plotting-in-pirate-seas:
Francis Rolt-Wheeler opened his Round the World with the Boy Journalists series with Plotting in Pirate Seas in 1921. His young hero sails to Haiti, the Black republic in the Caribbean. The roll of voodoo drums frightens the boy on his first night ashore. His father's strange disappearance weighs on him through every chapter.

The trail leads through the ruined citadel of King Christophe and out to the old buccaneer island of Tortuga. Cuba follows, with plots thickening in pirate seas once ruled by men like Morgan. Rolt-Wheeler mixes real history and geography into the adventure. Boys of 1921 got a Caribbean tour disguised as a mystery.
22186-for-the-liberty-of-texas:
Edward Stratemeyer wrote For the Liberty of Texas in 1900 as a boy's history of the Texas revolution. Stratemeyer, the busiest boys' author of his age, placed young heroes inside great events. Texas in 1835 rose against Mexican rule. The Alamo, Goliad, and San Jacinto gave the struggle its immortal names, and Stratemeyer's lads stand near them all.

The publisher's lists at the front advertise Stratemeyer's many series at a dollar and a quarter a volume. Inside, the story mixes real commanders with invented boys on scout and courier duty. Such books taught history as adventure to American schoolboys. This one keeps the Texas myth in its simple, heroic form.
22696-colonel-crockett-s-co-operative-ch:
Colonel Crockett's Co-operative Christmas is a tall-tale Christmas story starring Colonel Crockett, the legendary bear hunter of American folklore. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Davy Crockett yarns, half history and half brag, filled almanacs and story papers for a century.

The narrator's sample fix is pure Crockett: he wakes to find himself on a pinhead of an island, no bigger than a freckle on the moon. Sky surrounds him, except where the water is. And he has nothing to drink that water with. Cooperative gift-giving, frontier style, drives the Christmas plot from there. The story keeps the backwoods voice that made Crockett a folk hero: extravagant, funny, and impossible to kill.
23118-a-chinese-command-a-story-of-adven:
A gust at Kingston-on-Thames starts A Chinese Command, a story of adventure in eastern seas. A gust tears down the cottage chimney, driving smoke across the snug sitting room. Sparks scatter, hissing, over the hearth rug. A tall, fair young giant stamps them out, rousing himself lazily from his chair to do it.

That giant takes ship for China, where command, mutiny, and pirates wait in the manner of Harry Collingwood's sea tales, to whom this adventure is credited. Eastern seas in boys' fiction meant typhoons, junks, and narrow escapes in weekly parts. The Thames cottage opening promises the contrast the genre loved, quiet home against the China coast. The voyage delivers it at full sail.
23161-sodom-and-gomorrah-texas:
A snap judgment leads to disaster in Sodom and Gomorrah, Texas. An official had given a snap judgement, the tale says, and it led to disaster. The instructions are not clear. Nowhere, the complaint runs, does all that verbiage state how large a being must be before it counts as a person.

Counting people, in this story, is a technical problem with biblical stakes. Two Texas towns named for the cities of the plain invite exactly the comparison the title makes, and officialdom's vague orders give the comparison teeth. The excerpt's complaint, nowhere does it say how big, could head a dozen bureaucratic horror stories. Here it heads a short, dry piece of speculative fiction about measurement, mercy, and forms filled in too fast.
23751-southern-stories-retold-from-st-ni:
The Century Company gathered these Southern stories from St. Nicholas magazine into one volume in 1907. They had first appeared across nearly twenty years, from 1889 to 1907, and the collection keeps the magazine's voice: clear, lively, and written for young readers.

Contents include a real Uncle Remus story by Joel Chandler Harris, Margaret Minor's His Hero, and tales of the earthquake at Charleston and hiding places in war times. Other pieces treat Louisiana's purchase, queer American rivers, catching terrapin, and the city that lives outdoors. Together they give a young reader's tour of the South, its rivers, towns, and past.
24404-a-sermon-preached-on-the-anniversa:
Jonathan M. Wainwright, rector of Trinity Church, Boston, preached this sermon on the anniversary of the Boston Female Asylum for Destitute Orphans, September 25, 1835. It was published by request of the Board of Managers. Dutton and Wentworth of Boston printed it in 1835. Wainwright tells the board that he first declined to print the sermon, since it was not prepared for publication. It has been his practice to abstain from appearing in print when he properly could.

Yielding to the board's renewed request, though his conviction about such publications remains unchanged, he commits the sermon to them. He hopes its possession may gratify anyone interested in their excellent institution. His letter to the board is dated Boston, October 6, 1835. The sermon text is Proverbs, chapter twenty-two, verse nine: he that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed, for he giveth bread to the poor. Readers get an orphan asylum's anniversary sermon.
24694-peter-prim-s-profitable-present-to: Published at Philadelphia by Morgan and Sons, this tiny illustrated chapbook offers counting rhymes for little misses and masters. One, two, come buckle my shoe, and you lazy elf, pray do it yourself. Three, four, shut the door, and keep warm without thinking of the storm. Five, six, sticks for a currant cake follow, in neat engravings.
25483-in-the-time-that-was:
J. Frederic Thorne renders Chilkat legends into English in this Seattle volume, the first of a series. The tales were told by Zachook the Bear to Thorne, whom the tribe called Kitchakahaech the Raven. Thorne travelled with Zachook by dog-team, snowshoe, and canoe, and carried the stories in memory for many weary miles. He warns that English, stiff beside the gutturals of the original telling, must lose something of campfire and trail.

One legend tells of the time before time, when no water lay on earth or in the sea's bowl. Only Heen, the water, lived in a deep well among mountains, guarded day and night by Heenhadowa, the Thirst Spirit. He would give no drop to man, animal, or bird, not even enough to wet a mosquito's tongue. Judson T. Sergeant illustrated the book.
2593-the-life-of-stephen-a-douglas:
William Gardner wrote this life of Stephen A. Douglas, the Illinois senator known as the Little Giant, and the first volume in a series on his career. Douglas rose from a Vermont boyhood to dominate the Senate in the years before the Civil War.

Gardner follows his debates, his railroad schemes, and his rivalry with Abraham Lincoln, whose 1858 debates made both men famous. The book treats Douglas as a master of party politics in a nation splitting apart. Readers get a full portrait of a man who sought the presidency while his country slid toward war.
26020-apis-mellifica-or-the-poison-of-th:
C. W. Wolf, former district physician in Berlin, treats bee poison as a healing agent in Apis Mellifica, printed at Philadelphia in 1858. Wolf says a physician who has spent years prescribing for crowds owes the world his experience, if his conscience holds it useful. Forty years of practice, he claims, sanction every fact in his essay, and no fact is adopted lightly.

The book covers fever and typhoid gastric states that arise during erysipelas, scarlatina, rubeola, measles, and nettle rash. Wolf's method gives Apis, then waits. If no gain comes in three days, a psoric taint blocks cure, and one globule of Kali carbonicum on the fourth day may clear the way before Apis resumes. The essay is a homeopathic record of its age, framed as claimed cures.
26621-the-story-of-madras:
Glyn Barlow, M.A., wrote this city history for Oxford University Press in 1921, with maps and illustrations by the author himself. Fifteen chapters run from before the beginning through the beginning, Fort St. George, the wall, expansion, and outposts to churches, palaces, the sea, and the schools. Barlow closes by calling Madras no mean city, in a phrase that crowns his civic pride.

Chronological notes anchor the tale: the East India Company in 1600, Francis Day's acquisition of the site in 1639, French capture in 1746 and restoration in 1748. Clive's capture of Arcot, Lally's failed siege of 1758-59, and Wandiwash in 1760 mark the Anglo-French struggle. Chepauk Palace, Government House, and St. Mary's in the fort give the story its landmarks.
26870-on-the-uncertainty-of-the-signs-of:
William Hunter, physician extraordinary to the Queen, read this paper to the Medical Society on July 14, 1783, and it was printed at London in 1818 after his death. Its occasion was a young woman jailed for supposedly murdering her bastard child. A friend of rank believed her innocent, though local feeling ran high against her as cruel and unnatural. Hunter wrote his remarks down for the friend. The woman was acquitted, his letter believed instrumental.

Hunter argues that reason and justice demand inquiry into the circumstances, above all the agent's mind and motives, before judging such a death. A child may be still-born, and its signs may mislead. A woman who hides what happened to save her character will see that concealment read as proof of guilt. The paper warns that imagination can worsen any crime, and circumstances can soften even offensive acts.
26924-flash-lights-from-the-seven-seas:
William L. Stidger published these travel sketches with George H. Doran Company of New York in 1921, with an introduction by Bishop Francis J. McConnell and photographs by the author. McConnell warns that the narratives belong neither to the guide-book nor to scientific geography. They show what visiting the countries would feel like, through impressions made on a mind of sound purpose. Stidger dedicates the book to Mary I. Scott, who led him to the trail of dreams and travel.

Ten chapters flash by theme: flame, physical sights, faith, fear, frightfulness, feminine lights, fun, freedom, failure, and friendship. The opening chapter burns with fire everywhere, from poinsettia bushes bursting into flame overnight in Manila to the great Flame of the Forest tree. Later pages reach the walled city of Manila, Korean girls with American training, the Confucius tomb at Chufu, the Temple of Heaven at Peking, and Borobudur in Java.
2711-a-phyllis-of-the-sierras:
Bret Harte sets this novel where the great Sierra highway nears its summit, among pines, rock, and waste, where weary travelers turn aside for rest. Dusty passengers on the old overland coach have gazed with tired eyes at the same halts, and one such halt holds a Phyllis.

A young woman of the mountains, fresh and frank, meets a worldly visitor, and love grows between two very different lives. Harte writes with pastoral grace, letting the Sierras do much of the talking. The book offers a gentle romance of nature, innocence, and the pull of the road.
2720-the-pension-beaurepas:
Henry James wrote this tale of a young American in Europe who was not rich, and who had heard the Pension Beaurepas was cheap. A boarding house, he had also heard, is a capital place for the study of human nature, and he fancied a literary career.

The pension's guests, with their flirtations, economies, and national types, give him matter enough. James writes with light irony about Americans abroad learning the world. The tale delights as an early sketch of his great theme, innocence meeting Europe over breakfast. The pension's cheap rates prove dear in comedy.
27298-marvel-carbureter-and-heat-control:
The Marvel Carbureter Company of Flint, Michigan, issued this booklet for owners and mechanics working on the Model S carbureter fitted to Series 691 Nash Sixes. A carbureter measures fuel charges for an engine and mixes them with the right amount of air to form a combustible gas. The Model S does so with an automatic air valve under heat control.

Its claimed advantages are simplicity, quick starting in any weather, complete vaporization of fuel through controlled heat, economy, and ease of adjustment. The booklet explains the mixing chamber, float chamber, low speed and high speed nozzles, dash pot, and fuel metering valve. It is a clear, practical manual for one specific part.
27318-pung-chow-the-game-of-a-hundred-in:
L. L. Harr's Pung-Chow, the Game of a Hundred Intelligences, also known as Mah-Diao, Mah-Jong, Mah-Cheuk, Mah-Juck, and Pe-Ling, was published by Harper in 1922. It teaches the Chinese game to Western players. Harr learned it through more than twenty years among business and official circles in Canton, Shanghai, Tientsin, and Pekin.

His keen appreciation helped arouse the game's popularity in the Western Hemisphere, putting Pung Chow on the map west of Suez. The book covers drawing the original hand and the mandarins, also called flowers and seasons. The mandarins number eight, with two for each of the four suits, and the book notes the points that make a game a draw.
27579-stephen-arnold-douglas:
William Garrott Brown wrote this life of Stephen Arnold Douglas, number thirteen in the Riverside Biographical Series, published by Houghton, Mifflin in Boston and New York in 1902. Its portrait comes from a Brady photograph in the Library of the State Department at Washington.

Brown opens on the ten years from 1850 to 1860, a decade whose fascination, he says, is second only to the four years of war that followed. He traces the Whigs' downfall, the Know-Nothings' swift rise and fall, the Republicans' birth, and the Democrats' disruption. Chapters cover youth and the West, the House and the Senate, the great question, leadership, and the rivals.
27654-the-story-of-the-prophet-jonas:
William Tyndale's 1531 translation of the story of the prophet Jonas appears here with spelling modernized and nothing else altered. The first chapter opens with the word of the Lord coming to Jonas, son of Amithai, bidding him rise and go to Nineveh, that great city, and preach against its wickedness.

Jonas instead makes ready to flee to Tharsis, goes down to Joppa, pays his fare, and boards a ship. The Lord hurls a great wind into the sea, and a mighty tempest threatens the ship. The mariners cast out goods to lighten it, while Jonas lies under the hatches asleep. Lots are cast to learn whose cause troubles them, and the lot falls upon Jonas.
27794-fanto-mas:
Pierre Souvestre and Marcel Allain created Fantômas, the genius of crime who spreads terror through Paris, in this novel first published by Brentano's in 1915 and reprinted by Dover in 2006. Cranstoun Metcalfe translated it from the French.

The plot opens with dinner-table talk about a name that means nothing and everything, then follows murder, investigation, and a trial at the court of assize. Fantômas himself slips through disguises and traps, and the book founded one of the great criminal series of popular fiction. Later books kept the villain at large.
27861-kathay-a-cruise-in-the-china-seas:
W. Hastings Macaulay published Kathay, a cruise in the China seas, in New York with G. P. Putnam and Company in 1852. The book follows a sea voyage from American waters toward China, and it is dedicated to Mrs. Jane G. Sproston of Baltimore. Its Latin motto says that travelers crossing the sea change their sky, not their soul.

The contents trace sea-sickness, a shipwreck at the Islets of St. Paul, crossing the line, and arrival at Rio, then doubling the Cape and steering for Java Head. Macaulay writes as a seaman telling his story plainly, and the book preserves a mid-century American voyage to the China seas in firsthand detail.
27870-the-seven-seas:
Rudyard Kipling's The Seven Seas, published in New York by D. Appleton and Company in 1900 after an 1896 copyright, gathers poems of the sea, soldiers, and empire, dedicated to the city of Bombay. Contents include A Song of the English, The Merchantmen, McAndrew's Hymn, The Rhyme of the Three Sealers, and The Song of the Banjo.

A second section adds barrack-room ballads such as Back to the Army Again, Soldier an' Sailor Too, and The Sergeant's Weddin'. The collection shows Kipling at his most musical and imperial, celebrating ships, engineers, and soldiers with the rhythms that made him famous.
28106-tres-comedias:
Jacinto Benavente's Tres Comedias, edited by John Van Horne for American students in 1918, gathers three Spanish plays: Sin querer, De pequenas causas, and Los intereses creados. Benavente, a leading Spanish dramatist, writes comedies of manners in which small causes set off large quarrels, and created interests, or false motives, rule the stage.

Van Horne's edition, in Heath's Modern Language Series, adds notes and a vocabulary for learners of Spanish. The plays are printed in Spanish, with help for readers still building their skill. The volume suits students of Spanish drama and readers of Benavente's witty, observant comedies.
28497-myths-of-the-norsemen-from-the-edd:
H. A. Guerber's Myths of the Norsemen, published in London in 1909, retells northern mythology from the Eddas and sagas for general readers. Guerber had already written a companion volume on the myths of Greece and Rome, and here she turns to the colder, sterner gods of the north.

Chapters take up Odin, Frigga, Thor, Tyr, Frey, Freya, Heimdall, the Norns, the Valkyrs, Hel, Balder, and Loki, with giants, dwarfs, and elves beside them. Longer chapters retell the Sigurd saga, the Frithiof saga, and the Twilight of the Gods, closing with a comparison of Greek and northern myth. Illustrations by several artists accompany the tales.
28893-of-time-and-texas:
William F. Nolan wrote this short science fiction story about Professor C. Cydwick Ohms and his Time Door. In the year 2057, overpopulation torments mankind: colonizing the polar wastes failed, and enforced birth control could not be enforced. Ohms tells reporters he has one answer, and sweeps aside a red velvet drape to show a tall gleaming structure.

The professor insists his door is not a time machine in the popular sense, but a device built by exact calculation. Open it, take a single step, and presto, the past. The story's humor comes from Ohms's grand manner and the reporters' eager questions. Readers get a brisk, witty time-travel tale from a newcomer Nolan, as the magazine's introduction presents him.
29129-the-boy-settlers-a-story-of-early-:
Noah Brooks published this boys' story of early Kansas with Charles Scribner's Sons in 1891, illustrated by W. A. Rogers. Brooks dedicated it to John Greenleaf Whittier, whose patriotic songs inspired the book's prototypes. The settlers arrive in disputed territory, among the Delawares, and build their first home in a deserted cabin.

Chapters follow the fire spreading, polls at Libertyville, a lost boy, a great disaster, and watermelons dotting their own cornfield. The boys learn to fill cabin chinks with sod and to hold what they can get. Readers get a frontier adventure for young readers, warm toward its settlers and vivid about the work of making a Kansas home.
29413-the-voyages-and-adventures-of-capt:
Jules Verne wrote this Arctic adventure, translated from the French and published in Boston in 1876 by James R. Osgood and Company, copyrighted in 1874, with two hundred and fifty illustrations by Riou. Part one, The English at the North Pole, opens with the brig Forward, an unexpected letter, and Dr. Clawbonny, followed by a dog-captain and the voyage to sea.

Later chapters follow the great polar current, the entrance of Davis Strait, and the talk of the crew, as the brig is tossed like a child's toy. Verne's captain drives north toward a goal that consumes him. Readers get a classic polar adventure, richly illustrated, about obsession, ice, and the far north as Verne imagined it before any ship had reached the Pole.
29551-told-by-the-northmen-stories-from-:
E. M. Wilmot-Buxton retold the tales of the Northmen for young readers in this 1908 book from George G. Harrap of London. Its chapters draw on the Eddas and sagas: how all things began, how All-Father Odin became wise, how Loki wagered with dwarfs, and how Thor's hammer was lost and found. The apples of youth, the Fenris Wolf chained, and the pride of Thor brought low stand among them.

Later chapters tell of Balder the Beautiful, Hermod's journey to the underworld, and Loki punished at last. Wilmot-Buxton keeps the old stories plain and vivid, fit for reading aloud. Young readers and lovers of Norse myth will find a fine doorway into Odin, Thor, and Loki.
29621-wild-justice-stories-of-the-south-:
Lloyd Osbourne, author of Baby Bullet, gathered these stories of the South Seas in Wild Justice, printed in 1921 by D. Appleton and Company of New York, with copyrights from 1906 and 1921. Its contents run from The Renegade and The Security of the High Seas through Forty Years Between, O's Head, Professor No No, Captain Elijah Coe, Mr. Bob, and Old Dibs. A picture shows a woman telling Jack to come along with them.

Osbourne writes of seamen, renegades, and island justice, where law is rough and mercy rarer still. Each story stands alone, yet the sea binds them. Readers of South Seas fiction will find a strong, atmospheric collection from the age of Stevenson and his heirs.
29688-home-range-and-movements-of-the-ea:
Donald W. Janes wrote this 1959 paper for the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History, on home range and movements of the eastern cottontail in Kansas. Printed May 4, 1959, as volume ten, number seven, pages 553 to 572, with four plates and three figures, it measures how far cottontails roam. Earlier estimates, Janes notes, varied wildly, from one tenth of an acre to one hundred acres.

Such wide variation called for careful fieldwork, and Janes supplies it, tracking rabbits across Kansas ground. The paper serves wildlife biologists and managers who must know how much room a rabbit needs. Students of mammalogy will find a precise, classic study of a common animal's hidden geography.
30039-adventurers-of-the-far-north-a-chr:
Stephen Leacock chronicles the search for a northern sea route in six linked chapters, from the great Elizabethan navigators to the conquest of the Pole. Samuel Hearne walks overland to the northern ocean. Alexander Mackenzie descends the great river of the north, and Sir John Franklin sails into the tragedy that bears his name. Maps, portraits, and a view of the Arctic Council at work frame the narrative.

Published in Toronto and Glasgow in 1914, the book reads as popular history rather than a dry record. It stresses hardship, courage, and the slow cost of Arctic knowledge. Leacock closes with an epilogue on the Pole itself, plus a bibliographical note and an index. The volume serves both as a readable tale and as a guide to further reading on frozen-sea exploration.
30399-pythias:
Frederik Pohl tells Pythias, illustrated by Mel Hunter, a short tale opening with a murderer's admission. Granted, Larry Connaught did save my life, yet the manner of that rescue drove me to murder him. The narrator sits on the edge of a bed of woven strips of steel, with no mattress, only an extra blanket of olive-drab. He sits in a precinct jail, expecting the District prison and the death house.

A trial will be only a formality, since they found him holding the smoking gun while Connaught choked to death through a hole in his throat. He confessed, acting knowingly, with malice aforethought, in shooting Laurence Connaught dead. They execute murderers, especially because Connaught had saved his life. Extenuating circumstances, he doubts, would convince a jury, though Connaught and he were friends before the war parted them.
30963-a-knyght-ther-was:
Robert F. Young wrote this science fiction story, printed in Analog in July 1963, about a knight who is a little less than perfect. His horse has no metabolism, and his castle is far more mobile in time than it should be. The story opens with lines from Chaucer's Canterbury Tales on a worthy knight who loved chivalry, truth, honour, freedom, and courtesy from the time he first rode out.

Its hero is Mallory, a time-thief who brings the time-space boat Yore back into being in a secluded valley in ancient Britain. He types Castle, Early Sixth-Century on a panel, checks a three-dimensional screen at eight in the evening in summer, in the year 542. He finds oaks, beeches, a full moon, and a forest hiding his castle. Young mixes Arthurian legend with time travel, in a witty tale of a knight out of his age.
31008-frigid-fracas:
Printed in Analog Science Fact and Fiction in March and April 1963, with pictures by John Schoenherr, this science fiction story is by Mack Reynolds. The story opens by arguing that in any status-hungry culture, a man's assigned level follows reputation, not reality. Only the deliberately phony has real status. The story's hero is Major Joseph Mauser, Category Military, Mid-Middle Caste.

Mauser opens the tale drenched, in his own time's word for drunk. He has run through an auto-bar's list of potables, from cocktail, highball, sour, flip, punch, and julep to a Sloe Gin Fizz. He sits at a small table in a corner, not happy about it, since this is not that kind of binge. It is a satirical story of caste, status, and a soldier who plays the game his society forces on him.
31020-a-new-subspecies-of-pocket-mouse-f:
E. Raymond Hall's 1954 paper in the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History series names a new pocket mouse subspecies, Perognathus flavescens cockrumi. While mapping Kansas mammals, Hall found that mice of this species from south-central Kansas and adjoining Oklahoma carried no subspecific name. He described them from a female specimen taken near Danville, Kansas, in December 1939.

The paper sets out the animal's small size, buff upper parts washed with black, white belly and feet, and small skull. It notes that it runs about twelve percent smaller than its northern kin. Its range is given as south-central Kansas south into Dewey County, Oklahoma, making the note a compact, citable record for mammal researchers.
31046-a-new-pocket-mouse-genus-perognath:
E. Lendell Cockrum's 1951 paper names a new pocket mouse subspecies, Perognathus flavus bunkeri, from western Kansas. Comparing Kansas specimens with named forms, Cockrum found them distinct. He described the new form from an adult female taken at the Conard Farm, one mile east of Coolidge in Hamilton County, on July 1, 1936.

The diagnosis notes its large size, light buff upper parts sparsely mixed with black, white belly, and enlarged frontonasal and mastoid regions of the skull. Its range runs through western Nebraska, eastern Colorado, western Kansas, and western Oklahoma, and the short paper remains the citable source for this plains mouse.
31063-two-new-moles-genus-scalopus-from-:
Rollin H. Baker's 1951 paper names two new moles of the genus Scalopus, one from Mexico and one from Texas. The Mexican form, Scalopus montanus, came from a single animal caught in a pocket-gopher trap in the Sierra del Carmen of Coahuila. That animal came during a 1950 University of Kansas field trip that also collected across the Mexican state.

Its type, an adult male taken near Piedra Blanca in April 1950 by J. R. Alcorn, is medium and slender for the genus, with buffy-brown upper parts and a paler belly banded in Sudan brown. Known only from its mountain locality, it shows how much mammal diversity still hid in Mexico's northern ranges at mid-century.
31258-our-campaign-around-gettysburg-bei:
Published in Brooklyn in 1864, this memorial records what the Twenty-Third Regiment of New York State National Guards and associated regiments endured, suffered, and accomplished. Their campaign ran through Pennsylvania and Maryland during the second Rebel invasion of June and July 1863. Dedicated to Colonel William Everdell Jr., praised for relieving footsore men on the march and sharing every bivouac hardship, the book honors a soldier's friend.

Its preface answers the objection that the militia never fought at Gettysburg. Like the reserve of eleven thousand under General French at Frederick, they stood ready, offered their lives, and waited only for orders to hurry into battle. The volume preserves the militia's own memory of the campaign that made Gettysburg an epoch.
3129-the-story-of-pocahontas:
Warner retells the life of Pocahontas without the trimmings he distrusts. Captain Smith's vanity, he says, and the pride of descendants ennobled by the smallest rivulet of her blood, have dressed a simple story in romance. Strip those away and a child of remarkable intelligence remains, one who early showed tender regard for the white settlers.

She served them willingly and unwillingly, Warner notes, on the concurrent evidence of the records. The book follows her from the Virginia shore to her English marriage and early death. Stripped of gilt, the story honors its heroine more, not less, than the legend ever did.
31513-fishes-of-the-wakarusa-river-in-ka:
James E. Deacon and Artie L. Metcalf's survey of the fishes of the Wakarusa River in Kansas appeared as volume thirteen, number six, of the University of Kansas Publications. It runs pages 309 to 322, with one figure, and is dated February 10, 1961. It came as a contribution from the State Biological Survey and from the university's department of zoology.

The paper records the fishes found in the Wakarusa, a Kansas river system, and it gives researchers a dated baseline for the river's fauna. Its short compass suits its purpose: a careful local list, tied to place and to the survey work behind it, rather than a general treatise on fishes.
31524-the-price-of-the-prairie-a-story-o:
Margaret Hill McCarter's The Price of the Prairie, a story of Kansas, was published in Chicago by A. C. McClurg and Company, in a fifteenth edition, with five illustrations in color by J. N. Marchand. McCarter, author of The Cottonwood's Story and Cuddy's Baby, takes as her epigraph the line "At evening time it shall be light." An illustration shows a girl crying to Phil to crown her Queen of May, here in April, a glimpse of the Kansas springtime romance within.

The novel tells a Kansas story of settlement, hardship, and love, where the prairie itself exacts a price from those who claim it. McCarter writes of Kansas with the affection of a native, and her heroines meet the land's trials with faith and courage. Readers of regional fiction will find a popular, heartfelt novel of the prairie frontier, in its day a bestseller.
32060-confessions-of-con-cregan-the-iris:
Charles Lever's picaresque novel, published in Boston by Little, Brown and Company in 1913 with drawings by Phiz, follows Con Cregan, an Irish Gil Blas. Its contents trace Con Cregan from peeps at his father to a first step on life's ladder. They follow him through college, entered and left, and through high and low company, to a bold stroke for an opening in the world. The early chapters stay close to Irish life, family, and the scramble for a place.

The voyage out changes the scale. Quebec, a night in the lower town, and the St. Lawrence give way to a log-hut at Brazos, a night in a Texas forest, and the lazaretto of Bexar. Later chapters reach a placer, the fate of a gambusino, La Senhora, and a discovery. Readers get a roving first-person life story, where each new country offers a fresh opening and scrape.
32084-frontier-boys-in-the-south-seas:
Captain Wyn Roosevelt's Frontier Boys in the South Seas, published in New York by Hurst and Company with drawings by Rudolf Mencl, carries the Darlington brothers to new waters. The series follows Jim, Jo, and Tom Darlington, starting with a camp wagon on the trail west in the early days. They are presented as real American boys, resourceful and humorous, meeting thrilling adventures at every turn.

Earlier volumes took the brothers over the Overland Trail, through Colorado, the Rockies, and the Grand Canyon, and on to Mexico, the Coast, Hawaii, and the Sierras. The series claims a true picture of a picturesque period, when the nation set its face toward the vast unknown West and conquered it. This volume moves the same boys to the South Seas, where island adventure replaces the wagon trail.
33189-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, volume five, gathers the entries running from Andrew Carnegie to the start of Cas. Its articles include Carnegie, Casanova de Seingalt, Casas Grandes, Florence Estienne Méric Casaubon and Isaac Casaubon, Carniola, carnival, Carnivora, and the Carnots from Lazare to Sadi. The list goes on to Carnoustie, Carnuntum, Caro, carol, the Carolines, Carolingians, and cash, with shorter entries beside them. Transcriber's notes record corrections to Cartesianism and caste.

The slice mixes biography, geography, history, and science in the confident voice of early twentieth-century reference writing. Readers get the facts and judgments educated readers of the day were expected to trust, from a steel magnate to a Venetian adventurer. As a reference text it is dated, but as a record of how knowledge was ordered a century ago, it remains a useful window.
33220-first-fam-lies-of-the-sierras:
Joaquin Miller's sketches gather tales of the Sierras, from life in the Forks to Little Billie Piper, the first woman in the Forks, and Sunday in the Sierras. Published in Chicago in 1876, the contents run through Washee-Washee, unwritten history, a boy's courtship, a wedding, a parson's pursuit of love, and scenes of grit and blood. Miller, known for his Songs of the Sierras, writes as a man who knew the mining camps first-hand.

The book mixes humor, pathos, and frontier color, with a poet's eye for mountain light and camp talk. Its sketches are short and vivid, each standing alone yet building a picture of Sierra life. For readers of western lore, it is a lively, old-fashioned collection, full of rough characters and the raw, hopeful world of the gold country.
33231-history-of-the-spanish-conquest-of:
Philip Ainsworth Means's history, issued as a paper of Harvard's Peabody Museum, traces the Spanish conquest of Yucatan and of the Itzas, the Maya people of the Peten. It follows the long, hard campaigns by which Spanish forces sought to bring the peninsula and its last independent Maya kingdom under colonial rule. Means draws on chronicles and records to set out battles, missions, and the slow fall of Itza towns.

The study is scholarly and detailed, aimed at readers of American archaeology and colonial history. Its value lies in gathering a scattered story into one clear narrative, from first contact to final conquest. For those who study the Maya world, it remains a useful, careful account of a conquest that took far longer than the textbooks often suggest.
33412-observations-on-the-mississippi-ki:
Henry S. Fitch's Observations on the Mississippi Kite in Southwestern Kansas, published in October 1963, studies a graceful hawk in its prairie home. Issued as volume twelve, number eleven of the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History publications, from pages 503 to 519, the paper notes where kites hunt, nest, and roam in Kansas. Fitch writes with a field naturalist's care.

The paper suits readers of ornithology, offering a short, technical account of one bird in one place. Its tone is precise and factual, with observations gathered over seasons. For bird researchers, it is a useful, if narrow, source on a kite whose prairie life was then little known.
33503-the-sweating-sickness-a-boke-or-co:
John Caius's Sweating Sickness, a boke or counseill against the disease, is a Tudor doctor's guide to a terrifying epidemic, in the 1912 Cambridge edition of his complete works. Caius writes of a sickness that struck by unnatural seasons, as if winter had come out of course, and he counsels how to meet it. His text, in old spelling, keeps the voice of a sixteenth-century physician.

The book's value lies in its first-hand medical history, showing how a Tudor doctor reasoned about a new, deadly fever. Its tone is earnest and practical, aimed at readers who might face the sweat themselves. For students of plague and medicine, it is a rare, vivid source on a disease that haunted England and then vanished.
33661-the-affecting-case-of-the-unfortun:
Thomas Daniels swore on November 23, 1761, that this twenty-four-page pamphlet gives a just and faithful narrative of his case. Daniels had been tried at the Old Bailey in September 1761 for the supposed murder of his wife, by casting her out of a chamber window, and sentenced to die. He received his Majesty's most gracious and free pardon.

The pamphlet, drawn up and authenticated by Daniels himself and prepared for the press by an impartial hand, gives a circumstantial account of his wife's behavior. It follows her from his first acquaintance with her to the day of her death. For readers of eighteenth-century crime and law, it preserves a rare first-person defense: a condemned man's own story, told to clear his name after an extraordinary deliverance.
33780-the-haunted-pajamas:
Francis Perry Elliott published this comic novel in 1911, with pictures by Edmund Frederick. Its hero receives a pair of yellow pajamas sent from China, and from the night he first wears them his life turns strange. Friends, a young woman from Radcliffe, and a family with secrets all get drawn into the trouble that follows.

Chapters pile up shocks, warnings, and mix-ups as the pajamas seem to push their wearer toward drink, daring, and disgrace. Elliott keeps the tone light even when the stakes rise, and the mystery of the gift drives the plot to its end. It is an old-fashioned farce with a touch of the uncanny.
33806-the-camp-fire-girls-across-the-sea:
Margaret Vandercook sends her Camp Fire Girls across the seas in this 1914 novel, illustrated and published by the John C. Winston Company. The story opens two years later in Woodford, New Hampshire, on an April afternoon. A young man with clouded blue eyes strides past elm trees and yellow forsythia toward a brown cottage where a large touring car waits. Farewells, the wheel's revolution, and a cosmopolitan company follow.

Twenty-one chapters carry the girls Unter den Linden, through changes, Das Rheingold, other scenes, a meeting, an adventure and its consequences, an uncertain future, Richard Ashton, Betty's strange disappearance. Vandercook blends travel, music, and friendship in a popular girls' series novel.
33878-at-the-ghost-hour-the-house-of-the:
Paul Heyse wrote this tale, translated from the German by Francis A. Van Santford and published in New York in 1894, with decorations by Alice C. Morse. It opens in a provincial town of northern Germany, where old high-gabled houses bear names like The Good Shepherd, Noah's Dove, and The Rose of Sharon on their lintels.

The old families of that street prized inward light, while a new age of brisk enlightenment pushed past them. One by one the old houses gave way to bustling newcomers. Heyse's tale weighs faith, doubt, and change in a town caught between two ages.
34167-a-lady-s-captivity-among-chinese-p:
Amelia B. Edwards translated this account from the French of Mademoiselle Fanny Loviot, published in London by George Routledge and Company and in New York. Loviot dedicates the book to a lady friend who, hearing the strange and eventful episode, urged her, though she had never written a book, to write and publish it. The friend advised simplicity and nature over show.

The narrative that follows tells of a lady's captivity among Chinese pirates in the Chinese seas, in plain, direct style. Edwards, a noted translator, keeps Loviot's voice clear. The book offers a vivid Victorian tale of piracy and survival at sea.
34429-check-list-of-the-birds-of-kansas:
Harrison Tordoff made a check list of the birds of Kansas for the University of Kansas museum series. It came out in Lawrence in 1956. Kansas was one of the first states to get a full bird book, back in 1891. Tordoff says bird work in Kansas since then has lagged behind work in many other states.

The list aims to bring the state record up to date. It names each bird known in Kansas and notes its status there. Tordoff draws on an older state list and on the thesis behind it, plus help from many workers. Bird watchers and museum staff get a clear base for fresh field work in the state.
34465-a-little-book-of-christmas:
John Kendrick Bangs put four Christmas tales into this small book, and Little, Brown printed it in Boston in 1912. Arthur Becher drew the plates. Bangs opens with a toast in verse to Santa Claus, cutting any man who will not believe in the saint.

The Conversion of Hetherington leads the set, a long tale of a heart changed. Next comes the child who had all things but one, then Santa Claus and Little Billee. The House of the Seven Santas closes the book at good length. Plates show a red, cold, rough hand that seems too coarse for Santa, and guests of the night dropping in one by one. Warm fun and soft hearts rule the whole set.
34523-fishes-of-chautauqua-cowley-and-el:
Artie L Metcalf wrote Fishes of Chautauqua, Cowley and Elk Counties, Kansas, issued by the University of Kansas on May 6, 1959. The study runs from page 345 to page 400, with two plates, two figures, and ten tables. It came from the State Biological Survey of Kansas. Editors of the museum series were E Raymond Hall, Henry S Fitch, and Robert W Wilson.

Metcalf first describes the streams, climate, plants, and past of the area. The Arkansas River has low banks, a sand bottom, and clear water in the dry year 1956. The Walnut River shifts from sand below to gravel and rubble above. Later parts list each species with notes, compare stream faunas, and sum up the findings.
34554-selected-records-of-reptiles-and-a:
John Breukelman and Hobart M Smith reported selected records of reptiles and amphibians from Kansas in 1946. Their paper ran in the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History series. Work toward a handbook led Smith to survey the holdings at Kansas State Teachers College in Emporia. Many local records gathered there came from Breukelman and his students, notably Allen Downs.

The authors list only finds of note, skipping counties already held by the university museum. Among them is the first Kansas record of Rana sylvatica, the wood frog. Marks show which specimens Smith checked himself. Locality notes give county, distance, and direction for each find.
34571-the-pearl-story-book-stories-and-l:
Ada M Skinner and Eleanor L Skinner gathered tales of winter, Christmas, and New Year. Duffield and Company issued The Pearl Story Book in New York in 1919. Rights rest from 1910 with the same house. A plate by Maxfield Parrish shows shepherds gazing at the sky.

Names on the contents run from Lowell and Emerson to Hawthorne and Longfellow. Indian, Russian, and Japanese legends stand beside poems of snow and frost. Hawthorne's Snow-Image leads the winter tales with quiet fame. Families gain a rich store of cold-season tales for reading aloud.
34606-what-gunpowder-plot-was:
Samuel Rawson Gardiner, a fellow of Merton College, Oxford, wrote an inquiry into the Gunpowder Plot, published in London in 1897. Gardiner was known for long histories of England under James the First and of the Civil War. A front picture shows the river front of a house occupied by Whynniard. A caption argues what the words Prince's Chamber and House of Lords must mean in the view.

The title asks what the plot in fact was, signaling a fresh look at the evidence. Gardiner tests the received story of the 1605 conspiracy against documents and places. His student's history and school atlas are listed among his works. The book is short beside his multi volume histories.
35021-indian-stories-retold-from-st-nich:
Indian Stories holds true tales retold from a famed youth magazine. The book is one in a set of five that reprint tales for schools. Drawings by Frederic Remington dress the text of this volume. The tales bear rights dates that reach back to eighteen seventy seven.

Tales treat a gift of self, an eagle prize, and a feast day with tribes. A boys visit to a great chief earns its own long part in the set. Horse races and scalp lore of the plains fill the mixed bag for youth. The set mates the tales with twin books on the war of the states. Schools used the books to teach the past in tale form to the young.
35587-the-headless-horseman-a-strange-ta:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote The Headless Horseman, a strange tale of Texas, in this edition printed by George Routledge and Sons in 1888. The tale opens with a prologue at midnight on the prairie. A stag of Texas rests in his lair and hears the hoofstroke of a horse. The ring of steel on stone tells him that a man draws near, and he springs up to look back.

What the stag sees holds him still with fear and wonder. The horse is perfect in all its parts, saddled and bridled in full trim. The rider lacks the one thing that should crown him, his head. In clear moonlight the stag stares, then flees through the waters of the Leona.
35821-leo-the-circus-boy-or-life-under-t:
Captain Ralph Bonehill wrote Leo the Circus Boy, or Life Under the Great White Canvas, copyrighted in 1897 and published at Chicago. Bonehill had written The Young Oarsmen of Lakeview and Gun and Sled. A frontispiece shows Leo's first appearance in the ring.

The contents open with a row and its result, then put Leo to capturing a runaway lion. He leaves the farm and joins the greatest show on earth in the fourth chapter. A leap of great peril, a thunderstorm ride among the clouds, and a mad elephant follow. Criminal compacts and stolen circus tickets supply the villainy. Leo asserts his rights, gains his liberty, and makes new friends as the show travels. Boys' novels lived on such programmes. Bonehill rings the changes on the circus bill.
36118-a-crime-of-the-under-seas:
Guy Boothby gathers eleven tales of crime, gold, and the sea in a Ward Lock volume from London dated 1905. Stanley L Wood drew the plates, one of which shows a diver who drops a man with a cry that rings in his helmet. Boothby names past novels at the front, among them Doctor Nikola.

The title tale starts with three old friends in talk on the verandah of the Grand Oriental Hotel at Colombo. Each man had just reached Ceylon by a different road, and talk turns to strange trades in the East. Boothby warns that half the world does not know how the other half lives, and that the gap yawns wide in the East. Later tales treat a phantom stockman, Sacramento Nick's treasure, and Tommy Dodd and his rooster.
36215-famous-prima-donnas:
Famous Prima Donnas profiles the women stars of light opera, by Lewis Strang, printed in nineteen hundred. Page published it at Boston, and a third impression followed in nineteen o six. Strang had written lives of actors, actresses, and light opera stars before this. Twenty two chapters run from Alice Nielsen to Hilda Clark in the contents.

Nielsen opens the book, five years from a Kansas City church choir to stardom. Strang hesitates to rank her first, so swift and untested is her rise. Her youth and freshness are at once her charm and the doubt against her. Lillian Russell, Fay Templeton, and Edna May fill the next ranks of fame. Portraits show the singers in their best known parts on the stage. Marie Dressler and Marie Tempest close the list of the era's stars.
36695-right-living-as-a-fine-art-a-study:
Right Living as a Fine Art is a study by Newell Dwight Hillis of Channing's Symphony as an outline of the ideal life and character. Fleming H Revell printed it at New York in 1903. The book's centre is the short piece called My Symphony by William Henry Channing, printed here in full.

To live content with small means, Channing writes; to seek elegance rather than luxury, and refinement rather than fashion. To be worthy, not respectable, and wealthy, not rich; to listen to stars and birds, babes and sages with open heart. Hillis builds chapters on the symphony's themes: Channing's vision of the beautiful life, the largest wealth, and how knowledge becomes wisdom. Later chapters treat the disguises of inferiority and strength blossoming into beauty. The book holds that man's house must now have beautiful walls, and the speaker's truth be clothed in words of beauty.
37081-in-strange-company-a-story-of-chil:
Guy Boothby wrote a tale of Chili and the southern seas, first printed in 1894 and given by the author to his mother after ten years apart. Boothby had won readers with tales such as Pharos the Egyptian. The first teller, Luke Sanctuary, owns he is a man of peace who never left England.

The contents promise the truth about some money, a strange night, and flight from Chili. A ship named the Island Queen and a man's death close the first part.
