Then John Ramsay takes up the tale, with a mixed career, ship owning, and a curious quest. Later parts hold a jail break, an island, and rescue.
37210-the-breeding-birds-of-kansas:
Richard Johnston of the University of Kansas wrote this study of the birds that breed in Kansas. The Museum of Natural History at Lawrence issued it on May 18, 1964. It runs to some eighty pages with ten figures, in the museum's own line of works.

Johnston first maps where birds live in Kansas and what kinds of ground they use. Some kinds reach the edge of their range in the state, and he marks them. Breeding times come next: how they shift, what rules them, and how blood lines shape the dates. Then come full accounts of each kind, one by one. Bird men of the plains get a firm base for field work in this study.
37327-o-er-many-lands-on-many-seas:
Gordon Stables wrote a sea tale in a form dated 1884, told on board the brave ship Niobe. The ship lies becalmed in calm seas near a shore of yellow sand, with no wind and no cloud. Sails flap only with the roll of the hull, and the officer on deck scans sky and sea for change.

All on board know a blow is near, since the glass has fallen fast. If the wind comes from the east, the strong ship may still be dashed to bits on that shore. Heat, hush, and dread fill the first pages, with surf sound far off and sharks at the surface.
37633-societies-of-the-kiowas:
Societies of the Kiowa, by Robert Lowie, was published in New York in 1916, as part of the Anthropological Papers of the American Museum of Natural History. In his preface Lowie explains the trip behind the paper. Data from the Kiowa were wanted on points raised by study of other Plains tribes.

Printed Kiowa material by Mooney seemed to decide those questions implicitly. Still, Lowie thought it best to view the subject in the field. So he made a side trip to Anadarko, Oklahoma, in June 1915. There he enlisted Andres Martinez as main informant and interpreter. Martinez had been captured by the Apache as a boy, sold to the Kiowa, and lived much of his life as a Kiowa. He married native women and entered some men societies. Readers get field knowledge of Kiowa societies from inside.
3770-a-second-book-of-operas:
Henry Edward Krehbiel, the New York music critic, gathers essays on opera for listeners who want to know what they are hearing. Biblical operas open the book, from Handel and Rossini to Verdi and Saint-Saens, with notes on censorship, revamped scores, and the passage of the Red Sea set to music. Bible stories in opera and oratorio follow, with Adam, Noah, Abraham, and the Exodus weighed as stage matter.

A later chapter traces Lakme in America, from its Paris premiere in 1883 with Marie Van Zandt to New York gossip and rival sopranos. Krehbiel writes with a critic's ear and a historian's patience. Opera lovers will find the book a rich companion, full of backstage tales and clear guidance on works still in the repertory.
37742-fishes-of-the-big-blue-river-basin:
Minckley wrote Fishes of the Big Blue River Basin, Kansas, published at Lawrence in 1959 as a University of Kansas museum paper. The paper runs in volume eleven of the museum publications, with plates, figures, and tables. It is a contribution from the State Biological Survey of Kansas.

The contents open with the Tuttle Creek dam and reservoir, then describe the basin itself. Geology, climate, population, and land use set the stage before the streams are treated. Previous records of fishes are gathered, and the methods of the survey are stated. A river basin fish list sounds dry until a dam is rising on the river: then it becomes the record of what lived there before the water changed. Minckley's paper is that record for one Kansas river system, species by species and stream by stream.
37903-the-girl-crusoes-a-story-of-the-so:
Mrs Herbert Strang wrote The Girl Crusoes, a story of the South Seas, issued in London in 1912. Colour pictures are by N Tenison. The tale opens at Poppicombe station, where a train from London halts at noon. A boy porter grabs a paper, reads a few words, and lets out a wild war-whoop.

Contents move from leaving home and boarding the Elizabeth to a midnight wreck. The girls reach a fair island and make a home there. Chapters promise fishers, a small brown face, a tropical storm, and a shark. Later parts bring a prisoner in a cave and a desperate venture. The tale ends with a home-coming. Young readers get a castaway tale with girls as the heroes.
38279-how-john-norton-the-trapper-kept-h:
How John Norton the Trapper Kept His Christmas is a North Woods tale by Murray, printed at Boston in 1890. A frontispiece shows John Norton himself. The story opens in a cabin in the woods. A great fireplace stands piled high with logs, fiercely ablaze.

On either side of the broad hearth-stone a hound sits on his haunches, looking gravely into the fire. At a strong wooden table sits the old trapper, poring over a book. The book is large, with wooden covers bound in leather, brown with age and smooth with handling. His whitened head bows over the page, one finger marking the sentence. Murray, the famous Adirondack guide and writer, builds his Christmas on that fireside: an old man's scripture, his dogs, and the winter forest outside.
38766-songs-of-the-mexican-seas:
Joaquin Miller wrote Songs of the Mexican Seas, a book of poems from the Gulf coasts. Roberts Brothers issued the book in Boston in eighteen hundred eighty seven. Miller gave the book to Abbie on its gift page. His note is signed from Mount Shasta, California, that same year.

Each song, Miller says, was born where its scene is laid. True air and hue are his claim for the set. Some lines had served at a Dartmouth rite and in print. The Sea of Fire opens the book in Darien seas. Seas there will one day join by the hand of man, it sings. A great French master will weld the oceans in flame. Yucatan, Honduras, and lost gold rivers crowd the warm verse. Miller asks his own land, at last, for a fair hearing.
38856-goblins-and-pagodas:
Goblins and Pagodas is a book of poems and essays by John Gould Fletcher. Houghton Mifflin published it at Boston and New York in 1916. Fletcher thanks the editors of three little magazines for reprint leave. The Egoist, Poetry, and The Little Review had printed his symphony poems. A long opening essay sets out his view of the age. He calls his era one of research, experiment, and unrest.

Science and philosophy, he writes, have attacked the machine theory of the universe. The arts strip away inessentials to disclose pure form. All Europe has slid into a war whose end none can foresee. Against that shaking of every tenet, Fletcher seeks the fundamentals of poetic form. The symphonies in colour — blue, green, orange — embody his answer. The book mixes criticism with the poems themselves.
38891-the-cruise-of-the-alerte-the-narra:
The Cruise of the Alerte is the narrative of a search for treasure on the island of Trinidad, off Brazil. The front matter lists companion travel volumes of its series, among them Doyle's Great Boer War and Grogan's From the Cape to Cairo. The Alerte was a small yacht fitted out for the hunt.

Her owner had a chart and a story of buried pirate gold. The cruise tests the tale against storms, a barren island, and long digging in the sand. Books of this kind fed the treasure-hunting dreams of the late Victorian reader. The narrative stands between travel record and adventure tale, with a real voyage behind the romance.
39485-ghosts-and-family-legends-a-volume:
Mrs Crowe wrote Ghosts and Family Legends, a volume for Christmas, in 1859. Newby at London published it from Welbeck Street that year. Crowe was the authoress of the Night Side of Nature. Contents fall into evenings round a fire in a country house. The preface tells how the tales were gathered last winter.

Guests at a large mansion in the north of England told them. The first evening gives the lover's farewell and an appointment kept. The white cat, passing spirits, and a carrier fill later evenings. Prophetic dreams, a vigil, and a strange dog take their turns. The radiant boy, haunted houses, and a German inn follow in the list. Her own visit to a haunted house closes the first part. A second part gives legends of the earthbound in six tales. Crowe gives Christmas ghosts from fireside tellers.
39958-life-history-and-ecology-of-the-fi:
Henry Fitch wrote a study of the life history and habits of the five-lined skink, printed at Lawrence, Kansas, in 1954. It forms number one of volume eight of the University of Kansas Publications of the Museum of Natural History. It runs to one hundred fifty-six pages, with two plates, twenty-six figures, and seventeen tables. The skink's Latin name is Eumeces fasciatus.

Fitch tells how the lizards were got: by lifting rocks and seizing the skinks by hand before they could flee, and by pitfall traps of gallon cans sunk flush with the ground. Hand catching worked when cold made the skinks slow, but in hot weather most escaped. At the pond rock pile, shelter was so ready that traps took nearly all the catch. The study is a full field record of one small lizard's feeding, breeding, and ways.
40010-summer-cruising-in-the-south-seas:
Summer Cruising in the South Seas is a set of South Sea idyls in American prose. A publisher account at its front calls the book a classic in American literature. It presents a later series by the same author, The Island of Tranquil Delights, in these pages. Of the first collection Emerson is quoted as saying its author wrote too well to leave off.

 The sequel bids fair to attain rank alongside of the first collection in its judgment. There is a haunting quality about these idyls that must make them live, the account goes on. They are full of charming word pictures and of exquisite touches of dream life in fairyland. The idyls are sketches of Tahiti and its neighbours, written in a prose of scent and colour that made the South Seas a place of the mind for American readers.
40184-the-natural-cure-of-consumption-co:
Page wrote a health book for the folk on cure by plain life ways. Its rights claim is cut in this copy, with 1886 on its press. Page wrote How to Feed the Baby in his past small works. Ills of the lung, gut, and Bright's ill fill its title in full. Nerve pain, stiff joints, and colds share that grim long list.

How ills start and how to bar them is its sub-title's aim. Food, air, rest, and clean ways are its cure tools in sum. Drug free care is the book's whole proud badge in that age. Tables and rules fill its pages for home use by plain folk. Health fans of that day kept such books close at hand. Each claim is pressed hard.
40292-paris-vistas:
Helen Davenport Gibbons published 'Paris Vistas' with the Century Company in 1919, with sixteen illustrations by Lester George Hornby. The contents are dated like a life: childhood vistas in 1887-1888, at sixteen in 1899, a honeymoon promise in 1908, and its fulfilment in 1909-1910. Gibbons recalls a Scotch-Irish Covenanter grandfather who kept his whisky locked away and thought of Paris when he read of Babylon.

Later chapters settle into the Rue Madame pension and the Rue Servandoni, then reach the war years. Headings promise hunting Apaches, walks at nightfall, the Gothas and Big Bertha, the darkest days, and armistice night. The book closes with royal visitors, the first peace Christmas, and the revenge of Versailles, carrying one resident's Paris from childhood to peace.
40364-the-blue-raider-a-tale-of-adventur:
Blue Raider is a tale of adventure in the southern seas by Herbert Strang. Humphrey Milford and Oxford University Press issued it in nineteen twenty. Brock drew the pictures, from bound prisoners stumbling through forest on. Strang long list runs from Dick Trevanion to With Haig on the Somme.

Chapters open on a beach in New Guinea, then drums and a chimney follow. Mr Haan, in the toils, and the totem deepen the island mystery early. A reconnaissance, complications, and the cast of the die build the middle. The ordeal of Ephraim Meek, a forced landing, and Duk Duk rites come next. Flight and the attack on the village close the listed chapters here.
40366-mary-ware-in-texas:
Annie Fellows Johnston wrote Mary Ware in Texas, published in 1910 as part of her Little Colonel series. Mary Ware entered the series as the Little Colonel's chum in Mary Ware, the volume just before this one. The series had grown volume by volume since The Little Colonel Stories first gathered the early tales. Each book appeared in cloth with illustrations at the same price.

The publisher's list at the front shows the whole family of books. House parties, holidays, boarding school, Arizona, and a Christmas vacation carry the girls through the series. Mary Ware in Texas sends its heroine south, in keeping with the pattern of each volume taking the characters to a new place. Johnston's series was among the best loved American girls' books of its day, and this volume continues Mary Ware's story for readers who had followed her since her first appearance.
4045-omoo-adventures-in-the-south-seas:
Herman Melville's sequel to Typee follows a sailor who deserts his whaler and wanders the South Seas. In a sampled chapter, the ship's captain falls ill and dies, while a doctor who had refused the cabin relents to pay his old enemy a professional visit.

A warm bath is prepared by lowering a cask through the skylight and filling it with buckets of water, a scene that shows Melville's eye for shipboard life. The book mixes adventure, humor, and sharp notes on missionaries and traders. Readers who like sea tales with a roving, curious mind will enjoy Omoo as a lively companion to Typee.
40528-spanish-vistas:
Spanish Vistas, by George Parsons Lathrop, is a book of travel sketches of Spain. Harper and Brothers printed it in New York in 1883, with drawings by Reinhart. Lathrop gives the sketches to his mother, whose taste for travel first prompted his own.

A frontispiece shows a mandurra solo, a player caught mid-tune. The preface sets Spain beside Italy as brother to sister among lands. Both peninsulas jut south into the same sea, rich in art, history, and romance. Spain is the broader and more rugged of the pair. Its tongue, Lathrop argues, is the masculine growth of southern speech. Gutturals from Arabic roughen its vowels and linguals. The Greek spirit, he says, passed to Italy and left a soft grace. The spirit of Rome passed to Hispania, and left it strong and austere.
40614-gabrielle-of-the-lagoon-a-romance-:
Safroni-Middleton, author of Sailor and Beachcomber, wrote this romance of the South Seas, published by Lippincott at Philadelphia and London in 1919. A prologue sets the scene at night in the Solomon Islands, where a dim, weird light lies over the isle and pierces the forest depths.

Below the skies of Bougainville, marshalled in millions of stars, a tribe buries its dead in the forest and then gathers before the secret tambu stage. The tribal chief yells his call, and maidens and high chiefs in feather head-dresses squat in festival costume. A tambu dancer sways to bamboo fifes and bone flutes while Oom Pa, the aged high priest, performs on the monster tribal drum. A fore-and-aft schooner with yellowish sails lies at anchor beyond the shore lagoons, the one sign of the outside world in a scene the narrator calls super-primitive.
40659-materfamilias:
Ada Cambridge, author of The Three Miss Kings and Fidelis, published her novel Materfamilias with D Appleton at New York in 1898. The narrator tells her own story from its beginning. Her father in England wed a second time when she was about eighteen, and the bride was her governess.

The girl refuses to see another woman in her mother's place and tells her father he must choose. He chooses the new wife, and she leaves home for good. At her uncle's house she secretly weds his assistant after urging an elopement. Chapters move through a broken circle, a silver wedding, and a grandmother's role. Pride, exile, and family repair shape the long tale.
40705-tom-wallis-a-tale-of-the-south-sea:
Louis Becke wrote Tom Wallis, a tale of the South Seas, published by the Religious Tract Society in London in 1903. Becke had lived the life he wrote about, in Wild Life in Southern Seas and By Reef and Palm. Lancelot Speed drew the eleven illustrations. The story opens at a small, old seaport town north of an Australian city.

Chapters introduce Captain Ramon Casalle, Captain Sam Hawkins, and the notorious Bully Hayes, a real figure of the Pacific trade. Tom lights a fire on Misty Head, meets strangers on Wreck Reef, and sails north to the Solomons. A fight on board the Leonie, a boat voyage with Maori Bill, and a stay on Alofi Island follow. Becke writes the trading Pacific as he knew it: rough, bright, and dangerous.
40731-tenting-on-the-plains-or-general-c:
Tenting on the Plains, or General Custer in Kansas and Texas, by Elizabeth B Custer, was printed in New York by Harper and Brothers in 1895, under an 1887 copyright. Custer wrote Boots and Saddles and Following the Guidon. A plate shows smoking the pipe of peace.

She gives the book to him whose brave and blithe endurance made those who followed him forget half the hardship and the danger. Chapters open with good by to the Army of the Potomac and New Orleans after the war. A military execution, marches through pine forests, and out of the wilderness follow. A Texas norther and letters home fill the mid list. The text says General Custer was given scant time after the last gun to realize the blessings of peace. West fans get army wife life on the plains.
40828-the-closed-book-concerning-the-sec:
The Closed Book, Concerning the Secret of the Borgias is a tale by William Le Queux. This form is dated nineteen four. The first part is named for a hunch man. Its voice vows that these strange facts would not stand on record but for two ends. One is the worth of his find to men of lore. The next is his wifes wish that naught be hid.

The tale opens on a great day when he halts past the white, near blind house of a church head in Florence. That town lay still in the blaze of a July noon, its folk fled to the hills for air. Shut blinds, shut shops, and the song of heat bugs in burnt trees fill the scene. The town stands as a grim wreck of past glory, its rich cloth and fine arms no more sought past the world.
41017-south-africa-and-the-transvaal-war:
Louis Creswicke's South Africa and the Transvaal War reached its fifth volume with the disaster at Koorn Spruit, and the contents run to Lord Roberts's entry into Pretoria. Photographs of generals and staff, Methuen and Mackinnon among them, front the volume.

The chapters cover the Reddersburg mishap, prisoners escaping from Pretoria, the battle of Boshop, affairs at Mafeking, the siege of Wepener and its relief, and the great advance from Bloemfontein. Creswicke wrote contemporary history for a British public following the Boer War bulletin by bulletin. Sets like this one, issued while the war still ran, mix reportage, portrait, and pride, and they preserve how the empire told itself the story at the time.
41831-betty-leicester-s-christmas:
Sarah Orne Jewett wrote this Christmas story, printed in Boston in 1899, returning to a heroine from an earlier book. Jewett opens by speaking in her own voice about Betty Leicester, her story-book girl from the town of Tideshead. She says girls she meets keep reminding her of Betty, and that she loves the character too much not to write a little more about her.

Betty is in the middle of her sixteenth year, fresh from a summer in New England with her aunts Barbara and Mary. Back in London with her father, she finds life hard: she is nearer grown-up duties. One night she cries from homesickness for her four-poster bed at Tideshead. Jewett gives old readers a Christmas visit with a favorite girl.
41987-the-united-seas:
Robert Rogers wrote this tribute to the opening of the Panama Canal, and holds its rights of 1915. The United Seas marks the Panama-Pacific International Exposition at San Francisco. A motto heads it: blessed are the pathfinders who do not fear the seas.

Vision, the need of the hour, opens the book. Rogers holds that a person with no value for vision is neither helpful nor wise. The canal's opening means far more than shows on its face, he insists. No exposition like this one has been or will be, he claims. After the close of the world war, men need such a sight to gain heart for the work of building. His prose is part hymn, part plea.
42414-the-animal-world-a-book-of-natural:
The Animal World, a book of natural history, is volume five of the Young Folks' Treasury, published by the University Society at New York in 1909. Hamilton Wright Mabie edited the twelve-volume set, with Edward Everett Hale as associate editor. Theodore Wood wrote the animal text, and Ernest Ingersoll edited it. The advisers' list runs from Theodore Roosevelt and Grover Cleveland to Joel Chandler Harris and Charles Roberts.

Twenty-one chapters survey the animal kingdom for young readers: apes and gibbons, baboons, bats, the larger and smaller cats, the dog, weasel, bear, and seal tribes. Whales, rodents, wild oxen, elephants, marsupials, and birds of prey follow. The frontispiece shows tropical American humming-birds. The Treasury was a subscription set for the family shelf, and this volume keeps its natural history anecdotal and pictured, in the manner of Wood's popular animal books.
42622-the-book-of-christmas:
Thomas K Hervey wrote The Book of Christmas, a store of old season lore. Roberts Brothers issued the book in Boston in eighteen hundred eighty eight. R Seymour drew the plates of mirth that stud its pages. Rites, games, foods, and omens of Yuletide fill the thick volume.

Mixed roots of the feast, part church and part old heathen rite, open it. Court feasts and the Inns of Court show the season in state. The Lord of Misrule and Father Christmas lead the gay ranks. Ben Jonson’s Masque of Christmas speaks from the old stage here. Mince pie, mistletoe, waits, and carols mark the signs of the days. The Yule log, great candles, and the wassail bowl warm Eve night. Plum pudding and the boar’s head crown the day’s high feast. Boxing Day gifts and the wren hunt close the round of days.
4273-nature-cure-philosophy-practice-bas:
Henry Lindlahr, a Chicago physician, collected his writings on nature cure into this first volume of a series. He drew on his Nature Cure Magazine and other journals. His central claim is the unity of disease. Varied ailments, he argues, share common causes in lowered vitality.

The body, in his view, tries to cleanse itself, and treatment should build health rather than suppress symptoms. Lindlahr argues against a medicine that neglects preventive and constructive methods. He sets out diet, hygiene, and natural measures as the basis of cure. A long introduction frames the volume as a practical guide for ordinary readers.
43265-under-wolfe-s-flag-or-the-fight-fo:
Rowland Walker wrote this boys' tale of the fight for the Canadas, published by Partridge in London. A plate shows a cry of 'Stop, stop, we're coming down' at a moment of peril. Walker dedicates the book to the memory of his grandfather, a brave and chivalrous frontiersman in his words.

The book sits in Every Boy's Library, a series chosen for the boy of today, the publisher says. Robust and absorbing stories are the series promise in that list. Under Wolfe's flag, boys follow battles, scouts and hard marches from the French and Indian War in Canada.
43763-snap-dragons-old-father-christmas:
J H Ewing wrote Snap Dragons and Old Father Christmas, with illustrations by Gordon Browne, issued by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge. Snap Dragons stands first. Chapter one treats Mr and Mrs Skratdj, a family with a Russian sounding name who most certainly lived in England. Their peculiarity drives the comedy. They seldom seriously quarrelled, but they never agreed about anything.

Friends found it painful to hear the Skratdj pair constantly contradicting each other. Yet it meant nothing and was only their way, folk granted. If one told an anecdote, the other broke in with half a dozen corrections of trivial details. At dinner in a strange house, weather talk alone could start the duel. Ewing writes with warm humour for children and parents alike. Christmas games, tales, and family fun fill the small book.
43917-the-motor-rangers-through-the-sier:
The Motor Rangers Through the Sierras, a boys adventure tale by Marvin West, was copyrighted in 1911 by Hurst and Company of New York. West also wrote The Motor Rangers' Lost Mine. The Rangers are a party of boys touring the west by motor car. Nat Trevor is the eldest and most skilled of the group.

Joe Hartley sweats over a punctured tyre as the tale opens, and Ding-dong Bell stutters out that variety is the spice of life. Twenty five chapters bring a runaway auto, a rescue, and a scare for some rascals. The boys are lost in a petrified forest and treed two hundred feet up. A volley in a canyon, a fire in the forest, and a dash through the flames follow. Colonel Morello's fortress and a ride through the flume close the run.
44186-trees-every-child-should-know-easy:
Julia Ellen Rogers wrote this child's guide to the trees of America for Doubleday in 1909. Grosset and Dunlap kept Trees Every Child Should Know in print for years. The Glory of Autumn Trees heads its plates in colour.

How to Know the Trees opens the lessons, by leaf, bark, and bud. Autumn studies lead, for that is the trees' grand show. The nut trees come first: shagbark hickories, the disappointing hickories, black walnut, and butternut. The chestnut and chinquapin and the beech follow. The oak family takes the long middle: white oak, bur oak, live oak, and post oak in one group; black, red, and scarlet in the other. Easy talks for all seasons, as the title promises.
44514-last-of-the-incas-a-romance-of-the:
Gustave Aimard, a French writer of tales of the wild West, set a romance on the pampas in a London edition of 1875. The book opens with a long look at Patagonia, a land Aimard calls as little known as when the first Spanish ships touched it in 1508. He repeats the old tales of giants nine feet high, then turns to the true face of the land.

Two rivers, the Colorado and the Negro, water the dry plains. Cougars, foxes, and wild asses roam them, and sea lions crowd the coasts. The chapter names then promise councils of native chiefs, a farm under threat, and a chase of the great flightless birds. Siege plans, an attack on a town, and a cave of cougars build toward the last chapter. The tale joins a full account of the land to a plot of raid and rescue.
45841-the-ocean-wireless-boys-on-war-swe:
Captain Wilbur Lawton wrote The Ocean Wireless Boys on War Swept Seas, published by Hurst and Company at New York in 1917. Arthur O Scott drew the illustrations. Lawton had written the Boy Aviators and the Dreadnought Boys, and three earlier Ocean Wireless volumes. Forty-one chapters fill this one. The gold ship opens the tale, and war is declared in the second chapter. Icebergs ahead and a close shave follow at sea.

Smoke on the horizon, a shot at the rudder, and land ho come next. The armed cruiser, a message in code, and the cattle ship fill the middle. A hidden mine and the North Sea raise the danger. The Germans are coming, the Uhlans, and a court-martial follow in turn. Through bullet-racked air and a mysterious capture, the tale runs to Old Glory again.
45989-grace-harlowe-s-overland-riders-in:
Grace Harlowe's Overland Riders in the High Sierras is a girls' adventure tale by Jessie Graham Flower. The hosted edition was issued at Akron and New York in nineteen twenty three. Chapter summaries fill the contents in full sentences. Chapter one brings old friends together to plan a summer vacation in the saddle.

Shots and yells startle the riders at the end of that summary. Chapter two treats an interrupted sleep on a train. A salesman entertains passengers with tales of wrecks and hold ups. Chapter three gives the hold up of the Red Limited in full. The sheriff calls for volunteers, and the Overland girls offer their services. A treasure car is cut off from the train. Later summaries chase a missing lieutenant and outwit bandit guards.
46113-typesetting-a-primer-of-informatio:
A A Stewart wrote Typesetting, a primer of information about working at the case, published at Chicago in 1919 as number 16 of the Typographic Technical Series for Apprentices. The United Typothetæ of America's committee on education issued it. Contents open with introductory and preliminary suggestions.

Learning the case, units for measuring, spaces and quads, and a simple spacing table follow. Hair spaces and justifiers, leads and slugs, setting the composing stick, and the use of the composing rule come next. Setting type, justifying lines, emptying the stick, tying up the page, and taking proofs complete the craft sequence. Readers get the hand compositor's trade taught step by step, just as machine composition was ending it.
46728-decadence-and-other-essays-on-the-:
Remy de Gourmont wrote essays on the culture of ideas, Englished by William Aspenwall Bradley and printed at London in 1922. A portrait of Gourmont by Helene Dufau, never before published, fronts the book. The disassociation of ideas opens the set. Glory and the idea of immortality, success and the idea of beauty, and the value of education follow.

Women and language, Mallarme and the idea of decadence, style or writing, and subconscious creation come next. The roots of idealism close the volume. The essays were drawn from three French books of Gourmont's, the note says. Ideas, like pictures joined by habit, can be taken apart one by one and paired anew, he argues. English readers get a sharp French mind at play.
4696-the-witch-of-atlas:
Percy Bysshe Shelley addresses The Witch of Atlas to Mary, answering her objection that the poem holds no human interest. He asks whether a young kitten must catch mice to leap and play, or a silken-winged fly must climb the purest sky to earn its place. Content thee with a visionary rhyme, he pleads, and let the poem stand as fancy, not as story, false or true.

A winged vision comes to Mary's feet, beats its wings for fame, and fades, like a watery bow in twilight. Shelley builds the poem from that image, mixing myth, light, and playful argument. Readers get a short, musical Shelley vision poem, best read aloud, where imagination itself is the subject, and where beauty is defended against the demand for a plain moral or plot.
48451-cassell-s-history-of-england-vol-1:
Cassell's History of England, volume one of eight, runs from the Roman invasion to the Wars of the Roses. The King's Edition was issued by Cassell and Company in 1909, with many pictures, including colored and Rembrandt plates. The frontispiece is a portrait of King Edward VII, from a painting by Margetson.

The first chapter treats Roman rule in Britain. It covers the Celts and their customs, Druidism and Stonehenge, and Caesar's two invasions. Claudius, Caractacus, Boadicea's rising, and Agricola's campaigns follow in turn. A second chapter surveys the Roman remains left in Britain, before the story moves on toward the Saxon age.
48571-philip-of-texas-a-story-of-sheep-r:
Philip of Texas is a story of sheep raising in Texas by James Otis, published by the American Book Company in 1913. A map at the front shows the ground of the tale. The narrator is a boy whose father kept a plantation in Mississippi and dreamed of a sheep ranch in the West.

On his twelfth birthday the boy is given twelve ewes from his father's flock of seventy-two, as pay for his work as a shepherd. The family then sets out for Texas, and the chapters mix story with plain teaching. Readers learn how sheep are herded, what Texas fever is, and how land grants and Spanish measures work. On the trail come storms, northers, rattlesnakes, and Comanche Indians. The book is at once an adventure for boys and a small handbook of pioneer sheep farming.
48885-the-curse-of-pocahontas:
The Curse of Pocahontas is a tale by Wenona Gilman, with rights of eighteen ninety-five. It is number past one hundred of a cheap tale set. Past thirty parts fill it. The tale opens past a wife who sits past a rose plot in gold sun light, her small hands past a note in her lap.

Those hands look as if they had never known work, pale and thin as her face. She was once fair in a soft, slight way, with wide brown eyes like those of a meek child. A weak chin and a moan at the mouth mark her now. For five years she has held death close past her door, yet she is no near it than at the start. Her pride is her line past a famed maid of the old world.
48970-across-texas:
Across Texas, a boys adventure tale by Edward S Ellis, was published by T Nelson and Sons in 1894, in the Forest and Fire series. Ellis also wrote The Cabin in the Clearing. The hero is Nick Ribsam, of whom the author had much to tell in The Young Moose Hunters. Nick comes home to western Pennsylvania with his health restored by his Maine woods trip.

Thirty eight chapters carry Nick through to Texas. A letter and a telegram start the trip, and San Antonio sets the scene. Bell Rickard joins the cast, and strange proceedings pile up: a startling interruption, an intruder in camp, a race with an avalanche, and a sound of a pistol in the night. Ellis packs the road with tests of nerve and good shots.
49174-wagner-and-his-music-dramas:
Robert Bagar wrote a short book on Wagner and his great stage works. The book came out in New York in 1943. A New York music society holds the rights to the text. A front plate shows Wagner as a band chief at work. Bagar calls his fire to make the most fierce of any artist's.

Wagner sought to win all men to his own views, Bagar says. He scorned the old, the false, and the out-worn in art. His stage tales aim at saga force for soul and mind. Sweet, strong music floods each work he made. Self-denial stands as a mark in tale after tale. New fans get a brief, warm door into his world.
49287-travel-stories-retold-from-st-nich:
Travel Stories gathers tales retold from St Nicholas, the well known magazine for young readers, and the Century Co issued the book in 1920. Sixteen pieces fill the contents, each by a named writer. A frontispiece shows Victoria Falls on the Zambesi, setting the far-ranging tone at once.

William Haskell Simpson opens with the Grand Canon of Arizona, and Amy Sutherland follows with Rainbow-Land. Other pieces travel in India, chase the sunsets of all the yesterdays, and look at firecrackers, curious clocks, and letter-boxes in foreign lands. One tale mourns lost Rheims, and another goes out into big-game country. Motoring pieces in two parts bring the machine age into the mix of older wonders.
4946-madame-midas:
Madame Midas opens in early Australia, when gold fever had turned Melbourne into something like an enlarged camp. Robert Curtis arrives seeking fortune. He is a man of good family, expelled from Oxford for unorthodox views. He then married a pretty girl whose face was her fortune and who came of poor but honest parents.

Poverty and honesty prove poor capital on the goldfields. The novel follows Curtis and his wife through the rush's hopes and failures. The work arrives without a named author here. Readers get a colonial gold-rush story about class, marriage, and luck, set in a raw new city where fortunes were made and lost overnight.
50822-mammals-of-the-southwest-mountains:
Mammals of the Southwest Mountains and Mesas, by George Olin, is a field guide to the mammals of the desert Southwest. Edward Bierly drew the illustrations. The Southwest Parks and Monuments Association issued it in 1961 as number nine of its popular series. The contents begin with the hoofed animals of the region.

Bighorn sheep, pronghorn, and bison lead, followed by mule deer, white tailed deer, and elk. Rodents and rabbits come next, from snowshoe hare and pika to the tassel eared and Kaibab squirrels. Olin notes that the only point where four states meet is the corner of Utah, Colorado, Arizona, and New Mexico. With parts of California, Nevada, and Texas, that land holds the whole Southwestern desert. The guide served park visitors who wanted to know the animals of the canyons and mesas. Its plain accounts of habits and haunts keep it handy.
51176-the-captivity-sufferings-and-escap:
The Captivity, Sufferings, and Escape of James Scurry was written by Scurry himself and printed in London in 1824. Scurry says he was held prisoner for ten years in the lands of Hyder Ali and Tippoo Saib. The book promises no flowery words, but an artless tale where simple truth alone is to be found.

The preface calls the two rulers famed, and hated, for cruelty to prisoners of war in India. It says many such accounts had come out in England, and that men who escaped bore marks that backed the tales. Scurry adds his own register to that grim list. Readers get a first hand account of long captivity, hardship, and escape, told in plain words by the man who lived it.
51282-lords-and-lovers-and-other-dramas:
Olive Tilford Dargan wrote Lords and Lovers and Other Dramas, printed at New York in nineteen six. The title play is set in England in the thirteenth century, in the reign of Henry the Third. Its cast holds earls, bishops, a cardinal, and a Scottish princess. The first scene is a room in the Earl of Pembroke's castle, where the earl lies in bed.

The king waits on the dying earl with sorrow more like a son than a sovereign. Pembroke calls his son Richford to swear by God to serve the king, and pardons him on that one condition. His last words, he says, are kept for the king's ears, since a passing tongue stamps truth that cannot be erased. Two shorter dramas, the Shepherd and the Siege, fill out the volume.
51580-on-the-future-of-our-educational-i:
On the Future of Our Educational Institutions joins with Homer and Classical Philology in one volume by Friedrich Nietzsche. Kennedy translated the pieces, and Oscar Levy edited the English series. Foulis of Edinburgh and London issued this third volume in 1909. It formed part of the first complete authorized English Nietzsche.

The education piece gathers five lectures Nietzsche gave as a young professor. He held the chair of classical study at Basle when he delivered them. His aim in them was the raising of the human type itself. Genius, he held, must be sheltered and carefully grown to that end. The German schools of his day earn his open scorn in the lectures. They teach pupils only to get on in the struggle for life. True culture, he argues, belongs to a few chosen minds.
51817-big-bend-national-park-texas:
Big Bend National Park, in west Texas, takes its name from the great U-turn the Rio Grande makes along the Mexican border. This handbook, number 119 in the National Park Service series, was published at Washington in 1983. Its first part introduces the park and its history. Its second, with text by Helen Moss, studies the natural history from the river to the Chisos Mountains. Its third is a compact travel guide.

The park's three great features are the river and its canyons, the Chisos Mountains, and the Chihuahuan Desert. Chapters treat waterholes and springs, the greenbelt along the river, and mountains that seem to float in the desert air. Practical pages cover hiking, birding, floating the river, and the rules of desert travel.
51832-the-place-where-chicago-was:
Jim Harmon wrote this science fiction story for Galaxy Magazine, where it ran in February 1962, with pictures by Cowles. The opening lines boast that war is gone at last: peace came when the only ones left to kill were the killers.

The scene is late December 1983, and Abe Danniels is walking across country in heat no winter should hold. Half the families in America own their own helicopters, and the sidewalks of Jersey City move on their own power. Still, Danniels sweats his way from the New Jersey coast toward Illinois, past talking road signs, hunting a car that has to stop for him. Readers get a strange, hot walk through a changed America.
52106-the-origin-and-development-of-the-:
The Origin and Development of the Moral Ideas is a large study by Edward Westermarck, shown here in volume one of the second edition. Westermarck held posts at the University of London and at the University of Finland, and had earlier written The History of Human Marriage. The first edition came in 1906, the second in 1912, and this print in 1924.

The opening chapter asks where moral judgments come from. Westermarck argues that they grow from moral feelings, not from reason alone, and looks at why men treat them as fixed and true for all. He holds that the aim of his science is to study how men judge, not to lay down rules for how they should live.
52913-an-anglo-american-alliance-a-serio:
Gregory Casparian wrote An Anglo-American Alliance, a serio-comic romance and forecast of the future, illustrated and published by the author at Floral Park, New York, in 1906. Contents promise a young ladies' seminary, an initiation, a moonlight soirée, historical events of the twentieth century, a fistic duel, a regatta, and adventures of an astronomer of Ispahan.

Chapter one opens in the year 1960, with Earth rotating serenely despite dire predictions of charlatans and fanatics. The Diana Young Ladies' Seminary stands on picturesque hills at Cornwall on the Hudson, near West Point, in a bequeathed millionaire's homestead. Lord Cunningham as viceroy of India and a transformation close the forecast plot. Curious readers get amateur futurism.
53014-twice-born-men-in-america-or-the-p:
Harriet Earhart Monroe wrote this book on the new birth of men, printed in 1914. Its full head joins two frames for one theme. It is a study of the mind in the change of heart, seen by a mind of the faith at work in the halls that save men from the street. The author had made past books on the art of talk, on a maid of the mines, and on the sights of Washington.

The list of parts opens with the tale of how she came to the work. In January 1908 a great blow fell on her, and that blow led her to the halls. Then come the work of the halls, and tales that show the might of God to save.
53654-snowbound-for-christmas:
Snowbound for Christmas is a Christmas entertainment piece by Mackenzie, issued by the Paine Publishing Company of Dayton, Ohio. The hosted text opens with the publisher's catalogue of musical entertainments. Songs for school and parlour are offered at thirty five cents each. A patriotic song heads the list, meant for the entire school. A quarrel duet for a small boy and girl follows.

Jolly farmer lads and lasses is billed as a humorous action song. Lullaby Lane is praised in Stevenson's vein and can close a program. Such catalogues show how the main piece was sold and used. Christmas entertainments were a staple of school and church life. A snowbound title promises the stranded holiday setting. Music, recitation, and simple staging made these booklets practical.
53917-disraeli-a-study-in-personality-an:
Walter Sichel wrote Disraeli, a study of the man and his thought, put out in New York in 1904. Sichel had written a life of Bolingbroke and his times. Three plates show Disraeli as a youth and in the year 1852. A note at the start lays out the theme of the book.

Sichel holds that the gift of fancy is the key to great rule. He then sorts the life by theme, not by year. Parts deal with the vote, with work and the Young England group, and with trade. Church, crown, and the growth of rule abroad each get a part. Themes of the United States, Ireland, high life, and books close the set. A last part sums up the path of his rise.
53920-kittyboy-s-christmas:
Amy Blanchard's Kittyboy's Christmas was published by Jacobs at Philadelphia in 1898, illustrated by Ida Waugh. Kittyboy is a small black cat, lost on a snowy street corner after a dog chased him into an alley. His little mistress Annie Brady has been sent away to a Home as a nuisance by her uncle's family, and the cat was kicked aside as one too. Still, he keeps a happy confidence in humanity.

He follows a passer-by up the steps and slips in as the latch-key turns. In the warm room an elderly, portly man with keen eyes lights a cigar and unfolds his evening paper, not noticing the kitten blinking by the fire. The frontispiece shows a solemn-faced little midget of six clasping a battered doll. Blanchard wrote Two Girls and A Dear Little Girl in the same juvenile line.
54084-list-of-post-offices-in-canada-wit:
List of Post Offices in Canada was printed at Quebec in 1865. It was issued by order of the postmaster general. Offices stand in alphabetical order, and again by electoral counties. The name of each postmaster is given. Marks show which offices could grant and pay money orders. Others are flagged for selling bill stamps or law stamps. Postmasters were told to correct their lists from later notices. Any error in an office entry was to be reported at once.

The department's own officers head the volume. Inspectors are listed for Toronto, London, Kingston, Montreal, and Quebec divisions. Rates of postage for foreign countries are added at the end. The list freezes the young country's mail network on January 1, 1865, office by office.
54479-faery-lands-of-the-south-seas:
James Norman Hall and Charles Bernard Nordhoff wrote this travel book, Faery Lands of the South Seas, printed in 1921. The preface is signed at Tahiti on April 10, 1921. Chapter heads name stops such as Mataora, Rutiaro, and the Cook Group. One head tells of costly welcomes, and one gives the tale of an Englishman.

In the preface the authors say the islands draw them for the charm of life among folk with a far outlook on life. They seek the feel and sense of that life, not mere facts. All the islands described lie in the Paumotu, Society, and Hervey groups. Old island names stand in for chart names in some tales.
54499-in-the-strange-south-seas:
Beatrice Grimshaw wrote of her sails through the strange South Seas. Her book came out in London in 1907. She wrote From Fiji to the Cannibal Islands in past years. A Kipling verse on new made tropic towns heads her tale. Most men have their loves among lands, her first page starts.

Names on the map call like horn blasts to men at home, she writes. Grey north towns hold them while far isles sing in their ears. Peaks, streams, and isles tramp the map to gay tunes there. She sailed with a young Ulysses from the quay in her verse. Strange shores and wild folk fill her own road tale. Sea fans get her bright eye.
55183-satan-a-romance-of-the-bahamas:
Stacpoole wrote this sea romance, Satan, a romance of the Bahamas, copyrighted in 1920 and printed at New York in 1921. Stacpoole also wrote The Blue Lagoon and The Beach of Dreams. Thirty-six chapters in three parts carry the tale, and their heads promise a floating caravan, a portmanteau, a wreck, a mutiny, and a fight.

Chapter one is Palm Island. Under a star-crusted tropic sky the yacht Dryad rides at anchor, lifting lazily to the swell beyond the great Bahama bank. She is Skelton's boat, six hundred tons, turbine engined, and rigged with every new gadget. She anchored at sundown off a tiny gull-haunted island west of Andros. Aboard are Skelton, a precise and very churchly Christchurch man, down below writing his diary, and Bobby Ratcliffe, leaning on the rail and smoking.
55366-the-farmer-s-veterinarian-a-practi:
Charles William Burkett, editor of American Agriculturist, wrote The Farmer's Veterinarian as a plain guide to the ills of farm stock. The copyright dates to 1909, and this copy was printed in 1914 as part of the Farm Life Series. Its ten chapters start with how the animal body is built and go on to the signs of age in the teeth, wounds, and the cutting open of dead beasts.

Later chapters treat common drugs and their acts, the meaning of disease, and the cure of farm animals' ills. The book is rich in pictures, from the bones of a horse to the parasites of the hog. Burkett aimed his advice at the working farmer, in brief, clear words, so a man far from a trained animal doctor could judge what ailed his stock and what to do first.
55378-miss-mephistopheles-a-novel-sequel:
Miss Mephistopheles is a novel by Fergus Hume, sequel to Madame Midas. White of London issued the one volume novel in eighteen ninety. Hume also wrote The Mystery of a Hansom Cab and other tales. Thirty chapters carry the story from Faces in the Fire to the close.

Chapter heads promise Keith adventure, Prince Carnival, and a woman appeal. A Russell Street crime, an inquest, and a council of three build the mystery. A cipher, a bank note proof, and Naball finds drive the hunt. The tale opens on a wet and dismal Sunday in the city. Church bells sound hoarse as folk go to evening service in rain.
55673-list-of-post-offices-in-canada-wit:
Printed at Ottawa in eighteen seventy-two by order of the postmaster general, the list names each post office in Canada and its chief on the first of July that year. Alexander Campbell held the top post, with William Henry Griffin as his deputy. The book also names the heads of accounts, cash orders, and branch work.

Long tables give each office by town, county, and vote district for each province. Added parts list offices shut in the past year and offices that changed names. Rates for mail in Canada and to Britain, its colonies, and other lands close the book. It is a plain state record, made so post chiefs could check and fix errors in their own lines.
55763-the-boy-fortune-hunters-in-the-sou:
The Boy Fortune Hunters in the South Seas is a boys' adventure novel by Floyd Akers, published at Chicago in 1911. The series had already taken its boys to Alaska, Panama, Egypt, China, and Yucatan. The first chapter introduces Señor de Jiminez, and the narrator's uncle Naboth opens the talk. A proposition is advanced in the second chapter.

The boys meet queer people, survive a South Pacific typhoon, and suffer a freakish shipwreck. Pearl people, a pearl city, and a reef patrol fill the middle chapters. A king, a priest, and a boy stand at the tale's heart, with an execution threatened and a run for life. A capricious earthquake shakes the close.
56070-list-of-post-offices-in-canada-wit:
This official list of post offices in Canada, with the names of the postmasters on July 1, 1873, was printed at Ottawa by order of the Postmaster General. Eight sections organise the book. A memorandum for postmasters and a list of the department's principal officers and inspectors come first.

The main list of offices and postmasters runs to some one hundred and fifty pages. Later sections list offices closed in the past year and offices whose names changed. Ontario and Quebec offices are then rearranged by electoral districts and townships. Readers get a complete snapshot of the young Dominion's postal network, one village postmaster at a time.
56203-list-of-post-offices-in-canada-wit:
List of Post Offices in Canada is an official register printed at Quebec in 1864, by order of the Postmaster General. It gives every post office in the province on the first of January of that year. The Postmaster General of the day was Mowat, and his deputy was Griffin. The front matter names the department's officers, accountants, and inspectors. Toronto and London divisions head the inspector list. Then come the tables, thousands of rows long.

Each row gives the name of the post office, its township or parish, its county, and the name of its postmaster. Offices printed in italics could grant and pay money orders. Abbotsford in Rouville, with Mrs Eliza Fisk as postmaster, stands near the head. The list is a census of settled Canada on the eve of Confederation. It serves the genealogist and the local historian as raw gold.
56280-stories-from-the-operas:
Stories from the Operas, by Gladys Davidson, retells opera plots in plain prose for the general reader. Lippincott published it at Philadelphia. Davidson also wrote Two Hundred Opera Plots and The Old Testament Story. A long opening list thanks publishing houses across Europe for leave to retell their stories, and a frontispiece shows Isolda snatching the cup and drinking.

Contents are arranged by composer. Auber's Fra Diavolo opens the book, then Balfe's Bohemian Girl and Beethoven's Fidelio. Bellini contributes La Sonnambula and I Puritani, and Bizet Carmen. Donizetti, Flotow, and Gounod follow, Gounod with Faust. The credits map the rest of the range. Verdi gives Trovatore, Traviata, and Rigoletto. Wagner gives Lohengrin, Tristan, and the Ring. Puccini gives Bohème, Butterfly, and Manon Lescaut, and Strauss the newer Elektra and Rosenkavalier.
56334-list-of-post-offices-in-canada-wit:
List of Post Offices in Canada, printed in Ottawa in 1866 by order of the Postmaster General, gives every post office in the country as of January 1, 1866. Offices are set out in A to Z order and also by voting county, with the name of each postmaster. A short note asks postmasters to report any error in their own listing at once.

Front pages name the chief staff of the Post Office Department and its inspectors for Toronto, London, Kingston, and Montreal. A table of postage rates for foreign lands is added at the end. The book is a plain working tool, and today it maps how mail reached towns across Canada before Confederation.
56457-faery-lands-of-the-south-seas:
Faery Lands of the South Seas, by James Norman Hall and Charles Bernard Nordhoff, appeared in 1921. Harper held the rights; Garden City issued this printing in New York. The pair had come through the Great War and met in Paris after it. German cannon on the Place de la Concorde framed their postwar start there.

A slow approach to the tropics opens their island wanderings in the book. Chapters visit Mataora, Mauké, Rutiaro, and the Cook Group in turn. Tales of Tari house, Vaitia valley, and costly hospitality fill the middle. A debtor of Moy Ling and an Englishman story add local color. Tahitian tales and a final anchorage off the reef close it.
56633-the-city-that-was:
The City That Was is a health past book by Stephen Smith, a cure trained man. An Allaben house of New York holds its right claim of nineteen eleven. Smith led the city health board in the years round eighteen seventy. Its front cut shows a school hard by a slay pen in eighteen sixty five. A press note calls the book a tale of a great life save turn.

That turn is cast as the vast of the last century in that note. New York of eighteen sixty four stands bare in its dread main part. Smith led that search of the town and told its tale to law men. He wrote it as a chief hand in the work, not a far seer of it. The tale claims like towns world wide share that same past state.
56917-addresses-by-john-a-martin-deliver:
Addresses by John Martin is a set of speeches delivered in Kansas. The Kansas Publishing House at Topeka issued it in 1888 for private circulation. Daniel Wilder, a Kansas editor, supplies the introduction to the volume. That introduction paints the governor's office during recent busy years. During the legislative session the governor rarely rests ten minutes by day.

At night callers follow him to his hotel until midnight with pleas. Martin reaches the office at eight and stays until five or six. He never goes out for lunch during those long office days. He listens to crowds, dictates letters, and keeps placid self control throughout. Wilder's portrait frames the speeches as a record of public duty.
57144-ypres-to-verdun-a-collection-of-ph:
Sir Alexander Kennedy took the photographs gathered in this book, first published at London in 1921. Kennedy, a past president of the civil engineers, went over the war areas of France and Flanders with a camera after the Great War. The book walks the reader along the whole front, from the Ypres salient to Verdun.

More than a hundred plates show the Menin Gate, dugouts in the walls of Ypres, the tank cemetery at Hooge, and the guns on the mole at Zeebrugge. Later sections cover the Somme, Arras and Vimy, Rheims and Soissons, and the Marne back to Mons. Short text ties the pictures together. It is a sober record of what the battlefields looked like when the guns had just fallen silent.
57605-tales-from-the-operas:
Tales from the Operas, edited by George Frederick Pardon, was published in New York by Carleton and in London by Blackwood in 1864. This American edition of an English work is inscribed to the opera manager Max Maretzek. Pardon's preface says readers wanted the stories of the famous operas told plainly, with the force and spirit of the originals kept.

The tales retell plots that American audiences knew best. Donizetti leads with Lucrezia Borgia, Don Pasquale, L'Elisir d'Amore and La Figlia del Reggimento. Mozart's Don Giovanni, Verdi's La Traviata, Rigoletto, Il Trovatore and Ernani follow, with Bellini's Norma and La Somnambula and Rossini's Barber of Seville. The Venice of Lucrezia's masqued ball opens the first tale.
57695-the-savage-south-seas:
Norman H Hardy painted and E Way Elkington described The Savage South Seas. A and C Black published the book at London in 1907. A note warns that island names are spelt more than one way in common use. The first part treats British New Guinea. It opens with the discoverers and the story of New Guinea, the Solomons, and the New Hebrides. Port Moresby and its two native villages follow.

Huts on poles and in trees, native superstition, and crops of hair fill the early chapters. Love and grief in New Guinea get a chapter, with the charms used to win constancy. Dances and queer costumes, then outrigger canoes and the great Lakatoi trading vessels, follow. The Solomon Islands form the second part. Hardy and Elkington made the large colour-plate travel book of empire at its height.
58200-lakeland-words-a-collection-of-dia:
Lakeland Words collects the dialect words and phrases of Cumberland and Westmorland. Kirkby compiled the glossary. Wilson printed it at Kendal in 1898. Joseph Wright, the Oxford dialect scholar, wrote the preface. The price was half a crown.

A dedication addresses the wandering sons of the Lake Country. Wherever they are, it says, they still love the sound of the old twang. Entries give each word with a spoken example. Sentences in the North Westmorland dialect show the words alive. The order is roughly alphabetical only. A nag that will not obey earns a long dialect scolding in one entry. Blodder means to cry in an effusive way. Braun is a wild boar.
58216-history-of-atchison-county-kansas:
Sheffield Ingalls compiled a history of Atchison County, Kansas, illustrated and issued at Lawrence in 1916. His preface disclaims any reading of the logic or spirit of events. He meant only a plain narrative of the people and institutions of the county, across the sixty years since its birth.

The work took six months, and Ingalls owns its imperfections freely. He thanks George Remsburg, a local historian of marvelous ability, who wrote two chapters and most of the matter on the founding of cities and towns. Files of the Atchison Daily Globe and Andreas' History of Kansas supplied much data. School history came through the county superintendent, and the state society helped throughout.
58590-la-re-union-a-french-settlement-in:
La Reunion, a French settlement in Texas, by William Hammond and Margaret Hammond, was published at Dallas in 1958. A portrait of Charles Fourier opens the book. Fourier's teaching inspired Victor Prosper Considerant to plant the colony. Quotes from Considerant head the work, on liberty and the free unison of human forces. Chapters start with the founders of the colony and a piece called Au Texas.

Later chapters treat the society, the view Texans took of it, and the immigrants. The colony itself and its breakup close the main text. An appendix lists some settlers and prints the plan of the phalanstery. Acts that set up the colony in law are also printed. The study shows a utopian plan tested on Texas ground.
58816-simla-village-tales-or-folk-tales-:
Alice Elizabeth Dracott collected these folk tales from the Himalayas, published by John Murray at London in 1906 and dedicated to the one she loves best. Nearly sixty short tales fill the contents, from a lawsuit between the owl and the kite to the Anar Pari, or Pomegranate Fairy, at the end.

The first tale explains the cause of that lawsuit: the owl claims she is the oldest creature in the world, since she alone existed when the world was made. The kite, who says he lived in trees, is confuted, there being no trees at the beginning. A monkey who objects to criticism, the origin of death, the real mother, and the snake's bride follow. Rajahs' sons, viziers' sons, jackals, tigers, a faithful dog named Kulloo, the repeating figure of Sheik Chilli, and the story of Puran give the book its village cast.
59263-88-favourite-carols-and-hymns-for-:
88 Favourite Carols and Hymns for Christmas is a songbook of Christmas hymns, printed at Otley by William Walker and Sons. It gathers the carols and hymns a church or family would sing across the season, in words only, for use in services, schools, and homes.

The first hymn is Christians Awake, salute the happy morn whereon the Saviour of the world was born. Its verses tell the whole story: the hosts of angels chanting from above, and the glad tidings brought first to the watchful shepherds. The babe lies wrapt in swaddling clothes in a manger at David's city. Heaven's whole arch, the hymn ends, rings with hallelujahs. Such cheap collections put the standard Christmas repertory into every hand, and the count of eighty-eight in the title was the selling point.
59524-a-guide-for-the-dissection-of-the-:
Lawrence E. Griffin wrote this guide to the cut-up of the dogfish, in a third shape printed at Portland in 1922. He taught the science of life at Reed College. The first page clears a point of names. The small sharks that swarm on the coasts of the United States are called dogfish by the men who fish and by most folk. The dogfish of fresh streams is of a far split kind, and is not in view here.

Two kinds of shark are caught in count and used in lab work. They are the spiny dogfish, Squalus acanthias, and the smooth dogfish. The first is known at a glance by the sharp spine in front of each fin of the back. The guide leads the student knife in hand through that fish, part by part.
59594-betty-s-virginia-christmas:
Betty's Virginia Christmas is a tale by Molly Elliot Seawell, printed at Philadelphia and London in 1914, with colour pictures by Henry Soulen. Seawell also wrote The Sprightly Romance of Marsac and Little Jarvis. This copy is a third edition, and the book is inscribed to Betty Randol, called a tall sister of the lilies.

The contents promise a young soldier, a dormer window, a shadow of the past, and the flying feet of the dancers. The tale opens on Christmas Eve in lower Virginia, with a thin crust of snow over the flat land. The river and the great bay beyond lie frozen hard as steel, and the low sun casts a rose red light on the silver world.
59605-a-topsy-turvy-christmas:
A Topsy Turvy Christmas is a short Christmas entertainment printed by the Paine Publishing Company of Dayton, Ohio, and sold for fifteen cents. The title page credits the piece to Guptill. School and church groups used such pieces for holiday programs. The copy carries the publisher's lists of kindred goods at the back and front.

Those lists sell the entertainment songs of Edna Randolph Worrell at twenty-five cents each. Welcome songs, good-bye songs and marching songs fill the catalog, each with a short pitch. One duet asks the whole school to whistle the chorus. The little book thus served two ends: a play for the night, and a shop window for the next one.
59740-lost-mine-trail-big-bend-national-:
Lost Mine Trail is a small park guide for Big Bend National Park in Texas. The booklet sold for ten cents to those who took it home. A cover photo came by grace of Peter Koch. The guide takes its name from Lost Mine Peak and its old tale.

Legend says Spanish men found rich ore high on the peak long ago. Men held for life were made to work the mine in chains. They were led blind from San Vicente in Mexico so none could learn the route. The guide asks if the mine was real or just a campfire tale, and leads walkers up the trail.
59841-sestrina-a-romance-of-the-south-se:
A Safroni Middleton wrote a romance of the South Seas, by the author of South Sea Foam, published by George H Doran at New York. Verse heads the title page: life is our death, we dream reality, and imagination is omnipotence. Some image of a bright eternity flashes on time's mirror, the lines say. It will be reshaped from madness into immortal beauty of new dreams.

Sestrina's tale belongs to the Edwardian South Seas romance trade. Safroni Middleton sailed the Pacific and wrote from the islands. His books mix beachcomber life, native custom, and love stories. Doran issued many such romances to American readers hungry for the tropics.
6003-story-of-aeneas:
M. Clarke retells Vergil's story of Aeneas for young readers, opening with Vergil as prince of Latin poets and a guide to gods and goddesses. The tale runs from the wooden horse and the fall of Troy through harpies, the prophecy of Helenus, and the giant Polyphemus.

A great storm drives Aeneas to Carthage, where Dido's love, funeral games, and burning ships follow. The Sibyl of Cumae, the golden bough, and the regions of the dead lead on to Latium, King Latinus, and the final fight with Turnus. A map traces the hero's wanderings across the sea.
60144-under-six-flags-the-story-of-texas:
M E M Davis wrote Under Six Flags, The Story of Texas, held in 1897 and issued by Ginn and Company. Davis had writ books such as In War Times at La Rose Blanche. A front picture shows the main door of Mission San Jose at San Antonio. The book is given to the memory of E H Cushing.

Davis says she sought to sketch the tale of Texas in bold strokes. She calls it a tale of romance, bold plans, and bold deeds. First men push into wild land, then settlers fight for freedom and rights. The book traces the birth of a people and the rise of a state. Davis hopes the short reads wake a like care in the reader.
60270-deep-sea-hunters-in-the-frozen-sea:
Hyatt Verrill wrote Deep Sea Hunters in the Frozen Seas, a boys adventure novel printed at New York in 1923. Verrill also wrote the Radio Detectives series and The Real Story of the Whaler. Old Captain Pem sits on a wharf with his wooden leg outstretched, chaffing with his crony Mike.

The two old mariners, friends since an Antarctic cruise on the bark Hector, never agree on anything by habit. Boys aboard ship meet narwhals, icebergs, glaciers, whales, and a walrus hunt in frozen seas. Unavik, a native guide, spins yarns and rescues the boys when they are frozen in for winter. An Arctic Christmas warms the tale. Young readers get whaling adventure up north.
60516-list-of-post-offices-in-canada-wit: The List of Post Offices in Canada for 1874 names every post office in the young Dominion and the postmaster who kept it on July 1 of that year. Hunter, Rose of Toronto printed it by order of the Postmaster General. The main list runs to nearly 150 pages, town by town. Registers follow for offices closed and renamed. Separate lists sort the offices by province and electoral district. Genealogists get the Dominion's whole postal map at one date, with a name at every counter.
61210-this-way-to-christmas:
This Way to Christmas, by Ruth Sawyer, author of Seven Miles to Arden, was published by Harper in October 1916. Its hero is David, and the contents send him seeking the way to Christmas. A locked out fairy leads, a flagman is found, and tales interrupt the road: Barney's tale of the wee red cap, and a trapper's tale of the first birthday.

The opening chapter muses that stories begin and end themselves where they please, leaving authors as helpless as readers. Sawyer would have begun with David in a window nook at dusk, the hill country white with gathering snow, seven days before Christmas. A closing legend of Bridget adapts Fiona Macleod's telling, with fragments gathered in the north of Ireland.
61794-buccaneer-of-the-star-seas:
Buccaneer of the Star Seas is a star tale by Ed Earl Repp from Planet Stories of fall nineteen forty. Its tag tells of a curse laid by a sorcerer of the thirteen hundreds. Thou shalt be death free, that curse ran on Carlyle in its words. He roams the wild star seas in search of death and rich lost hulks. A sea of long lost space ships is his hunt ground in that tag.

A dread shiver runs through Carlyle as a great iron door slams at start. He walks Reading Gaol damp halls at the heels of an old turn key. Friar Bacon lock has slept six months, that key man grumps in the walk. Brimstone, coal, and salt saltpeter made a flash and roar in that cell. Nine years the Gray Friar has sat jailed for dark craft in that place.
62502-records-historical-and-antiquarian:
Records, Historical and Antiquarian, of Parishes Round Horncastle is a local history by J Conway Walter. The hosted text comes from the nineteen oh four edition. The pieces first appeared in the columns of a local newspaper, the preface says. A photo of the author with his signature stands at the front. Walter also wrote records of Woodhall Spa and neighbourhood.

In his preface Walter warns that some parishes a reader seeks may be missing here. Accounts of them ran in his earlier Woodhall Spa volume instead, he explains. That book treated parishes from Somersby in the east to Bucknall in the west. It aimed at visitors to a growing health resort. A further volume is proposed for the near future, he adds. He owns the book's faults freely, saying none could be more alive to them.
62841-betty-crocker-s-bisquick-cook-book:
General Mills issued 'Betty Crocker's Bisquick Cook Book' in 1956, offering 157 recipes and ideas from Betty Crocker of General Mills. The opening pitch is that a cook does nice things for the family more often because she starts so far ahead with Bisquick. Pancakes come first: beat two cups of Bisquick, one egg, and milk with a rotary beater, and pour onto a heated griddle for about eighteen pancakes.

Muffins bake at 400 degrees for fifteen minutes, and waffles, coffee cake, and dumplings dropped onto boiling stew follow. A photo lesson then teaches good biscuits: add milk all at once, beat the stiff dough fifteen strokes, knead gently eight to ten times, and roll half an inch thick. Baked at 450 degrees, the batch makes twelve biscuits, set close for soft sides or apart for crusty ones. Dinner biscuits, herb biscuits, and cheese bread vary the theme.
62996-the-jewel-of-bas:
Leigh Brackett wrote this weird novel for Planet Stories, where it ran in the Spring 1944 issue. The head note calls it a tale of gripping power. A boy-god sleeps through all time at its heart, with his Stone of Life beside him.

Two mortals must stem a flood of death: Mouse and Ciaran. Mouse stirs a thin stew in a small iron pot as the tale opens. She scolds Ciaran for stealing too small a joint of meat. He lounges on a moss-grown rock and takes her heat with lazy grey eyes. The androids the boy-god made, of stuff and force, plot to kill a world, and this pair stands in their path.
6305-a-fool-there-was:
Porter Emerson Browne begins by admitting that no man knows when this story began, perhaps a hundred years ago, perhaps ten thousand. What can be told is that John Schuyler came from clean bodied, clear eyed ancestors, Dutch and English. They gave him their virtues and plucked their vices from his garden of heredity. He inherits cleanness of body and soul, and a life of outdoor pleasure follows.

Schuyler yachts from Gravesend to Bar Harbor in his yawl Manana, motors, rides, and plays tennis, golf, squash, and racquets, swims, fences, and boxes with youthful ease. Browne quotes Kipling's fool and his prayer to a rag and a bone and a hank of hair. He writes a novel of a good man undone by a woman who does not care. The 1909 tale is lush, moral, and unflinching about folly.
63060-war-in-the-underseas:
War in the Underseas is a book of the great war at sea by Harold Wheeler, a fellow of a royal corps of past lore. His past books told of bold deeds of trade sea men and of the sea dogs of Britain. He was the man who set a famed lore sheet on its feet. The front words are sworn to a young man whose sire won fame in a raid on two ports of the foe.

The first words lay down the creed of the book in one hard line. Sea might, they say, choked the foe land and saved the world. While the foe hosts rode rough shod past most of Europe, the grip of the sea held firm. The tale that follows is the war of the boats that dive.
63867-captain-midas:
Captain Midas is a science fiction tale by Alfred Coppel, first printed in Planet Stories in the fall of 1949. Its blurb shows the captain of the Martian Maid staring at a torn derelict in the void. Here was treasure past his wildest dreams. How could he know his dreams should have been nightmares? The tale is told by an old spaceman, beached earthside on a small pension. Gold, he says, is a magic word still. Lust and gold go hand in hand.

A third word completes the set: cost. Pain, sorrow, agony are its other names. The old man had millions in his hands once, and calls the treasure cursed. His hearers think it a tall tale for the youngsters. He answers that his breed went to space for Number One, and kept what they found. But this find was different, and the tale tells why.
63953-as-it-was:
As It Was is a science fiction story by Paul Payne, from Planet Stories of November 1952. Its blurb paints a cruel cosmos where one lived only to be killer or killed. The One, a vast predator, proves that law by killing a hundred times a day. Thisbe the Second is named as its blood red hunting preserve in space.

Pritchard, the brightest name in big game hunting across Galaxy A, takes up the challenge. Dawn on Thisbe shows a magenta sun and orange flares over a purple sky. The hunt pits man famed skill against a beast that rules a whole world. Payne builds a pulp duel of hunter and monster from that first light.
64049-witch-of-the-demon-seas:
Craig wrote Witch of the Demon Seas, a novel of alien sorcery from Planet Stories in January 1951. Corun, a condemned pirate of Conahur, is offered a reprieve from the headsman's axe if he will guide a black galleon to the lost citadel of the Xanthi wizards. His lover, the blurb warns, is a witch herself.

Khroman the Conqueror, a huge black-bearded king in a plain white tunic, watches guards bring up the captured pirates at Tauros. The sorcerer Shorzon counsels public torture stretched over many days for the pirate chief. Khroman refuses: Corun was the bravest enemy Achaera ever had and deserves an honourable death. Sword and sorcery fans get pulp grandeur.
6447-proserpine-and-midas:
Mary Shelley's two unpublished mythological dramas, Proserpine and Midas, appear here edited with an introduction by A. Koszul. The editor came across the texts as early as 1905 and long feared overrating their worth, delaying print. The Shelley centenary year gave the occasion: a little monument to his wife's collaboration, taking its modest place among tributes to his memory.

The dramas matter, Koszul argues, as the proper setting for some of Shelley's most beautiful lyrics, so far read in undue isolation. They also stand as a literary sign of their times, an example of the classical renaissance the romantic period fostered. A mid passage weighs poets as proofs of mythology, testing Jupiter's attributes and acts against Bible revelation. The volume is scholarship and tribute at once.
64641-oh-mesmerist-from-mimas:
Roger Dee wrote Oh, Mesmerist from Mimas, a science fiction story printed in Planet Stories in January 1953. Mimas is a small inner moon of Saturn, home of the smileys, creatures that pour out an aura of peace and brotherhood. The narrator carries one in a small tungsten wire cage.

At the cargo declarations mart of Areopolis spaceport on Mars, the busy room falls silent as he enters. The hush is not for him, though he is known in odd corners of the solar system. It is for the smiley, one of the first two ever to reach Mars, young, healthy, and unmated. The creature radiates like a beacon in a meteor shower. Dee plays the wonder straight and lets the room full of hard traders melt. The title gives the joke away: the mesmerist is the pet.
65071-matthew-fontaine-maury-the-pathfin:
Charles Lee Lewis, a teacher at the United States Naval Academy, wrote this life of Matthew Fontaine Maury. The book came out at Annapolis in 1927, with a foreword by Commander Richard Byrd. Lewis spent the best part of four years at work on it.

Maury was a naval officer whose charts of winds and currents made sea travel far safer. The publisher notes that no life of him had yet come out in America. Lewis tells the story of a man who cut risk for sailors on all seas. The book also holds plates and a warm note from the Maury Memorial Association. It presents Maury as a true pathfinder of the seas.
65503-60-new-trimmed-gift-ideas:
Sixty new trimmed gift ideas fill a free booklet of instructions from the W M Wright firm of West Warren, Massachusetts, makers of braids and rick rack. Each plan lists the yards of net, felt, ribbon and trim needed, then gives plain steps for making the gift at home.

Early pages show tree figures, mother and daughter net aprons with gold loop braid, an apron dressed with five cloth shapes, and a gold rose stocking cut from white felt. Numbers in brackets name other trims that give the same effect, so a maker can use what her shop has in stock. The booklet sold the firm's trims by showing their uses.
65593-a-history-of-kansas:
Anna Arnold, author of 'Civics and Citizenship,' wrote this history of Kansas for school use. The state published it at Topeka in 1919, in a revised edition from a 1914 copyright. A view of Memorial Hall and the seal of the state of Kansas stand at the front.

The beginning of Kansas history opens the contents as chapter one. Kansas becoming a part of the United States follows in the scheme of the book. Arnold writes a clear state history for Kansas children, covering explorers, territory days, the fight over slavery, statehood and growth, in the plain order a classroom text requires.
65663-list-of-post-offices-in-canada-wit:
The Post Office Department of Canada printed this list of post offices with the names of their postmasters, as of January 1, 1860. Thompson and Company of Quebec printed it by order of the Postmaster General. Sidney Smith held that post, with William Henry Griffin as his deputy. Inspectors served districts at Montreal, Kingston, Toronto, and London.

Postmasters were told to fix their lists from the notices sent out over time and to report any error in how their office was set down. Offices printed in italics could grant and pay money orders. The roll then runs office by office, with county or parish and postmaster for each, starting in Canada East.
6586-the-cruise-of-the-kawa-wanderings-i:
Walter Traprock, as his publishers present him, sails the South Seas in the Kawa, with seventeen pictures and a map to mark the way. The dedication names island brides in loving, fanciful terms, and the publisher's note plays up the craze for tropic tales among American readers. To be unread in Polynesian lore, it jokes, was to be out of fashion.
