The cruise itself promises warm seas, strange shores, and the lure that drew so many writers south. Traprock's voice is that of a jovial traveler, keen on color and fun. The Cruise of the Kawa is a light, period piece of South Seas travel writing, best read as a window on its own eager age.
66247-winter-butterflies-in-bolinas:
Mary Barber wrote Winter Butterflies in Bolinas, published at San Francisco in 1918. Her subject is the Monarch butterfly, known across much of the United States but less known as a migrant. Barber tells how it flies hundreds and even thousands of miles, and how it gathers each year at one sheltered California haven.

Immense swarms reach Bolinas early in September, to a coast village about ten miles north of the Golden Gate. Barber paints the place first, its beach, bluffs, cottages, gardens, and cypress groves. She then traces the Monarch from a pale green caterpillar on milkweed, banded in glossy black, to a green chrysalis spotted with gold. The butterflies come from the Sierra Nevada and from the western ranges of the Rockies.
66828-the-pilgrims-first-christmas:
The Pilgrims' First Christmas, by Josephine Pittman Scribner, was copyright in 1913 and issued by the Pilgrim Press. Its first pages drop to a bleak day in December 1620. The Mayflower fights rain and snow off the coast, her rudder broke and her masts split.

Below deck, women and twenty small children wait with battened hatches. Mary Chilton moves among them, fair and strong, cheering the sick and the scared. She keeps the Billington boy out of harm and teases him with talk of St Nicholas Day. A shoe may hold a gift on Christmas morning, if he stays good. Young readers get a warm tale of want, faith, and cheer on the first crossing.
66957-the-book-of-christmas:
The Book of Christmas is a gathering of pieces on the feast, with an opening essay by Hamilton W. Mabie. Drawings by George Wharton Edwards go with the texts. The book came out in New York from the Macmillan Company in 1909. A picture of the Holy Night by Correggio stands at its front.

The contents open with a set of pieces called Signs of the Season. Among them are a poem by Alfred Tennyson on the near birth of Christ and an old English tract in search of Christmas. A piece by F. Marion Crawford on the Doge's Christmas shooting stands in the list. Pieces on Advent rites, the Glastonbury Thorn, and the kitchen at the feast round out the first part of the book as shown.
67216-a-united-states-midshipman-in-the-:
Lieutenant Commander Yates Stirling Jr wrote a boys' naval adventure in 1913, drawn by Ralph L Boyer. Stirling had written earlier midshipman books set afloat, in China, in the Philippines, and in Japan. A dedication honors sailors of all nations who died in small island wars. Such wars, he notes, are scarcely remembered at home.

A United States man of war boat lands on the beach of Ukula through a coral reef channel. Rival chiefs, discord among the whites, and plotting for power drive the plot. Smuggled arms, an attack on Ukula, and a cutting out expedition follow. Count Rosen takes charge at a key point in the tale.
67795-the-lhota-nagas:
Mills, an officer of the Indian civil service, wrote a study of the Lhota Nagas, printed at London in 1922. It came out by order of the government of Assam. Hutton, who led the study of peoples in Assam, added a first word and notes. Plates show dress, houses, and war gear.

Seven parts treat the people whole. The first covers their start, moves, looks, dress and arms. Home life follows, with the village, the morung hall, farms, food, games and song. Laws and customs treat marriage rules, goods, oaths, war and head hunting. Faith, tales, and speech close the work, with notes on their calendar and on human sacrifice.
68275-the-war-of-the-carolinas:
Meredith Nicholson wrote The War of the Carolinas, issued in Nelson's Library at London beside novels by Wells, London, and Norris. Verses by Bunner head the opening: the writer hopes to know her face when under the may he finds her.

The book opens with a prose address, To You at the Gate. A daisy meadow runs to a stone wall, and a girl stands at the gate at dusk, arms folded, watching the stars and the young moon of June. The narrator passed her once, and in other Junes kept tryst with moon and stars beside that gate, though she never came again. The tone is wistful and romantic from the first page.
68498-the-sky-sheriff-the-pioneer-spirit:
Thomson Burtis's Sky Sheriff appeared in the April 1923 issue of Blue Book Magazine. Its subtitle promises the pioneer spirit living again in the Texas Airplane Patrol. Rosenmeyer drew the illustrations. Seven men stand in line at the McMullen Flight airdrome under a blazing Texas sun. Six are tanned young flyers; the seventh, with flowing gray mustache and embossed cowboy boots, is Sheriff Bill Trowbridge, known from one end of the Rio Grande to the other.

Captain Perkins, the new commanding officer, introduces Sleepy Spears, fresh from the mechanics' school at Donovan Field. Sleepy and Tex MacDowell have flown to Laredo and crossed to the Bee hangout in Nuevo Laredo to gamble. They were fed Benedictine and mescal and broke. Trowbridge asks whether Perkins has handled wildcats before. The tale mixes the old sheriff's world with the new patrol's.
6862-the-belted-seas:
Arthur Colton opens The Belted Seas with verse on the earth's cold feet, temperate bosom, and huge, hot midriff, where the belted seas laugh around still Hesperides. Chapters run from Pemberton's and the Hebe Maitland to the Hotel Helen Mar, Sadler in Portate, and Torre Ananias. Why Captain Buckingham did not go back to Greenough, and the loss of the Anaconda, add mystery.

King Julius, the Kiyi proposition, the voyage of the Voodoo, and Flannagan and Stevey Todd carry the tale through tropic ports. Colton writes with a sea storyteller's gusto. The Belted Seas is a colorful, episodic novel of ships, traders, and far waters.
68631-a-visit-from-st-nicholas:
Clement Moore's A Visit from Saint Nicholas, issued by the Atlantic Monthly Press at Boston in 1921, is a gift-book printing of the famous Christmas poem. Blank lines at the front leave room for the giver's name and the child's, and pictures show Saint Nicholas at work in a home. The poem itself fills the little book.

It begins with the night before Christmas, when all through the house not a creature was stirring, not even a mouse. The stockings hang by the chimney, the children dream of sugar-plums, and a clatter on the lawn brings the father to the window. Down the chimney comes Saint Nicholas with his bundle of toys, his cheeks like roses and his belly shaking like a bowl full of jelly. Moore names the eight tiny reindeer: Dasher, Dancer, Prancer and Vixen, Comet, Cupid, Donder and Blixen.
68757-list-of-post-offices-in-canada-wit:
The List of Post Offices in Canada, with the Names of the Postmasters, was printed at Toronto in 1856 by Lovell and Gibson, by order of the Postmaster General. It gives the offices as they stood on the first of September, 1856, with a supplementary list running to the first of March, 1857. Offices printed in italics, a memorandum notes, may grant and pay money orders.

The principal officers are named at the front: Robert Spence, Postmaster General; William Henry Griffin, secretary; and inspectors for the Montreal, Toronto, Kingston, and London divisions. The list itself is a great table. For every office it gives the township in Canada West, or the township, seigniory, or parish in Canada East, the electoral county or division, and the postmaster's own name.
69068-the-country-christmas:
The Country Christmas is a children's story by Frances Margaret Fox, printed at Boston by Page in 1907. It belongs to the Cosy Corner Series. Barry illustrated it, and a plate shows the choosing of the Christmas tree. Fox also wrote Farmer Brown and the Birds, Betty of Old Mackinaw, and How Christmas Came to the Mulvaneys.

The Mulvaneys walk into this book too. Sally Brown remembered the Mulvaneys, the tale notes, and talked of them at first without cease. When she had lived in the country two months, her mother and brother Alfred begged her to change the subject. The story turns on a city child's first country Christmas: the tree, the snow, and the farm's plain plenty against remembered streets. Fox wrote short, warm books for young readers, and this is her holiday piece.
69093-history-of-scientific-ideas:
History of Scientific Ideas is a work by William Whewell, Master of Trinity College, Cambridge. It forms the first part of his Philosophy of the Inductive Sciences. This third edition ran to two volumes; the first came out in London in 1858 from John W. Parker and Son, printed at the Cambridge University Press. A Greek motto about passing the torch stands on the title page.

The preface to the edition states the change of title. The chapters now offered were first put out as part of the larger Philosophy, but the present title fits them best, it says. This part of the work is in the main a history: it traces the ideas on which the sciences rest, as they grew through time. The second part of the philosophy builds on that ground.
69174-the-golden-verses-of-pythagoras:
Putnam published The Golden Verses of Pythagoras in the Redfield translation in 1917, in the Knickerbocker Press series. The French original is the work of Fabre d'Olivet, scholar and mystic. He explained the verses and preceded them with a discourse on the essence and form of poetry among the principal peoples of the Earth.

The verses themselves are the ancient maxims ascribed to Pythagoras: know thyself, and nothing in excess, as the Greek motto on the title page runs. Fabre d'Olivet reads them as the deposit of a primordial wisdom. His hermeneutic interpretation treats poetry as the first language of that wisdom. The book is offered, in the dedication, to travellers who have turned their faces to the dawn. It belongs to the occult revival that kept Pythagoras a prophet.
69214-list-of-post-offices-in-canada-wit:
List of Post Offices in Canada, with the Names of the Postmasters on the 1st January 1863, was printed by order of the Postmaster General at Quebec in 1863. Its first pages name the heads of the mail: M H Foley in chief, his deputy, the cash desk, and the chiefs of the money order branch. Watchers for five zones are set out too, from Toronto to Quebec. A short note bids each postmaster mark flaws in his own line and write in at once.

Then the long roll runs town by town in ruled ranks: the office, its township or parish, its county, and the man who holds the stamp. Offices in italic type may grant and pay money orders. Record fans get a full snap of Canada's mail web on one cold New Year's Day.
69383-in-old-madras:
B M Croker wrote In Old Madras, a tale of Anglo Indian trade and army life. Hutchinson and Company issued the book in London from Paternoster Row. A Kipling line on the East’s call fronts its first page. Surf like guns and red dust open the tale in Madras.

Brown, Brown and Company rules the trade scene of the tale. The old firm rose in John Company’s first plain days there. War, mutiny, and famine left its grim beach house unshaken. Robert Clive may have walked its halls as a young clerk. Captain Mallender, fresh from England, waits in its bare front room. A London tailor’s thin suit and new white umbrella mark him. Mr Fleming and Monkey Parr, the partners, share a start at his card. Same name, same club, Parr says, and it gave him a shock.
69508-sculptured-tombs-of-hellas:
Percy Gardner wrote Sculptured Tombs of Hellas, printed in London in 1896 with thirty plates and eighty-seven engravings in the text. Gardner was professor of classical archaeology and art at Oxford. An Athenian grave verse heads the book: a man of Chios, whose life held few griefs and many joys, lies in Attic land. Contents open with burial customs in Greece. The laying-out of the dead, shown by vases, and the bearing-out follow.

The worship of the dead takes the second chapter. Beliefs as to the future life fill the third. Homeric beliefs, the visit of Odysseus to the world below, the islands of the blessed, and the sway of Orphism are treated. Paintings by Polygnotus at Delphi close that chapter. The so-called treasuries at Mycenae, in truth tombs, follow.
69527-the-war-against-germany-europe-and:
War Against Germany forms the pictorial record of the United States Army in the Second World War in Europe, first printed in 1951. The Center of Military History issued the book at Washington. Kent Roberts Greenfield led the whole Army history set as chief editor.

Seven parts trace the war in maps and plates. Build up in Britain and the air war come first, then the Normandy and north France fights. Rhineland, Ardennes and Alsace, and last the drive into central Europe close the arc. Text notes the huge task of shipping men and goods across the Atlantic while German submarines struck at peak force. Lists of short forms and credits end a book made to show, not just tell, the war.
6969-the-orations-of-lysias:
The orations of Lysias appear here in a handy literal translation, covering speeches numbered from the funeral oration to the panegyric. The contents list pleas for Callias, the olive tree, Polyaenus, Theomnestus, and Eratosthenes, with cases on the property of Eraton and Aristophanes, the grain dealers, Pancleon, and the cripple. Speeches against Philon, Eratosthenes, and Agoratus stand beside a reply on the overthrow of democracy.

The funeral oration opens with Lysias doubting that any words, even with long notice, could match the valor of the dead. He notes the city provides a speaker, and he takes up the task with modesty. The collection gives English readers direct access to Athenian law courts, politics, and plain forensic speech.
69923-fuzzy-wuzz-a-little-brown-bear-of-:
Fuzzy-Wuzz, a little brown bear of the Sierras, by Allen Chaffee, was copyrighted in 1922 at Springfield, Massachusetts, with drawings by Peter Da Ru. Chaffee wrote Twinkly Eyes, the Little Black Bear, and other animal tales. Thirty-five chapters follow a cinnamon cub through a year of mountain life, from his mother's cave to winter snow.

The first chapter shows Mother Brown Bear in the mouth of her rock cave above the falls, nuzzling her babies under twinkling stars. Later chapters bring a screech owl, ranger's children, coyotes, a spotted fawn, hunters, and a rattlesnake den. Fuzzy runs away, makes wild playmates, and meets a burro and a pinto pony. Chaffee writes warm nature tales for children.
70273-the-boy-who-brought-christmas:
The Boy Who Brought Christmas, a tale by Alice Morgan, was published by Doubleday, Page and Company in 1911, with pictures by John Jackson. Parts of the book hold earlier copyrights, from 1901 and 1904. Four long chapters make the whole: The Itinerant Christmas Tree, Creeds and Deeds, Unconscious Mentality, and Old-Time Religion.

The tale opens on a mountain road. Old Man Ledbetter jolts along in an ox cart, his plaited beard bound with a shoe string, his whipstock at his feet. His team turns at the ford and staggers into the Junaluska, water swirling about his feet. The scene sets a backwoods world of faith, custom, and Christmas keeping.
70325-mary-christmas:
Mary Ellen Chase tells a Maine tale of four children and a strange guest in a Little, Brown volume with rights held from 1926. Boston printings ran in 1926, 1927, and again in 1936 under the Atlantic Monthly Press line. A plate shows a tall, odd figure walking at a man's side as the children stare.

Chapter one, Concerning a Collar and Tie, starts in the slow days of the late nineties. Children then curtsied, said yes ma'am and no sir, and recited the books of the Bible by rote. On a warm June day the four Wescott children swing on a white gate under great elms. Later heads name a blue gingham dress, buried wealth, a crab-apple tree, and the Garden of Eden, which hints at faith woven through farm life.
70460-docas:
Genevra Snedden wrote a school reader on an Indian boy of Santa Clara, printed at Boston in 1899 and kept in print for decades. It joins the Heath set of extra readers. A first letter asks young readers a plain question. What folk do you like best to read about, white folk or Indians?

All children asked say Indians, the writer holds, since their ways differ so much from our own. The tales treat the Indians near the Pacific shore before white settlers came west. Docas grows from boy to man in the book. His children and grandchildren follow. The last tales, she owns, tell things that truly befell Indian children in old California.
70521-the-hermit-s-christmas:
The Hermit's Christmas, a story by David De Forest Burrell, was copyrighted by the American Tract Society in 1912. On Christmas Day the solitude of the hermit Theodore is broken in upon. Theodore, a gaunt man in a robe of goat's hair, stands at his cave door when the first intruder appears far below, sunlight glancing from his armor.

The climber is a Crusader knight, his helmet slung at his back, his horse left by the sea with a broken leg. He calls hoarsely for water in the name of all the saints, and the hermit brings a gourd full, which he drinks dry. Talk turns to the feast he had forgot: Christmas Day. The knight sighs for a hall in merry England, the boar's head and foaming ale. The hermit answers that dried goat's flesh is not a boar's head, but the day and the welcome are what matter.
70522-for-the-freedom-of-the-seas:
For the Freedom of the Seas is a tale of the great war at sea for boys by Ralph Henry Barbour. Wrenn made its plates. It was put out in nineteen eighteen at New York and London. The book is sworn to a man of a coast town, with the hand's hail. A long front list names the past books of the hand in their sets: school tales, sport tales, and tales of camp and of the road.

The list of parts gives the run of this tale. The way of the foe heads it. With the coast watch, the lone reef, and a fight past ground come next. A chance meet, on the great river of the foe's land, and past parts of the list fill the first run.
70700-journal-of-a-tour-in-marocco-and-t:
Journal of a Tour in Marocco and the Great Atlas, by Joseph Hooker and John Ball, was published by Macmillan in London in 1878. Hooker, director of the Royal Gardens at Kew, made the expedition of 1871 and kept careful notes. Prinsep's panorama of the Great Atlas from the city illustrates it.

The preface, signed by Ball, explains the long delay. Hooker wrote the greater part of the first two chapters, but his duties at Kew forced him to hand the completion to his fellow-traveller. His election in 1873 to the presidency of the Royal Society had intervened. Ball was himself busy with a memoir on the flora of Marocco, drawn from the journey's collections. An appendix adds a sketch of the geology of Marocco by George Maw. In Marocco, the preface argues, a few years' delay costs little: the country has barely changed in two centuries.
70702-the-children-s-book-of-christmas:
Dier compiled this children book of Christmas for Macmillan in 1911. The volume opens with the famed Is There a Santa Claus letter. Virginia O'Hanlon, eight years old, wrote to The Sun for truth. Papa said if you see it in The Sun it is so.

The editor answers that her little friends are wrong to doubt. They think nothing can be which their little minds cannot grasp. Yes, Virginia, there is a Santa Claus, the reply affirms. He exists as surely as love and generosity do, it says. The famous answer ran first in The Sun newspaper of New York in its day.
70859-legends-of-texas:
Frank Dobie edited Legends of Texas for the Texas Folk-Lore Society, number three of its publications, printed at Austin in 1924 in a second edition. His preface calls the assembling of his state's legends a joyful business.

Dobie spent three years talking with people, riding into remote places, and searching Texas material, yet wishes he had three more. The legends of buried treasure and lost mines are grouped by place, with the Llano and San Saba country first. He excluded tales not living among English-speaking Texans, while granting that most settler legends derive from folk of other races. The society issued the volume as its third publication.
70911-the-evolution-of-general-ideas:
The Evolution of General Ideas, by Ribot, studies how the mind builds broad notions from single things. Ribot taught at the Collège de France, and Welby made this authorised English version. Open Court printed the book at Chicago in 1899.

Ribot states his aim at the start: to trace how the mind abstracts and generalises. These two acts, he argues, follow a true evolution in set stages. They are present already in simple perception, the first step of knowing. From there they climb by clear steps to the high forms of pure symbolism. The front pages list sister works in the same line, on attention, the diseases of personality and of the will, and the psychic life of small organisms. Prices run from fifteen cents to a dollar and a quarter.
71003-tusayan-katcinas:
Jesse Walter Fewkes wrote Tusayan Katcinas, drawn from the fifteenth yearly report of the Bureau of Ethnology. The Government Printing Office put it out at Washington in 1897. Fewkes sets out the sequence of Tusayan rites through the year, with the names of months and their rites. He tells how the time for each rite was fixed and how the rites were grouped. Earlier notes on the katcinas are weighed with care.

The bulk of the work sorts the katcinas into full and short forms. Full rites such as Soyaluna and Powamu get long treatment, with plates of masks and dolls. Short rites such as Siocalako and Pawikkatcina follow in kind. A last part sets Tusayan dances by the side of Cibola dances. The work is a key source for Hopi rite and art.
71089-tall-tales-from-texas:
Mody C Boatright gathered tall tales from Texas, with pictures by Elizabeth E Keefer. The Southwest Press issued the book at Dallas, with rights from 1934. J Frank Dobie wrote a foreword on the art of the honest liar. The book is given to the author's father at the front.

A true liar knows his listeners know, Dobie writes with grave fun. Pecos Bill's birth, deeds, and exit fill three full chapters of windies. Wind, speed, beasts, and hair-breadth escapes sort the rest of the yarns. Folklore fans gain campfire tales told as the range itself told them.
71404-the-book-of-saint-nicholas:
The Book of Saint Nicholas was printed by Harper in New York in 1836, translated, its title page claims, from the original Dutch of Nicholas Oudenarde. It is dedicated to the societies of Saint Nicholas in New York, in a letter dated from Nieuw Amsterdam in July 1827.

The contents hold eleven pieces. The Legend of Saint Nicholas leads, followed by the Little Dutch Sentinel of the Manhadoes. Dutch named tales follow: Cobus Yerks, a strange bird in Nieuw Amsterdam, and Claas Schlaschenschlinger. The Revenge of Saint Nicholas and the Origin of the Bakers' Dozen come later, and the Ride of Saint Nicholas on New Year's Eve closes the book. In his advertisement, the author boasts of hanging up his stocking every Christmas and New Year without fail.
71547-a-journey-in-search-of-christmas:
A Journey in Search of Christmas, by Owen Wister, was copyright 1904 and published in New York and London, with illustrations by Frederic Remington. Wister had also written Lin McLean, Red Men and White, and The Jimmyjohn Boss. The hero here is Lin McLean himself, in a frontispiece portrait.

Contents are five chapters. Lin money talks joy, then Lin money is dumb. A transaction in boot blacking, turkey and responsibility, and Santa Claus Lin close the list. Pictures show Lin walking in charge of children, and a Mister Billy Lusk presented. The tale opens with a Governor descending the Capitol steps, a gift list in hand. He has put off the task till the latest day, as was his custom. Readers get a Western Christmas tale with a governor, a cowboy, and street children.
71587-the-long-arm-of-fanto-mas:
Souvestre and Allain wrote a fresh Fantômas tale of the great rogue's long arm. Allinson turned it into English. The book came out in New York in 1924. A bright job starts the tale, and a night fight comes next. Dark schemes and a fit of the shakes fill the first parts.

Hopes fall, and a man is held in the Lantern's grip. Fantômas sends his last word, and a wire comes from mid sea. The Blue Chestnut and Tom Bob on the spot build the mid hunt. A wall that bled and the Bois de Boulogne stand in the list. Fantômas meets Fantômas in a late, bold part's name. Crime fans get pace.
72080-ozymandias:
Ivar Jorgenson wrote 'Ozymandias' for the November 1958 issue of Infinity, with illustrations by Dan Adkins. Its blurb stages a quarrel: open strife between the military and scientific staffs, but which was mightier? The story opens in orbit over a planet dead about a million years. Colonel Mattern calls it worthless at once and wants to pack up and move on.

Mattern serves the General Staff, which put in seventy per cent of the budget expecting new weapons and strategic materials, not archaeology. Leopold, head of the scientific segment, invokes the limiting clause that reserves at least one hundred sixty-eight hours of research on any world they land on. Four archaeologists and seven military men watch their chiefs battle over the dust and the stumps of monuments below.
72859-ships-of-the-seven-seas:
Hawthorne Daniel writes of famed ships in a Doubleday, Page volume held under rights from 1925 at Garden City, New York. Franklin D Roosevelt wrote the introduction, and Francis J Rigney drew the plates for the book. Daniel gives the work to his wife Nelle, without whose aid it would never have been finished, he states.

A front plate shows the Santa Maria, the Niña, and the Pinta, called the most famous ships that ever sailed. The Niña, smallest of the three, bore Columbus home after the Santa Maria was wrecked, the caption notes. A source list names Holmes on ancient and modern ships, Clark on the clipper era, and Hollis on the frigate Constitution. The New York Public Library and the Naval Academy's Marine Museum lent help for the facts, Daniel adds.
73749-lost-ships-and-lonely-seas:
Lost Ships and Lonely Seas, a book of sea disaster tales by Ralph D Paine, was published by the Century Company of New York under copyrights of 1920 and 1921. Seventeen chapters gather true stories of wreck, raft, and open boat. Paine was a writer of the sea, and the tales rest on logs, trials, and survivors' accounts.

The brig Polly opens the book, a sodden hulk whose crew caught fresh water from a pistol barrel in a tin cup. The schooner Exertion fell among thieves, and the frigate Medusa met her famous tragedy. The Blenden Hall, the Wager man of war, and the Nottingham Galley follow. One crew rowed four thousand miles in an open boat. Captain Paddock on the coast of Barbary and the roaring days of piracy fill out the round of luckless seamen.
74473-australia-new-zealand-and-some-isl:
Frank Carpenter wrote this travel volume, Australia, New Zealand and Some Islands of the South Seas, printed at Garden City, New York, in 1924. It carries one hundred and twenty-six pictures from his own photographs. It stands in his world travels series, familiar talks about countries and peoples, with the author on the spot and the reader at home. The talks rest on three hundred thousand miles of travel over the globe.

Contents walk the far south. Queensland, Sydney, the land of the golden fleece, sheep stations, rabbits and dingoes, and thirsty lands come first. Melbourne, gold diggings, the three school subjects, the first peoples, kangaroos, and Tasmania follow. Then pearl fisheries on a northern island, the crossing to Wellington, the dominion of New Zealand, its women, its working men, its hot-spring country, and its Maori people.
7451-the-countess-of-escarbagnas:
Molière's Countess of Escarbagnas is a comedy of provincial manners, acted before the court at Saint-Germain-en-Laye on December 2, 1671, and at the Palais Royal in July 1672. It was never printed in Molière's lifetime, appearing only in 1682, after his death. Charles Heron Wall's translation gives it in English prose, with introductions and notes.

The persons tell the plot: the Countess herself, her son the Count, the Viscount in love with Julia, and two older suitors, Thibaudier and Harpin, both in love with the Countess. The comedy lies in the gap between the Countess's grand airs, learned at court, and the provincial world she rules. It is a sharp, small Molière, a good picture of French provincial life in his day.
74633-the-poor-count-s-christmas:
Frank Stockton wrote The Poor Count's Christmas, published in book form in 1927 by Frederick Stokes in New York, with pictures by Bensell. Stockton died in 1902, and the tale had lived in magazines before this edition. Its hero is Count Cormo, one of the kindest men in the world. Every day he gave to the poor; at Christmas his goodness shone brightest.

The Count had vowed that every child he knew should be happy on Christmas Day. Each year the neighbourhood children came to his castle for games, feasting, and fun. The pictures promise giants as well: a young giant named Feldar talks with a fairy on his forefinger and forces a castle gate. A procession approaches, and the Count adopts the young giant before the feast ends. Stockton mixes gentle humour with fairy tale, making a Christmas story of generosity.
75380-dimple-dallas:
Dimple Dallas is a girls’ story by Amy Blanchard, billed as the further fortunes of a sweet little maid. Jacobs of Philadelphia copyrighted the book in 1900. Pictures by Ida Waugh go with the tale. Blanchard had written A Sweet Little Maid and A Dear Little Girl before it.

The New Scholar is the title of the first chapter. Changes and trouble with a boy named Donald follow. A new doll, more trouble, and a lost child named Bubbles fill the list. Uncle Heath, shopping, and Christmas come in their turns. A happy new year, a pony, and a May party close the contents. Dimple’s world is school, home, and small storms weathered sweetly. Blanchard wrote whole shelves of such gentle books.
75482-maisie-s-merry-christmas:
Nina Rhoades's Christmas story for girls, drawn by Elizabeth Withington and published at Boston in March 1911, follows the Barton family through a winter abroad. The book opens at the Hotel de Nice, where Maisie startles her mother by wishing there was not going to be any Christmas at all. She is sick of the ocean crossing, of foggy London, of Paris, and of roses in place of snow.

Maisie longs for Morristown, for her grandmother, and for a real Christmas at home. Her parents, her Auntie Belle, and the talk of the Channel crossing frame the opening chapters. The volume also prints two more tales, Jill and Lill and How Reggie Saw the Sphinx, after the Christmas story ends.
75551-reminiscences-of-the-south-seas:
John La Farge, the painter, records his 1890 and 1891 travels in the South Seas in this volume, issued at New York in 1916. Forty-eight pictures from his own paintings and drawings made on the spot fill the book. A prefatory note explains that he meant a continuous narrative but left much in letters to his son Bancel and in his journal. Those materials were drawn on with care after his death.

The contents sail from Honolulu and Hawaii, with the volcano Kilauea, to a long residence at Vaiala in Samoa. Samoan voyages, courtship, and gift-giving fill the middle chapters. Tahiti follows, with the story of the limits of the Tevas and the lament of Aromaiterai. Fiji closes the travels, with the story of the fish-hook war and an expedition into the mountains of Viti Levu.
75654-the-story-of-utopias:
Lewis Mumford's The Story of Utopias, ideal commonwealths and social myths, was published by Harrap in London in 1923, with an introduction by Hendrik Willem van Loon. A saying stands as epigraph: a map of the world that does not include Utopia is not worth glancing at. The chapter heads are written as a story in themselves, each beginning with How.

The story runs from the Greeks, with Plato's Republic asking what will hold the ideal city together, down to Thomas More and the New World. Christianopolis and the new humanism follow; Bacon and Campanella are judged echoes of greater men. The eighteenth century makes men think furiously, and utopias spring from the soil of industrialism. Land schemes, Cabet's Icaria, Bellamy's Looking Backward, and Morris renewing the classic line fill the later chapters, as the will-to-utopia keeps men living in two worlds.
75962-the-freedom-of-the-seas:
The Freedom of the Seas, issued in 1916, gives Hugo Grotius's Mare Liberum in Latin and English on facing pages. Grotius first published the tract in 1608, anonymously, to claim the Dutch right to the East Indian trade. Ralph Van Deman Magoffin translated it, working from the Latin text of 1633. James Brown Scott wrote the introductory note for the Carnegie Endowment.

The timing was pointed. Since August 1914, Scott notes, freedom of the seas had been on every tongue, belligerent and neutral. Here in English for the first time stood the famous argument that made the phrase. Two sets of nearly two hundred footnotes serve the Latin and the English separately. The Oxford University Press printed the book at New York.
76620-mother-s-golden-guineas:
Annette Lyster wrote Mother's Golden Guineas, issued in London by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge with illustrations by F G Kitton. Lyster also wrote Grannie, Faithful, and The White Gipsy. The frontispiece shows Tom eyeing bright coins and thinking one might do.

Twelve chapters follow Tom from Burdeck, where he makes a horseshoe, to sea, where he is pressed into service. Chapters cover Old Gideon, the articles of war, a cutting-out expedition, and Tom's one hundred and fifty guineas. The last chapter is called Better Than Golden Guineas. Readers get a boys' sea story with a moral close, of the improving kind the Society favoured.
76926-florentine-villas:
Janet Ross describes the great houses around Florence in Florentine Villas, issued by Dent in London and Dutton in New York in 1901. Photogravures from Zocchi's etchings and line drawings by Nelly Erichsen fill the book. This printing was limited to 200 copies for England and 100 for America.

Ross dedicates the work to Margaret, Countess of Crawford and Balcarres, herself the owner of a fine Florentine villa. Twenty-three houses appear, from Villa Palmieri and Careggi to Castello, Gamberaia, and Pratolino. Medici names run through the list, with medals of Cosimo and Lorenzo set among the plates. Each chapter pairs a house with its gardens, owners, and past.
77296-a-lady-s-ride-across-spanish-hondu:
Maria Soltera told of her ride across Spanish Honduras in pieces first printed in Blackwood's Magazine, then as a book from William Blackwood and Sons in 1884. She dedicated the record to Archbishop Roger Bede Vaughan of Sydney. Plates show a hacienda near San Antonio and the pass beyond Goascaron.

Chapter one turns on pounds, shillings, and pence. From San Francisco she could sail to Panama and cross the isthmus, risking the Panama fever, or sail to Amapala and ride mules two hundred and nineteen miles to San Pedro Sula. She weighs sea-sickness, thunder, and cost in her Palace Hotel room in June 1881. Comayagua and Maniobar mark the road she took.
77524-jakie-s-christmas:
Lida B Robertson wrote Jakie's Christmas for the Christopher Publishing House at Boston in 1927. Robertson had won prizes for short stories on farm homes and bad boys. A plate shows Jakie dressed as fat old Santa Claus. The dedication praises kindness as a candle in darkness.

Jakie, a happy country boy, lives with his grandmother Mamsy in a log cabin in the Alabama backwoods. His parents and grandfather are dead, and Mamsy keeps a cow, pigs, turkeys, and chickens. Foxes took the young turkeys and hawks the chickens, so Mamsy must tell Jakie not to expect Santa Claus this year. Poverty and a child's hope drive the short Christmas tale.
77567-list-of-post-offices-in-canada-wit:
List of Post Offices in Canada is an official directory printed at Ottawa in 1870. Taylor printed it by order of the Postmaster General. It gives every office and its postmaster as of July 1, 1870. A memorandum asks any postmaster who finds an error in his office's entry to notify the department without delay.

Alexander Campbell heads the department as Postmaster General, with Griffin as his deputy. Inspectors are named by division, from Nova Scotia to London, Ontario. Offices that grant money orders are printed in italics, and savings bank offices carry a star. Abbott's Corners in Missisquoi, with postmaster Charles Hope, leads the alphabetical roll. A table of foreign postage rates is appended.
77668-diminutive-dramas:
Maurice Baring wrote a set of short comic plays that first ran in the Morning Post and were gathered in a book in 1911. Critics praise the ease, irony, and humor of the pieces. Baring invites readers to smile rather than to laugh, and to think while amused.

The first play puts King Henry the Eighth and Catherine Parr at a breakfast table in London. The King cracks a boiled egg, finds it raw, and grumbles that his wife cannot boil an egg as his dear Katie once did. Other plays treat the death of Alexander, Caligula at a picnic, Don Juan in failure, and dinner parties of Calpurnia and Lucullus. Later pieces take up Jason and Medea, King Alfred, and Xantippe with Socrates. Readers get brief, witty scenes that bend great history into drawing-room comedy.
77821-the-man-who-found-christmas:
The Man Who Found Christmas, by Walter Prichard Eaton, was issued at Boston by the Wilde Company, with a frontispiece by Walter King Stone. Eaton wrote also The Idyl of Twin Fires and In Berkshire Fields. A preface prepares the reader: a new generation has come since what is here recorded took place, some twenty years before the telling.

Much has changed, the preface grants. A mighty war has passed, when peace on earth seemed very far away, and the automobile has conspired to change our ways of life and feeling. The story mentions forgotten things: sleighbells. Young people today, Eaton writes, are supposed more sceptical of sentiment than of old, and so more sceptical of Christmas, the feast of sentiment. But young people were sceptical before, and if Christmas proved them wrong then, it can again.
77840-the-seals-and-whales-of-the-britis:
Thomas Southwell studies the great sea mammals in The Seals and Whales of the British Seas, from Jarrold and Sons of London in 1881, with illustrations. His introduction complains that no modern book devoted to the subject exists, though interest in these creatures has grown fast. Records lie scattered in the publications of scientific societies.

Southwell offers instead a cheap, plain, but trustworthy treatise, grown from papers in Science Gossip and brought up to date. New matter treats the claim of the Atlantic right-whale to a place in the British fauna. He hopes the book will help name stranded specimens now lost to science.
78328-the-story-of-life-in-the-seas:
The Story of Life in the Seas is a popular natural history by Hickson, professor of zoology at Owens College, Manchester, published in London in 1898 with forty-two illustrations. An outline classification at the front runs from protozoa through sponges, corals, worms, crustaceans and molluscs up to fish, turtles, birds and whales.

In his preface Hickson admits the sea has too many aspects for one small book. Some readers want the food fishes and whales, others the shapes and colours of shells, others the reef-builders that lay down the ocean bed. He offers instead a sketch of the lines of research zoologists are pursuing, gathering discoveries from books and journals the general reader never sees. The aim is modest and plain: to awaken a new interest in the life of the sea rather than to exhaust any part of it.
78374-little-merry-christmas:
Winifred Arnold wrote a sweet Yule tale of a child called Merry Christmas. The book came out in 1913 in boards at sixty cents. From her first step off the train, one cold night, her tale starts. Oatka Center, with snow in piles, is her new home town. Light and joy trail her into cold homes and cold hearts there.

Lem Perkins, her sour old uncle, heads the frost she must thaw. The whole town is led by a child's hand in Arnold's claim. Peace and good will crown the small realm she wins for them. The tale is called sweet and gay in the house's own brief. Young hearts and old share its warm spell. Brief and bright it runs.
7844-three-dramas:
Bjornstjerne Bjornson's Three Dramas gathers The Editor, The Bankrupt, and The King, plays born when the author's views were changing fast. Two were written during, one just after, three years abroad, spent mostly in southern Europe, after a decade of theater management and political work.

Bjornson had campaigned, with republican leanings, for truer equality between Sweden and Norway, arguing Norway was treated as a mere appendage. His exile restored his imagination and widened it, giving him distance from old orthodoxies. The three plays test press power, money failure, and kingship with new, sharper doubt.
78711-where-the-young-child-was:
Marie Conway Oemler wrote a set of Christmas tales for warm home reads. Her book came out in New York in 1921. George Avison drew its pictures. Oemler wrote Slippy McGee and A Woman Named Smith. Some tales first ran in Harper's Bazar and like sheets.

Where the Young Child Was leads, with a call back to Christmas Eve. The Spirit of the House and The Youngest Officer come next. Linden Goes Home and The Little Brown House fill the mid set. That Makes the World Go Round closes the book's list. Each tale turns on love in the feast's soft light. Oemler's warm hand suits the days well.
78842-a-scheme-there-was:
A Scheme There Was is a western story by W C Tuttle, one of his tales of the whittling sheriff of Mohave Wells. Buck Brady stops whittling to brush the damp lock of roan hair from his forehead. He considers two passengers on the Mohave Wells to Lone Mule stage. The girl does not look over eighteen, with hair the colour of spun gold.

The man with her is under twenty-five and delicate looking, with hair of nearly the same colour. Buck, the sheriff of the county, is tall and lean, with a long face and high cheekbones. He is slow moving and slow of speech, barely thirty-five and looking forty-five. Yet men in the Mohave swear he can draw and shoot faster than a rattler can strike. His obsession is whittling, hour after hour in the shade of his office.
79111-another-ace-for-ananias:
Tuttle wrote a west tale of a crew whose lies are a high art. Chuck Warner tells the tale in the first pages' talk. He ranks truth men George Washington and Telescope as tied. Telescope lacks the gift to lie, Chuck claims with a grin. His mouth goes dry when he tries, and he is caught each time.

Telescope holds he has a clean heart and can sleep sound. He grants he has lied some, but with poor luck at it. Chuck, Henry, and Muley can hang a false sign on him at will. He trusts all men, and that trust is his weak spot. Ananias, the famed liar of old, gives the tale its name. West talk in full twang rules it.
79135-assisting-ananias:
Assisting Ananias is a western story by W C Tuttle. Its narrator sits on a corral fence at the Cross J with two friends. One is Chuck Warner, described as the biggest liar on earth. The other, Magpie Simpkins, studies a Sunday newspaper. The paper carries a page on Ashburton De Puyster, a missing heir.

Ashburton ran away twenty years ago to fight Indians. A fortune of ten million dollars waits for him. Chuck is small, blue-eyed, and about the right age. He dreams of walking up to the family's door and claiming the money. Magpie warns him that proof, not ear-wiggling, wins such pots. Chuck does the arithmetic himself. At forty dollars a month the sum would take him twenty thousand, eight hundred and thirty-three years to earn. The comedy rests on a liar measuring himself against the one story too big to fake.
79300-myths-of-hellas:
Myths of Hellas, or Greek Tales, retells the myths of ancient Greece for children. Professor Witt, headmaster of a gymnasium at Königsberg, told the stories in German, and Frances Younghusband translated them into English with his sanction. Arthur Sidgwick of Oxford supplied a preface, and this fifth edition appeared from Longmans in 1891.

Younghusband dedicated the book to English children, noting that young readers welcome tales of wonder when the language is plain and the moral is not forced. The tales present the gods, heroes, and monsters of Greece in simple narrative form. The book took its place beside Kingsley's Heroes and similar collections, part of the great Victorian effort to put classical story into the hands of the young.
79404-the-international-crisis-in-its-et:
The International Crisis in its Ethical and Psychological Aspects holds six lectures given in February and March 1915 at Bedford College for Women in London. Oxford University Press printed them that year. The speakers were famed names in British thought.

Eleanor M Sidgwick opens on the morality of strife in relation to the war. Gilbert Murray treats herd instinct and the war, and A C Bradley treats world morality and a United States of Europe. L P Jacks writes on the changing mind of a nation at war. G F Stout treats war and hatred, and B Bosanquet treats patriotism in the perfect state. Sidgwick owns she has no special knowledge and speaks as a plain member of the public. Readers get first war thought at a high level.
79517-christie-s-christmas:
Pansy, the pen name of Isabella Alden, tells a family tale in Christie's Christmas, issued by Ward, Lock and Company. The contents promise a first journey, rides in the cars, a baby left in the train, and Christie as housekeeper, with letters and surprises along the way. The gift is owned up to near the close.

Oddly, the planning starts on a hot day in August, under the elm in the Tucker yard. Christie sews a long seam, Karl fans the flies off sleeping Nettie, and talk turns to Uncle Daniel and his ice house. Warm hearts fill this holiday tale.
9068-apu-ollantay-a-drama-of-the-time-of:
Apu Ollantay is an Inca drama set in Peru around 1470, in the days of the Inca kings. It was kept alive in memory by trained reciters, then first written down by Dr. Antonio Valdez, a priest of Sicuani, about 1770. Sir Clements Markham made this free English version in 1910 from a copy of that text.

The play tells of Ollantay, a great general who loves the king's daughter, a love the law forbids. War, prison, and a final act of mercy drive the plot to its close. It stands as the most famous work of Inca theater, a rare voice from a world soon to be broken by conquest.
9969-love-s-final-victory-ultimate-unive:
Horatio, an orthodox minister, argues in this book that love wins in the end: that universal salvation follows from universal atonement, on the basis of Scripture and reason. He opens with a warning from Carlyle against believing what seems incredible, then states his case plainly.

The table of contents weighs different theories of the soul's fate, including the immortality of the soul, against his own hopeful reading. Written as a letter to an eminent Methodist minister in England, the book is earnest and argumentative. Readers interested in theology get a sincere case for hope, made by a minister to his peers.
a-catechism-of-christian-doctrine-no-2-f: Januarius De Concilio presents the second Baltimore catechism for confirmation classes. Like its companion volume, it was ordered by the Third Plenary Council of Baltimore and approved by its bishops. Its questions and answers carry pupils further into doctrine as they prepare for confirmation. The book offers a clear and compact course for classroom and home use.
a-fool-there-was:
A Fool There Was, by Porter Emerson Browne, takes its title and its warning from Kipling's poem The Vampire. Browne prints the famous lines as his frontispiece. A fool made his prayer to a rag and a bone and a hank of hair. He called her his lady fair. The book appeared in 1909, with illustrations by Edmund Magrath and W W Fawcett. Browne dedicates it to Robert Hilliard.

The contents proceed in stately generalities: Of Certain People, Of Certain Other People, Two Boys and a Girl. A child meets a stranger, time passes, and an accident and an incident turn the road. Browne's story follows a strong man ruined by a woman who does not care, the theme Kipling's verses fixed in the period's imagination. The novel became a byword. Its title alone passed into the language for every brilliant fool who prays to his own destruction.
a-little-book-for-christmas: Cyrus Townsend Brady offers a little book for Christmas with greeting, advice, adventures, a carol, and a meditation. Three Christmas stories for all ages complete the volume. Brady, author of Christmas fantasies, writes for the American Criterion Society. The book suits family reading at Christmas time. Families can read the stories aloud by the fire at Christmas.
a-phyllis-of-the-sierras:
Bret Harte opens where the great highway of the Sierras nears the summit and the pines thin into rock and waste. Side paths slip off toward clearings, logslides, and a sawmill half hidden in the forest it is eating. In such a clearing lives the mill owner's family, and his daughter, a Phyllis of the mountains.

An English visitor, in California for his health, is taken in by the family and slowly drawn to the girl, whose direct, woodland ways unsettle his city habits. Harte sets the courtship against mill work, mountain weather, and the father's pride. The tale is one of his gentler Sierra romances, with the forest itself given the largest share of the telling.
a-review-of-the-resources-and-industries: Ithamar Martindale Howell presents this two-year report on the resources and trades of Washington for 1909, put out by order of the lawmakers. Sent to Governor Hay from Olympia in June 1909, the volume surveys the state's trades for free handout by the state's bureau for figures, farming, and new arrivals. Its first plate shows the new capitol to rise on base work already laid at Olympia.
a-second-book-of-operas:
Henry Edward Krehbiel continues his guides for opera listeners with a second book, organized by subject rather than by composer. The first chapter, Biblical Operas, ranges far. It runs from Handel and Rossini's Moses to Samson et Dalila and Goldmark's Queen of Saba. Detours treat censorship by the Lord Chamberlain and composers revamping their own music.

Later chapters treat famous works and their makers in the same anecdotal way, mixing plot, musical comment, backstage history, and sharp personal judgments. Krehbiel was America's leading music critic of his day, and he writes for the newcomer who wants to know what he is hearing and why it matters. The book assumes curiosity, not training.
a-visit-from-saint-nicholas: Clement Clarke Moore gives the night before Christmas in this illustrated edition of A Visit from Saint Nicholas, published at New York in 1862. Drawings by Darley, engraved by Orr, accompany the poem. Stockings hang by the chimney with care, children lie snug dreaming of sugar plums, and mamma in her kerchief and the narrator in his cap settle for a nap. A clatter on the lawn sends him to the window, where moonlight lies on new-fallen snow.
a-wonderful-night-an-interpretation-of-c: James Henry Snowden interprets Christmas in this wonderful night, published by Macmillan in 1919 and decorated by Maud and Miska Petersham. No two nights are alike, the jacket text says. One night stands above all others, the night that heard angels sing above the Birth of Bethlehem. The book treats the events and steps leading to that central wonder in terms of its significance today.
apu-ollantay-a-drama-of-the-time-of-the-: Clements R. Markham gives a free English version of Ollantay, an Inca drama kept alive in memory by Amauta performers until acting was banned after the 1781 rising. The play follows the general Ollantay, his love for a royal princess, and the clash between rank and desire at the Inca court. Markham adds notes on how the text reached writing through Antonio Valdez at Tinto. The result is both a stage story and a record of Quechua drama under colonial rule.
barbara-s-heritage-young-americans-among:
Deristhe L. Hoyt wrote this girls' art novel, issued in a third edition by W. A. Wilde with copyright in 1899. Hoyt, author of The World's Painters, sends young Americans among the old Italian masters. A detail from Titian's Assumption in Venice fronts the book. Barbara, Bettina, Malcom, and their elders cross two oceans to Florence, with Lucile Sherman joining the party.

Lessons in looking alternate with a mild mystery that unfolds to Howard by degrees. A coming-out party, a startling disclosure, and the road to Rome structure the tour. One drive back from Assisi leaves a jealous companion silent while the others praise St. Francis, whose heart overflowed with love to every living creature. Hoyt teaches Renaissance art through a story, as governesses once taught it on the grand tour.
britannica-1911-abel-thomas:
Thomas Abel, better spelled Abell, receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abel, an English priest of unknown birth date, served Queen Catherine and crossed to Charles the Fifth on her divorce business before 1528. Bradwell in Essex was his living on return.

Loyalty to Catherine never broke. His Invicta Veritas of 1533, printed under a false Luneberge mark, answered tracts for Henry's church claims. Six years in prison followed, in the Tower, where a carved bell with an A and his name still shows on the wall. Denial of the royal supremacy brought death at Smithfield in July 1540. Leo the Thirteenth beatified him, the entry closes, and Gillow's dictionary carries the record.
britannica-1911-abraxas:
Abraxas receives an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abraxas, or Abrasax, is a word cut on antique stones used as amulets, called Abraxas stones from it. The Basilidian Gnostics prized the word, if they did not coin its use.

Its Greek letters sum to 365, matching the 365 orders of spirits the sect ranged in ranks below the Supreme Being. Those orders filled 365 heavens, each lower than the last, and the lowest spirits made and govern the earth. The stones often bear a fowl-headed, man-busted figure ending in a serpent's tail. Abraxas in the entry's last line belongs with Abracadabra, its sister charm word.
britannica-1911-abu-nuwas:
Abu Nuwas (about 756-810) was an Arabian poet born in al-Ahwaz, with a Persian mother and a father from Damascus who served as a soldier. He studied at Basra and Kufa under noted scholars, and is said to have spent a year among desert Arabs to purify his language. At Baghdad he enjoyed the favour of the caliphs Harun al-Rashid and al-Amin.

Wine-songs are the heart of his reputation. Genial, cynical, and openly immoral, Abu Nuwas drew on Baghdad's upper-class life and mocked the stiff set form of the qasida. His collected verses, nearly five thousand in one collection, sort into ten headings from wine and hunting to renunciation of the world in his ascetic later days.
britannica-1911-achenbach-andreas:
Andreas Achenbach (born 1815) was a German landscape painter from Cassel who began his training at Dusseldorf under Schadow and at the academy there. Early work followed the pseudo-idealism of the German romantic school. Moving to Munich in 1835 brought him under the stronger influence of Gurlitt, and his talent turned to realism, making him the founder of the German realistic school of landscape.

Judgement in the entry is balanced. His landscapes show too much deliberate picture-making and lack personal temperament, yet he remains a master of technique and a historically important reformer. Fine works hang in Berlin, Munich, Dresden, and other German galleries. His brother Oswald, taught by Andreas, painted glowing colour effects around Naples and Rome.
britannica-1911-adams-thomas:
Thomas Adams (died about 1655) was an English divine. In 1612 he was preacher at Willington in Bedfordshire. Heaven and Earth Reconciled issued from that post. The Devil's Banquet came from there too. Wingrave in Buckinghamshire held him next as vicar. Works poured out in quick succession there. In 1618 he preached at St Gregory's in London. That church stood under St Paul's Cathedral. Sir Henry Montague kept him as observant chaplain.

Praise for his sermons runs very high. Collected in 1629, they placed him first among English preachers. Southey called him the prose Shakespeare of Puritan theologians. He equals Jeremy Taylor in brilliant fancies. He matches Thomas Fuller in wit, the entry says. Ardent Protestantism offended Archbishop Laud, though. That offence hindered his preferment throughout life.
britannica-1911-aeneas:
Aeneas is the famed Trojan hero, son of Anchises and Aphrodite, and a myth entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica weighs his legends. He is one of the great figures of Greek and Roman legendary history. In Homer he stands as the chief bulwark of the Trojans, next to Hector. The gods favour him and step in again and again to save him.

One legend has Aeneas stay in his own land after the fall of Troy. There he founded a new kingdom on the spot. Scholars now hold that tale to be of fairly late origin. The tale of his flight from Troy is later than Homer as well. Virgil set it out in its fullest form in the Aeneid. In that poem Aeneas carries his aged father on his back. He leads his little son Ascanius by the hand, and bears his household gods with him.
britannica-1911-agathias:
Agathias is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a Greek poet and writer of history in the Byzantine age. Born near the year five thirty six, he read law in two great cities. He worked as a court pleader but loved verse more than the bar.

The entry lists his love poems and a ring of short verse he gathered. Friends urged him to write the tale of his own times in prose. His five book tale takes up where a great prior work leaves off. Wars with Goths, Franks, and Persians fill most of its pages. The entry faults his sense but prizes the worth of his facts.
britannica-1911-aird-thomas:
Thomas Aird (1802–1876), a Scottish poet, spent twenty-eight years editing one newspaper and a single year editing another. The long post was the Dumfriesshire and Galloway Herald; the short one, the Edinburgh Weekly Journal. Born at Bowden in Roxburghshire, he had chosen a literary life after Edinburgh University, where Carlyle and James Hogg became his acquaintances.

His first book, Martzoufle, a tragedy with other poems, came out in 1826, and a long tale in verse, The Captive of Fez, followed in 1830. A gathered edition of his poems in 1848 won wide favour. Carlyle praised a healthy breath in them, like mountain air. De Quincey, Lockhart, and Dean Stanley stood among his many literary friends. Aird died at Dumfries in April 1876.
britannica-1911-alcidamas:
Alcidamas of Elaea in Aeolis, a Greek sophist and rhetorician of the fourth century B.C., is noticed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A sophist was a paid teacher of speaking and argument. Alcidamas was the pupil and successor of Gorgias, the famous master of rhetoric. He taught at Athens alongside Isocrates, who became his rival and opponent.

Two speeches survive under his name. One attacks Isocrates and argues that speaking on the spur of the moment beats written speeches. The other puts Odysseus accusing Palamedes of treachery at Troy, though it is generally thought spurious. Alcidamas held that the orator's highest aim was extempore power on any subject whatever. Aristotle criticised his pompous style, crowded with poetic epithets and far-fetched metaphors. His lost Messenian speech declared that all are by nature free.
britannica-1911-angstrom-anders-jonas:
Anders Jonas Ångström (1814–1874) was a Swedish physicist. He was born at Lögdö in Medelpad. Upsala University educated him. He became a docent in physics there in 1839. Practical astronomy drew him to Stockholm Observatory in 1842. He then took a post as observer at Upsala. In 1858 he gained the Upsala chair of physics. He held it until his death in 1874.

Terrestrial magnetism occupied much of his early work. He measured magnetic intensity across Sweden. He also reduced the magnetic data from a world voyage. Heat conduction and spectroscopy formed his main fame. His 1853 optical researches made a key point. An electric spark yields two superposed spectra. One comes from the electrode metal. The other comes from the surrounding gas. His son continued the family science. The younger Ångström devised a pyrheliometer in 1893. That instrument measures the sun's heat.
britannica-1911-ansted-david-thomas:
David Thomas Ansted is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English scholar of rocks born in London in eighteen fourteen. He was schooled at a Cambridge college and won its fellowship in time. A famed teacher there turned his mind to the study of stone.

The entry tells how he held a chair of that study in London for years. He served the chief society of the field as aide and as journal chief. In time the trade side of the work drew most of his hours. He toured mines and lands in Europe as a paid guide on rock wealth. His books range from school texts to guides on isles and water supply.
britannica-1911-antigonus-gonatas:
Antigonus Gonatas, who lived from about 319 to 239 BC, was a king of Macedonia. The 1911 Britannica article says he was the son of Demetrius Poliorcetes. On his father's death in 283 BC he took the royal title. He did not win the throne itself till 276 BC, after four rivals had held it in turn. He then beat back an invasion of the Gauls. He held the land without a rival till 274 BC.

That year Pyrrhus came back from Italy and seized near all of Macedonia. When Pyrrhus marched south, Antigonus won his realm back. A son of Pyrrhus drove him out once more, and once more he returned. The last part of his reign was calm. The piece says he won the love of his people by fair dealing and by care for the arts. Poets, thinkers, and historians thronged his court.
britannica-1911-aquinas-thomas:
Thomas Aquinas, born about 1227 and dead in 1274, was a scholastic philosopher of noble birth. The 1911 Britannica entry links his house to royal lines across Europe by blood. He was born at Roccasecca, his father castle in the Naples territories. School at Monte Cassino and six years at Naples university shaped his youth.

Dominican friars drew him, and at seventeen he took the habit against family will. Only the pope own plea overcame that fierce block by his kin at home. Superiors sent him to the Dominican school at Cologne for higher study. The entry opens the life of the thinker called the Angelic Doctor.
britannica-1911-aras:
Aras is a river of the Caucasus region. Araxes was its ancient name. Xenophon called it the Phasis. It rises south of Erzerum in Turkey. The Bingeul-dagh mountains give it birth. It flows east through Erzerum province. The Pasin plateau lies along its course. Russian Armenia receives it next. It passes between Ararat and Erivan.

The river forms the Russo-Persian frontier. Its course runs about 600 miles. The Zanga is its principal tributary. That stream drains Lake Gokcha by Erivan. The Aras is rapid and muddy. Snowmelt makes crossing it dangerous. In ordinary states it is fordable. It formerly joined the Kura river. In 1897 it changed its lower course. It now runs direct to the Caspian. Artaxata, Armenia's old capital, stood on its island.
britannica-1911-arethas:
Arethas, a Byzantine theological writer and scholar who lived from about 860 to 940, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia and was born at Patrae. He wrote a Greek commentary on the Apocalypse, avowedly based on that of Andrew, his predecessor in the see. Despite his own modest view, the work is no mere compilation.

Arethas drew additions from other sources and took special care in checking his references. His interest was not confined to theology. He filled the margins of his classical texts with many notes, a good number of which survive. He also had several manuscripts copied at his own expense. Among them were a famous codex of Plato and a manuscript of Euclid now at Oxford. Views have differed widely on when Arethas lived.
britannica-1911-aristagoras:
Aristagoras is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a Greek who died in 497 before Christ. He was kin by blood and marriage to Histiaeus. Histiaeus was tyrant of Miletus in that age. While Histiaeus was held at the Persian court, he ruled. He acted as regent of Miletus in his stead. In 500 he urged Persia to join an attack on Naxos.

He fell out with the Persian chief on that drive. That chief warned the isle folk of the attack plan. The drive failed and Persia turned cold on him. A note from Histiaeus then spurred him to revolt. He raised the flag of revolt in Miletus that year. When that revolt failed in full he fled to Thrace. He fell in battle there in the year 497. Aid from Athens for him helped spark a Persian invasion.
britannica-1911-aristobulus-of-paneas:
Aristobulus of Paneas is a short life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Jewish philosopher of the Peripatetic school. He is placed about the year 160 before Christ, and the article holds the middle of the second century most likely. He stood among the earliest of the Jewish Alexandrian thinkers whose aim was to wed Greek philosophy to the Jewish religion and show the two as one.

Only scraps of his work, apparently called Commentaries on the Writings of Moses, survive, quoted by Clement, Eusebius, and other church writers, but they show his object plainly. He strove to prove that the early Greek philosophers had borrowed much from parts of Scripture. He quoted lines from Linus, Orpheus, Musaeus, and others that closely match the Mosaic writings. Those quoted passages, the article states flatly, were plain forgeries.
britannica-1911-arnold-thomas:
Thomas Arnold, an English clergyman who lived from 1795 to 1842, is profiled at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as headmaster of Rugby school. Born at West Cowes on the Isle of Wight, he was the son of a customs officer. His father died in 1801, and his schooling passed to kin and then to schools at Warminster and Winchester.

From Winchester Arnold went to Oxford in 1811 as a scholar of Corpus Christi College. He became a fellow of Oriel in 1815 and stayed there until 1819. Those years went to classics, history, and deep study for ordination. Thucydides and Aristotle were the authors he read with most care. Their hold on his thought lasted all his life. The entry also notes a long, anxious search on points of faith. Once he was sure of the truth of his faith, that sureness held firm and clear.
britannica-1911-arras:
Arras is a city of northern France, chief town of the department of Pas-de-Calais, set on the Scarpe where the Crinchon joins it. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it 20,738 people in 1906 and praises its Flemish-style squares. Tall houses on the Grande and Petite Place stand on columns, forming arcades over the footway.

The town hall of the 1500s overlooks the Petite Place, its belfry rising 240 feet with a fine peal of bells. Vauban's walls are mostly gone, leaving a gateway and the citadel called la Belle Inutile. Oil works, dye works, breweries, and hosiery shops support the town, which also holds a great market for grain. As Nemetacum it was chief town of the Atrebates, and Saint Vaast founded its bishopric about the year 500.
britannica-1911-arundel-thomas:
Thomas Arundel, who lived from 1353 to 1414, was an archbishop of Canterbury. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his rise and fall. He was a son of the earl of Arundel and Warenne. Church posts came fast to a youth of his house.

Arundel became bishop of Ely in 1374, then chancellor of England. He moved to York as archbishop in 1388, then to Canterbury in 1396. He pressed his rights hard and warned London over unpaid tithes. When King Richard struck at the lords appellant in 1397, Arundel fell too. The Commons charged him and a banishment sentence passed. He left for Rome late that year, stripped of his see.
britannica-1911-as:
As is the subject of a measure article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The as was the Roman unit of weight and measure. It was divided into twelve parts called unciae. From that word come both ounce and inch in English. The as really meant any whole thing, which gives the English word ace.

The article gives the as for each kind of measure. For weight it was the pound, for length the foot, and for surface a land unit. It also stood for a whole inheritance in law. An heir to the whole estate was named from it. The as was also a Roman coin, of shifting weight across the ages. The oldest as was a rough bar of mixed metal, stamped with a sheep, ox, or sow. Wars drained the treasury and cut its weight step by step.
britannica-1911-asturias:
Asturias is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes an old province and royal tract in the north of Spain. The Bay of Biscay bounds it on the north, and three realms ring the rest. A new map of Spain gave the tract a fresh name in the last century.

The entry gives a count of more than six hundred thousand souls there. High chains of hills shut the land in on the south in a wall. Snow crowns the top peaks well into the heart of summer each year. Few roads for carts crossed those hills till rail lines came late. A thin strip of moor by the sea holds rich coal beds below.
britannica-1911-athamas:
Athamas, in Greek myth a king in Boeotia, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. He was son of Aeolus, king of Thessaly, in one account. His first wife was Nephele, a cloud goddess. They had two children, Phrixus and Helle.

His second wife Ino raised Dionysus as a girl to save his life. That act drew the wrath of Hera, the entry says. Athamas went mad and slew one of his sons. Ino fled and threw herself into the sea with her other son. Both were later worshipped as sea gods. Athamas fled Boeotia with guilt on him. A sign from an oracle led him to settle in Thessaly, where he wed a third wife.
britannica-1911-athenagoras:
Athenagoras is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a Christian writer of the second century who came from Athens. Little sure is known about his life. The facts rest on a short late note and on the heading of his main work.

The article sets the date of his chief work, an appeal for the Christians, at about the year 177. In that work he answers charges of godlessness and other crimes laid on Christians. He also makes a strong case against the many gods of pagan belief. A second work argues for the rising of the body after death. The text praises his clear style and his use of Plato and older writers.
britannica-1911-atlas:
Atlas, the endurer of Greek myth, is explained in a legend entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a son of the Titan Iapetus and brother of Prometheus. Homer calls him one who knows the depths of the whole sea. He holds the tall pillars that keep heaven and earth apart.

Those pillars were first thought to rest in the sea past the western horizon. As Greek knowledge of the west grew, the name moved to a hill in north west Africa. Later tales made him a king there who was turned to rock by Perseus. Still later he was read as a first astronomer who made the first globe of the heavens. In art he bears the heavens or the globe on his back. A figure of Atlas at the front of map books gave the name atlas to a bound set of maps.
britannica-1911-bache-alexander-dallas:
Bache, Alexander Dallas (1806-1867), was an American physicist, great-grandson of Benjamin Franklin, born at Philadelphia and graduated from West Point in 1825. He taught there, served as an engineers' lieutenant building coast forts, then held the chair of natural philosophy and chemistry at the University of Pennsylvania.

For the future Girard College, Bache spent 1836-1838 studying European schools and published a valued report. In 1843 he became superintendent of the United States coast survey. Winning Congress's strong support, he mapped the whole coast at once through many observing stations under one plan, gathering besides a vast store of magnetic and weather observations. He died at Newport, Rhode Island, in 1867.
britannica-1911-bacon-sir-nicholas:
Bacon, Sir Nicholas (1509-1579), was lord keeper of the great seal under Queen Elizabeth, second son of Robert Bacon of Drinkstone in Suffolk and educated at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge. Called to the bar in 1533, he rose through legal offices and gained estates after the monasteries were dissolved.

Elizabeth's accession in 1558 opened his great period: friendship with Cecil, his brother-in-law, brought him the great seal that December, a knighthood, and a privy council seat. He helped place Matthew Parker at Canterbury and presided over the Lords at Elizabeth's first parliament. Against Cecil he opposed war on France as too costly for poor England, yet favoured closer ties with foreign Protestants against the French and Scottish threat.
britannica-1911-badagas:
Badagas, a name meaning a Telugu man, are a tribe of the Nilgiri Hills in India, probably Dravidian by descent and Hindu of the Saiva sect in religion. They are thought to have moved into the Nilgiris from Mysore about 1600, after the Vijayanagar kingdom broke up.

A farming people, the Badagas are by far the most numerous and wealthy of the hill tribes, numbering 34,178 at the 1901 count. They pay a tribute in grain and other goods to the Todas, their neighbours. Their language is a corrupt form of Kanarese. The entry points readers to Breeks's account of the Nilgiri tribes and the district manual for fuller detail on their life.
britannica-1911-bahamas:
Bahamas, or Lucayos, are an archipelago of the British West Indies strung 630 miles from Florida toward Haiti between Cuba and the open Atlantic. The count runs to 29 islands, 661 cays, and 2,387 rocks, with 5,450 square miles of land and 53,735 people in 1901.

Andros is the largest island group, but New Providence, only eighty-five square miles, holds the capital Nassau and the most people. Shallow seas surround the chain, cut by deep channels: the Florida channel carrying the Gulf Stream, the Providence channels with the deep Tongue of Ocean, and the Old Bahama channel along Cuba. The entry lists the main islands group by group, from the Abacos and Eleuthera down to Mayaguana and Inagua, with Turks and Caicos joined in geography but not in rule.
britannica-1911-baker-thomas:
Baker, Thomas (1656-1740), was an English antiquary. He was born at Lanchester in Durham. His grandfather had defended Newcastle in the civil war. Durham free school educated the boy. St John's College, Cambridge, took him in 1672. A fellowship followed there.

Lord Crew gave Baker the Long-Newton rectory in 1687. A Sedgefield living was meant to follow. Baker refused to read James II's Declaration. That refusal cost him the bishop's favour. When William came, Baker refused the oaths instead. He resigned his living in 1690. St John's sheltered him for years. In 1717 the college deprived him of fellowship. His father's annuity was his whole income. He would not even register that annuity. In his books he signed himself ejected fellow. He left his library to the university.
britannica-1911-ball-thomas:
Thomas Ball (born 1819) was an American sculptor, born at Charlestown, Massachusetts, on 3 June 1819. Son of a house and sign painter, he taught himself portrait painting before turning to sculpture in 1851, starting with a bust of Jenny Lind. At thirty-five he went to Florence to study.

Florence stayed his base for more than thirty years, among a colony of artists that included the Brownings and Hiram Powers. He came home in 1897 to Montclair, New Jersey. The 1911 Britannica entry lists his chief works: the mounted Washington in Boston's Public Garden, called probably his best, statues of Webster and Sumner, and the Lincoln Emancipation group at Washington.
britannica-1911-baltzar-thomas:
Thomas Baltzar (about 1630–1663) was a German violinist, born at Lübeck. He came to England in 1656 and made a great impression on hearers such as John Evelyn and Anthony Wood. Nothing like his playing had been heard in England before, the entry says.

In 1661 Baltzar was made leader of the king's famous band of twenty-four violins. Hard drinking cut his career short within two years, and he died in 1663. The 1911 Britannica entry is short, but it makes one large claim for him. The instrumental music of Henry Purcell, in all likelihood, owes much to the mark Baltzar left on English playing.
britannica-1911-banas:
Banas, or Bunas, is the name of three rivers of India, and the 1911 Britannica entry tells them apart in a few lines. The first is a river of Rajputana. It rises in the Aravalli range in Udaipur, drains the Udaipur valley, and after a course of 300 miles flows into the Chambal.

The second Banas runs in the Shahabad district of Bengal. It forms the drainage channel between the Arrah canal and the Sone canal system, and at last falls into the Gangi nadi. The third rises in the state of Chang Bhakar, in Chota Nagpur in Bengal, and falls into the Sone near Rampur. Nothing more is claimed for any of the three.
britannica-1911-barclay-de-tolly-michael:
Michael Andreas Barclay de Tolly (1761–1818) was a Russian field marshal, born in Livonia and descended from a Scottish family settled in Russia in the 1600s. He entered the Russian army young and served against Turks, Swedes, and Poles, reaching major-general by 1799. At Pultusk and Eylau in the war of 1806 he won high praise and promotion.

His march over the frozen Gulf of Bothnia in 1809, seizing Umeo by surprise, made his name. Minister of war from 1810, he commanded one of the armies against Napoleon in 1812. The 1911 Britannica entry tells how his foreign birth fed attacks on him. Defeat at Smolensk forced him to give up chief command to Kutusov. He served on at Borodino all the same.
britannica-1911-barcochebas:
Barcochebas, also written Bar Kokba, means son of a star. Christian sources give the name to Simeon, leader of the Jewish revolt against Rome under Hadrian, in the years 132 to 135. The name does not appear in the Roman historians. Rabbinic sources call him Bar Coziba, son of deceit, a bitter later verdict on his failure.

Rabbi Aqiba had hailed him as Messiah, reading a prophecy of a star out of Jacob as pointing to him. At first Rome paid the rising little mind. The rebels struck coins in the name of Simeon, prince of Israel, and struck at Christians who would not join. The 1911 Britannica entry follows the Roman gathering of troops, the fall of fortress after fortress, and the end at Bethar.
britannica-1911-barnabas:
Barnabas, in the New Testament, is the surname the apostles gave, according to Acts, to Joseph, a Levite born in Cyprus. Like Paul, he was not one of the Twelve, yet like Paul he came to rank as an apostle. The Greek rendering of his name may be read as son of consolation or son of exhortation.
