The entry opens with a puzzle: no good origin for the name in that sense has yet been offered. A proposal from Bar-Nebo is weighed and found unfit for a Jew and a Levite. The 1911 Britannica entry, a long and learned one, then follows Barnabas through Acts. It traces his travels and work with Paul. It also weighs the comfort-giving sense of his name against the usage of the text.
britannica-1911-barnes-thomas:
Thomas Barnes (about 1785–1841) was a British journalist, born about 1785 and educated at Christ's Hospital and Pembroke College, Cambridge. Coming to London, he joined the famous literary circle of Leigh Hunt, Charles Lamb, and William Hazlitt. In 1817, on Dr Stoddart's retirement, he was appointed editor of The Times.

Barnes held that post until his death on 7 May 1841, when Delane succeeded him. The 1911 Britannica entry is short, and its weight sits in one judgment: Lord Lyndhurst voiced a very widely held opinion when he called Barnes the most powerful man in the country. A quarter-century at the head of the leading newspaper, in an age when editors spoke with that weight, is the whole of his claim on the record.
britannica-1911-barras-paul-francois-nic:
Paul François Nicolas Barras (1755–1829), a French count from a noble family of Provence, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. Born at Fox-Amphoux, he served as a gentleman cadet, sailed for India in 1776, and shared in the defence of Pondicherry before its surrender to the British in 1778. Back in France, he backed the Revolution, sat in the Convention for the Var, and voted for the death of Louis XVI.

Barras helped overthrow Robespierre in 1794, commanded the troops defending the Convention in 1795, and chose Bonaparte as a subordinate for the street fighting that followed. As one of the five Directors ruling France from 1795 to 1799, he took part in the Fructidor coup before Bonaparte overthrew the Directory in 1799 and ended his career. The entry also warns that his memoirs, published in 1895, contain clear errors.
britannica-1911-barrett-lucas:
Lucas Barrett (1837–1862), an English naturalist and geologist born in London, is the subject of a brief 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. In 1855 he joined a dredging trip from the Shetlands toward Norway and beyond the Arctic Circle, then sailed on other cruises to Greenland and Spain. Those voyages built his wide knowledge of where marine life is found, the central theme of his short career.

At Cambridge, Barrett helped Sedgwick in the Woodwardian Museum, gave lectures, found bird bones in the Cambridge Greensand, and drew a geological map of the district. Aged only twenty-two, he became director of the Geological Survey of Jamaica in 1859. There he fixed the age of rocks holding Hippurites fossils, and a new genus was named Barrettia after him. He drowned off Kingston in December 1862, aged twenty-five.
britannica-1911-basin-thomas:
Thomas Basin (1412–1491), a bishop of Lisieux and historian, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born probably at Caudebec in Normandy, he spent a childhood unsettled by the Hundred Years' War, then studied at Paris, Louvain, and Pavia. He attended the Council of Ferrara, became a professor of canon law at Caen, and in 1447 was made bishop of Lisieux. Both Charles VII and Louis XI employed him on public business.

Favour with Louis XI did not last. At the king's request Basin drew up a memorandum on the misery of the people. Yet in 1464 he joined the League of the Public Weal against Louis, who seized his bishopric's revenues. After exile Basin renounced the see at Rome and received the title of archbishop of Caesarea instead. His chief work, a history of Charles VII and Louis XI, is valued but marked by dislike of Louis.
britannica-1911-batangas:
Batangas is a town, port of entry, and capital of Batangas province on Luzon in the Philippine Islands, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands near the Batangas river, about a mile from its mouth on the Gulf of Batangas, and about sixty-five miles south of Manila. Its people numbered 33,131 in 1903. The United States kept a military post there, and the town had fine public buildings and homes.

Trade rests on rich farm land. The province is noted for good soil and hard-working people, and the town is its chief port. Exports are large: rice, fine coffee, cacao, sugar, Indian corn, horses, and cattle. The horses of Batangas are praised as strong and quick. Cotton is grown and woven into cloth by the women of the province. The speech of the place is Tagalog.
britannica-1911-bateson-thomas:
Thomas Bateson, also written Batson or Betson, was an English writer of madrigals in the early 1600s, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He is said to have been organist of Chester cathedral in 1599. He is also thought to have been the first man to take a degree in music at Trinity College, Dublin. Church music by him is known, but the entry makes clear that his fame does not rest on it.

Song for several voices made Bateson's name. A madrigal is a part-song for a small group of singers, sung without instruments. Bateson published a set of madrigals in 1604 and a second set in 1618. Both sets, the entry notes, had been reprinted in recent years before 1911, a sign that singers still valued them. His madrigals give him an important place among the composers of the age of Elizabeth and James. He died in 1630.
britannica-1911-bazas:
Bazas is a town of south-western France in the Gironde, 382 miles south-south-east of Bordeaux by rail. It counted 2,505 people in the town and 4,684 in the commune in 1906. A bishop sat here from at least the early 500s until 1790, and its old cathedral is Gothic work of the 1200s to 1500s.

Bits of the town’s ramparts and several houses of the 1500s still stand. White wine comes from the vineyards round it, and its Bazadais cattle are well known in trade. Bazas, the Roman Cossio, was capital of the Vasates tribe and suffered much bloodshed in the religious wars of the 1500s.
britannica-1911-becket-thomas:
Thomas Becket, the slain archbishop, opens a long life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London about 1118, he was known as Thomas of London. His mother came from Caen and his father from Rouen stock. The father had held high city office, then fell on hard times. Young Thomas learned first with the canons of Merton priory.

Later schooling in London and in Paris shaped the young clerk. At twenty-two he had to earn his bread as a notary. A family friend brought him to Archbishop Theobald's notice soon after. He joined that great household and went to Rome in 1143. At Bologna and Auxerre he took up the study of church law. That bent for law, the entry says, shaped his rise and his fall.
britannica-1911-beckington-thomas:
Beckington, Thomas is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English churchman and statesman of the fifteenth century. Thomas Beckington, also spelled Bekynton, was born near 1390 at Beckington in Somerset and died in 1465. He was schooled at Winchester and at New College, Oxford, then held a string of church posts and became dean of the Arches in 1423.

The article then follows his turn to state work. He went as an envoy to Calais in 1439 and to the count of Armagnac in 1442, while acting as secretary to King Henry the Sixth. On his return in 1443 he was made lord privy seal and bishop of Bath and Wells. The piece ends with his building work at Wells and with the Latin journals of his French missions, which still survive in print.
britannica-1911-belsham-thomas:
Thomas Belsham (1750–1829) was an English Unitarian minister born at Bedford. He was schooled at the dissenting academy at Daventry and taught there as assistant tutor for seven years. After a charge at Worcester he returned as head of Daventry, holding it until 1789.

Belsham gave up that post when he adopted Unitarian beliefs, then helped Joseph Priestley run a short-lived college at Hackney. From 1805 he ministered at the Essex Street chapel until his death. His Review of Wilberforce’s Practical View and his Evidences of Christianity won wide notice, and his rendering of Paul’s Epistles in 1822 is counted his weightiest work. Opponents’ journals still granted his force as a writer.
britannica-1911-belt-thomas:
Thomas Belt (1832–1878) was an English geologist and naturalist born and schooled at Newcastle-on-Tyne. A field club on Tyneside fired his boyhood love of natural history. In 1852 he went to Australia and worked the gold diggings for about eight years, learning ore deposits at first hand.

Belt ran gold mines in Nova Scotia, then in Wales at Dolgelly, where his study of the Lingula Flags rocks became a classic paper. Four years managing mines in Nicaragua produced The Naturalist in Nicaragua in 1874, a book of high merit that also argued for old glaciers there. Later journeys took him to Russia, Siberia and Colorado before his death at Denver.
britannica-1911-benedictus-abbas:
Benedictus Abbas (died 1194) was abbot of Peterborough, whose name clings by chance to the Gesta Henrici Regis Secundi, a prized English chronicle of the 1100s. He first appears in 1174 as chancellor to Archbishop Richard, Becket’s successor. Canterbury made him prior in 1175, and Henry II gave him Peterborough two years later.

As abbot Benedictus built much, ran his house’s money well and gathered a library. He admired Becket deeply and wrote on the martyr’s death and miracles, works that survive in print today. Scholars have shown he did not write the Gesta itself; he only had it copied for Peterborough, though the oldest copy carries his name.
britannica-1911-berchem-nicolaas:
Nicolaas Berchem (1620–1683), also written Berghem, was a Dutch painter born at Haarlem. His father, Pieter Claasz van Haarlem, taught him first, and Van Goyen, Jan Wils and Weenix taught him after. Why he took the name Berchem, in its several spellings, is not known.

Berchem produced an immense number of pictures, and his etchings and drawings were in great demand beside them. His landscapes win the highest praise in the entry, and many were finely engraved by John Visscher. His best canvases hang in the Amsterdam Museum and in the Hermitage at St Petersburg. The note is short: teachers, output, the esteem of his landscapes, and where the finest of them live.
britannica-1911-berenger-alphonse-marie-:
Alphonse Berenger, known as Berenger de la Drome, was a French lawyer and man of state. He was born at Valence in seventeen eighty five, son of a deputy of Dauphine. He entered the magistracy and became chief prosecutor at Grenoble in his career. He resigned that office on the restoration of the Bourbons in France. He then gave himself mainly to the study of criminal law.

In eighteen eighteen Berenger published a book on criminal justice in France. With great courage he attacked the special courts set up by the Reaction. Those courts, or military panels, were the chief tools of that regime. He urged a return to the old common law and to trial by jury. The book did much to discredit the policy of the state at the time. In eighteen twenty eight he was elected to the chamber of deputies.
britannica-1911-berhampur-madras:
Berhampur is a town of British India in the presidency of Madras, headquarters of the Ganjam district. It stands about nine miles from the sea and counted 25,729 people in 1901. The East Coast railway, linking Calcutta with Madras, stops there.

The town once held a military cantonment, sometimes called Baupur, with a wing of a native regiment, but the troops have been moved away. Silk cloth weaving is carried on in Berhampur, and sugar goes out in trade, with sugar-making among its industries. Its college, founded by government, is now kept up by the raja of Kallikota. The entry is a short district record: seat, station, lost garrison, silk and sugar.
britannica-1911-bermudas:
The Bermudas form a British colony of small islands and reefs in the Atlantic Ocean. They lie about 580 miles east by south of Cape Hatteras. The 1911 Britannica article describes an oval group 22 miles long. Its total area is only 20 square miles. Great Bermuda, called the Main Island, is the largest member. Islets thickly stud the Great Sound.

The article works through the geology of the islands in detail. Their rock is wind-blown limestone made of crushed shells. Climate, history, and settlement also get full treatment. A long list of authorities closes the piece. They range from Agassiz and Verrill on geology to Lefroy on discovery and settlement.
britannica-1911-bernard-sir-thomas:
Sir Thomas Bernard (1750–1818) was an English social reformer. He was the younger son of Sir Francis Bernard, governor of Massachusetts Bay. He was educated partly at Harvard. As a young man he served as his father's confidential secretary. That was during the troubles before the American revolt. He then practised in England as a conveyancer. A rich marriage let him give his time to the poor.

The 1911 Britannica entry lists his foundations one by one. In 1796 he helped set up the Society for Bettering the Condition of the Poor. A school for the indigent blind followed in 1800, and a fever institution in 1801. He promoted vaccination and fought the salt duties. With Count Rumford he also helped found the Royal Institution.
britannica-1911-best-william-thomas:
William Thomas Best (1826–1897) was an English organist, born at Carlisle, son of a solicitor. He chose music as his career and learned first from the cathedral organist. He gave special study to the works of Bach. Posts followed at Liverpool chapels and the Liverpool Philharmonic Society. A short London spell came in 1854 and 1855. In 1855 he returned to Liverpool as organist of St George's Hall.

His playing there soon became famous across England, the 1911 Britannica entry says. He played solo organ at all the Handel festivals at the Crystal Palace. He also inaugurated the great Albert Hall organ in 1871. Ill health forced his retirement in 1894. His recital series covered the whole field of organ music, old and new. His own Organ Pieces for Church Use show a strong, marked character.
britannica-1911-betterton-thomas:
Thomas Betterton, an English actor who lived from about 1635 to 1710, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Son of an under cook to Charles the First, he was born in London and trained as a bookseller's boy. He first stepped on stage in 1660, when the Cockpit theatre reopened. His gifts won him lead parts at once.

In 1661 Davenant took him to the new theatre in Lincoln's Inn Fields. Charles the Second sent him to Paris to study stage craft, and his return brought shifting scenes to the English stage. Ruined by a bad venture in 1692, he built a new playhouse and opened it in 1695. Age and gout drove him from the stage. Pepys, Pope, and Steele all praised his art, and his clean life stood out in a loose age.
britannica-1911-biddle-nicholas:
Nicholas Biddle (1786–1844) was an American financier, born in Philadelphia. He graduated at Princeton with high honours in 1801. From 1804 to 1807 he served as secretary to envoys in Paris and London. Back home he practised law and edited Dennie's Portfolio magazine. He prepared the History of the Lewis and Clark Expedition for the press in 1814. That work used the explorers' own journals.

Biddle sat in the Pennsylvania legislature in the 1810s. In 1819 Monroe made him a government director of the Bank of the United States. He became the bank's president in 1823, replacing Langdon Cheves. The 1911 Britannica entry centres on that bank administration. It points readers to Catterall's 1903 history of the Second Bank for the best account. A note on his nephew Charles closes the article.
britannica-1911-billaud-varenne-jacques-:
Jacques Nicolas Billaud-Varenne (1756–1819) was a French revolutionist, son of a Paris parlement lawyer. His upbringing was poor, under a weak father, a religious but immoral mother, and a libertine abbé. At nineteen he joined the Oratorians without taking vows. He left their college in 1785, married, and bought a lawyer's post in Paris. In 1789 he printed a three-volume attack on ministerial despotism at Amsterdam.

At the Jacobin Club he became one of the most violent anti-royalist speakers. After the king's flight to Varennes he demanded a federal republic in print. The 1911 Britannica entry follows his rise in the Convention and the Terror years. It then tracks his fall, deportation to Guiana, and flight to Haiti in 1816. He died of dysentery at Port-au-Prince. Memoirs printed under his name in 1821 are judged probable forgeries.
britannica-1911-binney-thomas:
Thomas Binney (1798–1874) was an English Congregationalist divine, born at Newcastle-on-Tyne of Presbyterian parents. He had only ordinary day schooling as a boy. He spent seven years working for a bookseller, then trained at Wymondley theological school. Short pastorates at Bedford and Newport came first. In 1829 he accepted the call to the historic Weigh House chapel in London. There his preaching drew crowds too big for the building.

A much larger chapel rose on Fish Street Hill, and the congregation moved in 1834. His foundation address attacked the state church's influence and sparked a long, bitter dispute. The 1911 Britannica entry defends his breadth of view against narrow labels. He wrote devotional verse, including the hymn Eternal Light! Eternal Light! His lecture book for young men sold 30,000 copies in a year. He died in February 1874 after months of suffering.
britannica-1911-birch-thomas:
Thomas Birch (1705–1766) was an English historian, born at Clerkenwell in London. His father made coffee mills for a living. The boy preferred study to trade, but his Quaker parents kept him from university. Even so he was ordained deacon in 1730 and priest in 1731. As a firm Whig he won the favour of Philip Yorke, the future Earl of Hardwicke. That friendship drove most of his later church preferments in several counties.

He joined the Society of Antiquaries in 1735 and the Royal Society soon after. He served the Royal Society as secretary from 1752 to 1765. The 1911 Britannica entry lists his many lives and memoirs, from state papers to a history of the Royal Society itself. A fall from his horse killed him in January 1766. He left his books and manuscripts to the British Museum. About £500 of his money raised the assistant librarians' pay there.
britannica-1911-blacklock-thomas:
Thomas Blacklock (1721–1791) was a Scottish poet who lost his sight to smallpox before he was six months old. Born at Annan in Dumfriesshire, the son of a bricklayer, he still gained schooling at Edinburgh and studied divinity at the university there. Friends who saw his early poems helped arrange that schooling.

His first volume of Poems came out in 1746, and in 1754 he became deputy librarian for the Faculty of Advocates through Hume's kindness. He later broke with Hume and backed Beattie's attack on him. Blacklock was also an early friend of Burns in Edinburgh and one of the first to see his gift. Ordained at Kirkcudbright in 1762, he soon resigned the post.
britannica-1911-blackwell-thomas:
Thomas Blackwell (1701–1757) was a Scottish scholar of Greek and Roman writing, based at Marischal College in Aberdeen. Born in Aberdeen, he took his master's degree there in 1718, became professor of Greek in 1723, and served as principal from 1748 until his death. He is credited with restoring Greek study in the north of Scotland.

His chief book, An Inquiry into the Life and Writings of Homer (1735), tried to explain why Homer stood above all poets before and after him. Letters Concerning Mythology followed in 1748, and Memoirs of the Court of Augustus came out in three volumes from 1753. The entry praises his learning and fresh thought but faults his weak order and many side paths.
britannica-1911-bodley-sir-thomas:
Sir Thomas Bodley, an English envoy and scholar who lived from 1545 to 1613, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He is famed as the founder of the Bodleian Library at Oxford. He was born at Exeter, but his father fled England under Queen Mary for his Protestant faith. The boy studied for a time at Geneva, where Calvin and Beza taught.

On Elizabeth's accession the family came home, and Bodley entered Magdalen College, Oxford. He took his first degree in 1563 and became a fellow of Merton College. He lectured on Greek and on natural philosophy, and served as proctor in 1569. After a tour of Europe he became a gentleman usher to Queen Elizabeth. He sat in Parliament for Portsmouth in 1584. The queen then sent him on missions abroad, to Denmark, France, and the Hague, where Spanish power had to be faced.
britannica-1911-boileau-despreaux-nicola:
Nicolas Boileau-Despréaux (1636–1711) was a French poet and critic who set the rules for classical verse in France. Born in Paris, the fifteenth child of a parlement clerk, he lost his mother at two and grew up delicate and ill-cared for. Sainte-Beuve is quoted blaming those years for his hard, unsparing outlook.

He studied theology at the Sorbonne, switched to law, and was called to the bar in 1656, but soon quit practice for letters. His ruling passion, the entry says, was hatred of stupid books. The Satires, the mock-epic Lutrin, and above all the Art poétique made his fame, and he rose to be royal historiographer. Later pages judge his grip on French taste and list the many editions of his works.
britannica-1911-bolas:
Bolas are a hunting and war weapon of South American Indians, made of stone balls tied to the ends of a hide or hemp rope. The entry quotes Charles Darwin's account from the Voyage of the Beagle. In the simple kind, two leather-covered stones are joined by a plaited thong about 8 feet long.

A second kind has three balls tied to a common centre. The rider holds the smallest ball, whirls the other two round his head, and throws. The balls fly like chain shot, wrap round the target, and cross and hitch fast. Gauchos used them on the pampas for centuries, chiefly to catch ostriches. The Eskimo use a like tool for birds, and Ratzel is cited calling the bolas a form of lasso.
britannica-1911-booth-edwin-thomas:
Edwin Thomas Booth (1833–1893) was an American tragedian. He was the second son of the actor Junius Brutus Booth. The entry gives half its space to the father. He was a London-born rival of Kean, famed for Richard III, Hamlet, Lear, and Shylock. His fits of fury on stage sometimes put fellow actors in real danger as they fenced.

Edwin first acted in earnest at the Boston Museum on 10 September 1849. He played Tressel to his father's Richard. He is drawn as lithe and graceful, with dark curling hair and soft, shining eyes. The later pages follow his rise to lead the American stage. They cover his playing in London and his own theatre in New York. They tell of the shadow cast by his brother's murder of President Lincoln. His farewell years close the account.
britannica-1911-boras:
Borås is a manufacturing town in the Elfsborg district of Sweden, 45 miles east of Gothenburg by rail, standing on the river Viske. It was founded in 1632 by King Gustavus Adolphus. Its growth was swift in the late 1800s, from 4723 people in 1880 to 15,837 in 1900.

By the entry's measure it stood among the first twelve towns of Sweden both for people and for the value of its factory output. Cotton work rules the place: many spinning and weaving mills are noted, and a technical weaving school trained hands for them. The short entry gives little beyond site, size, founding, and this one great trade, which explains the town's rise from a small market place to a mill centre.
britannica-1911-boreas:
Boreas, in Greek myth, is the north wind made a god. He was son of Astraeus and Eos, brother of Hesperus, Notus, and Zephyrus, and his home was Mount Haemus in Thrace, or Salmydessus near the Hyperboreans. His famous act was a seizure, not a courtship.

Having wooed Oreithyia, daughter of King Erechtheus of Athens, in vain, he carried her off as she danced at a festival or picked flowers by the Ilissus. On Mount Haemus they lived as king and queen of the winds, with sons Zetes and Calaïs and daughters Cleopatra and Chione. Athens later counted on his friendship, crediting his storms with wrecking Persian fleets at Athos and Sepias, and built him an altar by the Ilissus with a yearly festival, the Boreasmos.
britannica-1911-boudinot-elias:
Elias Boudinot (1740–1821) was an American revolutionary leader who presided over the Continental Congress. Born at Philadelphia of Huguenot descent, he studied law in Richard Stockton's office at Princeton, married Stockton's sister Hannah in 1762, and was licensed in 1760 to practise at Elizabethtown, New Jersey. He sided with the conservative Whigs as war approached.

He sat in the New Jersey provincial congress in 1775 and served as commissary-general of prisoners, with a colonel's rank, from 1777 to 1778. In Congress in 1778 and again from 1781 to 1783, he was its president from November 1782 to October 1783, briefly acting as secretary for foreign affairs as well. He sat in the House of Representatives from 1789 to 1795 and directed the United States mint from 1795 to 1805. In 1816 he helped found the American Bible Society and became its first president.
britannica-1911-bouilly-jean-nicolas:
Jean Nicolas Bouilly (1763–1842) was a French playwright and story writer whose Léonore stands behind Beethoven's Fidelio. Born near Tours, he held office under the revolutionary government and had a large share in organising primary schooling. In 1799 he retired from public life to write full time.

His works include the musical comedy Pierre le Grand (1790) for Grétry and the opera Les Deux Journées (1800) with music by Cherubini, besides L'Abbé de l'épée and other plays. For young and old readers he wrote Causeries d'un vieillard (1807), Contes à ma fille (1809), and Les Adieux du vieux conteur (1835). His Léonore of 1798, a tale of a wife rescuing her husband, formed the basis of the Fidelio libretto. He died in Paris in 1842.
britannica-1911-brock-thomas:
Thomas Brock (born 1847) was an English sculptor, chief pupil of Foley and later touched by the new romantic movement in art. His group The Moment of Peril came first in the list of ideal works, followed by The Genius of Poetry and Eve, pieces that mark how his art grew. Portrait work in marble and bronze fills much of the notice.

Busts of Lord Leighton and Queen Victoria, statues of Sir Richard Owen and Dr Philpott, bishop of Worcester. Memorial statues of Queen Victoria at Hove and elsewhere show his power as a portraitist, praised as sympathetic in feeling and sound and restrained in execution. His tomb for Lord Leighton in St Paul's cathedral earns special praise for refinement and beauty. In 1901 his colossal horseman of Edward the Black Prince went up in Leeds.
britannica-1911-bromley-sir-thomas:
Sir Thomas Bromley (1530–1587) was an English lord chancellor born in Staffordshire in 1530. Educated at Oxford and called to the bar at the Middle Temple, he rose fast through family influence and the patronage of Sir Nicholas Bacon, the lord keeper. Recorder of London in 1566 and solicitor-general in 1569, he sat in Parliament for Bridgnorth, Wigan and Guildford in turn.

On Bacon's death in 1579 he became lord chancellor. As an equity judge he showed great and deep knowledge, and his judgment in Shelley's case stands as a landmark in the history of English real property law. He presided over the commission that tried Mary, queen of Scots, in 1586. The strain of that trial and the weight of her execution broke his strength, and he died on 12 April 1587. He was buried in Westminster Abbey.
britannica-1911-browne-sir-thomas:
Sir Thomas Browne (1605–1682) was an English author and physician born in London on 19 October 1605. He entered Winchester school as a scholar in 1616 and Broadgates Hall, Oxford, in 1623, graduating in January 1626. A master's degree followed in 1629, then medical study and practice in Oxfordshire before years of travel redrew his course.

Between 1630 and 1633 he travelled in Ireland, France and Italy and took his medical degree at Leiden on the way home. Back in London in 1634, he settled in practice at Norwich in 1637 and married Dorothy Mileham in 1641. Their eldest son Edward became president of the Royal College of Physicians. In 1642 his Religio Medici, a private exercise directed to himself, was printed from a manuscript copy without his knowledge, drawing Sir Kenelm Digby's Observations. The stir forced Browne to issue a correct version in 1643, the episode the entry tells at length.
britannica-1911-buckle-henry-thomas:
Henry Thomas Buckle (1821–1862) was an English historian. He wrote the famous History of Civilization. This 1911 Britannica biography tells his story. He was born at Lee, in Kent, on 24 November 1821. His father was a wealthy London merchant. Weak health kept the boy from school. He read widely at home instead. Before he was twenty he ranked among the world's best chess players.

After his father's death in 1840, Buckle formed a vast plan. He would give all his reading to one great work. He worked ten hours a day for seventeen years. At first he planned a history of the middle ages. By 1851 he had chosen a history of civilization instead. The first volume appeared in June 1857. It made him a sudden celebrity in London. His mother's death in 1859 crushed him deeply. The entry follows his grief and his last years.
britannica-1911-bunsen-christian-charles:
Christian Charles Josias Bunsen, a Prussian envoy and scholar who lived from 1791 to 1860, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Korbach in the small state of Waldeck. His father was a farmer whom want drove to serve as a soldier. Bunsen studied at the town school and at Marburg.

At the age of nineteen he went on to Göttingen. He kept himself there by teaching and by work as tutor to a rich American. In 1812 he won the university prize for an essay on the law of inheritance at Athens. That early win set the twin course of his life. Learning and state service ran side by side for the rest of his career, the entry shows.
britannica-1911-burgess-thomas:
Thomas Burgess lived from 1756 to 1837 and was an English divine. The 1911 Britannica life opens at Odiham in Hampshire, his birth town. He was schooled at Winchester and at Corpus Christi College, Oxford. Before his degree he had already edited a reprint of Burton. In 1781 he put out an annotated work of Richard Dawes.

In 1783 he became a fellow of his college at Oxford. Two years later he was chaplain to the bishop of Salisbury. In 1788 he wrote in favour of a slow end to slavery. He urged that freedom for the enslaved should come by steps. In 1803 he was appointed bishop of St David's in Wales.
britannica-1911-campion-thomas:
Thomas Campion, an English poet and musician who lived from 1567 to 1620, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in London in February 1567. His father was a legal clerk of the Middle Temple. Orphaned young, he was raised by a stepfather who sent him to Cambridge in 1581.

Campion studied four years at Peterhouse and left without a degree. Classical letters, met there, shaped all his later work. He entered Gray's Inn in 1587, seemingly bound for the law. He had little love for legal study and was never called to the bar. In 1591 he seems to have sailed with an English force sent to aid the French king. By 1606 he appears with a doctor's degree in physic, from a place unknown. The rest of his life was given to verse and music.
britannica-1911-candlemas:
Candlemas, the church feast held each year on the second of February, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica rite entry. The feast marks the day Christ was shown in the Temple as a child. In the Greek Church it is called the Meeting of the Lord. In the West it is named for the cleansing of the Virgin Mary. It ranks as the old feast of Mary known to the church.

A walk tale from the fourth century shows the feast kept at Jerusalem then. It first fell in mid February, forty days past Epiphany. When Christmas was fixed, the feast moved to the start of February. Blessings of candles for the year gave the feast its English name. That rite spread late, in the eleventh century.
britannica-1911-caracas:
Caracas is the capital of the United States of Venezuela. It is the principal city of that republic. This long 1911 Britannica article describes it fully. It stands in an elevated valley of the Coast Range. The plain of Chacao stretches about 11 miles long. La Guaira, its port, lies 6.5 miles north-north-west on the coast. The city stands from 2887 to 3442 feet above the sea.

The Guaira river flows past the city on the south. Small streams run down through the streets from the north. North-east rises the Silla de Caracas, a twin-peaked mountain. Its summits reach 8622 feet, like a giant saddle. The Naiguatá peak stands still higher, at 9186 feet. The climate is often called one of perpetual spring. Yet it swings fast between extremes of temperature. The article covers streets, buildings, trade and history. It gives the city's growth and its place in the republic.
britannica-1911-caravellas:
Caravellas is a small seaport of southern Bahia, in Brazil. It stands on the Caravellas river, near its mouth. The river mouth is dangerously blocked by sandbars. This short 1911 Britannica entry gives the port's state. Its municipality held 5482 people in 1890. About half of them lived in the town itself. The rest were spread through the surrounding district.

Caravellas was once the centre of a busy whale fishery. That trade has since fallen into decay. The town is now the port of a railway. The Bahia & Minas railway ends at its wharves. The entry calls that line's traffic comparatively unimportant. The whole notice is a few lines long. It gives the site, the sandbars and the lost fishery. It leaves the port as a small, quiet place.
britannica-1911-carew-thomas:
Thomas Carew (1595–1645?) was an English poet of the Caroline court. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his life. He was the son of Sir Matthew Carew, a master in chancery. He was born at West Wickham, in Kent, early in 1595. At thirteen he matriculated at Merton College, Oxford. He took his degree early in 1611. He then studied law at the Middle Temple.

His father complained that he did little at the law. Carew was sent to Italy in an ambassador's household. He served Sir Dudley Carleton at Venice and the Hague. In 1616 he was dismissed for levity and slander. Finding new work proved hard for the young man. After his father's death in 1618 he joined Lord Herbert's train. He travelled with Herbert's embassies in France until 1624. The article follows his later career as a court poet.
britannica-1911-carte-thomas:
Thomas Carte (1686–1754) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English historian born at Dusmoon, near Clifton, and educated at Oxford. He first won notice in a controversy with Dr Henry Chandler over the Irish massacre, where he defended Charles I. His loyalty to the Stuarts kept him a non-juror. When the Atterbury plot came to light he fled to France, having served as Atterbury's secretary.

In France he gathered materials later bought and published by Dr Mead, and Queen Caroline's influence recalled him to England. His General History of England began appearing in 1747, and the entry values it for its vast, careful store of facts. But his claim that the Pretender had cured the king's evil cost him most of his patrons. He published four volumes by 1755 and a life of the duke of Ormond. His papers passed to Oxford.
britannica-1911-cartwright-thomas:
Thomas Cartwright (c. 1535–1603) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English Puritan divine born in Hertfordshire. He studied divinity at St John's College, Cambridge, but Mary's accession forced him out of the university, and he worked as a clerk to a counsellor at law. Under Elizabeth he returned, took fellowships at St John's and then Trinity, and popular service as chaplain to the archbishop of Armagh followed.

In 1569 Cartwright became Lady Margaret professor of divinity at Cambridge. From that chair he attacked the hierarchy and constitution of the Anglican Church, comparing them unfavourably with the primitive church. John Whitgift, as vice chancellor and master of Trinity, stripped him of the post in 1570 and of his fellowship in 1571. The struggle grew so sharp that Chancellor William Cecil had to step in. Cartwright then visited Beza at Geneva and returned to England in 1572.
britannica-1911-cautley-sir-proby-thomas:
Sir Proby Thomas Cautley (1802–1871) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English engineer and palaeontologist born in Suffolk. He joined the Bengal artillery in 1819 and later took charge of the rebuilt Doab canal for twelve years, from 1831 to 1843. In 1840 he reported on the proposed Ganges canal, meant to irrigate the country between the Ganges, Hindan, and Jumna rivers. That project became his most important work.

The Ganges canal was sanctioned in 1841, but work began only in 1843, and Lord Ellenborough's opposition hampered it. Ill health kept Cautley in England from 1845 to 1848. On his return he became director of canals in the North Western Provinces. The canal opened in 1854, and he then went home, was made a knight commander of the Bath, and sat on the council of India from 1858 to 1868. He also published studies, some with Dr Hugh Falconer, on the fossils of the Sivalik Hills.
britannica-1911-chamfort-sebastien-roch-:
Chamfort, Sebastien Roch Nicolas is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a French man of letters. Born in a village near Clermont in Auvergne in 1741, the son of a grocer, he won a bursary to a Paris college. He took the dress of a minor cleric but refused to become a priest, saying he loved honour, not honours. About this time he took the name of Chamfort.

The article follows a career built on wit. He lived by teaching and hack writing until his looks and ready talk brought him notice. A comedy in 1764 had some success, and in 1769 he won the French Academy prize for a eulogy of Molière. The article tells of years lived on friends' hospitality and a brief spell at court given up after a year.
britannica-1911-charles-thomas:
Welsh Nonconformist divine Thomas Charles, born at Longmoor in seventeen fifty five, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born of humble parentage near Saint Clears in Carmarthenshire. He was educated for the Anglican ministry at several schools, and at Jesus College, Oxford.

In seventeen seventy seven he studied theology under the evangelical John Newton at Olney. He was ordained deacon in seventeen seventy eight and priest in seventeen eighty. He added charge after charge in Somerset over the next years. Yet in June seventeen eighty three he resigned all his posts and returned to Wales. There he wed the orphan daughter of a flourishing shopkeeper. He had fallen early under the sway of the great revival movement in Wales. At seventeen he had been converted by a sermon.
britannica-1911-charondas: Charondas was a famed lawgiver of Catina in Sicily, covered in a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His date is unsure, though he clearly lived before Anaxilaus of Rhegium, since that tyrant later abolished his laws. His laws, first written in verse, were taken up by other Chalcidic colonies in Sicily and Italy. Aristotle found nothing special in them except that Charondas introduced actions for perjury, but praised how precisely they were drawn.
britannica-1911-chilas:
Chilas is a hill village in the North-West Frontier Province of India, dominated by a fort on the left bank of the Indus. The fort stands about 50 miles below Bunji and 4,100 feet above sea level. A British force occupied the place early in 1893, and a determined attack followed at once. Kohistanis from the Indus valley districts to the south-west made that attack, aided by men from Darel and Tangir.

Position gives Chilas its importance, since it flanks the Kashmir to Gilgit route by way of Astor. A metalled road now joins it to Bunji, the entry notes. It also commands a much shorter and more direct route to Gilgit from the Punjab frontier than the Kashmir road. By the Kashmir route Gilgit is 400 miles from the rail head at Rawalpindi, while the Kagan route would cut 100 miles, though unsettled country bars its general use.
britannica-1911-chippendale-thomas:
Thomas Chippendale (died 1779), the most famous of English cabinetmakers, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry warns that the facts of his life are very scant. He was the son of a cabinetmaker and wood carver of good name in Worcester. His father may have first shaped some of the forms that later marked the son's style.

The article points to chairs and settees made at Worcester when the great maker was still a boy. They match much of what the family works turned out as late as the seventeen-sixties. Traits of the early Georgian taste sit side by side with the laced splats of the Chippendale style. By 1727 father and son had moved to London, where the son's name was made.
britannica-1911-chodowiecki-daniel-nicol:
Daniel Nicolas Chodowiecki, a German painter and engraver of Polish descent, was born at Danzig in seventeen twenty six. Left an orphan young, he took up miniature painting to support himself and his mother. His father had taught him the first steps of that art. In seventeen forty three he went to Berlin. There he worked as a clerk in an uncle's office while painting in his free hours.

Chodowiecki won a name for miniatures painted for snuff boxes. The Berlin Academy gave him its yearly almanac to illustrate. A set of miniatures on the life of Jesus made him famed at once. He then gave up all work save painting and engraving. For some years few books came out in Prussia without his plates. A Berlin list of his works holds more than three thousand items.
britannica-1911-christmas:
Christmas, the feast of the birth of Jesus Christ, is the subject of a study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word means the Mass of Christ. The piece warns that its tale is bound tight to that of Epiphany. The great Church took up Christmas much later than that older feast.

Before the fifth century, no one date for the feast had won wide assent. Some kept the sixth of January, some the twenty-fifth of March, some the twenty-fifth of December. The first tie of that last date to the birth of Christ rests on a weak quote from an early writer. A firmer note of the date comes in a list of feasts from the year 354. Origen, as late as 245, called the very idea of a birthday feast for Christ a sin.
britannica-1911-churchyard-thomas:
Churchyard, Thomas (c. 1520–1604) was an English author, born at Shrewsbury about 1520, the son of a farmer who gave him a good education. After wasting his father's money at court he entered the household of Henry Howard, earl of Surrey, for four years. There he learned something of poetry from his patron, and some early poems may date from that time. In 1541 he began a long career as a soldier of fortune.

For thirty years he fought through nearly every campaign in Scotland and the Low Countries, serving Charles V in Flanders. He fought at Pinkie in 1547 and escaped after capture at Saint Monance. Later service took him to Ireland, the siege of Metz and Antwerp, where a rising forced him to flee in priest's disguise. His most popular poem, Shore's Wife, appeared in the Mirror for Magistrates in 1563.
britannica-1911-clanvowe-sir-thomas:
Clanvowe, Sir Thomas was an English poet whose name entered literary history only in 1896, when F S Ellis edited The Book of Cupid for the Kelmscott Press. Professor Skeat had found the author's name, Clanvowe, at the end of the best manuscript of that poem. The Cuckoo and the Nightingale had been printed by Thynne in 1532 as Chaucer's work. Successive editors kept that error for three centuries, linking Chaucer wrongly with Woodstock.

Skeat placed the poem's making in spring 1403, three years after Chaucer's death, since its queen can only be Joan of Navarre. Clanvowe, of a Herefordshire family near Wigmore, moved in the courts of Richard II and Henry IV and is said to have been a friend of Prince Hal. He was one of twenty-five knights who sailed to Barbary with John Beaufort in 1390. His poem shows a closer study of Chaucer's prosody than Occleve or Lydgate achieved.
britannica-1911-clarkson-thomas:
Thomas Clarkson is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article as a leader in the fight to end the slave trade. The entry tells how a head, or essay subject, on slavery moved him so deeply that he gave up a plan to enter the church. He chose instead to give all his strength to the cause of abolition.

His first step was to publish an English version of his prize essay, with additions, in June 1786. He then searched everywhere for facts about slavery. A group of twelve men formed a committee in May 1787 to work for abolition. Clarkson travelled from port to port gathering a large mass of proof. Much of it went into his tracts, and leading statesmen of the day looked kindly on the movement.
britannica-1911-cleynaerts-nicolas:
Cleynaerts, Nicolas (1495–1542) was a Belgian grammarian and traveller, born at Diest in Brabant on 5 December 1495 and educated at Louvain. He became a professor of Latin there, teaching it by a conversational method of his own. Manuals of Greek and Hebrew grammar followed, meant to simplify the difficulties of learners. His principle, revived in modern teaching, was that elaborate rules should wait until the learner has a working acquaintance with the language.

A desire to read the Koran led him to link Hebrew with Arabic and to plan peaceful missions to the Arabs through language study. He taught Greek at Salamanca, tutored Don Henry at the Portuguese court, and learned Arabic at Granada with a Moorish slave's help. In 1540 he set out for Africa and reached Fez, then a flourishing seat of Arab learning. Fifteen months of privation forced his return, and he died at Granada in autumn 1542.
britannica-1911-cockburn-henry-thomas:
Henry Thomas Cockburn was a Scottish judge and writer whose gifts showed late in print. The hosted text opens part way through its account, so his early life is not given here. What survives praises his speech in court. His style was marked by clearness, feeling and plain force. His talk in company was held to be without match among men of his time.

His skill with the pen became known only after he passed seventy years of age. His life of Lord Jeffrey came out in 1852. His Memorials of his Time appeared after his death, in 1856. Cockburn died on 26 April 1854. He died at his house of Bonaly, near Edinburgh. The fragment gives no account of his birth or training. Readers get the close of a life, not its start.
britannica-1911-coke-thomas:
Thomas Coke (1747–1814) was an English divine known as the first Methodist bishop. He was born at Brecon, where his father was a well-to-do apothecary. He studied at Jesus College, Oxford, taking his master's degree in 1770. A law doctorate followed in 1775. From 1772 to 1776 he served as curate at South Petherton in Somerset.

His rector dismissed him for taking up Wesley's open-air and cottage services. He then served on the London Wesleyan circuit. In 1782 he became president of the conference in Ireland, a post he held more than once. He first crossed to America in 1784 as superintendent of the Methodist societies there. In 1787 the American conference gave him the title of bishop. He sought the same title in England without success. He died at sea on 3 May 1814, bound for Ceylon.
britannica-1911-cole-thomas:
Thomas Cole was an American painter of land views who lived from eighteen one to eighteen forty-eight. He was born in England and came to America with his folk in eighteen nineteen. He learned the first steps from a roam face painter in Ohio. He then roamed the land and painted faces for small pay.

In New York his land views in a shop pane caught the eye of a famed painter. That man bought a work and found him rich backers. Fame rests on two sets of tale works on life and on realms. The entry holds those works cheap, and puts his true worth in his views of the wild.
britannica-1911-colebrooke-henry-thomas:
Henry Thomas Colebrooke is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an English scholar of the East. He was born in London in 1765. He was the third son of Sir George Colebrooke. Schooled at home, he showed skill in classics and maths by age fifteen. He lived in France from age twelve to sixteen. In 1782 he took a post in India.

In India he worked first on accounts at Calcutta. He moved to revenue work at Tirhut soon after. At Purneah he studied the wealth of that region. His book on Bengal farming and trade backed free trade with Britain. After eleven years in India, he took up Sanskrit. He was trusted to translate a great Digest of Hindu Laws. That task had been left undone by a past hand. The entry traces the start of a famed career.
britannica-1911-conecte-thomas:
Thomas Conecte (died 1434) was a French Carmelite monk and preacher born at Rennes. He travelled through Flanders and Picardy on his preaching rounds. There he lashed the faults of the clergy with force. He also lashed the rich dress of women, above all their tall head-dresses, called hennins. Immense crowds came to hear him preach.

Bold claims marked his teaching. A true servant of God, he taught, need fear no papal curse. The Roman hierarchy, he held, was corrupt at its root. Marriage, he said, was open to the clergy, since only some men have the gift of restraint. In Italy he brought changes to the rules of his order. Nicolas Kenton, head of the English Carmelites, fought that move in vain. Pope Eugenius IV had him seized at last. He was condemned and burnt for heresy. Monstrelet's chronicle tells the tale.
britannica-1911-copperas:
Copperas is green vitriol, or ferrous sulphate, with water bound in its crystals. Its name runs through French to a Latin phrase that means the flower of copper. The stuff shows a bluish-green colour to the eye. Its taste is harsh, inky and a touch sweet at once. Three trades draw on it in the entry's short account.

Dyeing takes one share of its use and tanning a second. Ink making takes a third share of demand. It also feeds the making of Nordhausen sulphuric acid, the fuming oil of vitriol. The hosted entry is short and names no source or vein for the salt. It sends readers to the entry on iron for more. Name, look, taste and four uses form the whole of its facts.
britannica-1911-coram-thomas:
Thomas Coram is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English friend of children born in Dorset in sixteen sixty eight. He began life at sea and rose to captain of a trade ship. He lived for some years in New England, farming and building boats.

The entry tells how the plight of lost children in London moved him to act. After seventeen years of work he won a royal charter for a home for such infants. The home opened its doors in seventeen forty with twenty small charges. State funds later swelled the work, then were cut when too few babes lived. His last years were spent in care of the home he founded.
britannica-1911-corneille-thomas:
Thomas Corneille, a French dramatist who lived from 1625 to 1709, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Rouen, nearly twenty years younger than his famed brother Pierre. His gift for verse showed early, in a Latin piece acted by his schoolmates. His first French play was staged in 1647.

At his brother's death he took the empty chair in the French Academy. He then turned to language work, editing the remarks of Vaugelas and making a dictionary of arts terms. A full rendering of Ovid's Metamorphoses followed in 1697. Though he lost his sight in 1704, he kept working to the end. His last labour, in 1708, was a large dictionary of geography and history in three volumes.
britannica-1911-coryate-thomas:
Thomas Coryate, an English traveller and writer who lived from about 1577 to 1617, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Odcombe in Somersetshire, a rector's son, he was schooled at Westminster and Oxford. He became a kind of court fool and joined the household of Prince Henry. In 1611 he published Coryate's Crudities, the tale of a five month walk through France and Italy in 1608.

Verses in mock praise by Jonson and Donne were bound in at the prince's order, and the book sold wide. In 1612 Coryate set out again, mostly on foot, for Greece, the Holy Land, Persia, and India. His letters tell of inscriptions copied and customs from Latin speech to the new use of forks. He learned Turkish, Persian, and Hindustani on the road, spent just three pounds between Aleppo and Agra, and died at Surat in 1617.
britannica-1911-coutts-thomas:
Thomas Coutts (1735–1822) was an English banker and founder of the banking house of Coutts and Company. He was born on 7 September 1735. He was the fourth son of John Coutts, an Edinburgh corn factor and dealer in bills of exchange. John Coutts became lord provost of Edinburgh in 1742. The family came first from Montrose and settled in Edinburgh about 1696.

After John Coutts died, the business split in two. One branch traded in Edinburgh and the other in London. James and Thomas Coutts, two of the sons, ran the London side. On James's death in 1778 Thomas stood as sole head of the firm. Under his hand the house rose to the highest rank in its trade. His set aim was a name for sound business and a fortune to match. He lived to gain both, and to enjoy them long. Great men of letters sat among his friends.
britannica-1911-couture-thomas:
Thomas Couture (1815–1879) was a French painter born at Senlis in the Oise. He studied under Baron Gros and under Paul Delaroche. In 1837 he won the Prix de Rome. From 1840 he showed history and genre pictures at the Salon. Medals came to him more than once in that hall. One canvas stands as his masterwork in the entry's judgment.

That canvas is Romans in the Decadence of the Empire, from 1847. It hangs in the Luxembourg in the entry's day. Three more works stand as fair samples of his hand. Love of Money, from 1844, hangs at Toulouse. The Falconer dates from 1855 and Damocles from 1872. The hosted entry is short and keeps to training, prize, shows and those four named works. No word on his teaching or his pupils appears in the piece.
britannica-1911-cranmer-thomas:
Thomas Cranmer, archbishop of Canterbury who lived from 1489 to 1556, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Aslacton in Nottinghamshire on 2 July 1489. He was the second son of Thomas Cranmer and Anne Hatfield. His schoolmaster was, by one account, a wondrously harsh and cruel man.

That charge stands out in an age when no schoolmaster spared the rod. His father taught him field sports such as hunting and hawking at home. Those sports stayed a joy of his in later life as well. Skilled horsemanship came from that early training at his home. At age fourteen his widowed mother sent him to Cambridge for study. He became a fellow of Jesus College in 1510 or 1511. He had soon to give that post up on his marriage, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-creech-thomas:
Thomas Creech (1659–1700) was an English classical scholar born at Blandford in Dorsetshire. He was schooled at Sherborne under Thomas Curgenven and entered Wadham College, Oxford, in 1675. In 1683 he gained a fellowship at All Souls. He served as headmaster of Sherborne school from 1694 to 1696 and received a college living in 1699. In June 1700 he hanged himself, an act the entry links to money trouble, disappointed love, and deep melancholy.

Creech's fame rests on his translation of Lucretius, published in 1682 in rhymed heroic couplets. He also published a version of Horace in 1684 and rendered the Idylls of Theocritus the same year. Later work includes the Thirteenth Satire of Juvenal in 1693 and the Astronomicon of Manilius in 1697. He translated parts of Plutarch, Virgil, and Ovid as well. His Lucretius remained the work by which readers judged him.
britannica-1911-creevey-thomas:
Thomas Creevey (1768-1838) was an English statesman born at Liverpool in March 1768. His father was a merchant of that city. Thomas went to Queen's College, Cambridge, and took his degree in 1789. He read law at the Inner Temple and was called to the bar in 1794. In 1802 he entered parliament for Thetford on the nomination of the duke of Norfolk.

Creevey was a Whig and a follower of Fox. His sharp mind and social gifts won him close ties with the leaders of his party. In 1806 he was made secretary to the Board of Control. When his party next held power in 1830, he had lost his seat. Lord Grey still gave him the post of treasurer of the ordnance. Lord Melbourne later made him treasurer of Greenwich hospital.
britannica-1911-crinagoras:
Crinagoras of Mytilene was a Greek epigrammatist who flourished during the reign of Augustus. A number of epigrams under his name survive in the Greek Anthology. The entry rests his date on a notice in Strabo. Inscriptions found at Mytilene add a public role to the literary one. They show him as one of the ambassadors sent from his city to Rome.

The two missions named fall in 45 and 26 before Christ, and they give the short entry its firm dates. His work reached modern readers through the Anthology, the great gathering of Greek epigrams. The entry closes with the modern edition of his epigrams by M. Rubensohn, published in 1888. Poet and envoy are the two roles the entry joins. Together they place a minor Greek voice inside his city's dealings with Rome.
britannica-1911-critias:
Critias was an Athenian orator and poet who became one of the Thirty Tyrants. In youth he studied under Gorgias and Socrates, then turned to political intrigue. In 415 before Christ he was jailed over the mutilation of the Hermae. In 411 he helped bring down the Four Hundred and worked for the recall of Alcibiades. Banished soon after, he fled to Thessaly and stirred the serfs there against their masters.

Back in Athens, Critias was made an overseer by the oligarch party. Under the Thirty, set up in 404 with Spartan backing, he proved the most cruel and unscrupulous of them all. He died in battle against Thrasybulus and the returning democrats. The entry also credits his varied gifts as poet, orator, historian, and philosopher. Fragments of his elegies survive, and he wrote tragedies and lives of famed poets.
britannica-1911-cubitt-thomas:
Thomas Cubitt (1788–1855) was an English builder born at Buxton near Norwich on 25 February 1788. At nineteen he sailed to India as a captain's joiner after his father's death. He came home two years later with a small capital and set up as a carpenter in London. His firm grew steadily, helped by his early move to join several trades in one builder's business. The London Institution in Finsbury Circus first made his name.

From 1824 Cubitt's vast operations raised whole ranges of London houses, Tavistock, Gordon, Belgrave, and Lowndes Squares among them. He weathered a financial panic that ruined many rivals. He pressed for better drainage of London and helped start Battersea Park, the first of the people's parks. Queen Victoria praised him in warm terms, and his firm built Osborne palace for her. He died at Denbies near Dorking on 20 December 1855.
britannica-1911-curely-jean-nicolas:
Jean Nicolas Curély, French cavalry leader who lived from 1774 to 1827, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a poor peasant of Lorraine. In 1793 he joined a regiment of hussars. He served with great note as a private and as a junior officer in the Rhine campaigns to 1800.

Yet after twelve years of service he still held no commission. At Afflenz in November 1805 he attacked a whole regiment of Austrian cavalry with just twenty five men and beat it. That feat won him the rank of lieutenant and a name as a man of the future. Two more campaigns brought two more steps up the ladder. At Wagram, as a captain of hussars, he topped that deed. With forty troopers he cut through the Austrian lines on a mission with despatches.
britannica-1911-dalyell-thomas:
Thomas Dalyell, a soldier who died in 1685, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Thomas Dalyell of Binns in Linlithgowshire. He sailed with the Rochelle expedition in 1628 and later served under General Munro in Ireland.

He was taken prisoner at Carrickfergus in August 1650, then banished from Scotland. He fought at Worcester in 1651, was captured, and was held in the Tower of London. He escaped abroad in May and joined the Highland rebellion of 1654, with a price on his head. When the royal cause looked hopeless, he entered the service of the tsar of Russia. There he won distinction as a general against the Turks and Tatars. Back in Britain, he was made commander in chief in Scotland in 1666 to subdue the Covenanters. He beat them at Rullion Green and used his powers with great cruelty.
britannica-1911-daniell-thomas:
Thomas Daniell (1749–1840) was an English landscape painter born at Chertsey, where his father kept an inn. Apprenticed to a heraldic painter, he yet loved romantic building and nature. Till 1784 he painted views and flower pieces in England. That year he sailed for India with his nephew William, and stayed ten years at Calcutta. His greatest work, Oriental Scenery in six volumes, was not finished until 1808.

Daniell showed Eastern subjects in London from 1795 to 1828 and published illustrated books in aquatint. Views of Calcutta, views in Egypt, and the excavations at Ellora stand among them. He became an Academician in 1799 and a fellow of the Royal Society. The entry adds his nephews William and Samuel, both artists who died before him. William shared the India years and made a voyage round Great Britain, while Samuel drew the scenery and animals of Africa and Ceylon.
britannica-1911-dareste-de-la-chavanne-a:
Antoine Elisabeth Cleophas Dareste de la Chavanne (1820-1882) was a French historian born in Paris of an old Lyons family. Trained at the Ecole des Chartes, he became professor of letters at Grenoble in 1844 and at Lyons in 1849, staying there nearly thirty years. He died on the 6th of August 1882.

His works cover the administration of France since Philippe-Auguste and the farming classes since Saint Louis. His eight-volume Histoire de France of 1865-1873, continued through the Restoration and the July government, was the best general history of its kind before Lavisse. The entry rates it above Henri Martin for accuracy, as Martin had improved on Sismondi.
britannica-1911-dareste-de-la-chavanne-r:
Rodolphe Madeleine Cleophas Dareste de la Chavanne (1824- ) was a French jurist born in Paris on the 25th of December 1824. He studied at the Ecole des Chartes and the Ecole de Droit, rose early in a legal career, and sat as counsellor to the court of cassation from 1877 to 1900. His first publication was an essay on Francois Hotman in 1850, and he gave all his leisure to legal history.

His writings range over the old laws of Iceland, the legal monuments of Hungary, and studies in the history of law. Greek law drew his best work, from Athenian bottomry loans to the law of Gortyne and the legal science of Plato, Aristotle and Theophrastus. He also helped edit a great collection of Greek legal inscriptions.
britannica-1911-darly-matthias:
Matthias Darly was an eighteenth-century English caricaturist, designer and engraver of wide range. He issued political caricatures, designed ceilings, chimney-pieces and mirror frames, engraved many plates for Thomas Chippendale, and sold his own work over the counter. His first certain piece is a coloured caricature of 1741, and his 1754 book of Chinese designs fed the craze for furniture in that style.

Darly's Strand shop was long perhaps the most important of its kind in London. With his partner Edwards he published political prints gathered yearly as the Political and Satirical History. His chief publication was The Ornamental Architect of 1770-1771, and his last caricature came in October 1780. His furniture designs travelled from pseudo-Chinese fancy to the Adam brothers' classical severity.
britannica-1911-de-keyser-thomas:
Thomas de Keyser is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a Dutch painter born at Amsterdam near fifteen ninety six. His father was a famed builder and carver of stone in that city. No sure tale tells who taught the boy the craft of paint.

The entry notes a side trade in hard stone that he ran for years. Four names are put forth by scholars as the true source of his skill. His fame rests most on his portraits of Dutch men and women. Those works glow with rich gold light and deep shade in his best mode. Most of his portraits are small in size, though some are life size.
britannica-1911-dekker-thomas:
Thomas Dekker, who lived from about 1570 to 1641, was an English playwright born in London. The 1911 Britannica article traces him through the diary of Henslowe, a theatre manager of the day. His name shows there again and again in the last years of the sixteenth century. He took loans and pay for plays, often written with men such as Jonson, Drayton, and Chettle. The pace of the list shows his pen was in hot demand.

In one year, from April 1599 to March 1600, a dozen play titles bear his hand. Most are now lost. Of three plays paid to him alone, only one has come down to us. That one is The Gentle Craft, printed in 1600 as The Shoemaker's Holiday. The article warns that the classical themes of his lost plays prove little of his schooling.
britannica-1911-delisle-joseph-nicolas:
Joseph Nicolas Delisle is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a French astronomer. He lived from 1688 to 1768. He was born at Paris in April 1688. A solar eclipse in 1706 drew him to astronomy. In 1710 he gained leave to lodge in the Luxembourg dome. He procured instruments and observed from that post. There he watched the total eclipse of May 1724.

In 1715 he proposed a diffraction theory of the sun's corona. He visited England and joined the Royal Society in 1724. Late in 1725 he left Paris for Saint Petersburg. The empress Catherine had summoned him there. He founded an observatory in that Russian capital. In 1747 he returned to Paris for good. He became geographical astronomer to the naval department. He set up a new observatory in the Hotel Cluny. Messier and Lalande were among his pupils there.
britannica-1911-elias:
Elias of Cortona is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a disciple of Saint Francis. He lived from about 1180 to 1253. He was born near Assisi of the working class. He became a schoolmaster at Assisi in time. He then worked as a notary at Bologna. In 1217 he headed the Franciscan mission to the Holy Land. 

When Francis was recalled from the East in 1220, Elias came too. He played a leading part in the young Franciscan order. In 1221 Francis made him his vicar general. He was the practical acting superior till Francis died in 1226. That chapter did not elect him minister general. The chapter of 1232 did elect him to that post. At the chapter of 1239 he was deposed. He built the basilica and monastery at Assisi. Those works were entirely his own creation.
britannica-1911-elmham-thomas:
Elmham, Thomas (died about 1420), was an English chronicler, probably born at North Elmham in Norfolk. He became a Benedictine monk at Canterbury and then, joining the Cluniacs, was prior of Lenton Abbey near Nottingham. He was chaplain to Henry V and went with the king to France in 1415. He was present at the battle of Agincourt.

Elmham wrote a history of the monastery of St Augustine at Canterbury, printed in the Rolls Series in 1858. He also wrote a Liber metricus de Henrico V, a verse life of Henry V. The entry judges it very probable that he wrote the famous Gesta Henrici Quinti, the best authority for Henry's life from his accession to 1416. That work is often called the chaplain's life. The entry is careful to add that Elmham did not write the Vita et Gesta Henrici V, a different work once credited to him by Hearne and others.
britannica-1911-elvas:
Elvas is an episcopal city and frontier fortress of Portugal, in the district of Portalegre, 170 miles east of Lisbon and ten miles west of the Spanish fortress of Badajoz. Its population in 1900 was 13,981. The city stands finely on a hill north-west of the river Guadiana. Seven bastions and the two forts of Santa Luzia and Nossa Senhora da Graça defend it.

Its late Gothic cathedral shows Moorish traces and dates from the reign of Emmanuel I. A fine aqueduct four miles long, finished in 1622, brings pure water, rising in four tiers of arches to 120 feet. The lowlands are fertile, and Elvas is famed for olives and plums, with brandy distilled and pottery made in the city. The entry traces the place from Roman Alpesa through Moorish hands to its final taking by the Portuguese in 1226. It twice withstood Spanish sieges, in 1658 and 1711.
britannica-1911-elyot-sir-thomas:
Elyot, Sir Thomas (about 1490–1546), was an English diplomatist and scholar, son of Sir Richard Elyot, a judge of common pleas. Neither the date nor the place of his birth is known for certain. Elyot himself says he was educated at home and was his own tutor from the age of twelve. In 1511 he went with his father on the western circuit as clerk to the assize.

Wolsey made Elyot clerk of the privy council, but he lost that post in 1530 and gained only the costly honour of knighthood. In 1531 he produced the Boke named the Governour, dedicated to Henry VIII, and the book advanced him in the king's favour. Late that year he went as envoy to the emperor Charles V, tasked with softening the emperor's view of Henry's planned divorce from Catherine of Aragon.
britannica-1911-emlyn-thomas:
Emlyn, Thomas (1663–1741), was an English nonconformist divine born at Stamford, Lincolnshire. He served as chaplain to Letitia, countess of Donegal, and then to Sir Robert Rich. In 1691 he became colleague to Joseph Boyse, the presbyterian minister in Dublin. From that office he was in effect dismissed after owning his unitarian views.

For publishing An Humble Inquiry into the Scripture Account of Jesus Christ in 1702, Emlyn was sentenced to a year's imprisonment and a fine of £1000. Through Boyse's help he was freed in 1705 on payment of £90. The entry calls him the first English preacher clearly to name himself “unitarian.” It quotes his diary, thanking God that suffering came only once his judgment was mature. In later years he preached much in Paul's Alley, Barbican, and he died in London in 1741.
britannica-1911-epaminondas:
Epaminondas (about 418–362 B.C.) was a Theban general and statesman, born of a noble but poor family. For his schooling he owed most to Lysis of Tarentum, a Pythagorean exile sheltered by his father. He first gains notice at Mantineia in 385, fighting on the Spartan side and saving the life of Pelopidas, his future colleague.

At the congress in Sparta in 371 Epaminondas refused to give up the Boeotian cities under Theban control, blocking a general peace. He then led the Boeotian army at Leuctra. His victory there, won by daring new tactics for the heavy infantry, made Thebes the leading land power of Greece at a stroke. In 370 he led a great host into Laconia, ravaged Spartan land, freed the Messenians, and rebuilt their capital at Messene. The entry judges his chief political feat the final breaking of Sparta's rule in the Peloponnese.
britannica-1911-erastus-thomas:
Thomas Erastus, a German-Swiss theologian who lived from 1524 to 1583, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born of poor parents, likely at Baden in Switzerland, in September 1524. In 1540 he was at Basel for the study of theology. Plague in 1544 drove him to Italy, where he read philosophy and medicine.

In 1553 he became doctor to the count of Henneberg, and in 1558 to the elector-palatine, while he taught medicine at Heidelberg. In the faith he followed Zwingli, and he spoke and wrote for the Zwinglian view of the Lord's Supper. He fought in vain the push by Calvinists to set up the church rule of Geneva at Heidelberg. When that rule came in 1570, one of its first acts was to cast him out of the church. The ban was lifted in 1575.
britannica-1911-erpenius-thomas:
Erpenius, whose original name was van Erpe, Thomas (1584–1624), was a Dutch Orientalist born at Gorcum in Holland on 11 September 1584. He entered Leiden university and took his master of arts degree in 1608. On Scaliger's advice he studied Oriental languages while reading theology. He then travelled in England, France, Italy, and Germany, learning from the scholars he met.

In Paris Erpenius grew close to Casaubon and took Arabic lessons from an Egyptian, Joseph Barbatus. At Venice he perfected himself in Turkish, Persian, and Ethiopic. Home again in 1612, he became professor of Arabic and other Oriental languages at Leiden in 1613. The States of Holland later made him their interpreter, answering the letters of Muslim princes. He died on 13 November 1624, leaving an Arabic grammar of 1613 among his chief works.
britannica-1911-erskine-thomas:
Thomas Erskine of Linlathen, a Scottish church thinker who lived from 1788 to 1870, is covered in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born on October 13, 1788, the youngest son of a law man in Edinburgh. He studied at Edinburgh and Durham and joined the bar in 1810. In 1816 he gained the family estate near Dundee.

Erskine then gave his life to the study of faith. His books and letters are praised for a graceful style and fresh thought. His views are likened to those of Maurice, who owed him his first true grasp of Christ's sacrifice. Erskine held that faith's truth is shown by its fit with man's inner needs, not by tests of past fact.
britannica-1911-erysipelas:
Erysipelas, also called the Rose or Saint Anthony's Fire, is an acute catching disease of the skin, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a medical entry. The name comes from Greek words for red and for skin. The cause is a germ of the streptococcus kind, and the sickness is present in most countries, with outbreaks at set seasons, above all in spring.

The entry holds that the poison is not very strong, but it can travel by bedding and by the clothes of a third person. Two forms are named, one tied to wounds and one that seems to start on its own, yet in all cases a cut or scrape is the likely door. In a mild attack the skin turns red, hard and thick, with small blisters at times. The redness spreads to sound skin near by, with pain, heat and tingling as it goes.
britannica-1911-ewing-thomas:
Thomas Ewing, who lived from 1789 to 1871, was an American lawyer and statesman in a 1911 Britannica life. He was born near West Liberty and raised in Ohio, where he joined the bar in 1816. He soon won high rank as a court speaker in Lancaster. As a Whig senator he fought to keep the national bank alive.

He served as head of the Treasury under President Harrison in 1841 and left when party ties broke. Later he became the first head of the new Department of the Interior. There he set the office in order and urged a rail line to the Pacific coast. The entry closes with notes on his sons and their careers.
britannica-1911-falashas:
The Falashas are the subject of a peoples entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name means exiles or strangers in Ethiopic. They are also called the Jews of Abyssinia. The entry places them as a people of Hamitic stock, akin to neighbouring groups, who profess the Jewish religion.

They claim descent from the ten tribes banished from the Holy Land. Another tradition makes their ancestor a son of Solomon by the queen of Sheba. The entry notes little physical difference between them and other Abyssinians. When they became Jews is uncertain, with accounts pointing to distinct eras. That uncertainty is left open in the text.
britannica-1911-fay-andras:
Andras Fay (1786-1864), Hungarian poet and author, was born on 30 May 1786 at Kohany in the county of Zemplin and was educated for the law at the Protestant college of Sarospatak. His Fables, first published at Vienna in 1820, showed satire and invention and won wide applause at home. Their originality and simplicity led readers to call him the Hungarian Aesop. The fables were translated into German and partly into English.

Fay also wrote poems, gathered in collections of 1807 and 1818, plus plays, romances and tales. Elected to the Hungarian diet in 1835, he led the opposition for a time. He founded the Pest Savings Bank and helped found the Hungarian National theatre. His earlier works fill eight collected volumes, and his later humorous novel of a doctor and his servant appeared in 1855. He died on 26 July 1864.
britannica-1911-fayetteville-arkansas:
Fayetteville is a city and the county-seat of Washington county, Arkansas, about 150 miles north-west of Little Rock. Its population grew from 2,942 in 1890 to 4,471 in 1910. It stands about 1,400 feet above the sea in the Ozark Mountain region, served by the St Louis and San Francisco railway. Fine scenery and nearby mineral springs have made it known as a summer resort.

The city is the seat of the University of Arkansas, opened in 1872, with colleges of arts, science, engineering, music and agriculture at Fayetteville and other branches elsewhere in the state. In 1908 it had 122 instructors and 1,725 students. The entry also notes a National cemetery with 1,236 soldiers' graves, a Confederate cemetery, coal deposits nearby, a rich apple-growing district, and manufactures of lumber, waggons, lime and flour. Settlement began between 1820 and 1825.
britannica-1911-ferrar-nicholas:
Nicholas Ferrar (1592–1637) was an English churchman, born in London in 1592. He was schooled at Clare Hall, Cambridge, and took his degree in 1610. For some years he had to travel for his health. Back in England in 1618, he took an active part in the Virginia Company. When that company lost its charter in 1623, Ferrar turned to state life and was chosen for parliament.

Ferrar soon chose to give his life to faith. He bought the manor of Little Gidding in Huntingdonshire and set up a small house of faith there. In 1626 Laud made him a deacon, and he refused all higher posts. At Little Gidding he lived a strict life of study and good works, near that of a monk. He died on 4 December 1637. Ten years later the house was spoiled and the group was broken up.
britannica-1911-fields-james-thomas:
James Thomas Fields, an American publisher and author who lived from 1817 to 1881, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, on the last day of 1817. At seventeen he went to Boston as a clerk in a bookseller's shop.

In 1839 Fields became junior partner in a publishing firm, known from 1846 as Ticknor and Fields. He published the foremost American writers of his day and was on close terms of friendship with them. He was also the American publisher of leading British writers, some of whom he knew well. The entry praises his rare mix of keen business sense and sound literary taste. He edited the Atlantic Monthly from 1862 to 1870 and retired in 1871.
