britannica-1911-fieri-facias: Fieri Facias, often shortened to fi fa, is a writ in English law used after a court gives judgment for a debt or for damages. The Latin words mean that you cause it to be made, and the writ goes to the sheriff of the district. The 1911 Britannica entry states plainly that it orders the sheriff to make good the sum owed out of the goods of the person who lost the case. Readers who need the wider picture are sent on to the main entry on execution.
britannica-1911-fitzherbert-thomas:
Thomas Fitzherbert, an English Jesuit born in fifteen fifty two, was heir to an estate in Staffordshire. His grandfather was Sir Anthony Fitzherbert, a judge of the common pleas. He was schooled at Oxford, where at twenty he was jailed for recusancy. On release he went to London and joined a group of young men. That group, founded in fifteen eighty, helped two famed Jesuit priests.

In fifteen eighty two Fitzherbert left for the continent and worked for Mary, queen of Scots. He wed that year and, after his wife died, went to Spain. The king there gave him a pension on a duke's advice. Plots against the English state fill his record in those years. In fifteen ninety eight he was charged in a plot to poison Queen Elizabeth. He later went to Rome and was ordained a priest there.
britannica-1911-flamel-nicolas:
Nicolas Flamel (about 1330-1418), reputed French alchemist and scrivener to the University of Paris, was born in Paris or Pontoise about 1330. He died in Paris in 1418 and left most of his property to the church of Saint-Jacques-la-Boucherie, where he was buried. In life he gave freely to charity from wealth he had made, whether by his craft, by shrewd speculation or money lending, or, as legend claimed, by alchemy.

The legend rests on a document said to be his, dated 1413. In it a book by Abraham the Jew, bought for two florins in 1357, teaches the transmutation of metals but hides the first matter. After twenty years of failure, a learned convert named Canches explains the secret, and in 1382 Flamel turns mercury into silver and gold. The entry answers the tale with parish records, treating the gold-making as fable and the man as a wealthy scrivener.
britannica-1911-fleming-sir-thomas:
Sir Thomas Fleming (1544-1613), English judge, was born at Newport in the Isle of Wight in April 1544. He was called to the bar at Lincoln's Inn in 1574. He represented Winchester in parliament from 1584 to 1601, then Southampton. In 1594 he became recorder of London, and in 1595 he was chosen solicitor-general in preference to Bacon. He kept that office under James I and was knighted in 1603, rising fast in royal favour.

In 1604 Fleming was made chief baron of the exchequer and presided over many important state trials. In 1607 he rose to chief justice of the king's bench. At the trial of the post-nati in 1608 he sided with the majority. They held that Scots born after James I's accession were entitled in England to the rights of natural-born subjects. Contemporaries, above all Coke, praised his great judgments, integrity and discretion. He died at Stoneham Park in Hampshire on 7 August 1613.
britannica-1911-foley-sir-thomas:
Sir Thomas Foley (1757-1833), British admiral, entered the navy in 1770. As a midshipman he saw much active service in the West Indies against American privateers. Made lieutenant in 1778, he served under Keppel and Hardy in the Channel. With Rodney's squadron he was at the defeat of De Langara off Cape St Vincent in 1780 and at the relief of Gibraltar. Still with Rodney, he shared in the great victory of 12 April 1782 in the West Indies.

In the Revolutionary War Foley served from the start. As flag-captain to Admirals Gell and Hyde Parker he was at Toulon in 1793. He fought in the actions off Toulon in 1795. At St Vincent he was flag-captain to the second in command. The entry follows him on to the Nile and beyond, through a career running from the American war to the age of Nelson.
britannica-1911-ford-thomas:
Thomas Ford, born about 1580, was an English musician. Little more is known of his life than that he was attached to the court of Prince Henry, son of James I. His works are few. Yet they suffice, the entry says, to show the high pitch of skill and musical knowledge the English school had reached at the start of the seventeenth century. His music consists of canons and other concerted pieces of vocal music, mostly with lute accompaniment for the singers.

The chief collection of Ford's works is Musike of Sundrie Kinds, set forth in two books in 1607. The music histories of Burney and Hawkins print specimens of his art. Together with Dowland, immortalized in one of Shakespeare's sonnets, Ford is the chief representative of the school that came before Henry Lawes. The notice is short, a single paragraph, standing between Richard Ford and Francis Forde in one shared file.
britannica-1911-fouquet-nicolas:
Nicolas Fouquet (1615-1680), viscount of Melun and Vaux, marquis of Belle-Isle, was superintendent of finance in France under Louis XIV. He was born at Paris in 1615, of an influential family of the noblesse de la robe. After schooling with the Jesuits he was admitted, at thirteen, as an advocate at the parlement of Paris. While still in his teens he held responsible posts. At twenty, in 1636, he could buy the office of maitre des requetes, the first step of a rapid climb.

From 1642 to 1650 Fouquet held intendancies in the provinces and with Mazarin's army. In 1650 he bought the post of procureur general to the parlement of Paris. During Mazarin's exile he stayed loyal, guarding the cardinal's property. The entry follows him to his height under the young Louis XIV, and to the fall his splendour at Vaux brought on him.
britannica-1911-fraas-karl-nikolas:
Karl Nikolas Fraas (1810-1875), German botanist and agriculturist, was born at Rattelsdorf near Bamberg on 8 September 1810. After the gymnasium at Bamberg he entered the university of Munich in 1830 and took his doctor's degree in 1834. Botany had his chief attention. In 1835 he went to Athens as inspector of the court garden. In April 1836 he became professor of botany at the university there.

In 1842 Fraas returned to Germany as teacher at the central agricultural school at Schleissheim. He became professor of agriculture at Munich in 1847 and director of the central veterinary college in 1851. For many years he served as secretary of the Agricultural Society of Bavaria, resigning in 1861. He died at his estate of Neufreimann near Munich on 9 November 1875. The entry lists his principal works on botany and farming at the end of the notice.
britannica-1911-freret-nicolas:
Nicolas Fréret (1688-1749), French scholar, was born at Paris on 15 February 1688, son of a procureur to the parlement. Tutors set him early to history, chronology, and mythology, though his father meant him for the law. At nineteen he was reading papers on Greek religion to a learned society. At twenty-six he entered the Academy of Inscriptions as a pupil.

His 1714 memoir on the origin of the Franks argued they were a league of South German tribes, not a free nation sprung from Greece or Troy. The Abbé Vertot denounced him, and a lettre de cachet put him in the Bastille for three months, which he spent on Xenophon. Freed in 1715, he rose to perpetual secretary of the Academy in 1742. His many memoirs test old documents, sort myth from fact, and trim the vast chronology claimed for Egypt and China. He died in Paris in 1749.
britannica-1911-freron-louis-marie-stani:
Louis Marie Stanislas Fréron (1754-1802), French revolutionist, was born at Paris on 17 August 1754, son of the critic Élie Fréron. His name stayed on L Année littéraire after his father death until the journal ended in 1790. A schoolfellow of Robespierre and Camille Desmoulins, he launched the violent paper L Orateur du peuple when the Revolution broke out.

Sent with Barras in 1793 to impose the Convention rule at Marseilles and Toulon, he won notice for the harshness of his reprisals. He then joined the Thermidoriens, led the jeunesse dorée, and drove the charges against Fouquier-Tinville and Carrier. Elected to the Council of the Five Hundred, he was refused his seat. In 1799 he went as commissioner to Santo Domingo, where he died in 1802.
britannica-1911-fuller-thomas:
Fuller, Thomas (1608–1661), an English divine and historian, was baptized at Aldwincle in Northamptonshire on the 19th of June 1608. He studied at Queens' College, Cambridge. His Historie of the Holy Warre, a history of the crusades, appeared in 1639, and The Holy State and the Prophane State followed in 1642. His Church History of Britain, the work of many years, made his name as a historian.

Fuller lectured at the Savoy in London, and he was fined £200 for words spoken in the pulpit, though the fine was never exacted. His Worthies of England, a county-by-county account of notable persons, was published by his son John in 1662, after his death. Lamb, Coleridge and Southey all praised his quaint and lively style.
britannica-1911-gabler-georg-andreas: Gabler, Georg Andreas (1786–1853), a German Hegelian philosopher, was born at Altdorf in Bavaria on the 30th of July 1786, the son of the theologian J. P. Gabler. He followed his father to Jena in 1804 and there became a keen disciple of Hegel. After school posts he was rector of the Bayreuth gymnasium in 1821 and general superintendent of schools in 1830. In 1835 he succeeded Hegel in the Berlin chair, and he died at Teplitz on the 13th of September 1853.
britannica-1911-gage-thomas:
Gage, Thomas (1721–1787), a British general and governor of Massachusetts, entered the army in 1741 and served in Flanders and at Culloden. He became lieutenant-colonel of the 44th foot in 1751 and served in America from 1754, taking part in Braddock's disastrous expedition of 1755. He rose to major-general in 1761, succeeded Amherst in command of the British forces in America in 1763, and became lieutenant-general in 1770.

In 1774 Gage was made governor of Massachusetts and charged with enforcing the Boston Port Act amid the gravest unrest. The fighting at Lexington on the 19th of April 1775 opened the American war, and after Bunker Hill he was superseded by Howe and returned to England. He became a full general in 1782 and died on the 2nd of April 1787.
britannica-1911-galchas:
Galchas is the name of the highland tribes of Ferghana, Kohistan and Wakhan, Aryan kinsmen of the Tajiks in the Pamir and Hindu Kush. The word may be the Persian galcha, clown or rustic, aimed at their uncouth manners, rather than the tale of a hungry raven withdrawn to the mountains. Benedict Goes, crossing the Pamir in 1603, described them as of light hair and beard, like the Belgians.

French writers have called them belated Savoyards of Kohistan, so closely do they match the Alpine or Celtic European type. D'Ujfalvy describes them as tall and bronzed or even white, with ruddy cheeks, hair black, chestnut or sometimes red, and eyes brown, blue or grey, never oblique. The Galchas are for the most part Sunnite Muslims.
britannica-1911-galena-kansas: Galena is a city of Cherokee county in the south-east of Kansas, on Short Creek near Spring river. Its population jumped from 2496 in 1890 to 10,155 in 1900, then fell to 6096 by 1910. The town stands where two railways cross, in a lead and zinc region whose deposits were found in 1877, the year Galena was incorporated. Smelters and foundries are its works, and the Spring river gives water power. Empire City, its rival across the creek, was annexed in 1907.
britannica-1911-galloway-thomas:
Thomas Galloway (1796-1851) was a Scottish mathematician, born at Symington in Lanarkshire on 26 February 1796. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him to Edinburgh university in 1812, where he stood out in mathematics. In 1823 he became a teacher of mathematics at the military college of Sandhurst.

In 1833 Galloway moved to London as actuary of the Amicable Life Assurance Office, the oldest body of its kind there, and stayed until his death on 1 November 1851. The entry calls him a heavy but largely unsigned writer. His best-known paper, on the proper motion of the solar system, appeared in the Philosophical Transactions in 1847. He also wrote the article on probability for the seventh edition of the Britannica, later printed on its own.
britannica-1911-gataker-thomas:
Thomas Gataker (1574-1654) was an English divine, born in London in September 1574 and educated at St John's College, Cambridge. The 1911 Britannica entry makes him preacher to Lincoln's Inn from 1601 to 1611, then rector of Rotherhithe. In 1642 he joined the Westminster assembly of divines, annotating Isaiah, Jeremiah and Lamentations for it.

Gataker disliked the Covenant and favoured episcopacy, and he was one of forty-seven London clergy who opposed the trial of Charles I. The entry lists his works, from On the Nature and Use of Lots of 1619, which drew charges that he favoured gambling, to his 1652 edition of Marcus Antoninus. Hallam is quoted calling that edition the earliest of a classical writer printed in England with fresh notes. His collected works appeared at Utrecht in 1698.
britannica-1911-gautier-d-arras:
Gautier d'Arras was a French trouvere who flourished in the second half of the 12th century. The 1911 Britannica entry is short, and it says plainly that nothing is known of his life except what his works show. His patrons included Theobald V, count of Blois, Marie, countess of Champagne, and Baldwin IV, count of Hainaut.

Two romances carry his name. Eracle, dedicated to Theobald, tells of a hero who becomes emperor of Constantinople as Heraclius, and the entry calls it a pure romance of adventure that won great popularity. Ille et Galeron, dedicated to Beatrix, wife of Frederick Barbarossa, treats a plot much like the lay Eliduc by Marie de France. The entry closes with the modern edition of his works by E. Loseth, in two volumes of 1890.
britannica-1911-gee-thomas:
Thomas Gee (1815-1898), a Welsh preacher and journalist who did not conform to the state church, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Denbigh, he went into his father's printing office at fourteen while still going to grammar school in the afternoons. In 1837 he went to London to learn more of printing. He came back to Wales the next year and threw himself into writing, schooling, and church work.

The article names his quarterly magazine and his Welsh encyclopedia among his works. His chief feat was the newspaper Baner Cymru, founded in 1857, which soon spoke with great weight in Wales. It helped stir the Welsh national movement. Gee also fought long and well for schools open to all faiths and for a new tier of schools between the basic and the high levels.
britannica-1911-georgetown-texas:
Georgetown, a city in Texas, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It is the county-seat of Williamson county. It stands on the San Gabriel river, north of Austin. Two rail lines serve it. Its people grew from 2,447 in 1890 to 3,096 in 1910.

The city is the seat of Southwestern University. That school is Methodist, and it teaches men and women together. It was formed in 1873 by the union of older colleges. Ruterville College was one of them, chartered in 1840. McKenzie College and Wesleyan College were others. Soule University also joined the union. The article lists the parent schools and their fates. Some closed, and one burned and was never rebuilt. The piece shows how a young university was built from the stock of frontier colleges.
britannica-1911-gesner-johann-matthias:
Johann Matthias Gesner, a German classical scholar and schoolmaster who lived from 1691 to 1761, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Roth near Ansbach on 9 April 1691, he studied at the university of Jena. In 1714 he published a work on the Philopatris ascribed to Lucian. In 1715 he became librarian and vice principal at Weimar.

Gesner was rector of the gymnasium at Ansbach in 1729 and of the Thomas school at Leipzig in 1730. On the foundation of the university of Gottingen he became professor of rhetoric there in 1734. He subsequently became librarian of that university as well in his tenure. His special merit lies in the attention he gave to the subject matter of the classical authors. His principal works are editions of Quintilian, Claudian, Pliny the Younger, and Horace, and a first sketch of universal learning in 1756.
britannica-1911-girtin-thomas:
Thomas Girtin (1775-1802) was an English painter and etcher, son of a well-to-do Southwark cordage maker. The 1911 Britannica entry says his father died while he was a child, and he was apprenticed to the mezzotint engraver Edward Dayes. There he soon made the acquaintance of J. M. W. Turner.

His architectural and topographical drawings quickly built his name. The entry credits his use of water-colour for landscape with creating modern water-colour painting, as against mere tinting. He exhibited at the Royal Academy from 1794 until his death from consumption on 9 November 1802. Turner is quoted in his praise: had Tom Girtin lived, Turner said, he himself should have starved. Fine examples of Girtin's work rest in the British Museum and the Victoria and Albert Museum.
britannica-1911-gorgias:
Gorgias was a Greek sophist and speech teacher of the fifth century before Christ, born at Leontini in Sicily. The 1911 Britannica entry tells how his town sent him to Athens. He went to seek help against a strong foe. He stayed on in Athens, lived by public speech, and taught the art of rhetoric to paying pupils.

The entry credits him with a key role in Greek letters. He brought rhetoric into Greece. He also helped spread the Attic tongue as the tongue of fine prose. It names his lost work on what does not exist, and two speech pieces that bear his name. It notes his place at the heart of a famed dialogue by Plato, then points readers to works on sophists and doubt.
britannica-1911-graham-thomas:
Graham, Thomas, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a British chemist. Born at Glasgow on the 20th of December 1805, he was a merchant's son. He went to the Glasgow university in 1819 to train as a minister. There the chemistry chair holder Thomson turned his mind to science.

He took his degree in 1824 and worked two years at Edinburgh. Back in Glasgow he taught maths and then chemistry for some years. In 1830 he took the chemistry chair at the Andersonian school. In 1837 he moved to the same chair at University College in London. In 1855 he became Master of the Mint in Herschel's place. He held that post till his death in 1869.
britannica-1911-gray-sir-thomas:
Sir Thomas Gray (died about 1369) was an English chronicler of the border wars. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica makes him son of a knight caught at Bannockburn. The younger Gray fought at Neville Cross in 1346, it says. Captured at Norham in 1355, he spent his prison years in study.

In Edinburgh Castle he read Gildas, Bede, and Higdon with care. Freed in 1357, he rose to warden of the east marches. His Scalacronica tells English history down to about 1362 in Norman French. Its real worth lies in the Scottish wars he knew first hand. Battles of Bannockburn, Byland, and Dupplin fill its later parts there.
britannica-1911-gray-thomas:
Thomas Gray was an English poet who lived from seventeen sixteen to seventeen seventy one. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the fifth and sole living child of Philip and Dorothy Gray. He was born in London on the twenty sixth of December seventeen sixteen.

Gray mother kept a hat shop in Cornhill with her sister Mary. His father, a money scrivener, was selfish and brutal in the home. Dorothy bore twelve children, of whom Thomas alone lived past youth. She saved his life as a child by opening a vein herself. At her cost he went to Eton in seventeen twenty seven.
britannica-1911-gresham-sir-thomas:
Sir Thomas Gresham (1519-1579) was a London merchant, founder of the Royal Exchange and of Gresham College. The 1911 Britannica entry makes him the only son of Sir Richard Gresham, a leading merchant and sometime lord mayor. His father sent him briefly to Caius College, Cambridge, then apprenticed him to his uncle, also a merchant, for eight years.

Admitted to the Mercers' Company in 1543, Gresham went that year to the Low Countries. There he traded and acted as agent for Henry VIII, with his headquarters at Antwerp. When the king's merchant Dansell mismanaged affairs in 1551, Gresham rose. The long article follows his financial service to three sovereigns, his rescue of the crown's credit abroad, and his two great foundations in London, which still bear his name.
britannica-1911-hakkas:
Hakkas are a people of south west China whose name means guests or strangers in their tongue. A 1911 Britannica entry places them chiefly in Kwang Tung, Fu Kien, and Formosa. Their origin was in doubt, with one view linking them to old north China stock. Their own tale puts them in Shantung as early as the third century before Christ.

They speak a tongue apart and differ in dress, looks, and custom from other Chinese. Their women do not bind their feet and move freely in public view. Hard work is their mark, and at Canton they supply most coolie labour. The Taiping rebel leader Hung was himself of Hakka birth.
britannica-1911-halyburton-thomas:
Thomas Halyburton (1674–1712) was a Scottish divine. He was born at Dupplin, near Perth, on 25 December 1674. His father was one of the ejected ministers. The father died in 1682. In 1685 his mother took him to Rotterdam to escape persecution. He attended Erasmus' school there. He returned to Scotland in 1687. He graduated at St Andrews in 1696.

In 1700 he was ordained minister of Ceres. In 1710 the synod of Fife recommended him for a chair. Queen Anne appointed him professor of theology at St Andrews. Overwork killed him after a brief professorial term. All his known works appeared after his death. Wesley and Whitefield commended them to their followers. Natural Religion Insufficient appeared in 1714. His Memoirs followed in 1715, and The Great Concern of Salvation in 1721.
britannica-1911-hardy-thomas:
Thomas Hardy, an English writer of tales, opens a long life in the 1911 Britannica. Born in Dorset in eighteen forty, he came of a house long set in the Frome vale. He learned at town schools, then trained with a church builder at Dorchester. Church plans and the care of old churches filled his first work years. He went to London in eighteen sixty two as an aide to a famed builder.

Verse and tales pulled at him while he drew plans by day. A first tale came out in print in eighteen sixty five. George Meredith read an early draft tale and told him to write one with more plot. Desperate Remedies came out in eighteen seventy one. Under the Greenwood Tree came next and showed his true gift, the text says.
britannica-1911-harrison-thomas:
Thomas Harrison, an English parliamentarian who lived from 1606 to 1660, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. A native of Newcastle-under-Lyme in Staffordshire, he was the son of a butcher who was mayor of that town. He was placed with an attorney at Clifford's Inn. When war began in 1642 he enlisted in Essex's lifeguards. He became a major of horse under the earl of Manchester.

Harrison fought at Marston Moor, Naseby, and Langport, and at the taking of Winchester and Basing. At Basing he was accused of killing a prisoner in cold blood. In 1646 he entered Parliament for Wendover. He served in Ireland in 1647, then sided with the army against Parliament. He called the king a man of blood who must be called to account. Wounded at Appleby in 1648, he showed great zeal in bringing the king to trial.
britannica-1911-hathras:
Hathras is a town of British India. It lies in the Aligarh district of the United Provinces. Agra is 29 miles to the south. Its population in 1901 was 42,578. A Jat chieftain held it at the end of the 18th century. His ruined fort still stands at the town's east end. The British annexed the place in 1803. Insubordination forced a siege of the fort in 1817.

Under British rule Hathras rose fast in trade. It now ranks second to Cawnpore in the Doab. Sugar and grain are its chief articles of commerce. Cotton ginning and pressing factories operate there. A cotton spinning-mill also works in the town. A light railway links it with Muttra. A branch joins the East Indian main line. The entry is a short gazetteer notice.
britannica-1911-hawksley-thomas:
Thomas Hawksley (1807–1893) was an English engineer. He was born at Arnold, near Nottingham, on 12 July 1807. Nottingham grammar school taught him until fifteen. Private study supplied his mathematics, chemistry and geology. In 1822 he was articled to a Nottingham architect. That firm also undertook engineering work. He became a partner, then moved to London in 1852. He practised actively past the age of eighty.

Water and gas supply formed his chief field. He used to say he had built 150 waterworks. Liverpool, Sheffield, Leeds and Oxford all owe him water. Stockholm and Barbados appear on his foreign list. Nottingham kept him as water engineer for fifty years. Its constant-supply system was the first of its kind. He designed drainage for Birmingham, Worcester and Windsor. London's main drainage question called him in during 1857. He presided over the civil engineers in 1872.
britannica-1911-hawksmoor-nicholas:
Nicholas Hawksmoor (1661–1736) was an English architect of Nottinghamshire birth. At eighteen he became a pupil of Sir Christopher Wren. His name links inseparably with Wren's and Vanbrugh's. Official posts came to him through Wren's influence. He was deputy-surveyor at Chelsea and Greenwich hospitals. Clerkships of the works at Whitehall and Westminster followed. He succeeded Wren as surveyor-general of Westminster Abbey.

Credit for many designs is hard to divide among the three men. Hawksmoor seems responsible for All Souls' Gothic towers at Oxford. Queen's College library and features are also his. Late in Queen Anne's reign he helped plan fifty new London churches. He designed five or six of them himself. St Mary Woolnoth (1716–1719) is his. St George's, Bloomsbury (1720–1730) is also his. Many of his drawings survive. He died in London in 1736.
britannica-1911-hearne-thomas:
Thomas Hearne (1678–1735) was an English antiquary. He was born at Littlefield Green, Berkshire, in July 1678. His father was the parish clerk there. A wealthy nonjuror neighbour, Francis Cherry, spotted his taste for study. Cherry sent him to Bray school for Latin. Then Cherry took him into his own house. St Edmund Hall, Oxford, matriculated him in 1696. Dr John Mill employed him comparing manuscripts.

The Bodleian Library made him assistant keeper after his 1699 degree. Second keeper followed in 1712. As a nonjuror he refused oaths to George I. Early in 1716 that refusal cost him his librarianship. He refused the Camden professorship rather than swear. Editing English chroniclers filled his Oxford retirement. His careful editions were often the only ones extant. The Rolls series alone superseded them. He died on 10 June 1735.
britannica-1911-heracleonas:
Heracleonas was an east-Roman emperor who reigned from February to September 641. He was the son of the emperor Heraclius and Martina. Near the end of his father's reign, through his mother's influence, he gained the title of Augustus in 638. On Heraclius's death he was proclaimed joint emperor with his half-brother Constantine III.

Constantine died early, in May 641, which left Heracleonas sole ruler for only a few months. Suspicion fell on him and on Martina that the two of them had murdered Constantine. That charge soon raised a revolt against them. Both were seized, mutilated and banished. The account closes there: nothing further is known of Heracleonas after 641, and his brief joint reign is the whole of his recorded rule.
britannica-1911-herbert-sir-thomas:
Sir Thomas Herbert (1606–1682) was an English traveller and author, born at York, where his forebears were aldermen and merchants. He entered Jesus College, Oxford, in 1621, then moved to Cambridge. In 1627 the earl of Pembroke got him a place with Sir Dodmore Cotton, sent as ambassador to Persia with Sir Robert Shirley. The party sailed by the Cape, Madagascar, Goa and Surat, and landed at Gambrun in January 1628.

Cotton and Shirley both died at Kazvin. Herbert went on through Persia, visiting Kashan and Bagdad. He came home by Ceylon, Mauritius and St Helena in 1629. In the Civil War he sided first with parliament, then attended the king from 1646 as a devoted royalist. The Restoration brought him a baronetcy in 1660. His chief work, the Description of the Persian Monarchy (1634), grew into Some Yeares Travels into Africa and Asia the Great. Its pages hold sketches of the dodo, cuneiform inscriptions and Persepolis.
britannica-1911-herodas:
Herodas is a literature article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Greek poet of the third century before Christ. His name is also spelled Herondas in the few places where he is named. He wrote short, funny dramatic scenes in verse under the Alexandrian empire. The pieces are called mimeiambics.

Mimes began as a Dorian form from south Italy and Sicily. They were scenes from the life of common folk, in the speech of the people. The most famed mimes were those of Sophron, from whom Plato is said to have learned character drawing. Two of the best idylls of Theocritus grew out of Sophron's work. Herodas, a younger man of the same age, did the like in his own manner. The article values his scenes both for their merit and as a new kind in Greek letters.
britannica-1911-heywood-thomas:
Thomas Heywood (d. c. 1650) was an English dramatist, a native of Lincolnshire born about 1575. He is said to have been schooled at Cambridge and made a fellow of Peterhouse. Henslowe names him writing for the Lord Admiral's company in 1596, and by 1598 he was a player in it, with a share. He belonged to other companies too, among them the Queen's Servants.

In 1633 Heywood claimed a whole hand, or at least a main finger, in two hundred and twenty plays. Only twenty-three survive, for he wrote for the stage, not the press. Charles Lamb called him a prose Shakespeare. His building of a play was strong, his characterization weaker, and he loved broad farce. His clearest success came in domestic drama, backed by real tenderness. His masterpiece is A Woman Killed with Kindness, acted in 1603 and printed in 1607.
britannica-1911-hicks-elias:
Elias Hicks (1748–1830) was an American Quaker, born in Hempstead township, Long Island, on the 19th of March 1748. Apprenticed as a carpenter at seventeen, he gave up the trade and farmed. By 1775 he felt openings toward the ministry, and in 1779 he began preaching tours between Vermont and Maryland.

Hicks attacked slavery even in Maryland, and his Observations on the Slavery of the Africans appeared in 1811. He helped win the act of 1817 freeing, after 1827, negroes born in New York who were not freed under the act of 1799. His preaching was practical, not doctrinal, and he fought any set creed. At Baltimore in 1817 he blocked a proposed creed for the American Society. His Doctrinal Epistle of 1824 led to a break in 1827–1828: his Liberal followers were called Hicksites by the Orthodox. He died at Jericho, Long Island, in 1830.
britannica-1911-high-seas:
The high seas, in international law, are all parts of the sea not under the sovereignty of states beside them. Claims were once made to dominion over wide margins: a hundred miles, sixty miles, or as far as the eye could see. Bynkershoek stated the limit that won out: the dominion of the land ends where the force of arms ends. Cannon-shot range thus fixed the margin called territorial waters.

Apart from territorial waters, certain bays and inland waters, and waters held territorial by long usage, all oceans form part of the high sea. Its use is free to all nations, bounded by respect for others' equal rights and by agreements between states. A test case arose over a collision in the inland sea of Japan. A British court at Shanghai called that sea part of the high sea, but Japan still treats it as her own.
britannica-1911-hippocras: Hippocras is the subject of a short drink article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Hippocras was an old healing drink or cordial. It was made of wine mixed with spices such as cinnamon, ginger, and sugar. The mix was strained through woollen cloths. The early English spelling was usually ipocras or ypocras. The word adapts a Latin phrase meaning wine of Hippocrates. The name came not from a recipe of the famed physician. It came from a strainer used by drug sellers, nicknamed the sleeve of Hippocrates.
britannica-1911-hobbes-thomas:
Thomas Hobbes was an English thinker who lived from fifteen eighty eight to sixteen seventy nine. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Westport in Wiltshire, the second son of a vicar, he lost his home young. His father fled after a church door quarrel, leaving three children behind.

An uncle, a rich glover at Malmesbury, took charge of the children then. Hobbes went to school at age four and learned Latin and Greek early. Before age fourteen he turned the Medea of Euripides into Latin verse. At about fifteen he entered Magdalen Hall at Oxford to study more. The entry notes he gained little from the formal logic taught there.
britannica-1911-hofer-andreas:
Andreas Hofer (1767–1810) was a Tirolese patriot, born at St Leonhard in the Passeier valley in 1767. He kept his father's inn, the Sandwirth as he was called, and traded in wine and horses with northern Italy. He fought the French from 1796 to 1805, first as a sharpshooter, then as a militia captain. When the treaty of Pressburg gave Tirol to Bavaria in 1805, Hofer led the agitation against Bavarian rule.

In April 1809 the Tirolese rose, and Hofer crushed the Bavarians at Sterzing on the 11th, making him the chief insurgent leader. Driven back once, the Tirolese won twice on the Iselberg in May, and Hofer entered Innsbruck in triumph. The emperor Francis promised him that no peace would part Tirol from Austria. Then the armistice of Znaim in July surrendered Tirol again, and Hofer's work was undone. The entry follows his stand for the Austrian house he loved almost to fanaticism.
britannica-1911-holcroft-thomas:
Thomas Holcroft (1745–1809) was an English dramatist and miscellaneous writer, born in Leicester Fields, London, in 1745. His father, a shoemaker who also let horses, fell into hawking pedlary, and the boy tramped with his parents. He became a stable boy at Newmarket, reading widely in the evenings and teaching himself French, German and Italian. Later he worked as a schoolteacher, prompter and strolling actor.

Holcroft's first play, The Crisis, reached Drury Lane in 1778, and Duplicity followed in 1781. In Paris as a newspaper correspondent he memorized Beaumarchais's Mariage de Figaro whole, and his translation, The Follies of the Day, played at Drury Lane in 1784. The Road to Ruin (1792) was his most successful melodrama; a revival in 1873 ran 118 nights. A member of the Society for Constitutional Information, he was indicted for high treason in 1794 but discharged without trial. He died in March 1809.
britannica-1911-holstenius-lucas:
Lucas Holstenius, the Latin form of Luc Holste (1596–1661), was a German humanist, geographer and theological writer, born at Hamburg. He studied at Leiden, among scholars such as Meursius, Heinsius and Cluverius, whom he joined on travels in Italy and Sicily. Failing to win a post at home, he left Germany for good, spent two years in Oxford and London, and moved to Paris.

At Paris the scholar Peiresc commended him to Cardinal Francesco Barberini, whose great Roman library he then ran. Converted to Catholicism in 1625, he still fought the strict censorship of the Congregation of the Index. Innocent X made him librarian of the Vatican. His learning was immense and his industry tireless, but he lacked the staying power to finish his vast planned works. His finished books are notes and editions on Cluvier, Porphyry and Eusebius, and a Codex regularum of the monastic rules (1661). He died in Rome in 1661.
britannica-1911-home-daniel-dunglas:
Daniel Dunglas Home (1833–1886) was a Scottish spiritualist, born near Edinburgh on the 20th of March 1833. His mother came of a family credited with second sight. He went with her to America and, on her death, was adopted by an aunt. There he came out as a spiritualistic medium, though he never sought money from his exhibitions. In 1855 he came to England and gave many séances to well-known sitters.

Robert Browning attended one séance and kept his contempt, giving his impression in the poem Sludge the Medium (1864). Home still kept many disciples and performed at several European courts. In 1866 a wealthy widow, Mrs Lyon, adopted him and settled £60,000 on him, then sued for its return as gained by spiritual influence, and won. In 1871 he appeared before the tsar of Russia. Back in England, Professor Crookes tested his claims in set experiments and declared them thoroughly genuine.
britannica-1911-hood-thomas:
Thomas Hood (1799–1845) was a British humorist and poet, son of a London bookseller, born on the 23rd of May 1799. His father died in 1811, and the family moved to Islington, where a schoolmaster woke his love of learning. He earned his first fee by seeing a new edition of Paul and Virginia through the press. A counting-house post followed, but the work hurt his always weak health.

Hood turned fully to writing and editing, working with surprising energy despite illness. In those years he composed the few poems the account calls immortal in English. The Song of the Shirt appeared without his name in the Christmas Punch of 1843. The Bridge of Sighs and the Song of the Labourer stand with it. Those poems seized the deep human interests of their time. At the same time his puns and comic verse made him the age's best-known humorist.
britannica-1911-hope-thomas:
Thomas Hope, English art collector and author of Anastasius, was born in London at about 1770 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of John Hope of Amsterdam. His line came from an old Scottish family of merchants in London and Amsterdam. At about age eighteen he set out on a long tour.

That tour took him through parts of Europe, Asia, and Africa in turn. Building and sculpture drew his eye most of all on the road. He made a large collection of the chief objects that caught his fancy there. Back in London at about 1796, he bought a house in Duchess Street and fitted it up in rich style. His own drawings guided that work in full. In 1807 he published sketches of his furniture in a grand folio volume. That book swayed taste in how homes were furnished and graced.
britannica-1911-hovenden-thomas:
Thomas Hovenden (1840–1895) was an American artist, born in Dunmanway, County Cork, Ireland, on the 28th of December 1840. He studied at the South Kensington art schools and at the National Academy of Design in New York, where he settled in 1863. Later he went to Paris and studied under Cabanel at the École des Beaux Arts. Most of his Paris years, though, were spent with the American colony at Pont-Aven in Brittany, painting the peasantry.

Hovenden came back to America in 1880 and became an academician in 1882. He drew wide notice with his canvas The Last Moments of John Brown, now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. His Breaking Home Ties, a scene of American farm life, was engraved and sold widely. He was badly hurt in a brave attempt to save a child from a train at Germantown station, near Philadelphia. He died at Norristown, Pennsylvania, on the 14th of August 1895.
britannica-1911-hutchinson-kansas:
Hutchinson is a city and the county seat of Reno county, Kansas. It stands on broad low land on the north side of the Arkansas river. Its people numbered 9,379 in 1900 and 16,364 in 1910. Three railways serve the city. Its chief public buildings are the Federal building and the county court house. The city has a public library, and the state keeps a work school for young offenders there.

Hutchinson sits in a region of stock raising, fruit growing, and farming. Wheat, Indian corn, and fodder are its main crops, and the city does a large trade in them. A huge bed of rock salt lies under the city and its lands. The making and shipping of salt is thus the city's chief trade, and it has one of the largest salt plants in the world. Other goods made there include flour, soda-ash, straw-board, and packed meats.
britannica-1911-hutchinson-thomas:
Thomas Hutchinson (1711-1780) was the last royal governor of Massachusetts. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his rise from a Boston merchant family. He graduated from Harvard in 1727 and worked in trade at first. Public posts followed from 1737, with long service in the General Court.

He pushed for sound finance and fought risky paper money schemes. In 1748 he carried a bill to redeem the old paper currency. He served as chief justice, then as governor from 1771 to 1774. A mob sacked his house in 1765 over the Stamp Act. He left for England in 1774 and advised the king there.
britannica-1911-hyde-thomas:
Thomas Hyde, an English Orientalist who lived from 1636 to 1703, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Billingsley, near Bridgnorth in Shropshire, in June 1636, he got his taste for language study from his father. His father, the parish rector, gave him his first lessons in them. At sixteen Hyde entered King's College, Cambridge, under the Arabic professor Wheelock.

After only a year at Cambridge, Hyde was called to London to help Brian Walton with the Polyglott Bible. Besides correcting its Arabic, Persian, and Syriac texts, he turned the Persian Pentateuch into Persian characters. Archbishop Ussher had thought that task near impossible even for a native of Persia. Hyde added the Latin version that goes with it. In 1658 he became Hebrew reader at Queen's College, Oxford. In 1665 he was made librarian-in-chief of the Bodleian Library.
britannica-1911-idas:
Idas, a figure of Greek legend, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a son of Aphareus, of the royal house of Messene, and brother of Lynceus. Homer names him in one passage only, and calls him the strongest of men on earth. He carried off Marpessa as his wife and dared to bend his bow against Apollo, who also sought her.

The article says Zeus stepped in and left the choice to the girl. She chose Idas, fearing the god would leave her when she grew old. The brothers are best known for their fight with the Dioscuri over a stolen herd of cattle. Idas claimed the whole spoil as the winner of an eating contest and drove the herd home. In the fight that followed, one twin was slain, Lynceus was killed, and Idas was struck down by lightning.
britannica-1911-iglesias:
Iglesias is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a town in Sardinia. It lies in the hills of the south-west of the isle. The town count for 1901 is 10,436 folk. A state school for mine engineers is based there.

The town's weight comes from its place at the heart of a mining district. Ore moves by a small rail line to Portovesme for shipping by sea. The entry gives the whole isle's mine yield for 1905 by weight and worth. Zinc ore made up the largest share of that yield. Lead, blende, and lignite are also named in the count. The town's old church, built by the Pisans, is noted at the end.
britannica-1911-irulas:
Irulas, a forest people of southern India, are the subject of a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Their name comes from a Tamil word for darkness, and the entry renders it as the benighted ones. They are found mainly in North Arcot, Chingleput, South Arcot, and Trichinopoly, and in the Malabar Wynaad. The branch in the Nilgiri hills lives a wild life on the lower slopes.

The article gives counts from the census of 1901. That branch numbered 1,915 people, while the whole count of those called Irulas came to 86,087. It points readers to books on the early peoples of the Nilgiris and to district manuals for North Arcot. Short as it is, the entry fixes the name, the home districts, and the scale of the group as officials then recorded it.
britannica-1911-jackson-thomas:
Thomas Jackson, head of Corpus Christi College at Oxford, is profiled in a short life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Jackson lived from 1579 to 1640 and was born at Witton le Wear in Durham. He studied at Oxford and became a fellow of Corpus in 1606. He soon rose to vice president of the college.

Later posts took him to church livings in Newcastle, Durham, and Oxfordshire. He became president of Corpus in 1630 and dean of Peterborough a few years later. In faith he moved from a Calvinist start toward an Arminian view. His chief work was a long set of notes on the Apostles Creed. Those notes first came out as twelve books with mixed titles. A full set of his works came out in London in 1673.
britannica-1911-james-thomas:
James, Thomas is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English librarian at Oxford. Thomas James was born at Newport on the Isle of Wight, near 1573, and died in 1629. He was schooled at Winchester and at New College, Oxford, and became a fellow there in 1593.

His wide knowledge of books, and his skill at reading old handwriting and spotting forged texts, won him a key post in 1602. He became the first librarian of the library founded that year by Sir Thomas Bodley. In 1605 he made a classed list of its books, then in 1620 swapped it for one in letter order. The deal of 1610, by which the Stationers' Company sent the library a copy of each book it printed, was his idea.
britannica-1911-jarry-nicolas: Nicolas Jarry was a French calligrapher born at Paris about 1620 and ranked among the best known penmen of the seventeenth century in his country. The 1911 Britannica entry notes that he was in the official employ of King Louis the Fourteenth at the French court. His most famous work is named as the Guirlande de Julie, dated 1641 in the entry. He died at some point before 1674, and the brief record leaves his later years and the rest of his output largely unstated.
britannica-1911-jean-d-arras:
Jean d'Arras was the name borne by French writers of the late middle ages, as this short 1911 Britannica article explains. One was a trouvère of the 1400s, about whose life nothing is known. With Antoine du Val and Fouquart de Cambrai he helped write a set of tales called the Évangiles de quenouille.

Those tales claim to record what a group of ladies said at their spinning, on a wide range of current beliefs. The article calls the work of real value for what it shows of life in that age, and notes many early printings, one in English by Wynkyn de Worde. A second Jean d'Arras, of the late 1300s, wrote a long prose tale of the fairy Mélusine for John, duke of Berry.
britannica-1911-johnson-thomas:
Thomas Johnson was an English wood carver and furniture designer of the 18th century, held in high repute as a craftsman and an artist in wood. His own designs, and his reworkings of other men's ideas, were marked by extreme showiness. He loaded them without mercy with thin, showy ornament.

One design, for a table in which a duck spills water onto a seated mandarin, is singled out as his most inept. His clocks carried scythes, hour glasses, and flashing sunbeams amid endless whirls and floral work. Yet he could at times produce a mirror frame or mantelpiece that was simple and grave. The entry judges him a bold copyist who outdid his rivals. He mixed the Chinese, Gothic, and Louis Quatorze modes in startling ways, and placed figures of men, animals, birds, and fishes in odd spots. He traded at the Golden Boy in Grafton Street, Westminster.
britannica-1911-kailas:
Kailas is a mountain in Tibet, the highest peak of the range that lies north of Lake Manasorawar, with a height of over 22,000 feet. Its segment sits in a hosted file shared with the Kain entry. In Sanskrit lore it is famous as the paradise of the god Siva. Hindus hold it the most sacred spot on earth, and it is a favoured goal of pilgrimage.

A track runs round the base of the mountain. The pilgrim takes three weeks to make the full round, prostrating himself the whole way. The entry is very short: the peak, its height, its place in Hindu faith, and the hard rite of the circuit. Nothing is said of climbs, routes, or the peoples of the district, and the notice rests on the sacred name of the mountain alone.
britannica-1911-kansas-city-kansas:
Kansas City, Kansas, is a city and the county seat of Wyandotte county. It stands on the west bank of the Missouri River at the mouth of the Kansas, about 800 feet above the sea. Only the state line splits it from its larger neighbour, Kansas City, Missouri, and it is the largest city in Kansas. Its people numbered 38,315 in 1890, 51,418 in 1900, and 82,331 in 1910.

Four railways serve it, with electric lines to Leavenworth and across the river. Bridges cross the Kansas. The city fills the low bottom land at the meeting of the rivers, then spreads over the highlands to the west, where the chief housing district lies. Its plan is regular. The long entry traces its growth to the stockyards and packing trade that made the twin cities a great market for the plains.
britannica-1911-ken-thomas:
Thomas Ken (1637–1711) was the most eminent of the English non-juring bishops and one of the fathers of modern English hymn writing. His segment sits in a hosted file shared with the Kempt and Kempten entries. He was born at Little Berkhampstead in Hertfordshire in 1637, the son of Thomas Ken of Furnival's Inn, of an old Somerset stock.

His mother was a daughter of the poet John Chalkhill, and his step sister Anne married Izaak Walton in 1646, a link that brought the boy under Walton's gentle and devout sway. In 1652 Ken entered Winchester College, and in 1656 he went to Hart Hall, Oxford. He gained a fellowship at New College in 1657 and took his degrees in 1661 and 1664. Anthony Wood notes that at the musical gatherings of the time, Thomas Ken of New College would sometimes be among them and sing his part.
britannica-1911-khevenhuller-ludwig-andr:
Ludwig Andreas Khevenhüller, an Austrian field marshal who lived from 1683 to 1744, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He came of a noble Frankish family settled in Carinthia. He first served under Prince Eugène in the War of the Spanish Succession. By 1716 he led Eugène's own dragoons, and he stood out at Peterwardein and Belgrade.

In the Polish Succession war he held chief command in Italy after Count Mercy fell at Parma. Made field marshal in 1737, he cut his way through a far stronger Turkish force at Radojevatz. His finest work came in 1742, when he drove the French and Bavarians out of Austria in days, took Munich, and forced a French corps at Linz to yield. He died at Vienna in 1744.
britannica-1911-kidd-thomas:
Thomas Kidd (1770-1850) was an English scholar of the classics and a schoolmaster. He was born in Yorkshire and schooled at Giggleswick. He went on to Trinity College, Cambridge. He held a string of school and church posts in his life. The last was the rectory of Croxton, near Cambridge, where he died on 27 August 1850.

Kidd was a close friend of Porson and of Charles Burney the younger. He wrote much for journals, chiefly on points of classical study. His name rests most on his editions of the works of other scholars. They include the minor works of the Dutch scholar Ruhnken and the tracts of Porson. He also gave out Dawes's Miscellanea Critica in a second edition. In 1817 he brought out an edition of Horace built on the text of Bentley.
britannica-1911-killigrew-thomas:
Thomas Killigrew, English playwright and wit, was born in Lothbury in London on 7 February 1612 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a son of Sir Robert Killigrew. As a boy he loved the stage so much that he played a devil for free entry. In 1633 he became page to Charles the First.

Loyalty to the royal house shaped his whole life. He wrote two tragi-comedies that came out in 1641 and followed Prince Charles into exile in 1647. At the Restoration he served Charles the Second at court. In 1660 he gained, with Sir William Davenant, a patent for a new playhouse. His company, the King Servants, moved in 1663 to the first Theatre Royal in Drury Lane.
britannica-1911-king-thomas:
Thomas King, English actor and playwright born in London on 20 August 1730, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Garrick saw him act as a strolling player in a booth at Windsor. Struck by the show, Garrick took him on for Drury Lane. He first played there in 1748 as the Herald in King Lear.

For eight years he led in comedy at the Smock Alley theatre in Dublin. In 1759 he came back to Drury Lane and held leading parts till 1802. An early triumph came as Lord Ogleby in The Clandestine Marriage in 1766. His crown came when he created Sir Peter Teazle in The School for Scandal in 1777. He wrote a string of farces and held shares in theatres. A love of gambling ate into his gains in time.
britannica-1911-kiowas: Kiowas, in a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry, are a tribe and stock of North American Indians. Their former range lay around two rivers in what became Oklahoma, Colorado, and New Mexico. A fierce people, they raided settlers in western Texas until 1868, when they were placed on a reservation. They broke out again in 1874 but were finally subdued the next year. About twelve hundred in number and settled in Oklahoma, they are the sole people of their language stock.
britannica-1911-kurumbas-and-kurubas:
The Kurumbas and Kurubas are aboriginal tribes of southern India, thought by some to be of distinct races. The Kurumbas come in two types. Those of the Nilgiri plateau speak the Kurumba dialect and live in a wild state. Those of the plains speak Kanarese and are settled in their ways.

The hill Kurumbas are a small people, with wild matted hair and scant beard. They look sickly, with big mouths, jutting jaws, strong teeth and thick lips. Their villages, called mottas, are groups of four or five huts, set in mountain glens or forests. At the census of 1901 their number was returned as 4083.
britannica-1911-laenas:
Laenas was the name of a plebeian family in ancient Rome, notorious for cruelty and arrogance. Gaius Popillius Laenas was consul in 172 B.C. and fought in the war against Perseus of Macedonia. When Antiochus Epiphanes of Syria invaded Egypt, Laenas was sent to stop him. Meeting the king near Alexandria, he handed him the senate's decree demanding the evacuation of Egypt. Antiochus asked for time to consider. Laenas drew a circle round him with his staff and told him to answer before he stepped out of it — and Antiochus submitted.

His son Publius Popillius Laenas, consul in 132 B.C., made himself hated by the democrats. As head of a special commission he took harsh measures against the accomplices of Tiberius Gracchus. In 123 Gaius Gracchus carried a bill against such commissions, and Laenas left Rome; a sentence of banishment from Italy was pronounced against him.
britannica-1911-largilliere-nicolas:
Nicolas Largillière (1656-1746) was a French painter, and this 1911 Britannica entry follows his early travels and training. He was born in Paris, the son of a merchant who took him to Antwerp at the age of three. As a lad he spent nearly two years in London.

At eighteen he left to seek his fortune in England, where Lely befriended him and employed him for four years at Windsor. His skill caught the eye of Charles the Second, who wished to keep him. But the fury against Roman Catholics after the Rye House Plot drove him to Paris. There Le Brun and Van der Meulen received him well. In spite of his Flemish training he built his name fast as a portrait painter, and the famous of the day flocked to his studio.
britannica-1911-le-blanc-nicolas:
Nicolas Le Blanc is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Le Blanc was a French chemist born at Issoudun in 1742. He trained in medicine and became surgeon to the duke of Orleans in 1780. At the same time he gave much study to chemistry and to a pressing trade problem.

The article tells how he sought to make soda from common sea salt. His key find was to add chalk to a mix of charcoal and soda salts. That step founded the great trade in man made alkali. A factory opened near Paris in 1791 with funds from his patron. The Revolution then took the works and forced him to reveal his method. The works came back in 1800, but he could not raise funds to restart them. He died by his own hand in 1806.
britannica-1911-legas:
The Legas are one of the Shangalla group of tribes, held to be among the purest types of the Galla race. They live in the upper Yabus valley in south-west Abyssinia, near the Sudan frontier. The article sets them apart in looks from the Negro Shangalla near them. They are of very light skin, tall and thin, with narrow, hollow-cheeked faces, small heads, and high foreheads. Their chiefs' families show more mixed blood.

The Legas are said to number more than a hundred thousand, with some 20,000 warriors among them. Yet they are a peaceful people, kind to their women and slaves, and keen farmers. Once free, they came under Abyssinian rule about 1900. Most are pagans by faith, though Islam has won many converts among them.
britannica-1911-linacre-thomas:
Thomas Linacre (about 1460-1524) was an English scholar and doctor. Canterbury was most likely his birthplace. The cathedral school there, under William Celling, fed his first love of Greek. Oxford took him about 1480. A fellowship at All Souls came in 1484.

Italy came next, in Celling's train to the papal court. Poliziano taught him at Florence, near the Medici princes. One of them later sat as Pope Leo X. Padua gave him his doctor's degree in medicine with high praise. Home again, he joined the bright Oxford circle of Colet, Grocyn, and Latimer. Court called him about 1501 to tutor Prince Arthur. Under Henry VIII he served as the king's own doctor. Great churchmen and statesmen filled his practice in London. Caius praised his hate of fraud and his faith to friends.
britannica-1911-linley-thomas:
Thomas Linley, who lived from 1732 to 1795, was an English musician of Bath and London. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Wells in Somerset. He studied music at Bath and settled there as a singing master. He also led the concerts of that city. From 1774 he helped run the Drury Lane theatre in London. There he wrote or pieced together music for many plays.

His songs and madrigals rank high among English works of the kind. The entry turns then to his gifted children. His eldest son Thomas was a fine violin player and a friend of Mozart. A younger son wrote glees and songs while serving in India. Three daughters won fame for singing and for beauty. The eldest wed Richard Brinsley Sheridan in 1773. That match tied the family's fate to the playwright's rise.
britannica-1911-lodge-thomas:
Thomas Lodge (about 1558-1625) was an English playwright and all-round writer. West Ham was his birthplace. His father had been lord mayor of London in 1562-1563. Merchant Taylors' School and Trinity College, Oxford, formed him. Degrees came in 1577 and 1581. Lincoln's Inn took him in 1578.

Debt and letters both grew fast in that soil. When Gosson's Schoole of Abuse struck at plays in 1579, Lodge struck back. His Defence of Poetry, Music and Stage Plays was banned, yet passed hand to hand. An Alarum Against Usurers came in 1584, fed by his own hard years. A first tale of his own, Forbonius and Prisceria, came the same year. Stage plays flowed from 1587, though most laid to him rest on guess. That he trod the boards himself is held not likely.
britannica-1911-lowndes-thomas:
Thomas Lowndes, who lived from 1692 to 1748, founded a chair of astronomy at Cambridge. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth to Cheshire land owners. In 1725 he was named provost marshal of South Carolina. He filled that post by deputy from home. He claimed a big part in the crown's purchase of Carolina. His patent for the post was given up, renewed, then resigned for good.

He then pressed a string of schemes on the state. They aimed to curb the wool trade with France and fix paper money in New England. One plan would draw salt for the navy from brine. The entry calls such plans unworkable. He died in May 1748 with a rich will. His Cheshire lands went to Cambridge for a chair. That gift set up the Lowndean chair of astronomy and geometry. The chair is the chief mark his name keeps.
britannica-1911-lowndes-william-thomas:
William Thomas Lowndes was an English book list maker of the nineteenth century. He lived from about seventeen ninety eight to eighteen forty three. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a London bookseller and worked with books all his life.

Lowndes chief work is a manual of English books in four parts. That work, from eighteen thirty four, took fourteen years to compile fully. It was the first planned work of its kind in the field. Despite its worth it brought him neither fame nor money in life. Poor and ill, he later listed books for publisher Henry Bohn.
britannica-1911-lysanias:
Lysanias is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a tetrarch of Abilene. Luke names him in the time of John the Baptist. The only Lysanias in secular history for that district is another man. That man was executed in 36 before Christ by Mark Antony. He was son of Ptolemy Mennaeus, ruler of an independent state. Abilene formed only a small portion of that state. Josephus adds a later note to the record.

Josephus says Claudius confirmed Agrippa in possession of Abila in 42. Caligula had already bestowed that land on Agrippa. The land is described as the tetrarchy of Lysanias. Some argue it cannot mean the man Antony executed. His father's realm was far larger than a tetrarchy. So some authorities assume a second Lysanias existed. That second man would match the date in Luke's gospel. The entry lays out a puzzle of names and dates.
britannica-1911-macdonough-thomas:
Thomas Macdonough (1786–1825) was an American sailor, born in the state of Delaware. His father had been an officer of the Continental Army. Macdonough entered the United States navy in 1800. In his long service as a lieutenant, he took part in the bombardment of Tripoli. On a later day he showed great firmness in a clash over a seaman. He fought the claim that the man was a deserter from the British navy and held him, though his ship lay under the guns of Gibraltar.

When war with England broke out in 1812, Macdonough was sent to cruise in the lakes. His base was on Lake Champlain. He saved New York and Vermont from attack by a bright win on that lake in 1814. With 14 ships and 86 guns, he beat a force of 16 ships and 92 guns under Captain George Downie.
britannica-1911-macias:
Macias is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Galician troubadour, or trovador. He flourished from about 1360 to 1390. He held some position in the household of Enrique de Villena. He is represented by five poems in the Cancionero de Baena. He is the reputed author of sixteen other poems. Macias lives by virtue of romantic legends around his name. The most popular version of his story is one man's telling.

According to that tradition, Macias loved a great lady. He was imprisoned at Arjonilla for that love. The jealous husband murdered him while he sang her praises. There may be some basis of fact for this narrative. The tale became a favourite subject with Spanish poets. Macias is mentioned as the Castilian equivalent of Cabestanh. He afforded a theme to Lope de Vega in one play. In the nineteenth century the romantic movement took him up again.
britannica-1911-maes-nicolas:
Nicolas Maes, who lived from 1632 to 1693, was a Dutch painter. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Dordrecht. About 1650 he went to Amsterdam and entered Rembrandt's studio. His early genre scenes use life size figures and deep glowing colour. Some were so close to his master's style that they pass as Rembrandt's. Works in Leipzig, Budapest, and London bear that wrong credit.

From 1655 to 1665 came his best period. He turned to small scenes of home life on a lesser scale. Women spinning, reading the Bible, or cooking were his loved themes. He kept much of the colour magic he learned from Rembrandt. In 1665 he moved to Antwerp and his style changed whole. Portraits in a loose elegance, kin to Van Dyck, replaced the warm home scenes. The shift was so sharp that some posited a second Maes.
britannica-1911-mahrattas:
Mahrattas is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on a people of India. They live in the region known by the old name Maharashtra, meaning great kingdom or region. That large tract runs from the Arabian Sea in the west to the Satpura mountains in the north. It takes in much of western and central India.

The entry says the root of the name Mahratta is not certain. The name marks no caste, sect, or tribe, it stresses. In its strict sense it covers the upper class from whom the generals of Sivaji mostly came. In a wider sense it covers all who live in Maharashtra and speak Mahratti as their mother tongue. Speakers of that tongue in India passed eighteen million in 1901.
britannica-1911-malebranche-nicolas:
Nicolas Malebranche (1638–1715) was a French thinker of the school of Descartes. He was born at Paris on 6 August 1638, the youngest child of a secretary to Louis XIII. His mother was the sister of a viceroy of Canada. Frail in body, he was taught at home by a tutor. He left home only to study thought at the Collège de la Marche and theology at the Sorbonne.

Malebranche had meant to take holy orders, but his love of study led him to refuse a stall in Notre Dame. In 1660 he joined the Oratory. He was urged to study church history and read Eusebius and other old writers with great pains. Yet the facts would not settle in his mind. A try at Hebrew under Richard Simon went no better. In 1664 he chanced to read Descartes on man, and the book moved him deeply.
britannica-1911-malet-lucas:
Lucas Malet was the pen name of Mary St Leger Harrison (1852-), an English novelist, and her work is noted in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Eldest daughter of Charles Kingsley, she was born at Eversley in 1852. She studied at the Slade school and at University College, London, and married a rector in 1876.

The entry lists her early books, from Mrs Lorimer in 1882 to A Counsel of Perfection in 1888. Her strong story The Wages of Sin, in 1891, drew great attention. The History of Sir Richard Calmady in 1901 did even better, and later novels include The Carissima and The Gateless Barrier.
britannica-1911-malik-ibn-anas:
Malik ibn Anas, who lived from about 718 to 795, founded a school of Islamic law. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives his quiet life at Medina. He was born and taught in that city all his life. Townsfolk held him as their top voice on faith and law.

Malik taught law, gave rulings, and sat as a judge in Medina. He held that an oath forced by power did not bind the swearer. Rulers had him scourged for that stand, yet feared to go further. A caliph later came to sit at his feet as a pupil. Late in life Malik withdrew to prayer and study. His chief book, the Muwatta, set out his teaching in full.
britannica-1911-malory-sir-thomas:
Thomas Malory is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Malory was the translator and compiler of the famed English classic the Morte d'Arthur. Who he was stayed an unsolved problem for long. At the end of the book the author asks readers' prayers for Sir Thomas Malory, knight. He says the book was finished in the ninth year of King Edward the Fourth.

The article follows a scholar's search for a man who fits all the facts. Such a man must be a knight, alive in 1469, and dead by 1485. The match found is a Thomas Malory of Newbold Revell. He sat in parliament for Warwickshire in 1445. He had served in France in the train of the earl of Warwick. He died in March 1470.
britannica-1911-manton-thomas:
Thomas Manton, an English Nonconformist divine, was born in Somerset in sixteen twenty. He was schooled at Hart Hall, Oxford, in his youth. A bishop ordained him deacon, but he never took priest's orders after that. He held that he was duly ordained to the minister's office already. He served as a clerk at the Westminster Assembly of divines.

Manton was one of Cromwell's chaplains and a trier under that regime. He held livings at Stoke Newington and at Saint Paul's, Covent Garden. He disapproved of the execution of Charles the First, the entry notes. In sixteen fifty eight he helped Baxter draw up the fundamentals of religion. He helped restore Charles the Second and became one of his chaplains. In sixteen sixty two he lost his living under the Act of Uniformity.
britannica-1911-march-auzias:
Auzias March, who lived from about 1395 to 1458, was a Catalan poet born at Valencia. The 1911 Britannica entry notes how little is known of his life in plain fact. He wed twice, died on the fourth of November 1458, and left several children born outside marriage. Wealth from his father and favour from Prince Carlos let him give his time to verse.

He followed Petrarch with open zeal, at times to the point of close copy in form. His love songs use scenes and turns drawn straight from that model. In his songs of death he found a brooding tone the entry calls his own. Faults of dark phrasing mar the work, yet the voice still stands out.
britannica-1911-marquesas:
Marquesas is an islands article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a chain of islands in the Pacific Ocean. They are also called the Mendana Islands, and they belong to France. The chain runs some two hundred and fifty miles from south-east to north-west. Its total land area is 490 square miles.

The southern group holds Fatuhiva, Motane, Tahuata, and Hivaoa, the largest of them. The north-western, or Washington, group is made of seven islands. Nukuhiva measures seventy miles round its coast. A ridge of mountains runs down the centre of each island. In Huapu that ridge reaches 4,042 feet. Rough spurs fall from it to the sea, cutting deep valleys. The rocks are basalt, trachyte, and lava, proof of the chain's volcanic origin. Plant life is rich in the valleys, the article notes.
britannica-1911-mathews-thomas:
Thomas Mathews, who lived from 1676 to 1751, was a British admiral born at Llandaff Court. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him into the navy, with captain rank by 1703. In the short war with Spain he led the Kent under Byng in action. From 1722 he led a small squadron to the East Indies against Malabar pirates.

No sea service followed until 1741, when he took the Mediterranean command at once. He also held envoy powers to Sardinia and other Italian courts in that post. The entry asks on what grounds so ill fitted a man was chosen. Want of skill and tact for both tasks is charged plainly against him.
britannica-1911-matthew-tobias:
Tobias Matthew, archbishop of York, who lived from 1546 to 1628, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Bristol, son of Sir John Matthew of Ross. He studied at Wells, then at two Oxford colleges in turn. He took his first degree in 1564 and caught the notice of Queen Elizabeth.

His rise through church and university posts was steady. He was public orator, head of an Oxford college, and dean of Christ Church. He then became dean of Durham, bishop of Durham, and at last archbishop of York in 1606. In debate he took on the Jesuit Edmund Campion, and his arguments were printed at Oxford. In the north he worked hard to force those who refused the English church to conform. He preached hundreds of sermons and held strict visitations across his province.
britannica-1911-may-thomas:
Thomas May, an English poet and historian who lived from 1595 to 1650, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Sir Thomas May of Mayfield in Sussex. He went to Sidney Sussex College at Cambridge in 1609 and took his degree three years later. His father lost the family wealth, so May made letters his trade.

He wrote comedies such as The Heir in 1620 and classical tragedies on Antigone, Cleopatra, and Agrippina. His best known work was a rendering of Lucan's Pharsalia in heroic couplets in 1627. Its success led him to carry the tale on to the death of Caesar. Charles the First became his patron and set him to write verse histories of Henry the Second and Edward the Third.
britannica-1911-mayhew-thomas:
Thomas Mayhew, an English maker of fine furniture in the 1700s, is noticed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the less famed partner of William Ince, and their firm traded as Mayhew and Ince. Most of what is known of his work comes from their joint book of designs. That book, The Universal System of Household Furniture, puts the names in the reverse order on its title page.

The text judges Mayhew with frank words: his designs are for the most part heavy and clumsy. Some are even wild in their excess. Yet he had a light touch in his use of the odd Chinese style then in vogue. Much of that Chinese work has been credited to Chippendale by mistake. Only books of designs, the text warns, let us sort out which maker did which piece.
britannica-1911-metaxas-andreas:
Andreas Metaxas, a Greek politician who lived from 1786 to 1860, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born on the island of Cephalonia. In the last years of the War of Independence he came to Greece with Capo d'Istria. Capo d'Istria appointed him minister of war for the new state.

When Capo d'Istria was murdered in 1831, Metaxas joined the provisional government that ruled until King Otho came in 1833. During the king's minority he served as privy councillor and as minister at Madrid and Lisbon. In 1840 he was recalled and made minister of war again. In 1843 and 1844 he was president of the council of ministers. He later served as ambassador at Constantinople from 1850 to 1854. He died at Athens on the nineteenth of September 1860.
britannica-1911-midas:
Midas is a mythology article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the name of several Phrygian kings. The first Midas was said to be the son of Gordius and Cybele, whose first priest he was. He returned the drunken Silenus to Dionysus and was rewarded with the golden touch. Starving, since his food turned too, he begged the god to take the gift back.

A second tale tells how Midas judged a music contest against Apollo and was given ass's ears. His barber, unable to keep the secret, whispered it into a hole in the ground, and the reeds that grew there proclaimed it to the world. The article then turns to history: the name Midas the king appears on an ancient tomb in Phrygia.
britannica-1911-middleton-thomas:
Thomas Middleton (about 1570-1627), an English playwright, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a London man and most likely born in London. No proof shows that he studied at either university, though he may match a man of his name entered at Gray's Inn in the fifteen-nineties. He began to write for the stage before the century turned.

By 1602 he was one of the settled playwrights of the manager Henslowe, whose diary notes plays he had a hand in. In one year he produced no fewer than six comedies of London life. The entry says he knew that life as well as Dekker did and painted it in truer colours. In 1613 he devised the Lord Mayor's pageant and wrote a show for the opening of the New River.
britannica-1911-mifflin-thomas:
Thomas Mifflin, an American soldier and politician, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Philadelphia in seventeen forty four of Quaker parents, he graduated at the college of Philadelphia in seventeen sixty. He sat in the Pennsylvania house in the early seventeen seventies as an ardent Whig.

In seventeen seventy four he was a member of the first Continental Congress. After war broke out he gave himself to raising and drilling troops. He was chosen major of a regiment. In June seventeen seventy five he entered continental service as Washington's first aide de camp. Two months later he gained a new post.
britannica-1911-moore-thomas:
Moore, Thomas is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the Irish poet famed for his songs and for Lalla Rookh. Moore was born in Dublin on the twenty-eighth of May 1779, the son of a grocer and wine merchant. His first verses saw print in 1793. At Trinity College, Dublin, from 1794, he became friends with Robert Emmet. The rising of 1798 and the hanging of Emmet in 1803 left a deep mark on him.

Moore took his degree in 1798 and went to London to study law, but song made him a social success first. His version of the Odes of Anacreon appeared in 1800; love poems as Thomas Little followed in 1801. In 1803 he sailed to a registrar's post in Bermuda, soon left a deputy, and came home by way of America and Canada.
britannica-1911-moran-thomas:
Thomas Moran, an American artist born in 1837, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Bolton, in Lancashire, England, in January 1837. In 1844 he emigrated with his parents to America. The family settled in Philadelphia.

He was apprenticed for some years to a wood-engraver. He then studied under his brother Edward and under James Hamilton. Later he studied in London, Paris, and Italy. In 1871 he joined the exploring expedition to the Yellowstone. Two years later he went down the Colorado with Major Powell's famed party. On those trips he made sketches for two large pictures. One showed the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone. The other showed the Chasm of the Colorado River. Both works were bought by the United States government. The piece ties an artist's fame to the survey of the West.
britannica-1911-morley-thomas:
Thomas Morley, an English composer who lived from 1557 to 1603, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a pupil of William Byrd, but little is known of his origin. A motet dated 1576, written when he was nineteen, helps fix the year of his birth. In 1591 his music was played for Queen Elizabeth at Elvetham.

In July 1588 Morley took a degree in music at Oxford, and in 1592 he entered the Chapel Royal. There he filled the offices of epistler and gospeller in turn. From the dedication of his first book of canzonets, he seems to have married in 1595. His wife's name was Margaret. In September 1598 he won a licence for twenty one years to print music paper and song books. That grant covered songs in English, Latin, French, and Italian.
britannica-1911-mozley-thomas:
Thomas Mozley, who lived from 1806 to 1893, was an English churchman and writer born at Gainsborough. The 1911 Britannica article says his father sold and printed books in that town. Mozley went from Charterhouse to Oriel College, Oxford. There he became the pupil and close friend of John Henry Newman. He was ordained in 1831 and took the parish of Cholderton in 1836.
