Mozley backed the Tractarian movement from its start. He wrote for its chief paper, the British Critic, and took over as editor from Newman in 1841. In 1843 he stood near to joining the Roman Church, but Newman urged him to wait. In the end he stayed an Anglican. From 1844 he wrote leaders for The Times for many years. His best known book is his tale of his Oxford days and of the movement, printed in 1882.
britannica-1911-mulji-kursendas:
Kursendas Mulji (1832–1875) was an Indian journalist and social reformer born on the 25th of July 1832. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells how his own family cast him off for backing the remarriage of widows. He became a schoolmaster and started a weekly Gujarati paper, the Satya Prakash.

In his paper he attacked the wrongdoing of the Maharajas, the born high priests of his own sect. They sued him for libel at Bombay in 1862, and he won on the main point. A cotton venture in England failed and brought him expulsion from his caste. In 1874 he was set to run a native state in Kathiawar during its chief's minority, and he died there in August 1875.
britannica-1911-nast-thomas:
Thomas Nast is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Nast was an American caricaturist, born in Landau, Germany, in 1840. His mother brought him to New York in 1846. At fifteen he was drawing for Frank Leslie's Illustrated Newspaper.

The article traces his rise at Harper's Weekly. His Civil War cartoons won wide notice, and Lincoln called him a fine recruiting sergeant. His attacks on the Tweed Ring in New York helped expose that corrupt circle. One caricature even helped police identify and arrest Tweed in Spain. Nast gave American politics lasting symbols: the donkey, the elephant, and the Tammany tiger. The entry closes with his lost fortune, a consul's post in Ecuador, and his death there in 1902.
britannica-1911-necessitas:
Necessitas is a myth article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the figure of Necessity in old Greek thought. In the Orphic system she stands for need in its stark, fixed form. She is named as mother of the Fates.

The article sets out her place in that scheme of the world. She is also wife of the Fashioner of the World and mother of Destiny. Her power cannot be withstood, and it tops the power of the gods themselves. The strife of the old gods is laid at her door. The world is said to turn on a spindle that rests in her lap. In the Egyptian scheme she stands at the birth of each child. Roman verse shows her walking before Fortune, with great nails and molten lead in her bronze hand.
britannica-1911-newton-sir-charles-thoma:
Sir Charles Thomas Newton was a British scholar of ancient remains and art. He lived from eighteen sixteen to eighteen ninety four. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Bredwardine in Herefordshire, he was schooled at Shrewsbury and Oxford.

Newton joined the British Museum in eighteen forty as an aide in antiquities. In eighteen fifty two he left to serve as vice consul at Mitylene. His aim was to explore the coasts and isles of Asia Minor. With funds from Lord Stratford he found carved stones at Calymnos isle. In eighteen fifty six he uncovered the Mausoleum of Halicarnassus, a world wonder.
britannica-1911-norton-thomas:
Thomas Norton, an English lawyer, lawmaker and verse writer who lived from 1532 to 1584, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London and schooled at Cambridge, he worked as a clerk to the Protector Somerset and wed Margery Cranmer, the archbishop's daughter. He wrote verse from his youth.

With Sackville, Norton wrote Gorboduc in 1560, the first English tragedy, staged before Queen Elizabeth at the Inner Temple. He sat in Parliament, went to Rome on law work, and let John Foxe print Cranmer's draft code of church law. His Calvinist zeal grew hard with age. As the man charged with pressing Catholics, he earned the grim name Rackmaster General. In time even the bishops feared him, he lost his post and was held in the Tower, and his health broke before his death in 1584.
britannica-1911-oldham-thomas:
Oldham, the geologist who led the survey of India, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life story. The hosted text gives his years as 1816 to 1878 and his birth place as Dublin. He took his first degree at Trinity College in 1836. He then studied works of building at Edinburgh, gaining skill in earth science.

Back in Ireland in 1839, Oldham helped with the survey of Londonderry. He led the Irish survey from 1846 and found an odd fossil, named Oldhamia, in 1849. In 1850 he was picked to run the Geological Survey of India, which he set up from scratch. He launched its Memoirs and Records and wrote a large report on India's coal in 1864.
britannica-1911-otway-thomas:
Thomas Otway, an English writer of plays who lived from 1652 to 1685, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Trotton in Sussex, the son of a clergyman. He studied at Winchester and then at Christ Church, Oxford. He left Oxford in 1672 with no degree.

In London he first tried the stage as an actor and froze with fright. He turned to writing, and his first tragedy was staged in 1675. His Don Carlos, drawn from a French tale, made real money for the house. The entry marks the two types found through his plays. One is the rash young man, much like Otway. The other is the soft, sad heroine seen later in his famed works.
britannica-1911-oudinot-charles-nicolas:
Charles Nicolas Oudinot, who lived from 1767 to 1847, was a marshal of France and duke of Reggio. The 1911 Britannica entry gives his birth at Bar le Duc to a plain Lorraine family. A love of soldiering took him into the Medoc regiment from 1784 to 1787. Low birth blocked all hope of rise, so he left as a sergeant.

The Revolution changed his luck, and in 1792 volunteers chose him lieutenant colonel. His brave defence of the small fort of Bitsch drew the eye of commanders. Regular rank and brigade command followed for conduct at Kaiserslautern in 1794. Service under Hoche, Pichegru, and Moreau kept his name high on the frontier.
britannica-1911-overbury-sir-thomas:
Sir Thomas Overbury, an English poet and essayist who lived from 1581 to 1613, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry calls him the victim of a famed crime. Born in Warwickshire, he studied at Oxford and then read law at the Middle Temple in London. He won favour with Sir Robert Cecil.

About 1601 Overbury met Robert Carr, then a young page, in Edinburgh. The two youths became close friends and came to London together. When Carr caught the eye of King James and rose fast, Overbury rose with him. He was knighted in June 1608. The bond broke over Carrs love for the countess of Essex. Overbury fought the match from the first and spoke of the countess in harsh terms. Carr told her what his friend had said.
britannica-1911-pache-jean-nicolas:
Pache, Jean Nicolas is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a French politician of the Revolution. Born in Paris in 1746 of Swiss parentage, he became tutor to a marshal's children. He rose through posts at the ministries of marine and elsewhere and spent some years in Switzerland with his family. He returned to France at the start of the Revolution.

The article follows his sudden rise and fall. He was chosen a deputy for Paris in September 1793 and made minister of war the next month. Though himself a Girondist, he angered that party by his poor work, and Marat's support kept him up. He helped bring down the Girondists, and was arrested that May. An amnesty saved him in 1795, and after a hospital post he retired from public life.
britannica-1911-paine-thomas:
Thomas Paine, who lived from 1737 to 1809, was an English writer who fired a revolution. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Thetford in Norfolk. His father was a Quaker stay maker. After years at sea and odd trades, Paine took up his father's craft in London. A post in the excise came in 1762, then loss of it.

A second excise post at Lewes let him shine in a Whig club. In 1772 he wrote a plea for better pay for excise men. In 1774 he was sacked again, in part to dodge his debts. A meeting with Benjamin Franklin in London turned his life. Franklin sent him to America with letters in hand. On the ninth of January 1776 he issued Common Sense in Pennsylvania. That tract urged a break with Britain and a republic.
britannica-1911-pal-kristo-das:
Kristo Das Pal (1839–1884) was an Indian publicist born in Calcutta, and his life is the subject of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Pal came from the Teli caste of oil men, a group placed low in the Hindu social order. He gained an English education at the Oriental Seminary and the Hindu Metropolitan College. He turned to journalism while still young.

In 1861 Pal became secretary to the British Indian Association, a body of Bengal landlords. That same year he took over as editor of the Hindu Patriot, a paper first issued in 1853. The entry traces his long editorship and his later public posts in Calcutta. Readers get a compact record of how one Indian editor rose to civic standing under British rule.
britannica-1911-pampas:
Pampas is the subject of a plain article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The pampas form a vast plain of Argentina. The name comes from a native word for a level open space. The plain runs from one river north to a great forested lowland. It stretches from the foothills of the Andes east to the coast.

The article puts its area at two to three hundred thousand square miles. Low ranges break its surface in the northwest and south. Apart from such breaks the plain looks perfectly level. It slopes gently from over two thousand feet in the west to near sea level at Buenos Aires. The east is humid, fertile, and grassy, with almost no native trees. The west is covered by shingle and sand. Settlers have planted foreign trees with success since Europeans arrived.
britannica-1911-parnell-thomas:
Thomas Parnell, an English poet who lived from 1679 to 1718, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Dublin, of a Cheshire family that had moved to Ireland. In 1693 he entered Trinity College, Cambridge, and took his degree in 1700. That same year he was ordained deacon, though still young.

Posts in the Irish church came fast, and in 1706 he was made archdeacon of Clogher. His wife died in 1711, and Swift says grief kept him ill near a year. In London he moved among Steele, Addison, and Pope, and sat in the Scriblerus Club. He wrote the life of Homer set at the head of Pope's translation. His best known poem is The Hermit, a moral tale in couplets. He died at Chester on his way home in 1718.
britannica-1911-pausias: Pausias, a Greek painter of the fourth century before Christ, is the subject of a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He belonged to the school of Sicyon. He began the custom of painting the ceilings of houses. His great skill lay in the rendering of foreshortening. The article quotes Pliny on his famous bull. Pausias painted the bull from the front, not in profile. Yet the full length of the body still showed. He painted the whole animal in dark colour. His figures thus stood out from a flat ground.
britannica-1911-pelias:
Pelias is a figure in Greek legend, a son of Poseidon and Tyro. The 1911 Britannica entry tells his tale in brief, stark terms. Tyro wed her father's brother Cretheus, king of Iolcus in Thessaly. Pelias and his twin brother Neleus were cast out as babes. A herdsman found them and raised them to manhood in secret.

Once grown, the twins were owned by their mother at last. After the death of Cretheus, Pelias seized the throne of Iolcus. To rid himself of Jason, he sent him to Colchis for the golden fleece. In Jason's absence he slew Aeson and kin of the young hero. Medea then tricked the daughters of Pelias into a grim act.
britannica-1911-pheidias:
Pheidias, son of Charmides, is held the great sculptor of Greece in a 1911 Britannica art life. Born at Athens near five hundred before Christ, his training is told in more than one way. Three teachers are named by old tales, from Athens, Argos, and Thasos. Of his life past his works, the text says, we know but a small part. Two tales of his death stand at odds with each other.

One tale says foes of Pericles struck at him and he died in jail at Athens. A second tale says he fled to Elis, made its great Zeus, and was slain there. Plutarch shows him as guide and head of the vast art works of Pericles. His fame in old days rested on bronze and on gold and ivory gods, not on marble.
britannica-1911-philetas:
Philetas of Cos, a poet and critic of the Greek world in Egypt, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He lived in the late part of the fourth century before the common count. He taught the son of Ptolemy the First of Egypt. He also taught a famed poet and a famed word scholar in their youth.

His thin frame made him a butt of jokes. Comic verse said he wore lead in his shoes so the wind would not blow him away. Too much hard study is said to have cut his life short. His love verse, most of it in praise of his dear Battis, was much prized by the Romans. Two great Roman poets name him with praise. One took him as a model and set him above his great rival. He also made a word book that glossed rare and dark terms for readers.
britannica-1911-phillips-thomas:
Phillips, Thomas is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English portrait painter of the Georgian age. Born at Dudley in Warwickshire on the eighteenth of October 1770, Phillips learned glass painting at Birmingham and came to London in 1790 with a letter to Benjamin West. West found him work on the windows of St George's Chapel at Windsor, and Phillips soon showed history pieces at the Academy.

After 1796 he gave himself mainly to portraits, and it was not long before he became the chosen painter of men of genius and talent. He joined the Royal Academy as an associate in 1804 and a full member in 1808. In 1824 he followed Fuseli as professor of painting, holding the post till 1832, and his lectures saw print in 1833. He died in 1845.
britannica-1911-picton-sir-thomas:
Thomas Picton, who lived from 1758 to 1815, was a British general whose career the 1911 Britannica entry follows in detail. He was born in Pembrokeshire and got a first army post at age thirteen. Service at Gibraltar and a captain rank followed, then his regiment was disbanded. He stopped a mutiny by bold action yet missed the reward he was promised.

After twelve quiet years at home he sailed for the West Indies in 1794. He fought in the taking of Saint Lucia and Saint Vincent and rose in rank. He then governed Trinidad so well that locals begged to keep British rule. The entry gives a full picture of a brave but hard edged officer.
britannica-1911-pietas:
Pietas is the Roman form of the sense of duty to god and man. The 1911 Britannica entry adds duty to the fatherland to that list. A famed tale tells of a poor young woman and her jailed parent. That parent lay in prison under death sentence, with no food given. The daughter got in and fed the parent with milk from her breast.

To honour that deep filial love a temple was raised at Rome. Manius Acilius Glabrio dedicated it in the year 181 before Christ. It stood in the Forum Holitorium, the grocers' market of that city. The spot was said to be where the young woman had lived. A second temple of Pietas stood near the Circus Flaminius in Rome.
britannica-1911-pinckney-thomas:
Thomas Pinckney, an American statesman and envoy born in seventeen fifty, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Charleston, South Carolina, he was the younger brother of a famed namesake. He was schooled in England and came home in seventeen seventy three. He was let to the bar the next year.

In the war for free rule his drill at a French war school made him of great use. He served more than one general in the south. At the battle of Camden he was hard hit and taken. He was held for more than a year. He then rose to lead his state as its head for two years. He led the meet that passed the new frame of rule for the union. He sat in the state house and then went as envoy to a great court abroad.
britannica-1911-pitt-thomas:
Thomas Pitt, an English merchant in India often called Diamond Pitt, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Blandford in Dorset in sixteen fifty three, he went to India while still young. From Balasore he made trading trips into Persia. He soon stood out among those who traded against the East India Company.

The entry tells how the Company had him seized twice, yet could not check him. In time it took him into its own service. In sixteen ninety seven he became president of Fort Saint George at Madras. There he worked hard to guard his employers' trade against a new rival company.
britannica-1911-polk-leonidas:
Leonidas Polk, an American soldier who lived from 1806 to 1864, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born at Raleigh, North Carolina, on April 10, 1806. He was a cousin of President James Knox Polk. Schooled at West Point, he then studied faith and took church orders in 1831.

In 1841 Polk was made bishop of Louisiana, after years as a mission bishop in the South West. His church work leaned hard on schools and colleges for the South. At the start of the Civil War he quit his bishop post and joined the Confederate army. He rose to lieutenant general and led a corps of the Army of Tennessee. He was killed near Pine Mountain in 1864.
britannica-1911-poussin-nicolas:
Nicolas Poussin (1594-1665) was a French painter born at Les Andelys in June 1594. His early sketches drew the eye of Quentin Varin, a local painter, whose pupil he became. He then went to Paris and worked in the studios of Ferdinand Elle and of L'Allemand. French art stood at a point of change at that time. The old system of training was in flux, and the schools that would replace it were not yet set up.

In the house of Courtois the mathematician, Poussin saw a store of prints after Italian masters. That sight fired his zeal for study. After two failed bids to reach Rome, he fell in with the chevalier Marini at Lyons. Marini set him to draw plates for his poems and took him into his household. In 1624 Marini made it possible for Poussin to join him at Rome at last.
britannica-1911-pownall-thomas:
Thomas Pownall (1722-1805) was a British statesman and soldier linked with the American colonies, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. Born at Saltfleetby in Lincolnshire, he studied at Trinity College, Cambridge, and worked for the board of trade and plantations. In 1753 he went to America as private secretary to Sir Danvers Osborn, the new governor of New York.

Osborn died soon after landing, but Pownall stayed to study the colonies and met Benjamin Franklin at the Albany Congress of 1754, starting a lifelong friendship. He became governor of Massachusetts in 1757 and backed Pitt's plans in the Seven Years War. Later, as a member of parliament, he at first opposed all plans to tax the American colonists.
britannica-1911-pratinas:
Pratinas was one of the oldest tragic poets of Athens, a native of Phlius in the Peloponnese. The 1911 Britannica entry places him about five hundred years before Christ. He vied with two other poets in the year when Aeschylus first wrote for the stage. His home near Corinth, where round dances of satyrs were said to start, may explain his taste for that kind of play.

The entry credits him with making satyr plays a form apart from tragedy. In them, the rough fun and wild dances of the satyrs were kept whole. He also wrote dithyrambs and choral odes, of which a large piece still stands. A tale in the entry says a wooden stage fell in one of his plays, and Athens then built a stone house for plays.
britannica-1911-privas:
Privas is a town of south east France, chief town of the Ardèche district. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places it south of Lyons near the Ouvèze river. The commune held 7,000 people in 1906. Courts, a prefecture, and schools for teachers stand in the town. A madhouse serves two districts from there. Silk milling is the main trade. Folk nearby rear silkworms and grow the mulberry trees they feed on.

Iron mines dot the land around the town. Trade runs in silk, leather, game, chestnuts, and fruit preserves. The town's past was rough. It stood as a stronghold of the reformed faith in the wars of religion. Royal troops failed to take it in 1574. In 1629 Louis the Thirteenth seized it and left it in ruins. The king at first banned all return to the site. Three years later the townsfolk won leave to come back.
britannica-1911-pytheas:
Pytheas of Marseilles was a Greek navigator and geographer, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica weighs what is known of his voyage. From him the Greeks got their first firm knowledge of western Europe and of the British Islands. He likely lived in the time of Alexander the Great.

The entry notes that his work is lost, so its form must be guessed from the titles under which it is quoted. They point to a geography treatise built from his own observations, not a plain tale of the trip. Polybius is cited to show Pytheas sailed at his own cost, visited Britain, and claimed to have crossed much of it on foot.
britannica-1911-quiller-couch-sir-arthur:
Sir Arthur Thomas Quiller Couch, an English writer known as Q, was born in Cornwall in eighteen sixty three. He was schooled at Newton Abbot, at Clifton, and at Trinity College, Oxford. After his degree in eighteen eighty six he lectured briefly in classics at Trinity. While at Oxford he published his first romance, in the vein of Stevenson's Treasure Island. More novels followed in quick order in the next two years.

After work in London journalism, Quiller Couch settled at Fowey in Cornwall in eighteen ninety one. His later novels include The Blue Pavilions, The Ship of Stars, and Hetty Wesley. In eighteen ninety eight he completed Stevenson's unfinished novel Saint Ives for publication. He was known from his Oxford days as a writer of fine verse. In eighteen ninety five he published a choice set of lyrics from two centuries.
britannica-1911-rambaud-alfred-nicolas:
Alfred Nicolas Rambaud, a French historian who lived from 1842 to 1905, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Besançon and trained at a top school in Paris, then in Germany. He was one of a band of young scholars fired by the German way of science. Their aim was to reshape the high schools of France.

His first deep work dealt with the Greek empire of Byzantium. A book on the tenth century there made his name as a master of that field. The war with Germany then turned his mind to France on the Rhine. Next he took up the past of Russia, and lived there to learn its tongue and ways. His short history of Russia ran through five editions by 1900.
britannica-1911-rickman-thomas:
Thomas Rickman, an English architect who lived from 1776 to 1841, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Maidenhead in Berkshire, where he helped his Quaker father as a grocer and druggist until 1797. He then worked at various trades until 1818. All his spare time went to sketching and measured drawing of old buildings.

In 1811 alone he is said to have studied three thousand church buildings. When the government granted funds for new churches in 1818, a design of his won an open competition. That launch made him an architect in full, and he moved to Birmingham. By 1830 he was one of the most successful architects of his day. He built churches in many towns and a new court at Saint John's College, Cambridge. All his work is in the Gothic style, strong on outward form.
britannica-1911-ridley-nicholas:
Nicholas Ridley is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was an English bishop and martyr from about 1500 to 1555. He came of an old Northumberland family line. He was the second son of a man of that house. He was sent to Cambridge at about the year 1518. An uncle paid for his keep at that school. He stood out there most of all in Greek studies.

He took a master grade in the year 1526. He then studied at Paris and at Louvain schools. On his return he took a post at his college. In 1534 he was a proctor for the school. He signed a decree against papal rule in England. He won note as a speaker and a debater. Leanings to the reformed faith showed in his work. Cranmer made him a chaplain in that same age.
britannica-1911-rotherham-thomas:
The 1911 Britannica article on Thomas Rotherham (1423-1500) gives the life of an archbishop of York. He was born at Rotherham in 1423. He was also called Thomas Scot. He studied in his home town. He had links with both Oxford and Cambridge. He entered the church and held livings in Worcestershire and London.

The article follows his rise under Edward the Fourth. He became keeper of the privy seal in 1467. He was bishop of Worcester, then of Lincoln. He became chancellor of England in 1475. In 1480 he was chosen archbishop of York. When Edward died, he stayed loyal to the widow. Richard the Third jailed him for it. He later gave buildings and funds to both universities. He also founded a college at Rotherham.
britannica-1911-rowe-nicholas:
Nicholas Rowe, who lived from 1674 to 1718, was an English playwright and writer. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him from baptism in Bedfordshire to Westminster School. He won a King Scholar place and then read law at the Middle Temple. On his father death he gained a fortune that freed him to write.

His first play reached the stage in 1700, set in old Persepolis. Tamerlane followed, with its hero drawn as William the Third and its foe as Louis the Fourteenth. That play was staged each year on the date of William landing for long after. His Fair Penitent won high praise from Johnson as a most pleasing tragedy.
britannica-1911-rowlandson-thomas:
Thomas Rowlandson (1756–1827) was an English caricaturist, and his life story opens a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. He was born in Old Jewry, London, in July 1756, the son of a city merchant. On leaving school he joined the Royal Academy as a student. At sixteen he lived and studied for a time in Paris.

In 1775 Rowlandson showed a drawing of Delilah visiting Samson in prison at the Royal Academy. Portraits and landscapes by him followed in later shows. He had a quick hand and a sure grasp of the figure. Teachers saw him as a painter of real promise. Then an aunt left him a sum of £7000, and he fell into the gaming life of the town. Want drove him at last toward caricature as a way to earn.
britannica-1911-ruddiman-thomas:
Thomas Ruddiman, a Scottish classical scholar who lived from 1674 to 1757, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Raggal in Banffshire, the son of a farmer, he studied at Aberdeen University. Through a patrons help he became an assistant in the Advocates Library in Edinburgh. Early work there gave him a name as an editor.

In 1714 Ruddiman issued his Rudiments of the Latin Tongue, long used in Scottish schools. A year later came his edition of the works of George Buchanan, in two large volumes. As a Jacobite he censured Buchanans free views in his notes, which drew fierce attacks. Still, his set stays the standard edition of Buchanan. He founded a sound printing business and became printer to the university. In 1730 he took charge of the Advocates Library itself. Doctor Johnson called him the stand in for Scottish learning in his age.
britannica-1911-russell-thomas:
Thomas Russell is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Russell was an English poet who lived from 1762 to 1788. He was born at Beaminster, son of a Dorset attorney. He was schooled at Bridport and at Winchester, then went to New College at Oxford in 1780. He graduated in 1784 and was ordained priest in 1786.

The article says he gave himself to the literatures of many tongues at Oxford. His health broke down, and he retired to Bristol to take the waters. He died there in 1788, aged twenty six. A thin book of his sonnets and poems came out the next year. The sonnets are called his best work. By them he takes his place as a forerunner of the romantic school. His topics broke with the narrow range set for poets of his century.
britannica-1911-rymer-thomas:
Rymer, Thomas is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English writer who held the post of royal record keeper. Thomas Rymer lived from 1641 to 1713 and was the younger son of Ralph Rymer, a Yorkshire landowner put to death for his part in a rising in 1663. The article follows his school days, his time at Cambridge, and his call to the bar in 1673.

Much of the piece deals with his work in print. His first books were translations, one from Cicero and one a French work on poetry, with a preface in defence of the old classical rules. Readers get a clear picture of a scholar whose fame rested on old records, old plays, and sharp views on how verse should be made.
britannica-1911-sampson-william-thomas:
William Thomas Sampson (1840–1902) was an American naval commander, born at Palmyra, New York. He finished first in his class at the U.S. Naval Academy in 1861. He rose to master that year and to lieutenant the next. He was executive officer of the Patapsco when she was blown up in Charleston Harbor in 1865. He later served on far stations and twice at the Naval Academy.

Sampson became commander in 1874 and led the Naval Academy from 1886 to 1890. He sat on the prime meridian conference of 1884 and on the Board of Fortifications. From 1893 to 1897 he ran the Bureau of Ordnance. About 95 per cent of the guns used in the Spanish-American War were made under his care. His views also shaped how guns and armour were placed and how crews were trained.
britannica-1911-scopas:
Scopas is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a great Greek carver in stone of the fourth century before Christ. He was most likely of Parian stock, the son of Aristander. Though classed as an Athenian, he worked far and wide, in Asia and in the Peloponnese.

The article links his name to two great works. One is the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, a wonder of the world. The other is the temple of Athena at Tegea. Stone heads from Tegea, now split between Athens and the local store, are held to be his own work. They show a bold style, with deep set eyes and strong feeling in the face. That sets him apart from Praxiteles, the text says. Scopas chose force and action over calm and soft charm.
britannica-1911-shadwell-thomas:
Thomas Shadwell is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English play writer born in Norfolk near sixteen forty two. He was schooled in Suffolk and at Cambridge but left with no degree. He then joined a law inn in London and turned to the stage.

His first prose comedy came out in sixteen sixty eight and set his path. For years he brought out a new play near each season. His best plays show the talk and tricks of low London life. The entry praises his hate of shams and his rough but sound morals. He is best known now as the butt of a famed satire by a rival poet.
britannica-1911-shelton-thomas:
Thomas Shelton (active 1612-1620) was the English translator of Don Quixote, as this 1911 Britannica article explains. In the dedication of his version of 1612 he told his patron, Lord Howard de Walden, a simple tale. He had rendered the book from Spanish in forty days for a dear friend. That friend could not read the original. Shelton worked not from the first Spanish printing but from one issued at Brussels in 1607.

When the second part came out at Brussels in 1616, Shelton translated that too, finishing in 1620. He issued a revised first part at the same time. His version became a classic among English renderings for its racy, spirited style. The article also traces what later research found about his life, including links with the earl of Suffolk's kin and work carrying letters from Dublin Castle.
britannica-1911-sheraton-thomas:
Thomas Sheraton, who lived from about 1751 to 1806, stands next to Chippendale as the most famed English designer of furniture. His life is told in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in poor state at Stockton-on-Tees. His schooling was slight, but he picked up drawing and geometry on his own. He seems to have been bound to a cabinet maker.

He was a strange mix of craftsman, inventor, artist, and man of faith. He is first heard of as a writer on points of religion. A Baptist, he brought out a work on the doctrine of regeneration at Stockton in 1782. Of his work as a maker of furniture nothing is known till he shows in London in 1790, at near forty years of age. His work there made him famed for all time, yet it never raised him out of deep poverty.
britannica-1911-simler-josias:
Josias Simler was the writer of the first book that deals with the Alps and the Alps just, who lived from fifteen thirty to fifteen seventy-six. He was the son of a priest at Kappel. He was schooled at Zurich past a famed church reform head, then at two more towns. He served as priest and then taught the new books.

He made new prints of a great list of all who had writ in three old tongues. His Alps book sums all that the old world knew of those hills, plus much from his friends. A twin work on the Swiss state was held the chief word on its rule for ages.
britannica-1911-simon-thomas:
Simon, Thomas is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English medallist and engraver of the Civil War age. Born in Yorkshire about 1623, Simon learned engraving under Nicholas Briot and gained a post at the Mint about 1635. In 1645 Parliament named him joint chief engraver. He cut the great seal of the Commonwealth and dies for its coinage, and he rose to chief engraver to the mint and seals. He made several fine portrait medals of Cromwell.

His fame rests on the crown piece of Charles the Second, struck during his contest with the Roettiers brothers in 1662. Around its edge Simon engraved a petition to the king, and the coin is usually held to be his masterpiece. He is believed to have died of the plague in London in 1665.
britannica-1911-simpson-thomas:
Thomas Simpson, an English mathematician who lived from 1710 to 1761, is given a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Market Bosworth in Leicestershire, he was a weaver's son whose father cared little for his schooling. The boy taught himself, let his weaving slide, and left home. At Nuneaton he fell in with a pedlar who told fortunes and took up casting horoscopes himself.

Simpson soon saw that trade as a fraud and gave it up. He wove by day at Derby and taught pupils at night, then moved to London. His first book, a Treatise of Fluxions of 1737, was marred by press errors and gaps. Works on chance, annuities, algebra, and geometry followed fast. In 1743 he became professor of mathematics at the Royal Military Academy at Woolwich. Two years later he joined the Royal Society.
britannica-1911-smart-sir-george-thomas:
Sir George Thomas Smart, an English musician who lived from 1776 to 1867, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in London, the son of a music seller. As a boy he sang in the choir of the Chapel Royal. He trained in music and grew skilled as a violinist, an organist, a singing teacher, and a conductor.

In 1811 he was knighted in Ireland after he led a run of fine concerts in Dublin. From then on he was one of the chief men of music in England. He led bands at the Philharmonic, at Covent Garden, and at town festivals across the land. In 1838 he became composer to the Chapel Royal. He knew the music of Handel by heart, knew Beethoven in person, and was a close friend of Weber, who died in his house.
britannica-1911-smith-sir-thomas:
Sir Thomas Smith, an English scholar and diplomat, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Saffron Walden in Essex in fifteen thirteen, he became a fellow of Queens' College, Cambridge, as a young man. He was soon made a public reader. He lectured on natural philosophy and on Greek.

In fifteen forty he went abroad to study in France and Italy and took a law degree at Padua. Back at Cambridge he led a reform of how Greek was pronounced. After much debate his views were adopted by all. With his friend Sir John Cheke he stood as a leading classic scholar of his age in England.
britannica-1911-southerne-thomas:
Thomas Southerne (1660-1746) was an English playwright born at Oxmantown, near Dublin, in 1660. He entered Trinity College in 1676. Two years later he was entered at the Middle Temple in London to read law. His first play, The Persian Prince, or the Loyal Brother, came out in 1682. It was built on a novel of the day.

The true interest of that play lay not in its plot but in its cast of public men in disguise. The loyal brother was a kind portrait of James II, and the villain was taken to stand for Shaftesbury. Southerne gained a post in the regiment of Princess Anne and rose fast to captain. His army life ended at the Revolution. He then gave himself to the stage in full. In 1692 he reworked a play for Dryden, and in 1694 he won a great hit with The Fatal Marriage.
britannica-1911-spence-thomas:
Thomas Spence, who framed a plan to make land a public good, fills a cause life in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Newcastle in seventeen fifty, he was the son of a net maker. A fight over common land rights in his town set his mind on the land cure. His plan set each parish as a self held whole town for its folk. Rent paid to the town board would stand as the sole tax of any kind.

His tract first sold by hand in the streets of his home town. In London he kept a book stall and wrote on for his cause. Jail terms fell on him twice for tracts the state found too hot. He died in London in September of eighteen fourteen at his stall work. His fans formed a band named for him to spread his plan.
britannica-1911-stanley-thomas:
Thomas Stanley, an English poet and thinker who lived from 1625 to 1678, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was the son of Sir Thomas Stanley of Cumberlow, in Hertfordshire. His mother was kin to the poet Richard Lovelace. He went up to Cambridge in 1637, at age thirteen.

Stanley took his master's degree in 1641 and seems to have moved to Oxford by then. He was wealthy, married early, and travelled much on the Continent. He was a friend and helper to many poets of his day. He wrote verse of his own and translated verse as well. His Poems came out in 1647. More works, among them Europa and Cupid Crucified, followed in 1649. The article gives a life of ease spent in the world of letters.
britannica-1911-staunton-sir-george-thom:
Sir George Thomas Staunton, an English traveler and scholar of the East who lived from 1781 to 1859, is covered in a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born near Salisbury on May 26, 1781. In 1792 he sailed to China with his father, who served on a royal mission there. He gained a good grasp of Chinese on that trip.

In 1798 Staunton joined the East India Company's post at Canton and rose to its chief. In 1805 he put a medical work into Chinese, bringing vaccination to China. He sat in parliament for many years from 1818. In 1823 he helped found the Royal Asiatic Society. His chief book rendered the basic laws of China into English in 1810.
britannica-1911-steele-thomas:
Thomas Steele lived from 1788 to 1848 and was an Irish politician and writer. The 1911 Britannica life opens with his birth in November 1788. His Somerset family had settled in Ireland in the 1600s long before. He was schooled at Trinity College in Dublin and at Magdalene, Cambridge. A large estate in County Clare came to him in time.

As a volunteer he fought against the Bourbons in Spain in 1823. Back in Ireland he threw himself into the cause of Catholic relief. He helped return Daniel O'Connell to Parliament for Clare in 1828. That famed election was a landmark in Irish public life for years. Steele himself was a Protestant, the entry notes with pointed care.
britannica-1911-stofflet-jean-nicolas:
Jean Nicolas Stofflet, who lived from 1751 to 1796, was a Vendean general for the royal cause. The 1911 Britannica entry gives his birth at Luneville as the son of a miller. He served long as a private in a Swiss regiment in French pay. Work as gamekeeper to a count filled his years before the Revolution.

When the Vendee rose for faith and king, he joined the rebels at once. Fights at Fontenay, Cholet, and Saumur showed his worth in the field. He rose to chief command of the royalist army in 1794 after a leader fell. Feuds with Charette and fresh defeats pushed him to a treaty in 1795.
britannica-1911-stone-nicholas:
Nicholas Stone, the mason who remade English sculpture, fills a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1586, he was a Devon quarryman's son of Woodbury. A London mason took the boy to learn the trade of stone. About 1603 he crossed to Holland to work under De Keyser. He wed that master's daughter and learned at his side there.

Stone came home about 1613 and set up work in Southwark. In 1619 James the First made him his master mason at court. Charles the First kept him in that same post from 1626. His hand is tied to the new Renaissance build craft in England. Great tombs by him fill Westminster Abbey and parish churches wide. Donne's shrouded figure at St Paul's is among his famed works.
britannica-1911-stothard-thomas:
Thomas Stothard (1755-1834) was an English painter and book illustrator from London. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his start as a silk pattern draftsman apprentice. Praise for drawings of poets he loved turned him toward art full time. He entered the Royal Academy in 1778 and rose to full member in 1794.

He drew one hundred forty eight designs for the Novelists Magazine alone. Series for Robinson Crusoe and The Pilgrims Progress won wide use. Small tasks such as tickets and almanac art gained grace in his hands. His designs are put at five thousand, with most of them engraved. Late works for Rogers poems show his fancy fresh in old age.
britannica-1911-stucley-thomas:
Thomas Stucley (c. 1525–1578), also spelled Stukely, was an English adventurer. He was the son of Sir Hugh Stucley of Affleton, near Ilfracombe, a knight of the body to Henry VIII. Some men of his time thought he was a son of the king. He served as a standard-bearer at Boulogne from 1547 to 1550. He then entered the service of the duke of Somerset.

When Somerset was arrested in 1551, a warrant was issued against Stucley as well. He got away to France and served in the French army. His skill in war drew the eye of Montmorency, and Henry II of France sent him to Edward VI with a note of praise. On his arrival in 1552, Stucley laid bare French plans to take Calais and land in England. Northumberland paid him no reward. He sought the French king's favour instead by claiming not to trust Stucley's tale.
britannica-1911-sully-thomas:
Thomas Sully lived from 1783 to 1872 and was an American painter of note. The Britannica life of 1911 opens at Horncastle in England, his birth town. His parents were actors who took him to America at age nine. They settled at Charleston in South Carolina, where his art training began. A French painter of small portraits gave him his first lessons.

He later studied with Gilbert Stuart in Boston and with Benjamin West in London. From 1810 he made Philadelphia his home for life. In 1837 he went back to London to paint Queen Victoria full length. His sitters ranged from Commodore Decatur to Thomas Jefferson and Lafayette. The entry ranks him among the best early painters of America.
britannica-1911-sutton-thomas:
Thomas Sutton, founder of Charterhouse school and hospital, who lived from about 1532 to 1611, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Son of a Lincoln official, he was schooled at Eton and most likely at Cambridge. He travelled in Europe and served great lords as secretary. Then he turned soldier, and in 1569 he helped put down the rising in the north of England.

In 1573 he took part in the siege of Edinburgh Castle. His wealth came from coal mines in Durham and from his marriage in 1582 to a rich widow. In 1611 he paid 13,000 pounds for the Charterhouse in London. On that spot he raised the hospital and school he had meant to build in Essex. He died at Hackney that year and was buried in the Charterhouse chapel, his wealth left to charity.
britannica-1911-sydenham-thomas:
Thomas Sydenham (1624-1689) was an English physician born in Dorset. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces broken study at Oxford due to civil war. He served as an officer for parliament before finishing his degree. A licence to practice in London came only in 1663 for him.

Fellow doctors distrusted him as a plain spoken innovator, it says. Letters quoted show barbs traded with peers who scorned new ideas. He still won warm friends among sharp minds of his day. His own claim was simple: few patients miscarried under his care. A late medical degree from Cambridge came in 1676, long after practice began.
britannica-1911-syntipas:
Syntipas is a literature article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a set of tales known in Europe as the Seven Wise Masters. Syntipas is the Greek form of Sindibad or Sendabar. He is cast as an Indian philosopher who lived near the year 100 before Christ. The tales went under his name.

They won immense popularity and appeared in many tongues of East and West. A Greek version, most likely from a Syriac one, survives from the eleventh century. It is the earliest specimen of Romaic prose. Its translator, plainly a Christian, kept most of the Oriental colour of the tales. The main frame is the same in all versions, though the tales inside it vary. A prince, bound to silence for a time on his tutor's advice, is tempted by his stepmother.
britannica-1911-szalay-ladislas:
Ladislas Szalay, a Hungarian lawmaker and writer of the past, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life note. Born at Buda in eighteen thirteen, he sat in the Hungarian diet after his studies. In eighteen forty eight he spoke for Hungary at the German diet in Frankfurt. He took part in the revolt of those years and had to flee. Safe in Switzerland, he wrote his past of Hungary there.

That work came out at Budapest in parts and runs to the year seventeen oh seven. He also wrote sharp studies of Pitt, Fox, and Mirabeau. Work on the law code of Hungary owes much to him, the text says. He came home in late life and died at Salzburg in eighteen sixty four.
britannica-1911-tallis-thomas:
Thomas Tallis, who lived from about fifteen o five to fifteen eighty five, is called the father of English cathedral music. He may have sung as a boy at old Saint Paul's in London. He is known to have been organist at Waltham Abbey. When that house was closed in fifteen forty, he got small sums for wages and reward. Not long after, he joined the Chapel Royal as a gentleman.

From that post Tallis worked hard for his art for the rest of his life. The entry says the English school owes him more than any other composer of his age. His early Service in the Dorian mode sets many church texts for four voices. Some parts use five voices instead.
britannica-1911-tanner-thomas:
Thomas Tanner, an English antiquary and bishop who lived from 1674 to 1735, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Market Lavington in Wiltshire and schooled at Queen's College, Oxford. He took holy orders in 1694 and became a fellow of All Souls College. He then served as chaplain to the bishop of Norwich.

Tanner rose to rector of Thorpe in 1706, canon of Ely in 1713, and bishop of Saint Asaph in 1732. His chief work is the Notitia Monastica, a short account of all the religious houses of England and Wales. It was printed at Oxford in 1695 and reprinted with additions twice. He also laboured forty years on a dictionary of authors of Britain and Ireland. It appeared only in 1748, after his death. His fine collection rests in the Bodleian Library.
britannica-1911-telford-thomas:
Thomas Telford, a British engineer of canals and works who lived from 1757 to 1834, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Westerkirk in Dumfriesshire, the son of a shepherd. As a boy he herded sheep and snatched what schooling he could. At fifteen he was put to a stonemason to learn the trade.

He taught himself Latin, French, and German in his spare hours, and wrote verse as a young man. Work on fine houses in Edinburgh and London trained his hand and eye. In 1793 he took charge of the Ellesmere canal in Wales. His great aqueducts for that work made his name as a canal engineer. The king of Sweden then sought his plans for the Göta Canal. He also took charge of the Caledonian Canal in Scotland.
britannica-1911-tenison-thomas:
Thomas Tenison, an English archbishop who lived from 1636 to 1715, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born at Cottenham on September 29, 1636. He went to Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, and took his degree in 1657. He was made a fellow two years later and was ordained in the same year.

As a vicar in Cambridge, Tenison cared for plague victims with great zeal. He later held posts at Norwich and at a large London parish. There he endowed schools, set up a public library, and kept many aides. He was a firm foe of the Church of Rome. That stand put him at the front of the fight in King James's reign.
britannica-1911-tiberias:
Tiberias is the subject of a town entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. The lake takes its modern Arabic name from the town. The entry gives its population as about four thousand, with more than half being Jews.

The town stands on a fertile but fever prone strip of plain between hills and shore. It was the seat of a sub governor under the governor of Akka. Latin and Greek hospices stood there, the entry notes. A Scottish mission ran a hospital and schools in the town. The early history of the city before Herod is treated as uncertain.
britannica-1911-tickell-thomas:
Tickell, Thomas, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of an English poet. Born at Bridekirk near Carlisle in 1686, he was a clergyman's son. He went to Queen's College at Oxford in the year 1701. He took his master's degree there in 1709 with credit.

He became a fellow of his college the next year after that. In 1711 he was made reader in poetry for the university. His rise in letters and life owed much to Addison's friendship. Addison got him a post as under-secretary of state in 1717. That gift stirred the anger of Richard Steele against him for good. In 1713 he brought out a poem called Prospect of Peace. In 1724 he took a top post in Ireland and kept it till death.
britannica-1911-tooke-thomas:
Thomas Tooke (1774-1858), an English economist, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at St Petersburg, he entered a large Russian trading house in London at an early age. There he gained sound practice in trade and became a known voice on finance and banking. He was one of the earliest backers of free trade.

The article says he drew up the petition of the merchants that was laid before the House of Commons. He gave evidence to several panels of Parliament, on foreign trade in 1821 and on the Bank Acts three times after. He was made a fellow of the Royal Society in 1821. His books attacked the policy later set in the Bank Act of 1844. He is best known for a history of prices and of the flow of money, in six books printed over near twenty years.
britannica-1911-torquemada-thomas:
Thomas Torquemada, chief judge of the faith courts of Spain, born in fourteen twenty, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a lord of a small town in Old Castile. He was born at Valladolid. He was the nephew of a famed church prince of the same name.

From his youth he felt a pull to a great order of friars. As soon as he was let, he joined that order in its house at Valladolid. His life books say he showed a strict life and a low bent from the start. Great posts were put to him in time. He gave signs that he would keep the plain life of a friar in spite of rank. In the house he said no to the top degree in church study.
britannica-1911-torres-vedras:
Torres Vedras is a town of Portugal in the district of Lisbon, north of the capital on a rail line. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its town count at the turn of the age. It stands on the left bank of a small river, and holds a Moorish fort and hot sulphur baths.

Old Roman texts and remains have been found there, though its Latin name is most likely of a later age. The town is famed in war annals for the lines that bear its name. A British general built that great chain of forts there to guard Lisbon in the wars with France. The piece closes with a later fight, when troops of one chief beat a rival force and took both castle and town.
britannica-1911-trevet-nicholas:
Nicholas Trevet was an English chronicler who lived from about twelve fifty eight. He died in about the year thirteen twenty eight. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The son of Sir Thomas Trevet, a judge, he became a Dominican friar.

Trevet studied at Oxford and in Paris, then spent his years writing. His chief work is Annales sex regum Angliae, a chronicle of English kings. It covers the years eleven thirty five to thirteen o seven in full. The work is prized most for the reigns of Henry the Third and Edward the First. Chaucer is thought to have drawn his Man of Law Tale from Trevet.
britannica-1911-tulsi-das:
Tulsi Das, the greatest and most famed of Hindi poets, lived from 1532 to 1623 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a Brahman born, by tradition, in 1532 in the reign of Humayun. Rajapur in the Banda district south of the Jumna is the most likely place. His father name and his mother name are both given in the entry.

Legend says his birth fell under an unlucky joining of the stars. His parents thus left him in infancy, and a wandering holy man took him in. With that guide he roamed to many holy places across the length and breadth of India. Parts of his own poems back that tale in some measure. He later studied, wed in his father lifetime, and had a son. His wife was a daughter of a man named in the text.
britannica-1911-tusser-thomas:
Thomas Tusser, an English poet of farm craft, gets a roving life in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Rivenhall in Essex near fifteen twenty four, he sang as a boy in a chapel choir. He was pressed for the King Chapel, then sang at Saint Paul in London. Hard school days at Eton left a droll tale in his verse. He won a place at King College in Cambridge in fifteen forty three.

Court work as a music man held him for ten years of his life. He then wed and took to farm life by the River Stour. His Hundred Good Points of Husbandry came out in fifteen fifty seven. Farm tries in more than one shire met with thin luck at best. He died in fifteen eighty with a small plot to his name.
britannica-1911-twining-thomas:
Thomas Twining (1735-1804) was an English classical scholar born at Twickenham. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes his father sold tea in London trade. Trade life repelled the son, so his father sent him to Cambridge instead. Sidney Sussex College made him a fellow in 1760 after study there.

Orders and marriage in 1764 fixed his life in Essex parishes from then. Fordham and Colchester were his homes till death in 1804 at home. His translation of Aristotle Poetics, with notes, built his fame in 1789. Music skill let him aid Charles Burney on his History of Music. Letters in print keep his country clergy life on record now.
britannica-1911-urquhart-sir-thomas:
Sir Thomas Urquhart, the Scots voice of Rabelais, is drawn in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1611, he was heir to an old house of Cromarty. Debt pressed his father hard all through the son's young years. The king gave the father a shield from his creditors in 1637. Young Thomas learned at King's College, Aberdeen, in his teens.

Spare hours went to the study of nature and its laws. Tours of Europe and a great library marked his next years. Creditors seized that library when his debts came due at last. A fierce Royalist, he fought in the Trot of Turriff rising. The king knighted him by his own hand in 1641. His first book of short poems came out that same year.
britannica-1911-ursinus-zacharias:
Zacharias Ursinus, a German theologian born at Breslau in fifteen thirty four, helped write the Heidelberg Catechism. He became a follower of Melanchthon at Wittenberg in his youth. Later he studied divinity at Geneva under Calvin himself. He also studied Hebrew at Paris under Jean Mercier. In fifteen sixty one he took a professor's chair at Heidelberg.

At the call of the elector Frederick the Third, Ursinus drew up the Catechism in fifteen sixty three. He worked on it with Kaspar Olevian at his side. When the elector died in fifteen seventy six, Ursinus lost his post. From fifteen seventy eight he held a chair at Neustadt until his death in fifteen eighty three. His works came out in print soon after he died.
britannica-1911-usas: Usas is a short myth entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She is the goddess of dawn in the old hymns of India. Some twenty hymns praise her as the most fair form in that song hoard. She rides a bright car drawn by red cows or bulls. She is the child of the sky, and the sun is her lover. The hymns say she cuts short the lives of men as she brings each day. Her name has all but died out with the old faith.
britannica-1911-vurjeevandas-madhowdas:
Vurjeevandas Madhowdas, a Hindu merchant of Bombay who lived from 1817 to 1896, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Gogia, in Kathiawar, of the Kapole Bania caste. His father came to Bombay for trade. The son was schooled in Bombay and set up a firm under the name Vurjeevandas and Sons.

He soon ranked among the richest merchants in Bombay. He was made a justice of the peace and a member of the Bombay Port Trust. He took a keen interest in the Royal Asiatic Society and in Bombay University. A prize there bears his name. He built the Madhow Bang in memory of his father. He gave it for the use of poor Hindus and endowed it with a large sum. The article shows wealth turned, in part, to public good.
britannica-1911-wakley-thomas:
Thomas Wakley, an English medical and social reformer who lived from 1793 to 1862, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Devonshire, he was apprenticed young to a Taunton apothecary, then went to London and qualified as a surgeon. He set up in Regent Street and wed a woman whose father governed Saint Thomas's Hospital.

Wakley's career had a violent start. In August 1820 a gang with a grudge burned his house and wounded him badly in a murderous attack. He was even suspected, wrongly, of setting the fire himself, but he beat the insurance firm that fought his claim. A friend of William Cobbett, whose radical views he shared, Wakley started the medical weekly the Lancet in 1823. In its pages he attacked the jobbery of the day, printed hospital lectures against the doctors' wishes, and exposed bad practice, fighting lawsuits that only grew his sway.
britannica-1911-walsingham-thomas:
Thomas Walsingham (died about 1422) was an English chronicler, and a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry records what is known of him. He was likely schooled at the abbey of St Albans and at Oxford. He became a monk at St Albans and passed most of his life there. For six years, from 1394 to 1400, he was prior of a Benedictine house at Wymondham in Norfolk.

At St Albans Walsingham had charge of the scriptorium, the writing room of the abbey. His chief work is the Historia Anglicana, a valued chronicle. It covers the years from 1272 to 1422. Some scholars hold that he wrote only the part from 1377 to 1392 himself. That view is disputed by James Gairdner, who is cited in the entry. The chronicle stays a key source for its period.
britannica-1911-webster-thomas:
Thomas Webster is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a British student of rocks born in the Orkney Isles in seventeen seventy three. He was schooled at Aberdeen and then trained in building design in London. One famed hall in the city was built from his plan.

The entry tells how he served a London society of rock scholars for years. He edited and drew for its journal and kept its collections in order. His own field work traced young rock beds on an island off the south coast. He showed how fresh water and sea beds lay mixed in those strata. A mineral found in his field bears his name to this day.
britannica-1911-werner-friedrich-ludwig-:
Zacharias Werner was a German poet, stage writer, and preacher born at Konigsberg in Prussia. From his mother, who died with her mind lost in faith, he took a weak and unstaid nature. His schooling did nothing to mend that flaw, the 1911 Britannica entry says in plain terms.

He read law at the college of his home town. The works of a French thinker and his German followers shaped his view of life more than law did. For years he swung hard between two poles. One was a lust for a state of nature, which led him into a run of rash and sad wed locks. The other was a fond love of the Church of Rome, shared by many of his school, which ended in his change of faith. His gift won him a state post in spite of his name.
britannica-1911-wilson-sir-robert-thomas:
Wilson, Sir Robert Thomas is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a British general. The son of the painter Benjamin Wilson, he was commissioned in 1794 and fought at Villers-en-Cauchies. He was one of eight officers to receive the emperor's special medal, with the order of Maria Theresa. In the campaigns in Flanders and Holland he repeatedly made his mark.

The article follows a career of soldiering and writing. Wilson served in Ireland, fought at Alexandria, and published an account of the Egyptian expedition. He wrote an early protest against flogging in the army. He served at the Cape, watched the battles of Eylau and Friedland as an attache in Prussia, and raised the Lusitanian Legion in Portugal. In 1812 he joined the Russian pursuit of the retreating French, and his account of it is highly valued.
britannica-1911-wolsey-thomas:
English cardinal and statesman Thomas Wolsey, born at Ipswich about fourteen seventy five, opens a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His father sold meat and other goods, and held some property. Town records show the father fined often, for stray pigs, bad meat, and like breaches of town rules.

Thomas was schooled at Magdalen College, Oxford. Details of his time there are not clear, the entry warns. College registers are flawed for those years. He is said to have taken his first degree at age fifteen. His first firm record is as junior bursar of the college in fourteen ninety eight. He rose to senior bursar the next year. He had to quit that post for using funds to finish the great tower without full leave.
britannica-1911-wright-silas:
Silas Wright, who lived from 1795 to 1847, was an American political leader from New York. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born at Amherst on the twenty-fourth of May 1795. He took his degree at Middlebury College in 1815 and joined the bar in 1819. He set up practice at Canton in the north of New York state. Posts came in quick order after that.

Wright sat in the state senate, then in the national House, then as state comptroller. He served in the Senate of the United States from 1833 to 1844, then as governor of New York. He led the state Democrats with Martin Van Buren in the group called the Albany Regency. As governor he used armed force to end the anti-rent rising of 1845.
britannica-1911-zumalacarregui-thomas:
Thomas Zumalacárregui (1788-1835) was a Spanish Carlist general, born at Ormaiztegui in Navarre, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. His father was a lawyer with some property, and the son was articled to a solicitor. When the French invasion came in 1808, he enlisted at Saragossa.

Zumalacárregui served in the first siege there, at the battle of Tudela, and through the second siege until taken prisoner in a sortie. He escaped and reached his family in Navarre, and for a short time served with a minor guerrilla leader known as the Shepherd. Grave and silent by nature, and strong in his faith, he disliked the disorderly life of the guerrillas. When regular forces were raised in the north he entered the first battalion of Guipuzcoa as an officer, and served in the regular army for the rest of that war.
camille-la-dame-aux-camilias:
Alexandre Dumas fils opens Camille by confessing he is not old enough to invent characters, so he will narrate a true story instead. The narrator buys a keepsake at the auction of a dead courtesan's effects, then learns from her lover Armand Duval how Marguerite Gautier lived and loved. The lady of the camellias becomes literature's most famous consumptive heroine.

Armand's father forces their separation, Marguerite sacrifices herself in silence, and letters written on her deathbed reach Armand too late. Dumas turned the novel into the play that made his fortune; Verdi's La Traviata remade it as opera. This English text, plainly translated, keeps the twenty-seven chapters' direct, tearful momentum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abdias:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Abdias treats a minor prophet whose name comes from Greek for Hebrew Obadiah, meaning Yahweh's servant or worshipper. The fourth and shortest minor prophetic book, with just twenty-one verses, bears Abdias' name.

In the book's title the name is usually taken as a proper name. Some recent scholars treat it as an appellative, since Scripture often calls a true prophet the servant of Yahweh. Scripture gives no distinct information about this writer. Nothing is known of Abdias' family, station, birthplace or manner of death, the entry stresses, beyond the inference from his work that he belonged to the Kingdom of Judah.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achimaas:
Achimaas is the name of two or three biblical figures, and this entry sorts them out. First, he was father of Achinoam, wife of Saul. Second, as son of Sadoc the priest, he served David as a swift-footed messenger during Absalom's rebellion. He brought news of enemy movements from Jerusalem, and after the battle where Absalom was slain, he was first to reach the king with news of victory.

David called him a good man. This Achimaas may be Solomon's prefect of Nephtali, the king's son-in-law. The entry thus links a messenger's speed to a court career, while marking the identification of the prefect with the messenger as probable rather than certain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acuas:
Acuas pioneered Manicheism's spread in the Christian Orient. Probably a Mesopotamian by birth, he introduced the heresy into Eleutheropolis in Palestine. The Manichaeans were sometimes called Acuanitae after him, a mark of how closely his name stuck to the movement he carried into Palestine and beyond.

St. Epiphanius calls him a veteranus, an imperial ex-soldier, dating his propaganda to the fourth regnal year of Aurelian, 273. The entry cites Cowell in the Dictionary of Christian Biography, and its short compass rests on that single patristic witness alone for date and career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-addas:
Addas ranked among Manes's three original disciples. According to the Acts of Archelaus, he carried Manes's heretical teachings into Scythia, later taking a similar mission East. He was also commissioned to collect Christian books, a task that set him travelling with a purpose beyond preaching.

Cyril of Jerusalem calls him Baddas, while Photius cites a work of his, entitled Modion, from Mark 4:21, which Diodorus of Tarsus refuted. Also mentioned: Addas and Adimantus's work against Moses and the Prophets. The entry cites Cowell in the Dictionary of Christian Biography, and its brief record rests on patristic witnesses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adonias:
Adonias, Hebrew Adoniyah, meaning Yahweh is Lord, was King David's fourth son, born in Hebron during his father's sojourn there. Nothing is known of Adonias until his father's last days, when he suddenly emerged as a competitor for the crown. He was then thirty-five and comely in appearance.

Since Absalom's death he ranked next in succession by birth, and he hoped to secure the throne as his father's death drew near. A younger son, Solomon, stood in his ambition's way, since the aged king had chosen Solomon, son of Bethsabee, as successor. Relying on his father's past indulgence and present weakness, Adonias built a quasi-royal state around chariots, horses, and fifty footmen. He then won Joab and the religious leaders to his cause. The entry follows his bid, defeat, and death, and notes a Levite of the same name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agathias:
Agathias, Byzantine historian and man of letters, was born about 536 at Myrina in Asia Minor. He died at Constantinople in 582, or 594 by some accounts. He is a principal authority for Justinian's reign from 527 to 565 and is often quoted by church historians. Probably educated at Constantinople, he spent time at Alexandria, returning to the royal city in 554 to take up law and become a successful pleader at the bar.

Literary tastes, however, soon had him producing nine books of erotic poetry, the Daphniaca, plus epigrams and sonnets, many preserved in the Palatine Anthology. He also wrote marginal notes on Pausanias's Periegetes. Last in whom sparks of classic epigram fire can be traced, he turned at thirty to history. He composed five books On the Reign of Justinian, covering 552 to 558, on wars with Goths, Vandals, Franks, Persians, and Huns. He continues Procopius, a poet beside Procopius the soldier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alagoas:
Alagoas, a South American diocese in eastern Brazil, depends on Bahia. By Leo XIII's decree of 2 July 1900 it left the Diocese of Olinda. The state of Alagoas forms it, bordered by Pernambuco to the north and northwest, the Atlantic to the southeast, and Sergipe to the southwest. Its area is 22,583 square miles, with a population of 648,009 counted in 1890.

Monsignor Castilho de Brandao, the first bishop, lives in the capital city, Maceio, a town of 12,000 inhabitants. He was consecrated at Belem de Para on 7 September 1894 and transferred to this see on 5 June 1901.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ampurias:
An Italian diocese in Sardinia, suffragan of Sassari, Ampurias also bears the names Castelsardo and Tempio. The see of Civita, now Tempio, dates to 304 through Saint Simplicius, while Ampurias itself was erected in 1113. Julius II united Civita to Ampurias in 1506. Gregory XVI later raised the collegiate church of Saint Peter in Tempio to a cathedral.

After a vacancy from 1854 to 1871, the united diocese came under Bishop Antonio Maria Contini, transferred here in 1893. Ampurias counted 11,200 Catholics in eight parishes with twenty-five secular priests. Tempio counted 26,200 Catholics in seventeen parishes with forty-four priests, a portrait of a small Sardinian church at the turn of the century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
Strengnas, in Sweden, covered Nykoping, Stockholm south of Lake Malar, and the southern half of Orebro. In 829 Saint Anschar and Witmar reached Bjorkoe, or Birca, an island trading centre on Lake Malar, and were welcomed, making many converts. Anschar returned to Germany in 831 as first Archbishop of Hamburg. Ebbo's relative Gautbert built a church at Bjorkoe, but heathens drove him out in 837 and slew his relative Nithard.

Anschar sent Ardgeir in 844, though he stayed briefly, and revisited Bjorkoe in 853, when a law tolerating Christianity passed. Rimbert worked there until 865. Unni visited in 936 and died there. The city was destroyed in 1066. About 1080 Saint Eskil, an English bishop, was killed for disturbing a heathen sacrifice at Strengas. Botvid, a native convert, preached until his murder. Laurentius Andreae taught Lutheranism at Strengnas. Bishop Gregerson was beheaded in the Stockholm massacre of 1520, and Magnus Sommar, from 1528 to 1536, closed the Catholic line.

In Sweden, Westeraas covered Vestmanland, Stora Kopparberg, and Fellingsbro in Orebro. Its see began at Munktorp. The English Cluniac Saint David moved it to Westeraas about 1100, not 1050; he had been Munktorp's abbot, became its bishop, and is a patron of its cathedral. Before 1118, Sigtuna was split into Upsala and Westeraas, and Henry, Sigtuna's bishop in 1134, moved to Westeraas.

Pagan worship survived to 1182. Charles, bishop from 1257 to 1277, gave generously, and Israel Erlandsson, bishop from 1309 to 1332, mined Dalecarlian copper and wrote Saint Eric's life and miracles. Otto, bishop from 1501 to 1522, finished it. Peter Sunnanvader, bishop from 1522 to 1523 and once Sten Sture's chancellor, was executed for alleged treason in 1527. The last Catholic bishop, Petrus Magni, served from 1524 to 1534, consecrated at Rome in 1524. In 1527 the Diet of Westeraas made the Swedish church Protestant and cut it from Rome, yet Magni kept his see until death, consecrating bishops under protest in 1528 and 1531.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andres-perez-:
Andres Perez de Ribas, pioneer missionary and historian of northwestern Mexico, was born at Cordova in Spain in 1576 and died in Mexico in 1655. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1602, came to America, and finished his novitiate in Mexico in 1604. In the same year he was sent to Christianize the Ahome and Suaqui of northern Sinaloa, the former friendly, the latter just subdued after a hard campaign.

Within a year he had both tribes in towns, each with a well-built church, and most baptized. In 1613, as Sinaloa superior, he helped subdue a hostile mountain tribe. In 1617 he began converting the powerful Yaqui of Sonora, gathering most into towns within a few years. Recalled to Mexico in 1620, he became provincial. After a visit to Rome in 1643 he turned to study and writing. His reputation rests on his history of the Jesuit missions of Mexico, published at Madrid in 1645.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-annas:
Annas, son of Seth, succeeded Joazar as high-priest in A.D. 6 or 7, appointed by Quirinius, come to Judea for Archelaus's territory. Deposed in A.D. 15 by Valerius Gratus, he was followed by Ismael, Eleazar, son of Annas, and Simon, until Joseph Caiaphas, who retained Roman favour from A.D. 18 to 36. But deposition did not end his ascendency: five sons became high-priests, and Caiaphas was his son-in-law.

References to Annas and Caiaphas as joint high-priests, or to Annas alone as high-priest, have given rise to many hypotheses. They are not strictly accurate, but they testify to his ascendency. Annas is more than a chronological landmark. According to John's common text, after His arrest the Lord is brought directly to Annas, in whose palace an unofficial, preliminary interrogatory takes place. The Synoptists omit this episode entirely. The common text here seems disturbed, as Maldonatus remarked.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-de-he:
Spanish historian Antonio de Herrera y Tordesillas was born at Cuellar in 1559 and dead at Madrid in 1625. He served three kings as grand historiographer, or chief historian, of America and Castile. After study in Spain and Italy and secretarial work for Vespasiano Gonzaga, Philip II gave him the post. He held it through the reign of Philip III and into that of Philip IV. His body was taken back to Cuellar for burial in the church of Santa Marina.

His most famous work is the General History of the Deeds of the Castilians on the Islands and Mainland of the Ocean Sea. It covers 1472 to 1554 in eight blocks of ten years each. Printed at Madrid in 1601 and reprinted and revised in later editions, it remains the article's centrepiece. The entry suits readers who want the official chronicler of Spain's American enterprise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aristeas: Aristeas is the name Josephus gives to the author of a letter. It ascribes the Old Testament's Greek translation to six interpreters sent from Jerusalem into Egypt at the request of Alexandria's librarian. The letter is the usual account behind the Septuagint version, the Greek Old Testament. Josephus cites it in his Antiquities, and the entry points readers to the article on the Septuagint for the fuller story of that translation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arkansas:
Arkansas, one of the United States, lies between Missouri to the north and Louisiana and Texas to the south. Mississippi and Tennessee lie to the east, and Texas and Indian Territory to the west. It covers 53,335 square miles between latitudes 33 and 37 north and longitudes 89 and 95 west. Its boundaries are set out in detail in the state constitution, beside the Act of Congress of 15 June 1836 that admitted Arkansas as a state. Its motto is Regnant populi, the people rule.

Its name came from a tribe of Indians, called Quapaws or Ozarks and Alkansas by Illinois Indians and other Algonquins. A General Assembly resolution of 1881, noting confusion over pronunciation, ruled that the name be spoken in three syllables. Its final s stays silent, and the a in each syllable sounds alike. The long article moves from borders and name to history, government, and Catholic life in the state.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-armella-nicol:
Armella Nicolas, popularly called La bonne Armelle, the good Armelle, was a holy French serving maid held in high veneration by the people, though never canonized by Rome. Born at Campénéac in Brittany on 9 September 1606 to poor peasants George Nicolas and Francisca Neant, she died on 24 October 1671. Her youth passed in the pious, simple life of hard-working country folk.

At twenty-two her parents wanted her to marry, but she chose service in nearby Ploërmel, where she found more scope for pious works and spiritual needs. After some years she moved to Vannes, served several families, and spent a year and a half as portress at the Ursuline monastery. There she befriended Sister Jeanne de la Nativité, telling her details of her spiritual life. Jeanne noted them down and later shaped them into Armella's life, since Armella herself could neither read nor write.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arras:
Arras, in Latin Atrebatum, is a diocese covering the Pas-de-Calais department in France. At the Concordat, the dioceses of Arras, Saint-Omer, and Boulogne merged into one Arras diocese. It answered to Paris from 1802 to 1841, when Cambrai became an archdiocese again and Arras returned to it as suffragan. Early in the sixth century Remi of Reims placed Vedastus, or Vaast, teacher of Clovis after Tolbiac, in the Arras see, where he died about 540.

His successors Dominicus and Vedulphus are both honoured as saints, and after Vedulphus's death the see moved to Cambrai, returning to Arras only in 1093. Later bishops include Cardinal Antoine Perrenot de Granvelle, councillor to Charles V, bishop from 1545 to 1562 and afterwards archbishop of Malines and viceroy of Naples. Another is François Richardot, celebrated preacher, bishop from 1562 to 1575.
