catholic-encyclopedia-1913-association-o:
Association of ideas is, first, a principle in psychology accounting for the succession of mental states, and second, the basis of a philosophy called Associationism. The fact was noted by some of the first philosophers. Aristotle indicates three laws of association that underlie nearly all later lists, and Thomas Aquinas, commenting on Aristotle, accepts and illustrates them at length. Hamilton gives great credit to the Spanish humanist Vives, who lived from 1492 to 1540, for his treatment of the topic.

Association is therefore not a discovery of English psychology, as often claimed, though English psychology gave it an interpretation never given before. The name comes from Locke, who headed a chapter of his Essay with it but used it only to explain peculiarities in character. Applied to mental states in general, it became a system explaining memory, habit, and thought by linked ideas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-athenagoras:
Athenagoras, a Christian apologist of the later second century, is known only as an Athenian philosopher converted to Christianity. Only two genuine pieces survive: his Apology, or Embassy for the Christians, plus a Treatise on the Resurrection. Early Christian literature mentions him only in accredited quotations from his Apology within a fragment of Methodius of Olympus, who died in 312. It also mentions him in untrustworthy biographical details in Philip of Side's Christian History, about 425.

His treatises may have circulated anonymously for a time and been taken for another apologist's work. His writings show erudition and culture, power as philosopher and rhetorician, keen grasp of his age's intellectual temper, and tact and delicacy in handling powerful opponents of his religion. The Apology's date is fixed by internal evidence, and the entry presents a learned Athenian pleading for Christians before emperors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auguste-nicol:
Auguste Nicolas was a French apologist, a defender of Christianity, born at Bordeaux in 1807 who died at Versailles in 1888. He studied law, entered the magistracy, and served as justice of the peace at Bordeaux from 1841 to 1849. From 1842 he published apologetic writings that soon made his name known among Catholics. In 1849 he joined the ministry of worship to run church property business, later became inspector general of libraries, and ended as councillor at the Paris appeals court.

His books defended Christianity as a whole and in its chief dogmas, fitted to the minds of his time. He argued from philosophy, good sense, and authority, but also from tradition and the groping moral sense of mankind. The entry faults him fairly: his testimonies were often apocryphal, his reading of them uncritical, and his apologetics soon dated as critical studies revived. His works also show, at times, the layman without full theological training.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-banaias:
Banaias, Hebrew for 'Jehovah hath built up,' names several Bible men, the most famous being Joiada's priest-son. He ranked most valiant among the thirty and captained the third company for the third month. He seems to have been both priest and principal officer at David's court. A text naming Joiada as Banaias's son may swap the two names by false reading.

Banaias won fame by three feats of strength and courage. He slew two lion-like Moabite champions, killed a lion in a pit, and vanquished a giant Egyptian hero. He commanded the king's guards, the Cerethi and Phelethi, and sat on David's council, though short of the first three. He backed Solomon's throne claim against Adonias's intrigues, then put Adonias to death at Solomon's command.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartolomeu-di:
Bartolomeu Dias was a famous Portuguese navigator and discoverer of the Cape of Good Hope, who died at sea in 1500. By 1481 he had sailed to the Gold Coast with Diogo d'Azambuja, and he served as court cavalier, warehouse superintendent, and sailing-master. On 10 October 1486, John II named him head of an expedition to sail around Africa's southern end. Its chief purpose was to reach Prester John, the Christian African king of recent report.

After ten months' preparation, he left Lisbon in late July or early August 1487 with two fifty-ton caravels and a supply ship. His brother Pero commanded the supply ship, and interpreters were carried to explain the expedition to coastal peoples. Sailing past the Congo's mouth, he followed the coast to Walfisch Bay. No official report of the cape expedition has been found; Barros's account and a Columbus-owned manuscript note remain key sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-book-of-miche:
The Book of Micheas, sixth among the Twelve Minor Prophets, gathers the preaching of Micheas of Moresheth, a contemporary of Isaiah. Born near Geth, he ministered at Jerusalem under Kings Joathan, Achaz, and Ezechias, roughly 740 to 698 before Christ, though no addresses survive from before Ezechias. His book falls into three parts, each treated in turn.

Chapters one to three announce Samaria's fall for its sins, threaten Jerusalem, and rebuke prophets, priests, princes, and judges, ending with Sion ploughed as a field. Chapters four to five promise the nations' conversion to Yahweh's law and a Messianic peace, with a king born at Bethlehem-Ephrata. The final chapters, debated by critics over post-exilic origin, complete a prophet whom Jeremiah's defenders later cited, since Ezechias repented at his word and Jerusalem was spared.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-book-of-tobia:
The Book of Tobias opens by sorting out the several men named Tobias, then treats the canonical book itself. Earlier Tobias figures include a Levite sent to teach in Juda and a returnee from Babylon bearing silver and gold for a crown. Others are a family that could not prove its genealogy, an Ammonite foe of Nehemiah's wall, and the father of Hircanus. Chief among them stands Tobias the Elder, hero of the book that bears his name.

In the Vulgate and some Hebrew texts, father and son share the name Tobias, while Greek versions call the father Tobit. The original text, thought to be Hebrew, is lost, and an Aramaic version likely shaped the Greek texts we hold. Jerome, not yet knowing Aramaic, made the Vulgate with a rabbi versed in both Aramaic and Hebrew, rendering the tale into Latin for the Western Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-british-hondu:
British Honduras, a vicariate matching the Crown colony of 7,562 square miles, about the size of New Jersey, holds some 40,000 people, 23,500 of them Catholic. It lies south of Yucatan across the Rio Hondo, facing the Bay of Honduras, with Guatemala to south and west. Only about 14,000 Catholics are reached with regularity by the vicar and his Jesuit helpers.

Eight churches with resident priests and fifty-five chapels serve the vicariate under Frederick Hopkins, titular Bishop of Athribis, with six Jesuit priests, four clerics, and four lay brothers from Missouri province. English buccaneers settled it without legal right in the 1600s, and it passed from Trinidad's vicariate to Jamaica's in 1836. Seven thousand Yucatan refugees in 1848 swelled its Catholic flock and brought Jesuit missionaries in their wake.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brother-azari:
Brother Azarias, born Patrick Francis Mullany near Killenaule in 1847, became a leading American Catholic educator, essayist, and philosopher. Schooled at home, in Deerfield, New York, and at Utica's Christian Brothers Academy, he entered the Brothers of the Christian Schools at New York in 1862. He taught at Albany, New York, and Philadelphia, then held the mathematics and literature chair at Rock Hill College from 1866.

President of Rock Hill from 1879 to 1886, he spent two years researching in Paris and London libraries. He then taught literature at De La Salle Institute until his death at Plattsburgh in 1893. His funeral at Saint Patrick's Cathedral showed his wide influence. He wrote for the Catholic World and the American Catholic Quarterly, lectured on Aristotle, church and state, and religion in education, and died preparing a History of Education.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-candlemas:
Candlemas, also called the Purification of the Blessed Virgin and the Presentation of Christ in the Temple, is kept on 2 February in the Latin Rite. Under the Mosaic law a mother kept forty days of purification after a son's birth, then brought a lamb and a dove to the temple. Forty days after Christ's birth Mary kept this law, redeemed her first-born, and received purification through Simeon's prayer, with Anna the prophetess present.

Jerusalem kept the feast early, and the pilgrim Egeria attests it in the first half of the fourth century as the fortieth day after Epiphany, with a procession and homily. It spread through the Church and settled on 2 February once Rome's Christmas feast of 25 December took hold. Justinian imposed it across the Eastern Empire in 542 in thanks for the end of a great plague at Constantinople.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canelos-and-m:
Canelos and Macas is a vicariate apostolic in Ecuador, split from Napo in 1886 and since 1893 one of four missionary vicariates under Leo XIII's concordat with Ecuador. Dominicans run it, having sent the first missionaries soon after the Spanish conquest. It answers to the Congregation of Extraordinary Ecclesiastical Affairs, not to Propaganda.

Canelos town, in the Andean foothills near the Bobonaza springs, takes its name from the cinnamon plant growing thickly there, and dates from the first conquest, though natives often destroyed it. Macas, farther south on the Upano, was once Sevilla del Oro for its gold mines, but fell into decay when native attacks forced the mines' abandonment. Missionaries gather orphans of Indians killed in tribal wars and teach them trades, building Christian settlements.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-capitolias:
Capitolias was a titular see of Palestine under Scythopolis in Palestina Secunda, a city of the Decapolis. Its coin era begins in 97 or 98, placing its founding under Nerva or Trajan. Geographers from Hierocles to Georgius Cyprius mention it. Lequien lists six of its bishops across the fourth to seventh centuries.

Antiochus attended Nicaea in 325 and Ananias attended Chalcedon in 451. The last named, Peter, is said to have died at Saracen hands, though he seems to have been only a priest of the city. By the twelfth century the see ranked as an independent archbishopric. Fourteenth- and fifteenth-century Latin titulars are also recorded. Ruins at Bet-er-Ras near Irbid are now identified as the site.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caracas:
Caracas is the metropolitan archdiocese of Venezuela, with Barquisimeto, Calabozo, Guayana, Mérida, and Zulia as suffragan sees. The see dates from 1530, soon after the Spanish conquest. It kept its residence at Coro until 1637, stood vacant from 1721 to 1727, and rose to archdiocesan rank in 1803. Archbishop Juan Bautista Castro, named in 1904, was its eighth metropolitan and thirty-fourth bishop.

The city, founded in 1567 by Diego Losada, sits at the foot of the Silla de Caracas and links to La Guaira by a twenty-three-mile railway. Earthquakes have battered it, one in 1812 killing 12,000 people, and Drake plundered and burned it in 1595 before Bishop Manzanillo rebuilt the cathedral of Santa Anna. A university founded in 1822 and a recent Eucharistic Congress mark a church the entry still calls Catholic at heart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-casas:
Bartolomé de las Casas was born at Seville, probably in 1474, and died at Madrid in 1566. His family came from France to Seville, and his father sailed with Columbus on the second voyage. Bartolomé studied law at Salamanca before Ovando took him to Hispaniola in 1502. He became a secular priest in 1510, after winning the trust of the island governors. He turned his life to the condition of the Indians under Spanish rule.

His schemes met failure in Venezuela, yet the Crown still gave him chances, and he took up the Bishopric of Chiapas in southern Mexico. Though he did not draft the New Laws for the Indies of 1542, those enactments owed much to his influence with government and clergy. His Brevísima Relación of 1552, a passionate and one-sided account of Indian destruction, shows an advocacy that grew only fiercer with age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chachapoyas:
Chachapoyas is a Peruvian diocese founded by Pius VII in 1803 as Chachapoyas and Maynas. Gregory XVI made it a suffragan to Lima in 1843 under the shorter name of Chachapoyas. The change of name marks the diocese's settled place in the Peruvian church, no longer joined in title to the Maynas region.

The diocese counts about 96,000 souls divided into 45 parishes. Its episcopal city, also called Chachapoyas, holds about 6,000 people and possesses a fine cathedral. The whole entry is a compact statistical portrait: foundation, metropolitan link, parishes, population, and cathedral, without a longer history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-l-a-t:
A musical biography of Charles Thomas, the French composer best remembered for the operas Mignon and Hamlet. Born at Metz in 1811, he won the Paris Conservatoire's Grand Prix in 1832 after prizes for piano and harmony. He then spent years writing ballets, motets, short sacred songs, and a requiem mass. Comic opera brought him wider notice, and in 1852 he became professor of composition at the Conservatoire.

Mignon, staged in 1866, won him the opera-going public, and Hamlet followed in 1868 as a five-act work. On the death of Auber in 1871 he became director of the Conservatoire, a post he held until his death in 1896. Sacred pieces such as his Solemn Mass of 1857 sit alongside the stage works, and the entry credits his dramatic instinct while judging him just short of the first rank.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-stant:
An entry on Charles Stanton Devas, an English political economist who treated economics from a Catholic standpoint. Born at Woodside in 1848 to Protestant parents, he was received into the Catholic Church before Oxford, earning a first class in law and history at Balliol College. His career was devoted to religion, and he was among the first to oppose an economics that ignored history and ethics.

Devas published The Groundwork of Economics in 1883 and the Manual of Political Economy in 1892, a textbook used in English-speaking schools and seminaries. Studies in Family Life of 1886 argued that Christianity is essential to social well-being, and his last book, The Key to the World's Progress of 1906, defended the faith directly. He wrote often for the Dublin Review and the Month, spoke before learned societies, and died in 1906, a loss felt keenly amid the controversies raised by Socialism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chiapas:
In southern Mexico, the Diocese of Chiapas covers almost the whole state of that name. Its seat is San Cristóbal de Las Casas, once called Ciudad Real, and it borders the dioceses of Guatemala, Tabasco, and Tehuantepec. Erected in April 1538 by Pope Paul III, it became the centre of a successful missionary movement through its first bishop, the great Bartolomé de Las Casas.

The baptismal register begins in 1541, and Dominican brothers gathered the Indians into settlements. They taught them crafts they still practise and Christian doctrine in their own tongue. The diocese has since been ruled by thirty-six bishops. Its life, as recorded, includes a cathedral chapter of seven canons, fifteen secular priests, and six Jesuits in the city. A seminary, a Marist primary school, a girls' school run by the Sisters of Divine Providence, a good cathedral, and nineteen other churches complete the picture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chibchas:
An entry on the Chibchas, also called Muyscas, the settled Indian peoples of the highlands of Colombia. Next to the Quechuas of Peru and the Aymaras of Bolivia, they were the most striking of the settled peoples of South America. They held the present departments of Boyacá and Cundinamarca in the early sixteenth century. Today they no longer form autonomous tribes and are practically extinct as a distinct people.

Chibcha lore tells of Bochica, an old man from the eastern plains who taught a new way of life at Sogamoso. Their religion mixed belief in many spirits with offerings of gold, emeralds, and crops. Shamans acted as healers, diviners, and oracles, while councils ruled each tribe and an elected war chief led in battle. About 1470 the people of Bogotá rose against Tunja, and by 1538 the Spaniards under Quesada had virtually conquered them, seizing great wealth in gold and emeralds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christmas:
An entry on Christmas, the feast of Christ's birth, tracing its name, its early celebration, and its customs. The Old English word, Cristes Maesse, meaning the Mass of Christ, is first found in 1038, while French Noël comes from Latin Dies Natalis, birthday, and German Weihnachtsfest from the sacred vigil. Christmas was not among the earliest feasts: Irenaeus and Tertullian omit it, and Origen notes that Scripture shows sinners, not saints, marking birthdays.

The first evidence comes from Egypt about the year 200, when Clement of Alexandria records theologians dating the birth to May or April. Basilidian Christians kept Epiphany with the Nativity on 6 or 10 January, and the December feast reached Egypt between 427 and 433. The entry follows the feast through Cyprus, Mesopotamia, Armenia, and Asia Minor, weighing rival dates and the customs that gathered around the December celebration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cleophas:
Cleophas, in Catholic English versions, names two persons in the New Testament. In Greek the names differ: Cleopas, short for Cleopatros, and Clopas. The first, Cleopas, was one of two disciples meeting the risen Lord at Emmaus. The second, Clopas, appears in John, where a Mary is called Mary of Clopas, generally translated as Mary the wife of Clopas.

Many think Clopas the Greek form of Alphaeus. They identify Mary, mother of James, with Mary, wife of Clopas, and thus Alphaeus with Clopas. Heth rarely becomes Kappa at a word's beginning. Clopas would suppose Halophai rather than Halpai. Syriac versions render Clopas with Qoph, not Heth. Others see Clopas as a substitute for Cleopas, with eo contracted to o, as Mishnic Hebrew renders Cleopatra by Clopatra. Even if the names differ, one man may have borne both, and the identity of Alphaeus and Clopas remains open.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cosmas:
Cosmas of Jerusalem, an eighth-century hymn-writer of the Greek Church, grew up as foster-brother to St John of Damascus. The two boys shared a Sicilian teacher, also named Cosmas, then became monks together at St Sabas near Jerusalem. In 743 Cosmas left the monastery to serve as bishop of Maiuma, Gaza's port.

Learned prose comments on Gregory of Nazianzus sit beside the poetry for which Greek worship remembers him. His canons, artistic liturgical chants, began as adornments for Jerusalem services and spread through Constantinople's influence across the Orthodox Church. Not every hymn bearing his name is certainly his, since his teacher wrote hymns too.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-a:
A short reference entry gathers the church councils held at Arras, a town in northern France. It explains what each meeting set out to settle. Written for the Catholic Encyclopedia, it treats these gatherings as local moments when bishops defined belief and ordered church life. They were not grand assemblies of the whole Church.

Its focus falls on two moments. A council in 1025 confronted heretics who rejected the sacraments, with special insistence on Catholic belief in the Eucharist. Two councils in 1097, led by Lambert of Arras, dealt with monasteries and with men and women dedicated to God. Readers looking for a quick, dated outline of Arras will find the essentials here, with sources cited for further checking.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dallas:
A diocesan entry presents Dallas, created in 1890 for 108 counties of northern and north-western Texas plus El Paso, covering one hundred and eighteen thousand square miles. The city of Dallas, population 95,000, stands at the centre of a circle holding nearly half of Texas's people. Settled chiefly from Kentucky, Illinois, and Indiana, it grew rich on cotton and minerals as a distributing centre.

As late as 1868 only one Catholic family lived there, served as a mission from Collin County by Father Joseph Martinere, whose visits crossed hundreds of miles of swamp and forest. By 1892 the diocese held 15,000 Catholics and 30 priests. Its first bishop, Thomas Francis Brennan, born in Tipperary in 1853, was consecrated in 1891 and transferred to Newfoundland two years later. By 1908 the diocese counted 60,000 Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-deo-gratias:
A liturgical entry on Deo Gratias, Latin for thanks be to God, an old formula of gratitude in the Latin Church. Scripture gives the words in Paul's letters to Corinth, and the Mass uses them as the server's answer to Epistle and Prophecies. Breviary use is wider still, answering lessons in Matins and short readings in Prime and Compline.

Rules carve out exceptions, such as Ember Saturday, Good Friday, and Holy Saturday, where the flow of the rite must not break. Greek churches do not pair the formula with the Epistle, and Mozarabic and Old Gallican use places it after the lesson title. Outside worship the phrase even became a name, borne by a bishop of Carthage and by the deacon addressed in Augustine's teaching treatise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-covarru:
Diego Covarruvias was born at Toledo in 1512. He became a professor of canon law at Salamanca at twenty-one and was later charged with reforming that old university. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry calls him the Bartholo of Spain. It praises a legal mind whose learning was matched by beauty of phrasing and clearness of style.

His writings ranged across civil and canon law, and he took part in the Council of Trent. He left a treatise on punishments and a catalogue of the kings of Spain. The entry also notes his wide reading in the sciences that bear on law. His work shaped Spanish courts long after his death at Madrid in 1577.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dionysias:
Dionysias was a titular see in Arabia, named in the lists of Hierocles and Georgius Cyprius. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry counts three Greek bishops, at Nicaea in 325, at Constantinople in 381, and at Chalcedon in 451. A fourth, Peter, is known from an inscription, and fifteen or sixteen Latin titular bishops appear through the fifteenth century.

Waddington identified Dionysias as Soada, modern es-Suveda, the leading town of a Damascus district rich in inscriptions. Inscriptions prove it was built by a lord builder named Dionysos and that it held a bishop's see. Gesenius placed it instead at Shohba, but the entry judges that town too far from Damascus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epistle-of-ba:
The Epistle of Barnabas survives in a triple tradition of its Greek text, and this entry traces its manuscripts before turning to its message. Until 1843 only eight manuscripts were known in Western libraries, all from one source, and none held chapters one through five, verse seven. Since then two complete manuscripts have appeared: the fourth-century Codex Sinaiticus and the eleventh-century Jerusalem Codex.

An old Latin version of the first seventeen chapters, perhaps from the late fourth century, is too free to restore the text. The Sinaiticus remains the chief authority. The letter names neither author nor readers. Its aim is to impart perfect wisdom, an exact knowledge of God's plan of salvation. The first part urges the faithful, freed from Jewish ceremonial law, to practise virtue and flee sin. The second part reads the Law allegorically, as pointing to Christian virtues and institutions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eudoxias:
Eudoxias was a titular see in Galatia Secunda, Asia Minor, under Pessinus as suffragan. Only Hierocles and Parthey mention it. Aquilas in 451 and Menas in 536 are the two bishops known, and the life of Saint Theodore of Sycæ speaks of another near the end of the sixth century.

Nobody knows the town's original name. Eudoxias may honour either the mother or the daughter of Theodosius II. Perhaps it was Gordion, where Alexander the Great cut the famous knot. Perhaps it stood at modern Yürme in the vilayet of Angora. Others instead match Eudoxias with Akkilaion, whose site is unknown, and put Germe at Yürme.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ezechias:
Ezechias ruled Juda as Achaz's son and successor. Second Kings 18 says he began to reign in the third year of Osee of Israel, at age twenty-five, and reigned twenty-nine years. His mother was Abi, daughter of Zecharias. Scholars dispute his accession year, but the common reckoning runs from 726 to 697 before Christ.

Pious and pleasing to God, he was a strenuous reformer, and Scripture likens him to David. He cleansed the Temple closed by Achaz, restored the neglected Passover, and rooted out idolatry. Soon after his accession he cast off the Assyrian yoke laid on his father. Struck by mortal sickness, he prayed, and Isaiah promised fifteen more years. Sennacherib in 701 ravaged Juda's towns and besieged Jerusalem, but the angel of the Lord slew 185,000 besiegers in a night.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flavias:
Flavias was a titular see of Cilicia Secunda, said to be identical with the city of Sis. Nothing is known of its early name and past beyond the names of several bishops. Alexander, later bishop of Jerusalem, founded the Holy Sepulchre's library in the third century. Nicetas attended Nicaea in 325, and later bishops are named down to Eustratus about 868.

Sis was besieged by Arabs in 704 and served as capital of Lesser Armenia from 1186 to 1375. Egyptians captured and burned it in 1266, and conquered it for good in 1375. In medieval times it was the religious heart of Christian Armenians. It still houses an Armenian catholicos, with bishops, towns, and convents under him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fogaras:
Fogaras is a Greek-Rumanian archdiocese in Hungary, seated since 1733 at Blaj. Made a diocese in 1721, it joined the restored see of Alba Julia in 1853. Its head now bears the title Archbishop of Fogaras and Alba Julia. Since the Rumanians came back to Catholic unity in 1697, eleven men have held the see.

The archdiocese counts 440,000 Catholics, 720 priests, 705 parishes, and as many churches. Its seminaries, college, and press stand at Blaj, with schools for 60,000 pupils. The city of Fogaras, 6,000 souls on the Aluta, saw its fortress figure in the Turkish wars. In 1849 Hungarians were beaten there by Russians; in 1848 Rumanians protested union with Hungary at Blaj.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-arias:
Francis Arias, born at Seville in 1533 and dead there on 15 May 1605, was a Spanish Jesuit writer of ascetical treatises, books that guide the spiritual life. Received into the Society of Jesus at twenty-six, he taught scholastic theology at Cordova and moral theology at Trigueros, serving as rector at Trigueros and Cadiz. A brilliant student at Alcala and an apostle in his native Seville while still a secular priest, he gave his life to prayer and penance. He cared for Black people, Moors, and inmates of hospitals and prisons.

His works include Spiritual Profit, a treatise on the Rosary, Imitation of Our Lady, Imitation of Christ, and Mental Prayer. The Use of the Sacraments, The Promises of God, and The Turpitude and Grievousness of Sin complete the list, most of them translated into several languages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-bay:
Francisco Bayeu y Subias, born at Saragossa on 9 March 1734 and dead at Madrid on 4 August 1795, was a distinguished Spanish painter of religious and historical subjects. He studied at Tarragona under Jose Luzan Martinez and won first prize at the academy. He went on pension to Madrid's San Fernando Academy under Antonio Gonzalez Velasquez, where he caught the eye of Raphael Mengs, court painter to Charles III. Recalled by the king on Mengs's advice, he worked on the palaces of El Pardo and Aranjuez and the new Royal Palace at Madrid.

Painting with and partly under Mengs, he became devoted to his style and is counted with his school. The Prado catalogue calls him a mannered painter best appreciated as a fresco painter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-nic:
Francisco Nicolas Borras, born at Cocentaina in 1530 and dead at Gandia in 1610, was a Spanish painter and priest whose life's work fills a monastery. Going young to Valencia to study under Vicente Joanes, he became that master's finest pupil, and his works resemble Joanes's so closely that some have been taken for the master's. Ordained priest and assigned to his native place, he gave every spare moment to painting, and the Hieronymites of St. Jerome at Gandia hired him for their high altar picture.

He loved the monastery and its brothers so much that he asked no payment but membership in the order, receiving the habit in 1575 and final vows the next year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-para:
Francois Para du Phanjas, born at the castle of Phanjas in Champsaur in 1724 and dead at Paris in 1797, was a French Jesuit writer on physics and philosophy. Admitted to the Society in 1740, he taught mathematics and physics and later philosophy at Besancon, where many pupils distinguished themselves in science and apologetics. He was esteemed for learning and a conciliatory temper. On the suppression of the Society the Archbishop of Paris and Princess Adelaide gave him a pension.

In 1791 he took the oath to the new authorities but took it back once the pope had spoken. His Theory of Sensible Beings, five volumes in 1772 and four in 1788, is both an encyclopaedia of physics and a philosophy of science. It was followed by Principles of Calculation, theories of new discoveries in physics and chemistry, and a Theory of Insensible Beings in 1779.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frederick-luc:
Frederick Lucas, a member of Parliament and journalist, founded the Tablet, the weekly Catholic paper that still runs today. Born in Westminster in 1812 to a Quaker corn merchant, he studied at a Quaker school and University College, London. He was called to the bar in 1835. Drawn first to the Oxford movement, he entered the Catholic Church in early 1839 after reading Milner.

In May 1840 he launched the Tablet, fought off a rival edition from his own printers in 1842, and kept the paper on bold, outspoken lines. Irish priests backed him, and in 1849 he moved its offices from London to Dublin. Returned to Parliament for Meath in 1852, he won standing as a leading Catholic voice there before his death at Staines in 1855.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gavin-douglas:
Gavin Douglas, a Scottish prelate and poet born about 1474, gave Scotland its first great Virgil in Scots. Third son of Archibald, Earl of Angus, called Bell-the-Cat, he studied at Saint Andrews and Paris. He held a Lothian benefice and wrote most of his verse as a country parson. In 1501 he became provost of Saint Giles at Edinburgh, then abbot of Arbroath and bishop of Dunkeld.

Douglas wrote the allegory Palace of Honour and two shorter poems, King Hart and Conscience. His fame rests on his free Scots Aeneid, each book headed by an original verse prologue. Politics undid him. Tried by Regent Albany for seeking promotion through the queen, he spent a year jailed in Edinburgh Castle. Stripped of his see, he escaped to England in 1521 and died of plague the next year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heraclas:
Heraclas, bishop of Alexandria from about 231 to 247, appears as a pupil of Origen's teacher of philosophy, attending his lectures five years before Origen himself. Origen later converted him and his brother Plutarch, the first of Origen's pupils to win martyrdom, and chose him as assistant in the catechetical school to teach beginners. Made priest by Bishop Demetrius, he headed the school when Origen was condemned in 231 and soon succeeded Demetrius as bishop.

He deposed Origen from the priesthood and banished him on his return to Alexandria. He later deposed Ammonius, bishop of Thmuis, for allowing Origen to preach, restoring him only after the people's plea and giving the see jointly to him and Philip. He was followed by Dionysius, who records his custom of receiving heretics without rebaptism after public examination of conduct. He also added twenty suffragan sees in Egypt, and his feast entered the Roman martyrology on 14 July.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermas:
Hermas was the author of The Shepherd, an early Christian book that once ranked beside Scripture in many churches. Written in the first or second century, it was read aloud in worship and quoted with reverence by Clement of Alexandria and Origen. It was even bound with the New Testament in the great Sinaitic Bible. Some early writers treated it as Scripture, while others called it useful reading but not an authority for faith.

The book speaks through visions, commands, and parables given by a shepherd figure, urging repentance and a return to good works. It offers Christians who have fallen a single fresh chance of restoration, a teaching the author presents as newly and clearly published. The entry traces the book's standing, its date and authorship debates, and its many ancient translations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herodias:
Herodias was a Hasmonean princess whose marriage choices led to the death of John the Baptist. Daughter of Aristobulus, son of Herod the Great, she first married her uncle Herod Philip and bore a daughter, Salome. Seeking higher standing, she left him for another uncle, Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee. John rebuked that union, and Herodias used her daughter's dance to win the prophet's head.

Josephus adds a political motive, saying Herod feared John's hold over the people, and the entry notes both accounts may be true at once. Later, when her brother Agrippa became king, she pushed Antipas to seek a royal title at Rome, but he met a treason charge instead and was banished to Lyons. Herodias refused the emperor's kind offers and chose exile beside him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ibas:
Ibas, in Syriac Ihiba or Hiba, was bishop of Edessa, elected in 439 as successor to Rabbulas, an ardent supporter of Cyril, and dead in 457. His policy ran just the reverse, inclining strongly to Theodore of Mopsuestia's doctrines. His reign was most disturbed: Dioscorus's partisans secured his deposition at Ephesus's Second Synod, the Robber Synod, in 449.

Chalcedon restored him in 451, and Ibas holds an important place in dogma's history. His one authentic writing is the celebrated letter to Maris of Beit-Ardashir, a subject debated at six councils. Monophysites accused him of Nestorianism, and he plainly sympathized with Antioch's school, whose masters were Diodorus, Theodore, and Theodoret. He taught for years at Edessa's Persian School and spread Theodore's fame among future Persian bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-iglesias:
Iglesias is a suffragan diocese of Cagliari in Sardinia, its city standing near the ruins of ancient Sulci. The land abounds in thermal springs, and mines, above all Monte Porri, yield lead, iron, and manganese. Many fortifications built by the Pisans, once masters of Sardinia, still stand. James II of Aragon seized the city in 1323 after long resistance, opening his conquest of the whole island.

Sulci had held a bishop's see since the seventh century at least. After its decline the bishop lived at Tratalias, and in 1503 the see reunited with Cagliari. Re-established in 1763, it received Giovanni Ignazio Gautier as bishop. Its cathedral, built by Pisans in 1285, has since been restored, and the diocese counts twenty-four parishes with seventy-three thousand souls, plus a boys' school and a girls' school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-isaias:
Isaiah, foremost among the writers the Hebrew Bible calls Latter Prophets, is praised in Ecclesiasticus as the holy prophet, great and faithful before God. His name means “Yahweh is salvation.” It appears in two Hebrew forms. Yeshayahu appears in the book's text and historical writings. Yeshayah titles his collected sayings. Greek renders it Esaias, Latin usually Isaias. Four other men of the same name appear in the Old Testament.

From his own opening verses we learn he was son of Amoz, and the entry builds his life and book from there, sorting authentic sayings, historical setting, and later additions. Readers get a prophet whose words shaped Jewish hope and Christian reading alike, with the name puzzles and text questions laid out before the message itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste Dumas, a French chemist and senator born at Alais in 1800 and dead at Cannes in 1884, began as a pharmacist's hand at Geneva. A memoir on the nervous system written with Prévost brought him to Paris, where he tutored at the Polytechnic and taught at the Athénée.

Dumas fixed the vapour densities of elements, worked out formulas for alcohols and ethers, and founded the law of substitution in carbon compounds, showing chlorine replacing hydrogen. With Boussingault he studied water and air, and with Stas, carbon dioxide. In 1829 he helped found the Central School of Arts and Manufactures, training engineers for French industry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-grancola:
Jean Grancolas, a French theologian and liturgist born near Châteaudun about 1660 and dead in Paris in 1732. He took his Sorbonne doctorate in 1685 and served as chaplain to Louis XIV's brother. His funeral speech for that prince displeased the duke of Orléans, who dismissed him, ending his court eloquence.

Grancolas then gave himself to liturgy, comparing rites with ancient accounts. His first book treated the age of sacramental ceremonies, followed by a study of dipping the host in the wine. Drawn next to controversy, he attacked Quietism in 1693 with a history of Molinos, his teaching, and his condemnation, judging the mystic movement by sacramental doctrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jeremias:
Jeremias, Hebrew Irmeyah, possibly meaning whom Jehovah appoints, is the name of seven or eight Old Testament men besides the prophet, and this entry sorts them out. They range from a father-in-law of kings to chiefs, warriors, and priests scattered through Kings and Chronicles.

Among them are Jeremias of Libnah, father of Hamutal, mother of kings Jehoahaz and Zedekiah. Others are a Manassite chief at the Assyrian deportation and Benjamite bowmen who joined David at Ziklag. Gadite braves also came to David in the desert, and a priest fathered the Rechabite chief Jaazaniah.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-malalas:
John Malalas was a sixth-century Byzantine chronicler who created the type of the popular Byzantine chronicle. A Monophysite born at Antioch, where he spent most or all of his life, he took his surname from the Syriac word for rhetor, pointing to Syrian origin. He lived under Anastasius I, Justin I, Justinian I, and Justin II.

His Chronographia began as a chronicle of Antioch and grew into a general history of the world to Justinian's last years, in eighteen books. The last, a Constantinople chronicle, is evidently by an orthodox hand. Writing not for the cultured but for laymen and monks, Malalas gratified naive curiosity with legends, anachronisms, and repetitions in the earliest important monument of low Greek. Yet later chroniclers from Evagrius to Theophanes quoted and copied him freely.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-st-th:
John of St. Thomas, born John Poinsot, was a Portuguese Dominican and foremost interpreter of Aquinas in seventeenth-century Spain. Born at Lisbon in 1589 to noble parents, he studied at Coimbra and Louvain, taking a bachelor's degree in theology young. He joined the Dominicans at Madrid in 1612, taking his religious name.

As professor of philosophy and theology at Alcala he ranked among the most learned men of his time. He held the university's two principal theology chairs in 1630 and 1640 and drew the largest audiences its faculties had ever seen. His nine-volume philosophical course and nine-volume theological commentary on the Summa rank among the best expositions of Thomas, and his courtesy never hurt an opponent. Refusing many dignities, he accepted the post of royal confessor to Philip IV only from obedience in 1643, dying at Fraga in 1644.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-zonaras:
John Zonaras was a Byzantine chronicler and canonist of the twelfth century. Under Emperor Alexius Comnenus he served as commander of the imperial bodyguard and first secretary of the imperial chancery. He later took monastic vows at Hagia Glykeria on one of the Princes' Islands, now Niandro.

There he wrote his Epitome of Histories, a world chronicle from creation down to the accession of John Comnenus in 1118. It is superior in form and content to most Byzantine chronicles and widely used through the Middle Ages. It is especially valuable for its excerpts from the lost books of Dio Cassius. His other important work, a commentary on the canons of the Apostles, of various Eastern synods, and on the Fathers' canonical letters, survives in the great Patrologia editions alongside his history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-athias:
Joseph Athias was a Spanish-born Jewish printer at Amsterdam who shaped the Hebrew Bible's printed form. Born probably at Cordova early in the seventeenth century, he died at Amsterdam in 1700. His Hebrew Bibles of 1661 and 1667, checked against good manuscripts, became the base for nearly all later editions.

Careful printing did not save the editions from faults in vowel points and accents, and the 1667 text drew a bitter attack from the scholar Samuel Desmarets. Athias answered with a work beginning Caecus de coloribus. He also issued a manual for scribes and a Judeo-German Bible translation that set off a sharp rivalry with Uri Phoebus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-caipha:
Joseph Caiphas was the Jewish high priest at the time of Jesus' trial and death. Named to the office by the Roman procurator Valerius Gratus about AD 18, he held it until Vitellius removed him about AD 36. His father-in-law Annas, high priest from AD 6 to 15, still wielded great influence, which explains why Luke names both men together.

The entry gives Caiphas the most blameworthy part in the moves against Jesus. It quotes his council argument that a single death could spare the people. It notes that John's Gospel reads those words as prophecy and records the meeting in his house that planned Jesus' arrest. Tradition places that house on Jerusalem's Hill of Evil Counsel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-epipha:
Joseph-Epiphane Darras was a French church historian who lived from 1825 to 1878. Born at Troyes, he trained in its seminaries, taught there after ordination, and lost his post over a eulogy of a bishop disgraced by Napoleon. He then tutored Prince Eugène de Bauffremont and gave himself to historical study.

A foe of Gallicanism and a defender of the Holy See, Darras served as secretary to French bishops at the Vatican Council. His four-volume General History of the Church appeared in 1854, and his chief work, a history of the Church from creation, reached twenty-five volumes before his death. Critics faulted his method, but the books found wide use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-josias:
Josias, or Josiah, was a pious king of Judah who reigned from 639 to 608 BC. He took the throne at only eight, the son of Amon and grandson of Manasseh. In the eighteenth year of his reign, repairs to the Temple uncovered the Book of the Law, and its threats against disobedience frightened the king.

Josias consulted the prophetess Huldah, published the Law before the people, and bound them in a vow of obedience. He then purged idol worship in Judah, Jerusalem, and northern Israel and celebrated a splendid Passover. Thirteen years later he died at Megiddo, fighting Pharaoh Necho II on his march against Assyria. Kings and Chronicles agree in substance on his reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-cardenas:
Juan Cárdenas was a Spanish Jesuit moral theologian praised by St. Alphonsus Liguori. Born at Seville in 1613, he joined the Society of Jesus at fourteen and served as rector, master of novices, and provincial. Through a busy life he wrote small ascetical works, meditations on Christ crucified, and lives of holy women and men.

Cárdenas is chiefly remembered for his Crisis theologica bipartita of 1670, which attacked extreme laxism in clear, profound prose and defended moderate probabilism against laxists and rigorists alike. The book stirred a storm of controversy, and its 1680 supplement restated his case. Later editions add his notes on propositions condemned by the pope in 1679.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kansas:
Kansas, the central state of the Union, was admitted on 29 January 1861. It spans about 82,144 square miles, roughly four hundred miles east to west and two hundred north to south, bounded by Nebraska, Missouri, Colorado, and Oklahoma. Eleventh among the states in area, it dwarfs Massachusetts nearly tenfold. Its undulating surface slopes from about 3,650 feet at the western border to 850 feet in the east, drained by the Missouri, Kansas, and Arkansas rivers into the Mississippi system.

The climate is described as mild and healthful, with winter averaging thirty-one degrees and summer seventy-four. Beyond physical geography, the article treats population, education, law, and history in full. Parents had to send children aged eight to fourteen to school, and Catholic church and school property stood vested in the diocesan bishop as trustee. The historical section runs through settlement, the Civil War years, and the state's later growth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-livias:
Livias was a titular see in Palestina Prima, a lesser bishopric under Caesarea, twice named in the Bible as Betharan. Alexander Jannaeus seized it from an Arab king around 80 BC, and it took the name Betharamphtha.

Herod Antipas walled it strong and renamed it Livias for the wife of Augustus, whom Josephus calls Julia, hence also Julias. Nero later gave it with fourteen villages to Agrippa the Younger, and the Roman general Placidus took it in war. Three bishops are recorded, at Ephesus in 431, Chalcedon in 451, and Jerusalem in 536, and today the site is Tell er-Rameh, twelve miles from Jericho.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luis-de-varga:
Luis de Vargas was a Sevillian painter and holy man, born in 1502 and dead there in 1568. His talent aimed at God's glory. Before a great altarpiece he went to confession and Communion, and kept a coffin in his room to mind death. He lived simply, mild and generous to the poor.

His street fresco of Christ Bearing the Cross drew condemned men to pray before execution. Trained at Seville under Campana's influence, he spent twenty-eight years in Italy, chiefly Rome, studying Perino del Vaga and meeting Vasari. Back home, his Purification and his Temporal Generation crown his work. The latter, famed as La Gamba, shows Adam's foreshortened leg as he adores the Christ child.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luis-ignatius:
Luis Ignatius Penalver y Cardenas was first Bishop of Louisiana and later Archbishop of Guatemala, born at Havana in 1749 and dead there in 1810. Of wealthy noble stock, he took a theology doctorate in 1771 and served as provisor and vicar-general from 1773.

Made first bishop when Pius VI split Louisiana and the Floridas from Cuba, he entered New Orleans in July 1795 and issued rules for parish priests that December. He visited a diocese as wide as the later Purchase, from Iberville to Natchitoches to Pensacola, and reported ignorance and lax discipline on return. Promoted to Guatemala in 1801, he built a hospital and schools at his own cost, resigned in 1806, and left 200,000 dollars to the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lysias:
Lysias, a titular see of Phrygia Salutaris, appears in Strabo, Pliny, Ptolemy, Hierocles, and the Notitiae episcopatuum. Antiochus the Great likely founded it about 200 B.C., and some of its coinage survives.

Ramsay locates it by ruins between the villages of Oinan and Aresli, on the Oinan plain a little north-east of Lake Egerdir, in the vilayet of Konia. Its bishops sat as suffragans of Synnada, tying the small see to the wider Phrygian church. Lequien records three of its bishops, all under Synnada: Theagenes, at Sardica in 344, Philip, at Chalcedon in 451, and Constantine, at Constantinople in 879.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-madras:
Madras is an archdiocese in India, covering about 40,350 square miles, with some 50,000 Catholics among over seven million people. Secular clergy, European and native, with Mill Hill missionaries of St. Joseph, serve 47 churches and 135 chapels through 59 priests, aided by brothers and 262 sisters of several orders.

From 1606 the districts belonged to the Padroado see of San Thome. A Capuchin mission begun in 1642 became a prefecture, then in 1832 a vicariate, and by the brief Multa Praeclare of 1838 took San Thome's jurisdiction. Vizagapatam in 1849 and Hyderabad in 1851 trimmed it, and on the hierarchy's establishment in 1886 Madras became an archdiocese, with Nagpur added in 1887.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-malachias:
Malachias, in Hebrew Mal'akhi, was one of the twelve minor prophets. His book closes that collection. Whether Mal'akhi is a personal name or a title has divided scholars. Many modern writers refuse to read it as a proper name at all.

His book runs to three chapters in Hebrew. Its date is argued from clues within. The Temple stands, and worship has grown slack. The discourses fit a short span just before Nehemiah's mission. They fit neither the first years after the return from Babylon nor Nehemiah's own stay in Jerusalem. Its weight lies in two directions. One is light on Old Testament criticism and the history of the Pentateuch. The other is doctrine, notably on divorce, on the coming messenger, and on the famed passage in chapter 1, verses 10 and 11, read by many as pointing to a universal sacrifice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manuel-chysol:
Manuel Chrysoloras was the first teacher of Greek in Italy. He was born at Constantinople about the mid-fourteenth century and died at Constance on 15 April 1415. He first came to Italy as envoy of Emperor Palaeologus, begging aid from Christian princes while Constantinople stood under siege.

In 1396 Florence's humanists, Salutato and Niccoli among them, called him to teach Greek literature. He later taught at Milan and Pavia. In 1404 he served as Palaeologus's ambassador in Venice, and visited Rome and England. He worked hard for union of Greek and Latin Churches. In 1413 John XXIII chose him to help fix a council site with Emperor Sigismund, and Constance was chosen. His works include tracts on the Holy Ghost's procession, letters, a Latin Plato's Republic, and the first modern Greek grammar, the Erotemeta of 1484, studied by Linacre and Erasmus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mariano-payer:
Mariano Payeras was a Franciscan missionary, born at Inca on Majorca in 1769 and dead in 1823. He took the habit at Palma in 1784 and left Spain in 1793 for the College of San Fernando in Mexico. He served California missions at San Carlos, Soledad, San Diego, and Purisima Concepcion from 1796 to 1823.

From 1815 to 1820 he served as presidente of the missions and vicar forane of the Bishop of Sonora, to whom California belonged. In 1819 San Fernando chose him comisario-prefecto, and he visited all twenty missions from San Diego to San Rafael, over six hundred miles apart. He led parties into native lands seeking sites for new missions, and six months before his death joined a trip to Russian settlements in Sonoma County, likely hastening his end. At Purisima he wrote an Indian-language catechism, used but never printed. Bancroft praised his even ability, business sense, and firm character.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mary-of-cleop:
Mary of Cleophas appears only in John 19:25 among those standing at the cross. Comparing the cross lists seems to identify her with Mary, mother of James the Less and Joseph, named in Mark 15:40 and Matthew 27:56. 

In resurrection narratives she is called Mary of James in Mark 16:1 and Luke 24:10, and the other Mary in Matthew 27:61 and 28:1. Her tie to the Blessed Virgin is obscure too. James is called son of Alpheus, and Jerome identified Alpheus with Cleophas, brother of Joseph by Hegesippus's account, making Mary the Virgin's sister-in-law and stretching sister in John 19:25 to cover it. Grave difficulties block that match: Luke names both Cleophas and Alpheus separately, and Cleophas, or Clopas, scarcely derives from Aramaic Alpheus, more likely shortening Cleopatros.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mathathias:
Mathathias is the name of ten biblical persons, a variant in Hebrew and Greek of both Testaments, uniform as Mathathias in the Vulgate. The name means gift of Jah, or Jahweh, like Theodoros. In Hebrew the first four are called Mattith Jah. Their stories span Ezra, Nehemiah, Chronicles, Maccabees, and Luke.

Third, a Korite Levite, eldest son of Sellum, in charge of frying cakes for temple worship. Fourth, an Asaph musician before the ark. Fifth, an Idithun Levite musician at the ark's Jerusalem entry and leader of David's fourteenth musician group. Sixth and greatest, father of the five Maccabees who fought Seleucids for Jewish liberty. Seventh, Absalom's son and Jonathan's captain at Asor. Eighth, Simon the high priest's son, murdered with father and brother at Doch. Ninth and tenth, two ancestors of Jesus in Luke 3:25-26.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mennas:
Mennas, Patriarch of Constantinople from 536 to 552, owed his throne to a pope's visit. Early in 536 Pope St. Agapetus came to Constantinople on state business pressed on him by Theodahad, the Gothic king. Empress Theodora had just brought Anthimus there from Trebizond, where he had been archbishop, and he shared her Monophysite leanings. Agapetus at once cast Anthimus out and made Mennas patriarch.

Anthimus fell partly because shifting from see to see broke canon law, and partly for doubtful orthodoxy. Whether he could return to his old see was still open when Agapetus died. Mennas pursued the case at a Constantinople synod that same year, with five Italian bishops at his right hand for the Apostolic See. Anthimus, not coming to clear his orthodoxy, was cast out with several followers. In 543 Justinian, with Mennas behind him, put out his famed edict against Origen's teaching and called a local council on it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moses-bar-cep:
Moses Bar Cephas, a Syriac bishop and writer born at Balad about 813, died on 12 February 903. He is known through an anonymous Syriac biography and references in Bar Hebraeus. He took up monastic life early and later became bishop over Beit-Ramman, Beit-Kiyonnaya and Mossul. He received the name Severus on his elevation. For ten years he also oversaw the neighbouring diocese of Tagrita.

A Jacobite of the Monophysite branch, he was the most voluminous writer of his sect in his day. His works include a complete commentary on Old and New Testaments. Now only fragments survive, on Genesis, the Gospels and the Pauline Epistles. He also wrote a four-book treatise on predestination and free will kept in the British Museum. He wrote a commentary on Aristotle's Dialectica, a Hexameron in five books at Paris, and treatises on paradise and the soul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicetas:
Nicetas, or Niceta, was Bishop of Remesiana, or Romatiana, in what is now Serbia, born about 335 and dead about 414. Recent research has clarified this ecclesiastical writer's identity. Gennadius of Marseilles, in his catalogue of writers, mentions Niceas, bishop of Romatiana city, crediting him with a six-book work for catechumens and a small book on a fallen virgin. No other writer or bishop of that name is known.

This Niceas is therefore without doubt the same as Nicetas, Bishop of the Dacians, contemporary and friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola. Gennadius compared with Paulinus's Carmina, plus agreement in time, proves the identity. In Dacia, where Paulinus places his friend's bishopric, stood Romatiana, now Bela Palanka, on the great Roman road from Belgrade to Constantinople. Paulinus mentions Nicetas often, especially in Carmen 27 and Carmen 17, written for his 398 pilgrimage to Nola for Saint Felix's grave.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-onias:
Onias names several Jewish high priests of the third and second centuries BC, whose stories run through Josephus and Maccabees. Onias I, son of Jaddua, held office twenty-three years after Alexander's death, exchanged friendly letters with Sparta's Arius, and saw Egypt and Syria trade mastery of Palestine.

Onias II, son of Simon the Just, loved money and refused Ptolemy's tribute of twenty talents until his nephew Joseph's tact averted invasion. Later bearers of the name built a rival temple in Egypt, and the entry sorts their tangled histories with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orthosias:
Orthosias was a Phoenician port town and a titular see, a former bishop's seat kept in the lists. It stood under the metropolitan of Tyre in Phoenicia Prima. First named in 1 Maccabees 15:37, the town is placed by Pliny between Tripoli and the River Eleutherus. Strabo sets it near that river, while later road lists set it between Tripoli and Antaradus.

Four bishops are recorded from the fifth century onward, beginning with Phosphorus. Two fourteenth-century Latin titulars appear in Eubel's hierarchy. Sixth-century Antioch lists make Orthosias a suffragan of Tyre. A tenth-century list confuses it with Antaradus, or Tortosa. Coins of Antoninus Pius found on the Eleutherus, stamped with Astarte, fixed the site near the River El-Barid, at ruins called Bordj Hakmon el-Yehoudi.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ozias:
Ozias means Yahweh is my strength. It is the name of six Israelites in the Bible, sorted here one by one. First stands Ozias, King of Judah from 809 to 759 before Christ, son and heir of Amaziah. Chosen king at sixteen, he reigned fifty-two years in a way pleasing to God, though he tolerated the high places. The chronicler adds that leprosy struck him for seizing the priestly task of burning incense in the Temple.

The other five are lesser figures. One is Ozias son of Uriel, father of Saul of Caath. Another is Ozias whose son Jonathan kept David's country treasures. A third is Ozias son of Harim, a priest forced to give up a strange wife under Ezra. A fourth is Ozias son of Misha, a ruler of Bethulia. The fifth is Ozias, an ancestor of Judith. King Ozias also appears among the Saviour's forebears in Matthew's gospel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patras:
Patras is a metropolitan see in Achaia, one of its twelve ancient cities, built near Mount Panachaicon from three districts, Aroe, Antheia, and Mesatis. After the Dorian invasion Patreus planted a Laconian colony there and gave it his name. In the Peloponnesian War it backed Athens, and in 419 before Christ Alcibiades urged long walls to its harbour. Ruin followed, until Augustus restored it after Actium with a military colony.

Commerce, above all weaving, made it prosperous again. An earthquake struck in the sixth century, then Slav ravages, but in 807 it beat off Slav attacks and won metropolitan rank from Nicephorus I. Dependent on Rome until 733, it then answered to Constantinople. Tradition credits Saint Andrew with its evangelisation, a famed stylite lived there in the tenth century, and William of Champlitte seized it in 1205.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pelotas:
Pelotas was a new Brazilian diocese carved out of Rio Grande do Sul in 1910. When Pius X raised São Pedro do Rio Grande into the archbishopric of Porto Alegre, he gave it four suffragans. Pelotas, formed from twenty-four parishes in the south-east of the state, was one of them. Its cathedral, dedicated to St. Francis of Paula, stood in the city of Pelotas on the São Gonçalo.

The entry sketches the diocese's human geography rather than its church history. Pelotas itself was a handsome trading city of about 25,000 people, busy above all in the cattle trade, with a Jesuit college. Its seaport, Rio Grande, held about 20,000 more, and Bagé, São Lourenço, São José do Norte, and Boqueirão were the other chief centres. The population was almost entirely Catholic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-hormi:
Hormisdas was elected in 514 and died at Rome on 6 August 523. He came from a wealthy, honourable family of Frosinone. Married before higher orders, he was father of the future Silverius. Under Symmachus he served as deacon and stood by him through the Laurentian schism, acting as notary at the 502 synod. Ennodius of Pavia already expected this pious, wealthy, well-born deacon to reach Rome's see.

Chosen the day after Symmachus's funeral, he cleared the last traces of the Laurentian schism in Rome. From the start he bent his mind to the Greek church and the Acacian schism, born of Zeno's Henoticon. Anastasius clung to the Henoticon and leaned toward Monophysitism, persecuting bishops who resisted. Hormisdas sent his confession of faith, the Formula Hormisdae, to Constantinople for reuniting bishops to sign. Scythian, Illyrian, Dardanian, and Epirus bishops signed it, and the breach began to close.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-praxeas:
Praxeas was an early foe of Montanism, known to us only through Tertullian's book Against Praxeas. His name in a heresy list tagged to Tertullian is an old editor's fix for Noetus. An Asiatic, he swelled with pride as a confessor for a short spell in prison. Rome took him warmly about 190 to 198. That pope had meant to own the gifts of Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla. The plan was public enough to bring peace to Asia and Phrygia, but Praxeas talked the pope into taking his letter back.

He reached Carthage ere Tertullian left the Catholic fold, about 206 to 208. There he taught Monarchian doctrine: having driven out the Paraclete, he now crucified the Father. Tertullian refuted him, and Praxeas gave a written recantation. By then Tertullian himself stood outside the Church, and Monarchianism had sprung up anew.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rabbulas:
Rabbulas, Bishop of Edessa, spent his last years as a foremost foe of Nestorianism. This encyclopedia entry tells that his father was a heathen priest, his mother a Christian. Eusebius of Chalcis and Acacius of Aleppo converted him, and he became a monk. For a time he admired Theodore of Mopsuestia, until some unknown quarrel drew a public rebuke from Theodore at a synod. In 412 Rabbulas became Bishop of Edessa, and he died in 435.

His anonymous panegyrist claims he opposed Nestorius from the first and denounced the heresiarch to his face. Yet at the Council of Ephesus he stood with John of Antioch, and his name appears on two letters denouncing Saint Cyril's teaching. The entry also notes the claim that Rabbulas authored the Peshitto, the Syriac Bible version. Overbeck's edition of the panegyric, with Bickell's translation, remains the chief source for his life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-hermas:
Hermas is the name set down in the Roman Martyrology for 18 August, alongside Serapion and Polyaenus, as martyrs who died in Rome for the faith. Greek calendars give the same three names for the same day, yet their historical notes offer nothing about the circumstances or the time of the martyrdom. The ancient Martyrologium Hieronymianum does not list these names under that date at all.

A different feast on 28 August honours the Roman martyr Hermes and others buried in the catacomb of Hermes and Basilla, together with two Alexandrian martyrs, Polienus and Serapion. The writer suggests the two groups are the same people, with the earlier date arising from a copyist's slip between XV and V Kalends of September. Hermas is also the name of a priest companion of Nicander of Myra, feasted on 4 November.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-marutha:
Maruthas, bishop of Maypherkat in Mesopotamia and friend of John Chrysostom, died before 420. Honoured by Latin, Greek, Coptic, and Syrian Christians alike, he filled his cathedral city with martyrs' relics until it earned the name Martyropolis, city of martyrs. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia sketches a bishop who worked across empires.

Sent by Theodosius II to the Persian court, he won King Yezdigerd's respect through courtesy, holy living, and skill in medicine, despite the jealousy of the Magi, the Persian priests. He attended councils at Constantinople and Antioch and held synods at Ctesiphon for the Persian Church. The entry also warns readers not to confuse him with a later Monophysite bishop of the same name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-thomas:
Saint Thomas here means the island diocese of São Thomé and Principe in the Gulf of Guinea, erected on 23 November 1584 as suffragan of Lisbon. It passed to the metropolitan of San Salvador in Brazil in 1676 and back to Lisbon in 1844. After its last bishop died in 1847 the see stood vacant, ruled as a vicariate from 1865. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia surveys two cocoa islands.

São Thomé, found uninhabited on 21 December 1470 and settled from 1485, covers 358 square miles and counted 37,776 people in 1900, mostly of African slave descent. Fertile and famed for cocoa, its capital on the Bay of Santa Anna held 6,000 souls. The entry traces colonisation, church building, and the long vacancy, giving a compact picture of Catholic life on a remote Atlantic outpost.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salmas:
Salmas, a Chaldean see in Persian Azerbaijan, belonged in ancient times to the archdiocese of Adhorbigan. Its Nestorian bishops are known from the fifth to the seventh centuries, and Jacobite bishops appear in the Middle Ages. By at least the late eighteenth century the Chaldean Catholic archdiocese of Azerbaijan had joined with Salmas, and the union has lasted ever since. Its short entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia gives the modern picture in figures.

The diocese counted 8,000 faithful, ten priests, thirteen parishes or stations, and twelve churches or chapels, with its seminary at Ourmiah and primary schools run by the Sisters of Charity. Town and province of Salmas are rich in marble, orchards, and vineyards. The entry suits readers tracing Eastern Catholic churches in Persia on the eve of the First World War.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-san-leon-del-:
San León del Amazonas, a prefecture apostolic in Peru, covers the forest country east of the Andes known as la Montaña. Drained by the Marañón and Amazon with their tributaries except the Ucayali, it reaches the borders of Ecuador, Colombia, and Brazil. Though the region fell within four dioceses, many pagan tribes once taught by Jesuits roamed beyond civilisation's reach. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia explains a missionary carve-up.

Moved by the tribes' plight, Peru's bishops, with government approval, asked Propaganda late in the nineteenth century to take up the work. By decree of 5 February 1900 the eastern wilderness was split into three prefectures directly under Propaganda, San León being the northernmost. The entry sets out the prefecture's bounds and the task facing its missionaries among peoples subject to no laws.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sebastiao-bar:
Sebastião Barradas, Portuguese exegete and preacher, was born at Lisbon in 1543 and died at Coimbra in 1615. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1558, taught Scripture for many years at Coimbra and Évora, and his preaching burned with such zeal that people called him the Apostle of Portugal. His short entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia rests on two books.

His Commentaria on the harmony and history of the Gospels, four volumes printed at Coimbra from 1599 to 1611, is called a treasure house for Gospel preachers. It was often reprinted in Germany, Italy, and France, last at Augsburg in 1642. His Itinerarium of Israel's children from Egypt to the promised land, printed at Lyons in 1620, serves as a useful commentary on Exodus. The entry leaves a preacher-scholar of the Counter-Reformation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-babylas:
St. Babylas was bishop and martyr, successor of Zebinus as bishop of Antioch in the reign of Emperor Gordianus, from 238 to 244. He was the twelfth bishop of that eastern metropolis. This entry follows a man who, during the Decian persecution in 250, he confessed his faith unwaveringly and was cast into prison, where his sufferings killed him. He was therefore honoured as a martyr.

John Chrysostom and the Acts of the Martyrs relate further that Babylas once refused an emperor, over wrongdoing, permission to enter the church, ordering him to take his place among the penitents. Chrysostom does not name the emperor, while the Acts name Numerianus. It is more probably Philip the Arabian, of whom Eusebius reports that a bishop would not let him enter the Christian gathering at the Easter vigil.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-barnabas:
St. Barnabas, originally Joseph, is styled an apostle in Holy Scripture. This entry follows a man who, like St. Paul, is ranked by the Church with the Twelve, though he was not one of them. He was born of Jewish parents on Cyprus about the start of the Christian era. A Levite, he spent much time in Jerusalem, probably even before the Crucifixion. He appears to have settled there, where his relatives, the family of Mark the Evangelist, also had their homes.

He owned land near Jerusalem, and a rather late tradition recorded by Clement of Alexandria and Eusebius makes him one of the seventy disciples. Acts, however, favours the view that he was converted shortly after Pentecost, about 29 or 30, and at once sold his property and gave the proceeds to the Church. The entry follows his missions with Paul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-felicitas:
Felicitas, a noble Roman lady, is honoured with seven sons as martyrs of 10 July, though the record invites caution. The Depositio Martyrum of about the mid-fourth century lists seven martyrs of that day, buried in four different catacombs along the Via Salaria and Via Appia. Sixth-century Acts, cited by Gregory the Great, call all seven her sons. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 sets the early list against the later Acts.

Felix and Philip rested in Priscilla's catacomb, Martial, Vitalis, and Alexander in the Jordanorum cemetery, Silanus in that of Maximus, and Januarius in Praetextatus's. A note adds that Novatians stole Silanus's body. Whether motherhood or martyrology joined them, the entry shows how Rome's feast calendar grew from tombs, lists, and stories into a family of saints.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gildas:
Gildas the Wise, born in the year of the Britons' victory at Mount Badon, is a saint whose lives disagree with each other. Born about 516 and dead at Houat in Brittany in 570, he is called Badonicus for that birth year, 493 or 516 by different reckonings. Two biographies survive, one by an unknown Breton monk of Rhuys in the eleventh century, the other by the Welshman Caradoc in the twelfth. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 weighs both and finds them unchronological.

Some critics, from Ussher to Colgan, split him into two or more saints, inventing surnames like Albanicus and Hibernicus to fit the contradictions. The general opinion, from Lanigan to the Bollandists, holds to one Gildas, with discrepancies explained by lives drawn up in separate countries. The entry leaves readers with a single wise Briton seen through two cloudy mirrors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-leonidas:
Leonidas is a name shared by several martyrs, and this entry sorts them before honouring the best known. The Roman Martyrology lists a Leonides of the Thebaid, dead with companions under Diocletian, on 28 January. Another appears in a long list under Diomedes on 2 September, and one with Eleutherius on 8 August. A Leonidas, bishop of Athens about the sixth century, is kept on 15 April. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 adds a martyr of 16 April with Callistus and Charysius.

Best known of all is Leonides of Alexandria, father of the great Origen. Eusebius records his martyrdom under Septimius Severus in 202, condemned to death by the governor. The entry thus moves from calendar confusion to a firm Eusebian fact: a father whose death left a son to become the Church's most learned writer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-matthias:
Chosen by lot to replace Judas among the Twelve, Matthias is the subject of this careful, sceptical entry. His name, from the Hebrew Mattithiah, also means gift of God. Acts places him among the seventy disciples, present from the baptism of John to the Ascension. It records how Peter proposed filling the vacant apostleship. Matthias won the lot over Joseph Barsabas.

Beyond that scene, the entry warns, every detail grows vague and contradictory. Nicephorus sends him preaching in Judea and Colchis before crucifixion, while other traditions place his death at Sebastopolis. Later legends, relics, and feast days get brief notice. Readers meet an apostle famous chiefly for one moment, ringed by uncertain tradition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-menas:
Menas, an Egyptian soldier martyred under Diocletian about 295, drew pilgrims for centuries to a desert shrine. Serving in the Roman army in Phrygia, he left the ranks when edicts against Christians were proclaimed and hid in the mountains in fasting and prayer. At a great festival he stepped into the circus, professed his faith openly, and after scourging and torture was beheaded.

His body was carried to Egypt, where miracles at his grave in the Mareotic desert drew thousands. A sanctuary city grew there, with a basilica raised by Arcadius, baths, and a holy well. Arab conquest and doctrinal strife later buried the site in oblivion until excavations in 1905 began to uncover it. The entry joins a martyr's legend to a rediscovered pilgrimage city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-olympias:
Olympias, a wealthy deaconess of Constantinople, spent a great fortune on the Church and stood by John Chrysostom in exile. Born about 361 to an illustrious family, she was orphaned young and married Nebridius, prefect of Constantinople, in 384 or 385. Widowed soon after and childless, she refused every new marriage proposal.

Bishop Nectarius consecrated her deaconess, and she built a convent beside Constantinople's principal church, gathering relatives and companions into community life. She funded churches, hostels, and clergy, and kept loyal to Chrysostom when he was banished, suffering exile herself. She died on 25 July 408, probably at Nicomedia. The entry draws a portrait of riches turned wholly to charity and loyalty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-papias:
Papias, bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia and an Apostolic Father, prized living voices over books. Irenaeus calls him a hearer of John and companion of Polycarp. His work in five books, an exposition of the Lord's sayings, survives only in fragments, chiefly through Eusebius.

Its preface shows his method: he questioned followers of the elders for what Andrew, Peter, Philip, Thomas, James, John, Matthew, Aristion, and the elder John had said. He trusted oral tradition passed from the Lord's disciples more than much speaking or foreign precepts. Later writers also cite his remarks on the Gospels of Mark and Matthew and on the millennium. The entry gathers fragments that still shape study of the early Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-sabbas:
Sabbas, a Cappadocian hermit, founded the great Laura of Mar Saba in the gorges of the Cedron. Born at Mutalaska near Caesarea in 439, he entered a Basilian monastery at eight, reached Jerusalem in 456, and spent five years in a cave as disciple of Euthymius. In 483 he founded his laura south-east of Jerusalem, restored in 1840.

When monks opposed his rule and demanded a priest abbot, Patriarch Salustius ordained him in 491 and made him archimandrite of all Palestinian monasteries in 494. Opposition drove him to a new laura near Thekoa. A strenuous foe of Monophysites and Origenists, he visited Anastasius in 511 and Justinian in 531 to sway them. He died in his laura on 5 December 532.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-thomas-aqu:
Thomas Aquinas, philosopher, theologian, and Angelic Doctor, towers over medieval thought and Catholic schools. Born at Rocca Secca in the kingdom of Naples in 1225 or 1227, he was son of Count Landulph of Aquino and Theodora of Teano. He was sent as a boy oblate to Monte Cassino. He studied at Naples and joined the Dominicans against his family's furious opposition.

He studied under Albert the Great at Paris and Cologne. He taught at Paris and in Italy. He wrote the Summa Theologiae, the Summa contra Gentiles, commentaries on Aristotle, and hymns for Corpus Christi. His synthesis joined Aristotelian philosophy to Christian doctrine with unmatched clarity. Called to the Council of Lyons, he died at Fossanova on 7 March 1274. Universities, colleges, and schools claim him as patron.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-suidas:
Suidas, author of perhaps the most important Greek lexicon, is himself almost unknown. Nothing survives about him except that he lived near the middle of the tenth century, apparently at Constantinople, and was probably a churchman devoted to letters. His lexicon, though, stands among the most valuable documents of Greek philology, grammar, and literary history.

Half dictionary and half encyclopedia, it explains words by the philology of its day and preserves details and quotations from authors otherwise lost, from Homer's scholiasts to Polybius, Josephus, and George Hamartolus. Its chief source for ancient history was Constantine VII's encyclopedia, and its words follow a phonetic ordering called antistoichia. Editions by Gaisford, Bernhardy, and Bekker followed the Milan printing of 1499.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tamaulipas:
Tamaulipas is a Mexican diocese, suffragan of Linares. It covers its state of 31,758 square miles plus two parishes in northern Vera Cruz. Its people numbered 249,253 in 1910. Bishop and governor live at Ciudad Victoria, 2,467 feet up, with 17,861 people. Father André Olmos came from Burgos in 1528 and first preached the Gospel here. He laboured until his death at Tampico in 1571.

Franciscans founded the Guardianship of San Salvador in 1530 with twelve convents. Zacatecas fathers took the missions in 1748. They passed to Mexico's Santo Evangelio province in 1768. Planned as early as 1722, the territory became a vicariate in 1860. Pius IX made it a bishopric in 1869. It joined Linares in 1891, and now counts three parish schools, six Catholic colleges, and ten Protestant colleges.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tanagra-hella:
Tanagra was a titular see in Hellas, suffragan of Corinth. This Boeotian town stood on the fertile right bank of the Aesopus. It was also called Poemandria. In 457 BC the Athenians lost to Spartans near Tanagra. The next year they beat the Boeotians and mastered Boeotia, though the city walls were destroyed. In 426 the Athenians invaded again and beat Tanagrians and Boeotians together.

Its people were famed for frugality, loyalty, and hospitality. Its land yielded Boeotia's best wine despite little wheat, and its town was known for fighting-cocks. Under Augustus, Tanagra and Thespiae led Boeotia. Temples to Dionysus, Themis, Aphrodite, Apollo, and Hermes crowded the town. The gymnasium held a portrait of the poetess Corinna. Slav invasions later wrecked it, and only one bishop, Hesychius in 458, is known.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-texas:
