Texas takes its name probably from Tejas, a friendly tribe met by early Spanish explorers. The state is bounded by Oklahoma, New Mexico, Mexico, the Gulf, Louisiana, and Arkansas. It lies between 25°50' and 36°45' north and 93°30' and 106°30' west. It covers 265,896 square miles, of which 3,498 are water. Four natural provinces run from south to north.

Nearest the coast lies the Coastal Plain, with Coast and Black Prairies and a Tertiary area. The Coast Prairie runs thirty to fifty miles inland, a flat, almost treeless clay tract along the coast. Rainfall shapes its products: rice in the wet east and north, sugar-cane and fruit in the centre, and cotton with range cattle in the drier southwest. Irrigation aids sugar-cane, sorghum, and cotton there, and the ground holds oil fields. The entry then covers the state's history and Catholic life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-pious-fun:
Money for California's missions, gathered as the Pious Fund, is traced here from 1697 onward. Donors in Mexico, private persons and religious bodies, gave to Jesuits so they might spread the Catholic faith in what was then California. Early gifts passed straight to missionaries, among them Juan Maria Salvatierra and Francisco Eusebio Kino.

Larger later gifts took the form of property held by donors for mission use, its income devoted to that end. In 1717 capital sums passed to the Jesuits, who ran the fund until their expulsion from Mexico. Spain's crown took over in 1768 and held it until Mexican independence, after which claims and courts tangled its fate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theonas:
Bishop Theonas of Alexandria, who led that see from about 283 to 301, is the figure sketched in this brief entry. Eusebius's Chronicle and Jerome's version date his episcopate, and in his day Achillas, made presbyter at Alexandria with Pierius, grew famous. A church dedicated by Alexander, Athanasius's predecessor, to Theonas also survives in Athanasius's apology to Constantius.

Fame clings most to a letter from Theonas to Lucianus, chamberlain to Diocletian, long quoted for its lifelike picture of a Christian at the imperial court. Batiffol first, then Harnack, judged it a forgery, and Bardenhewer agreed. Dacherius first printed it from a transcript said to come from Jérôme Vignier. The Roman Martyrology keeps Theonas on 27 August.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thynias:
Thynias is a small island in the Black Sea, a titular see subject to Nicomedia in Bithynia. Only 1,421 yards wide, it was first called Apollonia for its temple of Apollo, then Daphne, giving the name Daphnusia found in the lists of bishoprics. Its later name comes from the Thynii, a Thracian people who held the Bithynian coast.

Three bishops of Daphnusia are named by Le Quien: St. Sabas, honoured on 1 May, and Leo, present at the Eighth Ecumenical Council in 878, besides John, exiled there and martyred under Copronymus. Legend says the relics of Zoticus, Anicetus and Photius were kept on the island. Now called Kefken or Kerpe-Adasi, it lies off the coast west of the Bosphorus, where a Latin fleet besieged it in 1261.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tiberias:
Tiberias, a titular see subject to Scythopolis in Palestine, was founded on its lake in AD 17 by Herod Antipas, who named it for the Emperor Tiberius. Tombs found at the site kept Jews away at first, so Herod peopled it with foreigners and folk of low standing. Jerome links the site with Reccath, Emath and Cenereth, towns of Naphtali, and the town measured a little over three miles round.

Though the lake bears its name and the Gospels mention it often, Christ himself seems never to have lived there. After Antipas died in 41, Nero gave the town to Agrippa the Younger. In the Jewish revolt its people wavered between parties until Josephus, governor of Galilee, took it after several tries. It then submitted to Vespasian untouched, and late in the second century the Sanhedrin moved there from Sepphoris with its Talmudic school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-timbrias:
Timbrias was a titular see in Pisidia, subject to Antioch, whose exact site is unknown. The Roman Curia lists it as Thymbrium, a name spelled many ways in documents, while coins call its people Timbriadeon. Later forms include Timbriada and Thymbriada. Strabo mentions it, and its coins, bearing the river Eurymedon, point to the upper part of that river's course.

The town probably lay in the plain called Yilandi Ovassi, in the region of Konya. Church writings mention it as late as the thirteenth century. Le Quien names three bishops: Constantine, at Constantinople in 680 and 692, John at Nicaea in 787, and Theodosius at the Photian council of Constantinople in 879.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-troas:
A suffragan of Cyzicus in the Hellespont, first called Sigia, then enlarged by Antigonus as Antigonia Troas and again by Lysimachus as Alexandria Troas. Faithful to Rome in the war against Antiochus, it became Colonia Alexandria Augusta Troas, adorned by Augustus, Hadrian and the rich grammarian Herodes Atticus, whose aqueduct still stands.

St. Luke joined St. Paul here for the crossing to Europe, and Paul's friends spent a week with him at Troas, where Eutychus was restored to life. Paul also left his cloak and books with Carpus here, and St. Ignatius of Antioch stopped at Troas on his way to Rome, while its bishops run from Marinus in 325 to Peter in the ninth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ulfilas:
Ulfilas, also spelled Ulphilas, was the apostle of the Goths, a missionary, Bible translator, and inventor of an alphabet. He was born probably in 311 and died at Constantinople in 380 or 381. Though Gothic in speech and sympathy, he sprang from Cappadocian captives carried off in Gothic raids under Valerian and Gallienus. Sent young to Constantinople as hostage or envoy, he served as lector in the church. He was consecrated bishop in his thirtieth year by Eusebius of Nicomedia, the famed Arian bishop.

Back among the Goths north of the Danube, Ulfilas gave them letters of their own and turned the Scriptures into their tongue. That feat shaped Gothic Christianity for generations. His Arian teaching, learned from Eusebius, put him at odds with the Nicene church, and the entry weighs his doctrine fairly against his achievement. Readers meet a bridge figure between empire and barbarian world, whose alphabet outlived his theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Santo Tomás at Manila was founded in 1619 by the Dominican Miguel de Benavides, Archbishop of Manila. Innocent X bestowed the pontifical university title in 1645, and Philip IV of Spain bestowed the royal university title that same year. Attached to it stands the College of San Juan de Letran. After a five-year course there in Latin, Greek, English, mathematics, natural history, botany, mineralogy, physics, chemistry, and philosophy, the successful student earns a Bachelor of Arts.

The university may confer doctorates in theology, philosophy, civil and canon law, medicine, pharmacy, literature, and science. Its departments all lie within the walled city. It reached its greatest prosperity in 1897, just at the end of Spanish rule. The entry sketches its faculties, its colleges, and its long service to learning in the Philippines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vedas:
The Vedas are the sacred books of ancient India, and the Sanskrit word veda means knowledge, above all sacred book. Widely taken, the term covers not only sacred texts but the vast theological and philosophical writings joined to them: Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upanishads, and Sutras. Usually, though, veda means only the four collections of hymns and prayers, the Samhitas, made for different rites: Rig-Veda, Sama-Veda, Yajur-Veda, and Atharva-Veda.

Only the first three counted as canonical at first, with the fourth winning that rank after long struggle. Vedic language is an artificial literary tongue, fully formed, not a mere popular dialect, resembling later classical Sanskrit while differing from it. The entry describes each collection, its contents, and its ritual use, and sets out what scholars knew of their age and making.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-amia:
John Amias was an English martyr born at Wakefield who died at York on 16 March 1589. He worked as a Wakefield cloth merchant until his wife died, then shared his property among his children and took priesthood at Reims in 1581. Of his missionary life little is known.

Arrested at the house of a Mr Murton in Lancashire, he was taken to York and tried alongside two other martyrs, Dalby and Dibdale. Anthony Champney, Dean, witnessed their execution and left an account in his history. Other accounts note that Amias went to his death as joyfully as if to a feast. He was declared Venerable in 1886, and the entry gives a brief life of a late vocation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-lou:
Louise de Marillac Le Gras was the Paris-born foundress of the Sisters of Charity of St Vincent de Paul, later canonized in 1934. Born in 1591 to Louis de Marillac, she lost her mother early, was raised partly by an aunt at Poissy, and studied arts and philosophy under a tutor.

As a girl she longed to join the Capuchinesses, but her director dissuaded her. Instead she married Antoine Le Gras, secretary to Marie de' Medici, and devoted herself to their son, born in 1613, and to works of charity. Widowed in 1625, she placed herself under Vincent de Paul's direction. Together they built a community of women serving the poor, the sick, and abandoned children, work that grew from her own long habit of never tiring of charity. She died in Paris in 1660.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zacatecas:
Zacatecas is the Mexican diocese suffragan to Guadalajara, nearly matching the state of the same name, with 475,863 people in 1910. Its bishop and the governor live in Zacatecas city, 25,905 people at 2442 metres above sea level. Spain settled the land between 1546 and 1548, and its first parish, founded in 1569, belonged to Guadalajara. Franciscans came in 1567, Augustinians in 1576, Dominicans in 1604, Saint John's order in 1610, Jesuits in 1616, and Mercedarians in 1701.

Father Margil's College of the Propagation of the Faith, opened 4 May 1721, sent missionaries to Texas, French Louisiana, and Tamaulipas. It took over Jesuit missions in Tarahumara and Lower California after the expulsion. When Mexico sought a San Francisco bishopric in 1836, the college's Francisco Garcia Diego was consecrated first bishop in 1849. In the 1859 persecution the college's religious were jailed. Pius IX erected the Zacatecas diocese in 1863, with two seminaries, 144 parish schools, and nineteen colleges serving about seven thousand students.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zacharias:
Zacharias was the Hebrew prophet who, with Haggai, spurred the building of the second Temple. Son of Barachias, son of Addo, he rose in the eighth month of Darius's seventh year, 520 B.C., just two months after Haggai began. The two prophets' urgings raised the Temple, as Ezra 5 and 6 record. Addo was among chief priests who returned with Zerubbabel in 538 B.C., and sixteen years later a Zacharia of Addo's family appears as chief priest, most likely the prophet himself.

Christ's charge about a Zacharias slain in the Temple most likely points not to this prophet but to Zacharias son of Jehoiada, since Ezra shows no such Temple murder. His book, one of the Minor Prophets, opens with a call to return to Yahweh and eight night visions. Horsemen in a myrtle grove bear news of world rest yet promise comfort and rebuilding for a new Jerusalem without walls.
christmas:
Robert Haven Schauffler edited a Christmas anthology for the Our American Holidays series, meant for students and teachers. Copyright dates to 1907, though this printing is dated 1968 at New York. Contents divide into origin, celebration, and significance. Prose and verse are mixed throughout, as the series promised.

Francis Church's famous question, Is There a Santa Claus, opens the book. Phillips Brooks contributes O Little Town of Bethlehem. Kate Douglas Wiggin, Reginald Heber, James Russell Lowell, and Dinah Mulock all appear in the first section alone. A Leigh Hunt fancy appears later: that all England shakes hands on Christmas Day, link by link, from Dover to John O'Groats. School and home reading was the aim, with the best-known pieces gathered in one place.
critias:
Plato's Critias, translated by Benjamin Jowett, is the unfinished second part of a planned trilogy following the Timaeus. Jowett's introduction explains that Critias was to show the ideal state in a patriotic war, a mythical conflict shadowing Athens against Persia. The dialogue stops unfinished, mid-sentence, just as Zeus rises to speak.

Critias describes Atlantis: its kings, canals, metals, and armies. He also paints the fertile Attica of nine thousand years before. Its soil has since washed away, he says, though even the remnant could support a vast army. The fragment matters less as history than as the source of every Atlantis since. Jowett's analysis helps readers separate Plato's political fable from later occult embroidery.
dave-darrin-s-second-year-at-annapolis-o:
The second year at Annapolis fills this Dave Darrin book by H. Irving Hancock, marked MCMXI and drawn with pictures. Dave and Dan are now youngsters, the third class at the Naval Academy. Twenty chapters trace the year.

A question of midshipman honour opens the tale, over a deed Dave calls a shame. Pennington pushes too far and asks for a fight, then meets an accident at sea. A gale, a grim watch from the waves, and hunger till raw fish tempts fill the sea chapters. Fights by rule, with seconds, settle scores ashore. Dan faces a board and keeps his place. The book is Academy life as a code of honour, told for boys.
doe-osti-2572520-ier-516-zirconium-test-:
Preliminary design LA-UR-25-23659, by Gregory Siemers, Nicholas Thompson, and Jesson Hutchinson and issued July 21, 2025, plans a set of critical tests on zirconium. IER 516, the Zirconium Test Assembly, is a joint Los Alamos and French project. Its tests will check the nuclear data files for zirconium and its hydride, where past files hid errors that canceled each other out.

Ten early tests were designed for the Comet machine at the National Criticality Experiments Research Center, all fueled with highly enriched uranium. A swarm search in the MCNP code tuned each design to react most strongly to the data under test, across slow to fast neutron energies. Six use zirconium metal alone. Polyethylene moderates the slow-neutron cases best, and beryllium the mid-energy ones. Four more tests target the heat-scattering rules for the hydride in its delta and epsilon forms.
doe-osti-2575184-advanced-processing-of-:
Final report DE-FE0032139, from the Energy and Environmental Research Center at the University of North Dakota, covers April 2022 to July 2025. Alexander Azenkeng led the team, with Nicholas Stanislowski, Jason Laumb, and university colleagues. The goal was to upgrade coal and coal waste into graphite pure enough for fast-charging lithium-ion battery anodes, a market now supplied mostly from abroad.

The process chain starts with selecting and characterizing carbon feedstocks. Physical and chemical cleaning steps strip out mineral matter, and a heteroatom reduction step removes the sulfur, nitrogen, and oxygen that spoil battery performance. The cleaned carbon then goes through graphitization, ordering its layers into the structure anodes need. Sections walk the full route from raw sample to product testing. The work was sponsored by the Department of Energy and the North Dakota Industrial Commission's lignite program.
doe-osti-2584063-measuring-vibronic-coup:
Final technical report DE-SC0021232, from Munira Khalil and Brandi Cossairt at the University of Washington, measures how ligands grip nanocrystal surfaces and steer their excited states. The organic ligands coating a semiconductor nanocrystal are not packaging; their vibrations couple to excitons and govern how fast energy relaxes and where charge goes. The team paired nanocrystal synthesis with ligand-specific nonlinear spectroscopy to quantify those interactions.

One highlight used temperature-dependent infrared spectroscopy on myristic acid capped indium phosphide magic-sized clusters. A custom Markov chain Monte Carlo fitting routine extracted the relative energies of carboxylate binding shapes. The chelating mode beat the monodentate one by 0.7 plus or minus 0.3 kilocalories per mole; the syn-syn bridging shape was more stable by 1.1 plus or minus 0.5. Numbers like these let chemists choose ligands deliberately for photocatalysts and photonic materials. Four papers, two dissertations, and a trained cohort came out of the award.
doe-osti-2587230-code-coverage-status-of:
Micheal Smith of Argonne National Laboratory documents the code coverage of DASSH-F in report ANL/NSE-25/48. DASSH-F is the steady-state thermal-hydraulic code inside the Argonne Reactor Code system for fast reactor design. It replaced the older SE2-ANL software. The question here is narrow and vital: which lines of the code do the existing test problems actually run?

Coverage was measured with the Intel Fortran compiler's code coverage tool, which required changes to how DASSH-F is compiled. Tables give coverage submodule by submodule, with notes on linked DIF3D modules. Most uncovered code turns out to be error messages and debugging output that tests can safely skip. Seven features, though, are genuinely untested. Smith names them and suggests added test problems to cover them, noting that DASSH-F verification work is still ahead and should absorb most of the findings.
doe-osti-2587737-financial-analysis-of-t:
Quentin Ploussard, Matija Pavicevic, and Ao Yu of Argonne National Laboratory wrote this financial analysis, ANL-25/44, of a set of managed river flows. During water year 2024, Glen Canyon Dam released smallmouth bass flows. These release patterns aim to hinder the invasive smallmouth bass in the Colorado River below the dam, where the fish threatens the native ecosystem. Changing releases changes hydropower output, and this report prices the change.

The method mirrors the team's other dam studies. Dam operations are modeled with and without the flow program, following the hourly, daily, and monthly rules that govern the dam. Bypass operations began on July 8, sending part of the water past the turbines through bypass tubes instead. Hourly scheduling by the Western Area Power Administration's marketing office in Montrose, Colorado, frames the generation pattern. Financial chapters then convert the lost and shifted generation into dollars.
doe-osti-2589421-annual-site-environment:
SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory report SLAC-R-250221, dated September 2025, is the site's Annual Site Environmental Report for calendar year 2024. Prepared for the Department of Energy under contract DE-AC02-76-SF00515, it is required of all major Department sites. SLAC is run by Stanford University in Menlo Park, California, and hosts particle physics and X-ray science facilities.

Chapters track air and water monitoring, waste handling, radiation protection, and cleanup duties across the site. Some programs, such as stormwater sampling, follow a season running from October 2023 through June 2024. Management review found the site's environmental systems effective overall. Neighbors, regulators, and staff can use the volume as the public record of how the laboratory watched and limited its footprint during 2024.
doe-osti-2998586-final-report-for-sc0016:
Samuel Thomas of Tufts University wrote this final report for Energy Department award DE-SC0016423, with Chad Risko of the University of Kentucky as co-investigator. The project studied conjugated materials, the carbon-based materials used in organic electronics such as flexible screens and solar cells. Its question was how side chains attached to these molecules control the way the solid packs together.

The team made molecules whose fluorinated side rings stack against the main backbone, and compared them with plain controls. Twisted backbones, held by that stacking, shifted their glow one way when ground or pressed. Flat backbones without the stacking shifted the other way. Crystal structures confirmed which molecules stacked and which did not. The results give chemists a design rule: side-chain stacking can set both packing and color response in these materials.
doe-osti-3000743-microreactor-assembly-t:
Zhaopeng Zhong, Ahmed Abdelhameed, Nicolas Stauff and co-workers at Argonne describe a shipping cask model in ANL/NSE-25/9 Revision 2. Before a microreactor's fuel can travel by road, analysts must prove the load can never go critical, even in a crash or flood. This report works one full example for industry to copy: a gas-cooled microreactor assembly using HALEU fuel in TRISO particle form. Design variants run with and without yttrium hydride moderator.

The cask adapts Y-12's ES-3100 container, built for enriched uranium, enlarged to swallow the whole assembly. Calculations used the CSAS6 sequence of SCALE 6.3.2 with a continuous-energy neutron library, following federal guidance. Cases covered normal shipment, an intact cask flooded with water, and a damaged cask at its worst water content. Every case kept a large margin below criticality, even in an endless stack of casks. Sensitivity checks against benchmark experiments complete the validation.
doe-osti-3003930-smokeless-chimney-using:
Vi Rapp of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and Noel Putaansuu of Acumentor LLC close CRADA FP00018151 in report LBNL-2001714, dated October 30, 2025. The project, Smokeless Chimney, tested whether smoke opacity can steer a wood heater's combustion. Poorly run wood stoves emit heavy particulate pollution. Standard particle instruments cannot sample hot, dense flue gas directly.

The device under test is the Octoring, an opacity sensor that shines light through the stack flow and reads color and density. Over 18 months the team ran three Octorings on cordwood and pellet heaters across wide operating conditions. The evaluation is among the first thorough ones for wood heater smoke. The conclusion is measured: opacity monitoring is a sound foundation, but more development is needed before a robust commercial product.
doe-osti-3005926-lilith-an-enduring-plut:
C. Kostelac, J. Hutchinson, G. McKenzie, K. Stolte, and R. Little of Los Alamos propose a replacement for a legend in a slide deck, LA-UR-25-28663, dated October 2025. Jezebel, a bare plutonium sphere assembly, ran from 1954 to 1977 and has anchored fast plutonium-239 data validation for seventy years. It cannot be rerun: its operators are gone, parts are gone, and its documentation is thin.

The proposed assembly, Lilith, is designed to endure for a century with simple geometry and low uncertainties. The deck compares candidate configurations, with plutonium masses in the tens of kilograms and neutron generation times of a few nanoseconds. Gains claimed span nuclear data validation, methods testing, dosimetry, and reactor kinetics. The need has sat in the criticality safety program's mission documents for over a decade, and a 2022 futures panel ranked it first.
doe-osti-3009355-conference-support-50th: Short technical report for DOE award DE-SC0025676, organized by Sujith Puthiyaveetil and Josh Vermaas, documents grant support for the 50th Midwest/Southeast Regional Photosynthesis Conference. The meeting ran October 25 to 27, 2024 at Turkey Run State Park in Marshall, Indiana, with 85 participants and four keynote speakers. DOE funds waived registration for all students and trainees for 2,500 dollars and paid seven travel awards of 350 dollars each, chosen by abstract quality and financial need with undergraduates first.
doe-osti-3011852-2024-buildings-technolo:
Documentation for the 2024 Buildings Technology Baseline dataset comes from Mark Butrico and Rebecca Ciraulo of Guidehouse with Nathan Moore, Eric Wilson, and Jared Langevin. The baseline harmonises building technology data across the Energy Information Administration, the NREMDB database, and the Scout tool. Identifier tables map each technology or measure across the three sources at the most granular level available.

Price data collected from the NREMDB fed a retail price regression for 2023. Typical and high performance characteristics came from the EIA Buildings Data Report for 2023 to 2050. The November 2025 document explains the dataset structure for users of the baseline.
doe-osti-3014280-national-hydropower-fis:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4039, dated January 2026, is the user guide and methodology for the National Hydropower Fish Passage Database. Paul Matson, Bryan Bozeman, Christopher DeRolph, Gbadebo Oladosu, Debjani Singh, and seven others wrote it. The database inventories the ladders, lifts, and bypasses that help fish past American dams. It was built partly from the stakeholder questionnaire the same team ran.

The guide explains the database philosophy, terminology, and data dictionary. Passage types are grouped into simplified categories, so records from different sources can be matched. If two sources describe the same facility, it receives one identifier. Downstream bypasses and upstream fish ladders are split into subtypes. Common variants differ enough to matter. The methodology lets regulators and researchers query one national inventory instead of dozens of partial lists.
doe-osti-3019911-symposium-mt02-statisti:
T Haxhimali and K Wu of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory closed an Army Research Office grant in LLNL-TR-2015206, February 2026. The grant supported symposium MT02 at the Materials Research Society's Fall 2025 meeting. Its theme was statistical mechanics-based computational tools for phase transformations in complex materials. The report records the symposium's scope and content. Talks spanned modeling methods for how materials change phase, and the experiments that test those models. One thread reached orbit: ZBLAN fluoride glass fibers crystallize when made on Earth.

Convection in the melt stirs the glass, and the resulting defects scatter light, limiting transmission. Space-based experiments confirmed that removing convection preserves the fiber's quality. A symposium report cannot carry a field, and this one does not try. It documents who gathered, what was presented, and where the Army's sponsorship advanced the conversation. Program officers use such reports to judge whether a meeting earned its grant.
doe-osti-3022231-understanding-spectral-:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2011353, by C. Harthcock, is the abbreviated report for LDRD project 23-ERD-006, which studied how the precursors of laser-induced damage in dielectric optical coatings depend on wavelength. Damage precursors are the microscopic coating defects that grow into failure sites under repeated high-power laser shots, a limiting problem for large laser facilities.

Outcomes highlighted here include published findings in high-impact journals, invited conference talks, and direct support to programs including the National Ignition Facility and other high-average-power laser efforts. The project also stood up and qualified a new wavelength-agile damage test capability, letting researchers probe the same defects at several wavelengths. It also supported two postdoctoral fellows who joined the laboratory's optical materials team.
doe-osti-3022260-annual-supply-chain-for:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-7A40-93857, by Brittany L. Smith and eleven colleagues, reviews the United States photovoltaic supply chain for 2024. It tracks modules and batteries, structural and electrical balance-of-system parts, and recycling, then closes with installation trends, manufacturing jobs, and the domestic content of systems installed that year.

The headline numbers set the scale: 47.1 gigawatts of direct-current capacity installed in 2024 brought the national total to 224.1 gigawatts, supplying 7 percent of United States electricity. Vulnerability concentrates in the crystalline-silicon module and battery storage chains, still dominated by manufacturing in China, while cadmium telluride modules and balance-of-system components rest on stronger footing. About two-thirds of 2024 capacity went into utility-scale systems with single-axis tracking and large bifacial silicon modules.
doe-osti-3022392-one-earth-energy-feed-p:
A technical report from AECOM and Trimeric Corporation was prepared for the Illinois Storage Corridor CarbonSAFE Phase III project under DOE agreement DE-FE0031892. It sets the process design basis for carbon capture at the One Earth Energy ethanol plant in Gibson City, Illinois. Fermentation gives off a nearly pure carbon dioxide stream. The plant would compress and dry up to about 458,000 metric tonnes per year. The gas goes to injection into a saline aquifer roughly four miles away.

Normal operation means 1,290 metric tonnes per day across 355 operating days, matching 160 million gallons of yearly ethanol output. The process pairs a multistage centrifugal blower with a five-stage reciprocating compressor to reach wellhead pressures up to 1,500 psig. Triethylene glycol dehydration after the fourth stage cuts water to 10 pounds per million standard cubic feet. New cooling capacity and a new electrical substation are flagged as site needs.
doe-osti-3023069-april-2025-semiannual-c:
Madison C Hsieh and Katie A Hill of Savannah River National Laboratory report leaching test results for decontaminated salt solution from the Salt Waste Processing Facility. Their report, SRNL-STI-2025-00713, dated December 2025, covers the April 2025 semiannual composite sample. The test used is the Toxicity Characteristic Leaching Procedure, which shows what harmful substances might wash out of treated waste.

Samples were made with a water-to-premix ratio of 0.59, matching the Saltstone grout that will hold the waste. Tables report total mercury and methyl mercury in milligrams per liter, alongside results from the April 2024 and October 2024 semiannual samples for comparison. Qualifier flags mark results detected at or below the limit of quantitation, and values that were not detected.
doe-osti-3023314-understanding-spectral-:
Colin Harthcock of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory reports project 23-ERD-006 in LLNL-TR-2011352, dated March 2026. High-energy laser systems are limited by damage inside their own optics, and this work asks how that damage risk changes with laser wavelength. The materials in question are dielectrics, the glass-like coatings and crystals that steer and shape the beams.

Attention centers on hafnia and silica multilayer coatings, used on transport mirrors at the National Ignition Facility for their damage resistance. Tiny flaws drive failure: vacancies, interstitials, and nanobubbles left when ion beam sputtering traps inert gas such as argon inside dense hafnia films. Those defects promote absorption, which seeds damage. The report ties precursor types to spectral response so optics can be made harder to hurt.
doe-osti-3367725-microreactor-assembly-t:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL/NSE-25/9 Revision 3, by Zhaopeng Zhong, Ahmed Abdelhameed, Nicolas Stauff, and colleagues, is the companion model description for shipping a whole microreactor assembly rather than just its core. Like its sibling report, it exists to support a criticality safety validation basis: the cask model's assumptions, geometry, and materials are frozen in print so reviewers can audit them.

Calculation tables vary water intrusion inside the cask, tracking the multiplication factor as internal flooding changes. One case family steps water fractions from zero to full across assembly positions, with uncertainties near one ten-thousandth. External flooding scenarios complete the matrix. Revision 3 keeps the shipped configuration's safety analysis current as the design evolves.
doe-osti-3377667-u-s-distribution-transf:
National Laboratory of the Rockies slides from June 2026 present phase three of a study of United States distribution transformer demand. Four authors are printed: Killian McKenna, Sherin Ann Abraham, Wenbo Wang, and Zephyr Zink, of the laboratory's Distribution Edge and Grid Planning and Analysis Center work. Earlier phases appeared as reports in February 2024 and November 2024.

Distribution transformers step voltage down for electrical service and remain in short supply, with delays and rising prices across the industry. The deck characterizes the transformers now in service, then models future growth. Commercial and industrial demand is driven mainly by new customers and per-capita load growth, while data centers are modeled separately because of their expected scale. A regional analysis and demand management strategies close the deck.
doe-osti-3399432-development-of-post-con:
Development of Post-Consumer Textile Waste Degradation Protocol and Related Downstream Transformations, CRADA final report NLR/TP-2800-99333 from July 2026, closes agreement CRD-22-22875. Michelle Reed is the National Laboratory of the Rockies technical contact and cited author. Funding came from the Advanced Manufacturing and Materials Technologies Office.

Worn-out clothing is one of the largest unrecycled waste streams, because blended fabrics resist every simple recovery route. A degradation protocol is the recipe that breaks such textiles down in a controlled way, and downstream transformations are what the broken-down material becomes next: feedstocks instead of landfill. The cooperative project developed that protocol with a partner. The report closes the agreement at the summary level cleared for public release.
doe-osti-3400052-storing-affordability-b:
Storing Affordability: Battery Storage as an Asset to Reduce Data Center Cost Shifts, a Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report dated June 2026 by Devyn W. Powell and Erik Anderson, takes up the politics of the data center boom. New computing load raises total electricity demand; whether it raises or lowers everyone else's bills depends on how much new utility cost the load drags with it.

Three scenarios structure the analysis. Minimal load growth with rising utility costs leads to higher bills. Load growth with minimal new utility costs leads to lower bills, as fixed costs spread over more sales. When both load and utility costs rise, bill impacts vary. Battery storage enters as the tool of the title: an asset that can shave the peaks that drive new infrastructure spending, blunting the cost shifts that would otherwise land on ordinary customers.
doe-osti-3407756-financial-analysis-of-t:
Argonne report ANL-26/34 studies the money side of special water flows at Glen Canyon Dam during 2025. Quentin Ploussard, Matija Pavicevic, and Ao Yu wrote the study. The flows were meant to curb smallmouth bass below the dam. Changed flows also change power output.

Schedulers at the Western Area Power Administration office in Montrose, Colorado set hourly plant output under set rules. Those rules include limits tied to each reservoir and its environmental needs. The study weighs lost or shifted power value against the flow plan. Dam managers get a clear cost picture for a fish control choice.
doe-osti-3409959-fy26-status-update-on-a:
Argonne status update by Xuan Zhang and Edward J. Listwan covers Fiscal 2026 testing for the Alloy 709 code case. Alloy 709 is a steel meant for hot nuclear service. A code case would let builders use it under set rules.

Past heats came from several campaigns, including 40,000 pounds in Fiscal 2022 and 38,000 pounds in Fiscal 2023. A multi-lab round robin in Fiscal 2018 picked electro-slag remelting as the final production route. A treatment of 10 hours at 775 degrees Celsius was also set. Long tests toward 100,000 hours will decide the design basis. The update keeps the long test program on record for code case reviewers.
doe-osti-3818144-technoeconomic-analysis:
A National Laboratory of the Rockies study dated September 2026 sizes solar and storage for three Alachua County buildings in Gainesville, Florida. Ally Pantaleo Acquaviva and Clayton Pokorny are the printed authors. The lab's REopt platform searched for the cheapest mix of rooftop panels and batteries at each site.

At the Facilities Management Office, a local installer's fifty-four kilowatt design was checked against the roof, which could hold fifty-six to fifty-eight kilowatts. A thirty percent tax credit shapes the sums. The Environmental Protection lands building fits a smaller array, between eighteen and thirty-eight kilowatts. That range swings with load, panel price, and credit eligibility, so sensitivity checks were run.
doe-osti-3874828-the-role-of-water-on-mi:
How water vapour poisons the getter inside tritium production rods is studied in Los Alamos report LA-UR-26-28115, issued September 11, 2026. Bianca Ceballos leads, with Tanner Finney as co-lead and three teammates. The nickel-plated getter soaks up hydrogen isotopes inside the rod. Stray impurity gases can coat its surface and slow that uptake. Water is one suspect gas.

A custom balance rig weighs the getter as gases flow over it. Lines can run dry or humid, with moisture set by a chiller and checked by a dew point sensor. Samples first bake in air at four hundred degrees to clear old water and grime. Runs then hold at three hundred fifty degrees for up to two days per gas mix. Alternating dry and wet helium runs show how the getter answers each switch. Results feed getter life forecasts for the production program.
doe-osti-3912519-fluka-monte-carlo-analy:
Brookhaven technical note NSLSII-ESH-TN-448, dated July 29, 2026, pairs simulation with dose measurement at a synchrotron front end. Eleven authors are printed, led by João Saraiva. The setting is the 20-ID instrumentation front end of the National Synchrotron Light Source II. A permanent magnet quadrupole is set to be irradiated near the beam stop before ring testing. The goal is to learn how a samarium cobalt magnet's field degrades as dose climbs.

FLUKA Monte Carlo runs mapped the photon spectrum and expected dose around the stop. Radiochromic films then measured real doses above and below the vacuum chamber. Three campaigns logged exposures of very different lengths, the longest running hundreds of hours. Photon energies reach roughly one hundred kiloelectronvolts at the test spot. The note supports the magnet research effort for the light source upgrade. Its data tell engineers what dose the test magnet will accumulate.
dutt-mahabharata-later-parvas:
Dutt's 1905 volume gathers the Mahabharata's closing books in English prose. The span runs from the great horse rite to the ascent to heaven. The Pandavas' last journey brings the vast epic to its end.

Yudhishthira's horse roams free while armies guard its path across India. Then come the club fight, the great departure, and the walk to heaven. A lone dog keeps faith with the king to the last gate. Heaven and hell both hold shocks for the weary heroes there. The majestic close rewards readers who made the long road with them here. Sorrow and wonder share the final pages in equal measure.
england-over-seas:
Lloyd Roberts sings the emigrant's divided heart in England Over Seas, a book of verse published by Elkin Mathews in 1914. The opening poem sets white cliffs and green fields against the pull of new lands abroad. Titles like The Homesteader, Husbands Over Seas, and The Trail from Napoli mark the book's ground: settlers far from home.

Many poems turn to Canadian woods and waters, with berry pickers, frog flutes, musk-rats, and winter winds. A girl in moccasins and beads laughs among the pines in one hunting piece. Spring madness, scarlet trails, and dead days mark the seasons of exile. The closing pieces face the year's end and the winter harvest. Homesickness, not adventure, is the steady note.
eryxias:
Benjamin Jowett translated the Eryxias with an appendix warning. The dialogue, he says, is not by Plato. An imitator of the second or third generation after Plato wrote it. Aristotle and every early authority leave it unmentioned. Its persons are Socrates, Eryxias of Steiria, Erasistratus, and Critias, walking in the porch of Zeus. Their subject is wealth.

Socrates presses whether money is a good in itself or only in its uses, quoting Prodicus and turning the rich men's boasts against them. Jowett finds the style middling yet the thoughts surprisingly modern. The piece survives as evidence of how quickly Plato's manner became a school exercise, and its question, what riches are for, stays fresh.
folklore-of-the-santal-parganas:
Bompas translates the tales of a people of Bengal in Folklore of the Santal Parganas, dated 1909. Cecil Henry Bompas, of the Indian Civil Service, gathered the stories of the Santals in their own district. The contents run to more than a hundred tales, in parts: Bajun and Jhore, the cruel stepmother, Karmu and Dharmu, the laughing fish, and the magic cow among them.

The sampled tale opens with a raja and rani who long for a son. They make pilgrimages to many shrines, in vain. A Jugi, a holy man, reads their palms and fears to speak. At last he tells them they can never have a child unless they part, the raja to go away and the rani to live with another man. Bompas gives the tales plainly, as they were told to him, with their hard turns left in.
four-dimensional-vistas:
Bragdon explores the fourth dimension as a key to freedom, miracles, and the failure of common sense. His chapters climb a dimensional ladder from the cosmos to the corpuscle. Symmetry, isomerism, and the electric current are read as hints of a greater space containing ours.

Dreams carry one of his arguments. A dream's second can seem to last half an hour, yet the whole proves incredibly brief afterward. The body, he suggests, is an organ of many stops, playing richer music in sleep. Claude Fayette Bragdon, an architect by trade, ranges on to curved time, clairvoyance, and relativity.
freytag-die-technik-des-dramas:
Every student of drama knows Freytag's pyramid: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, catastrophe. Gustav Freytag built that model in Die Technik des Dramas, published in 1863 and given here in German. The Technique of the Drama became the standard theory of play structure for the stage and, later, the screen.

Freytag analyzes Greek tragedy, Shakespeare, and the German classics to extract his rules of construction. Scenes, acts, and turning points each receive practical, craftsmanlike treatment. Playwrights and screenwriters have been taught from his scheme ever since, often without knowing his name. The German text gives the theory in its original, confident voice. No book on playwriting has carried wider influence.
gaslight-sonatas:
Fannie Hurst gathers seven tales of city life in Gaslight Sonatas, published in 1918 and dedicated to her parents. The stories bear titles such as Bitter-Sweet, Sieve of Fulfilment, and Get Ready the Wreaths. Most turn on poor and working women in New York. Hurst opens by noting how big grim counts of the poor move no one, while one known face does.

A laundress's daughter, a wage-earning girl felled by typhoid, and women worn down by loss pass through the tales. Small homes, low pay, and sharp class gaps shape their choices. Hurst writes with warmth and bite, in a rich, musical style. The tales plead for the poor as real people, not as counts in a report.
gorgias:
Plato's Gorgias, in Benjamin Jowett's translation, brings the great Sicilian rhetorician to Athens, where Socrates asks whether rhetoric is an art or a knack like cookery, flattery dressed as medicine. Gorgias agrees that knowing justice makes a man just, and the trap begins. His pupil Polus and the brutal Callicles take up the fight in turn.

Jowett's introduction warns that the dialogue's digressions often outshine its thesis, yet a natural unity binds beginning to end. Callicles defends nature's right of the stronger against law and shame. Socrates answers with the health of the soul and a closing myth of judgment. The Gorgias remains Plato's fiercest attack on power without justice.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BaumlerThomas_B: Thomas Baumler is the title-name of this declassified US government document from the Internet Archive. The entry lists nothing else - no date, no bureau, no subject beyond govdocs. No public-domain text has been located. Kept as a thin named record.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HorockNicholas_: A memorandum dated February 20, 1975 records a phone call from Nicholas Horock. Horock worked in the Washington office of The New York Times. His call went to an employee of Bernard-Fain Carpets, Inc., an unlikely pairing of a national newspaper and a carpet firm. The memo preserves the call's date, caller, and destination, but not what the two discussed.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-IconoclastDalla:
A reader wrote to Doug Baker of the Dallas Iconoclast on June 2, 1975 about the physical evidence of the assassination. The letter discusses photographs and a mark on the concrete around a manhole. Its author cannot be identified from the text, but the subjects are the small, hard details researchers wrote to editors about.

Underground papers like the Iconoclast opened their columns to this traffic. A mark on concrete could carry a theory of a shot, and readers argued such marks for years. The letter preserves one citizen's evidence, sent to the local paper that would print it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LethridgeDougla:
On December 17, 1967, an unnamed researcher wrote this memorandum about finding Douglas Lethbridge. Lethbridge was a veteran of the Bay of Pigs, the failed 1961 invasion of Cuba. The writer reached him through Alberto Fowler and recorded a dinner conversation with him on tape. The author's own name cannot be recovered from the text.

The memo is a field note from the private investigation of the Kennedy assassination. At that moment, the Garrison inquiry in New Orleans was pulling in anti-Castro veterans as witnesses and suspects. A taped dinner with one of them, arranged through an intermediary, shows how that research was actually done: through introductions, shared meals, and a running tape recorder.
govdocs-archive_org-ompleteUnabridgedTho:
Thomas Aquinas, the Dominican friar and theologian, spent his last years writing the Summa Theologica, a huge summary of Christian teaching. It is organized in three parts, covering God, human life and morals, and Christ. Aquinas left it unfinished at his death in 1274.

Inside, nearly every topic is argued the same careful way: a question is posed, objections are stated, an answer is given, and each objection is met. That method, called scholastic, trained students for centuries. The Summa became the cornerstone of Catholic theology teaching, and the complete text here lets readers study Aquinas whole rather than in excerpts.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va:
Cryptolog was the National Security Agency's in-house periodical, written by signals intelligence staff for each other. In 2018 the Archive posted 136 publicly released issues of it. This Cyber Brief supplements that popular resource with newly released material from the same long-running publication.

An agency's internal magazine shows its craft culture in a way official reports do not. Cryptolog carried technical articles and shop talk for the people who intercepted and decoded foreign communications. Adding more of it gives researchers a deeper run of a source that reveals how NSA staff thought about their own work.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_indonesi:
President Suharto's long rule over Indonesia collapsed in May 1998 amid protests and economic crisis. This briefing book, posted in July 2018, draws on recently declassified documents from the Clinton administration. They show Washington working to preserve close ties with the Indonesian Armed Forces through the fall.

American officials knew the military was involved in kidnappings and disappearances of student activists at that very moment. Still, they treated the army's central role as the key to political stability. The documents record a familiar trade in plain terms: human rights concerns were noted, filed, and subordinated to keeping a partner institution in place.
herodias:
Gustave Flaubert set Herodias in the citadel of Machaerus above the Dead Sea, its basalt peak ringed by four valleys and walls like a crown of stone. Herod Antipas keeps John the Baptist, Iaokanann, in a pit below the palace while his wife Herodias plots against the prophet who condemns their marriage. The opening pages survey fortress, town, and tetrarch.

At the birthday feast, Salome dances and asks for the prophet's head, while Roman and Jewish factions crowd the hall. Cries of woe against Sadducees and Pharisees rise from the pit as spectators press closer. Flaubert rebuilt the scene from Josephus and archaeology with jeweler's precision, making one of his Trois Contes a study in lust, faith, and empire.
johnson-history-yorubas:
Samuel Johnson wrote The History of the Yorubas, released in 1921. His brother Obadiah edited the manuscript after the author's death. A Yoruba clergyman tells his own people's past in this book.

Kings, wars, and old traditions fill Johnson's vast, careful narrative. He drew on oral lore, court memory, and his own wide travel. The work stands as a founding text of African written history. An African voice claims the past from inside, with pride and proof. No study of the Yoruba world starts anywhere else with real profit today. Johnson's work survives as a near miracle of preservation in its own right.
la-bas:
J.-K. Huysmans published his French novel Là-bas in 1891. This English version, translated by Keene Wallace, appeared privately in 1928. Its first chapter shows writers debating the book's dark subject.

One speaker defends writing about Gilles de Rais, a notorious historical figure. He also defends the raw language of naturalist fiction. Hospital, latrine, and workshop words, he says, fit the matter. The novel became famous for its interest in evil, faith, and the occult. The debate in chapter one sets the book's whole direction. Faith, art, and horror pull the characters in opposed ways.
lesser-hippias:
Plato's Lesser Hippias is a short dialogue on truth and lying. Benjamin Jowett translated this edition and added notes on Plato's works. His appendix warns that genuine and spurious writings are hard to separate.

Aristotle's testimony, Jowett says, is the best external evidence available. In the dialogue, Socrates questions the sophist Hippias. They ask whether a person who errs on purpose is better than one who errs by chance. Achilles and Odysseus serve as their test cases. The talk ends in puzzlement, as Socrates often leaves it. Hippias prides himself on never telling a falsehood. Socrates turns that pride into a thorny puzzle about skill.
love-s-final-victory-ultimate-universal-:
Love's Final Victory argues that all souls will at last be saved. Its author signs himself Horatio, an orthodox minister. The subtitle states his ground: Scripture and reason, fairly read. A fierce line from Carlyle opens the book as a warning against false belief.

The contents survey rival theories of the world to come. Chapters attack the cruelty of older views on hell and election. They ask what becomes of the heathen and of infants. Conditional immortality and eternal punishment both come under fire. The author pleads for charity toward those who disagree. His book is a bold, kind challenge to the doctrine of endless loss.
madame-midas:
Madame Midas is a novel of mystery and gold by Fergus Hume. Its prologue, 'Cast Up by the Sea,' opens on a wild, bleak coast. Headlands jut into foaming water above a half-mile of yellow sand. Black cliffs rise behind, loud with nesting seagulls.

From that shore the tale moves to the Australian gold country. Madame Midas is a widow who has struck gold and grown rich. Greedy men circle her fortune, and crime follows the gold. Hume had won fame with The Mystery of a Hansom Cab. Here he mixes shipwreck, mining, and murder into one plot. It is rousing colonial melodrama, full of twists.
meyer-us4936961-method-for-the-productio:
Stanley A Meyer's United States Patent 4,936,961, granted June 26, 1990, is a method for the production of a fuel gas. It is the last of the eight water fuel cell patents gathered here. By 1990 Meyer had spent a decade patenting each part of his claimed system.

The method splits water with pulsed power, gathers the gas, and readies it for burning. Meyer said the gas could run cars and heat homes at almost no cost. No outside test ever backed that claim. A patent records a described method, not a proven one, and an Ohio court ruled his claims fraudulent in 1996.
mystic-isles-of-the-south-seas:
Frederick O'Brien opens this travel book with a Tahitian greeting, Ia Ora Na. He calls it a simple record of his days and nights. No science or exact knowledge is claimed, he warns. He went to the islands with one thought: to play.

O'Brien writes of Tahiti and Moorea as the merriest world he knew. Songs, dances, reefs, and lagoons fill his pages. He sailed, swam, and feasted with island folk and odd whites. The book comes before his White Shadows in the South Seas. It is a light, fond chronicle of leisure under the equator's bright skies.
nasa-tm-19660015397-observations-on-puls:
G R Cresswell, of the University of Alaska's Geophysical Institute, and T N Davis reported observations of pulsating auroras in November 1965. Most auroras shimmer, but pulsating ones blink on and off across wide patches of sky. The watchers used an image orthicon television camera, a sensitive early video device. Their study covers activity in the phase after an auroral display breaks up.

Pulsating patches are hard to record on ordinary film. A television camera could follow their rhythm in real time. Knowing when pulsations occur, and how they spread, tests ideas about the particles behind them. The report preserves careful watching from Alaska, then the center of American auroral research.
nasa-tm-19680020531-measurements-in-the-:
Robert G. Stone, Joseph Fainberg, and J. K. Alexander of Goddard Space Flight Center report antenna measurements from a sounding rocket in this paper, part one of a study. The rocket flew through the ionosphere measuring antenna reactance, a measure of how the antenna interacts with surrounding plasma. Readings varied in step with the rocket's spin period.

The variations split into parts tied to the full spin period, half the period, or a mix of both. Which part dominated depended on the experiment setup, flight path, and plasma conditions. Explaining the data required modeling both the plasma itself and the disturbance the moving rocket creates. The authors show plasma patterns inferred from the reactance records.
nasa-tm-19720008960-wave-growth-in-a-str:
Wave Growth in a Strongly Turbulent Plasma is a NASA preprint numbered X-641-71-321, whose author names the scan renders poorly. It treats electric waves moving through a plasma already churning with strong turbulence. In such a plasma, the turbulence itself changes how fast a wave can grow or fade.

The authors derive an equation for the average growth or damping rate of an electrostatic wave in a whole ensemble of turbulent plasmas. Strong turbulence bends particle paths while the wave grows, carrying particles into and out of resonance with it. Because of that, the growth rate depends on particle speeds near the wave speed, not only exactly at it. Two orbital effects emerge: the average orbits shift, and particles disperse around them, together broadening the resonance.
nasa-tm-19720010401-bleed-cycle-propella:
Albert F Kascak and Annie J Easley of the Lewis Research Center calculated pump performance for a gas core nuclear rocket in March 1972, as NASA TM X-2517. In that engine concept, the nuclear fuel itself is a hot gas. Propellant must be pumped to extreme pressures to feed it. A bleed cycle taps some propellant to drive the pump turbines. The study covered pressures from five hundred to five thousand atmospheres.

For an engine pressure of one thousand atmospheres, the numbers came out clearly. The bleed flow cost about a tenth of the specific impulse. Pump work and propellant preheat needs were also computed. At very high performance levels, extra energy sat available in the moderator. Gamma rays and neutrons supplied that surplus.
nasa-tm-19720019611-as-511-facilities-an: AS-511 Facilities and Environmental Measurements Program is a NASA document listing the monitoring planned for an Apollo Saturn flight. AS-511 was the vehicle stack for the Apollo 16 mission. The catalog record describes a list of facilities and environmental measurements to watch during the effort. Each entry carries an identification number and a description. It also gives the sensor's working range and the recorder type used. Drawings show where each measurement sits. The hosted sample is unreadable scan noise. No readable list entries survive in the sample provided.
nature-cure-philosophy-practice-based-on: Nature Cure, by Henry Lindlahr, carries the subtitle Philosophy and Practice Based on the Unity of Disease and Cure. The hosted sample holds only a Project Gutenberg header, so it preserves no readable content from the book itself. The title and subtitle alone state the claim: disease has one root, and cure follows the same unity. No year for the book is given in the sample or the record. Readers should treat this note as a title level guide only.
nibsy-s-christmas:
Jacob August Riis first published Nibsy's Christmas in 1893, and Books for Libraries Press reprinted it at Freeport, New York, in 1969. A picture shows Nibsy dressed as Santa Claus. Riis inscribed the tale to Queen Louise of Denmark, friend of the afflicted in his childhood home.

The story opens on Christmas Eve on New York's East Side. Darkness closes in on a cold, hard day. Light from a delicatessen and a corner saloon falls on men with empty dinner pails. They hurry home with coats buttoned tight, heads bent against the blast from the river. Christmas in the tenements is Riis's ground.
novelas-cortas:
Don Pedro A. de Alarcón, a member of the Spanish Academy, wrote the short novels in Novelas Cortas. W. F. Giese, of the University of Wisconsin, edited this school edition with notes and a vocabulary. Ginn and Company published it in Boston, New York, Chicago, and London. Spanish students were its first readers.

Contents open with La Buenaventura, then La Corneta de Llaves and Las Dos Glorias. El Afrancesado, Viva el Papa, and El Extranjero follow. El Libro Talonario and Moros y Cristianos come next, the latter the longest piece. El Año en Spitzberg closes the tales. An idiomatic commentary at the back explains hard phrases for learners.
old-christmas:
Washington Irving wrote these sketches of an English Christmas. They are set at Bracebridge Hall in the countryside. The contents move from the stage coach to Christmas dinner. Irving laments that old holiday customs are fading fast. He recalls games, feasts, and rural joys of former times.

The sketches show hosts, guests, and poor neighbors at the feast. Good fires, rich food, and welcome for all fill the hall. It says the pieces helped shape the American idea of Christmas. Warmth and gentle humor run through every scene. An old song in the text bids welcome to the poor. It says the poor were not chased from the gates.
omoo-adventures-in-the-south-seas:
Herman Melville wrote this sea narrative about the South Seas. The contents list dozens of chapters aboard the Julia. Early chapters describe the ship, crew, and forecastle life. The ship touches at Dominica and other islands. Tattooers, gales, and coral islands fill the voyage.

Later chapters center on Tahiti and the town of Papeetee. The crew defies the consul and faces the French. Some sailors land in the local calaboose prison. Doctor Long Ghost provides humor among the men. Melville draws on his own whaling years for detail. The book mixes adventure, satire, and island life.
on-the-indian-sect-of-the-jainas:
Georg Bühler wrote this essay on the Jaina sect of India. He read it in Vienna on May 26, 1887. James Burgess edited this English translation in 1903. Burgess also added an outline of Jaina mythology. Bühler knew the Jains and their religious books well.

The preface hopes Indian readers will welcome the translation. German works were sealed books to most of them, Burgess says. The essay gives a succinct account of the sect. Its long note defends the Jaina tradition as authentic. Burgess adds a fuller account of the Tirthankaras. Those figures stand at the center of Jaina worship.
podcast-dannyjones-MxF7TzYzfAs:
Journalist Ben Swann joins Danny Jones to discuss the darkest corner of the Epstein record as Swann presents it. It concerns classified videotapes he says Epstein kept. Their contents, in the episode's phrase, would end society if released. Swann argues the blackmail archive, not the trafficking alone, is the real story and the real leverage.

Jones works through what can actually be shown: the cameras documented in Epstein's properties, the tapes investigators reported, and the gap between that record and Swann's fullest claims. The strongest assertions remain unproven, and the recording keeps them as the guest's. For followers of the case, the episode offers the blackmail theory in its most developed popular form, argued by a broadcaster who has staked his comeback on it.
podcast-joerogan-JIArjzI3gas:
Former Texas governor Rick Perry and ibogaine advocate W. Bryan Hubbard join the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2477. Perry, once U.S. Secretary of Energy, now backs psychedelic treatment for veterans. Hubbard has led the policy fight to fund that research. Their pairing is itself the story.

They tell Rogan why ibogaine, a strong plant psychedelic, drew them in, and what veterans report after treatment. The talk covers the politics of getting a banned drug studied at all. The episode shows an unlikely alliance, a conservative politician and a reform advocate, making the same case to Rogan's huge audience.
podcast-joerogan-q7hWj2iS0As:
Lawrence Wright, the Pulitzer Prize-winning author and New Yorker writer, talks with Joe Rogan in episode 1588. Wright is known for Going Clear, his book on Scientology, and The Looming Tower, on the road to 9/11. Few guests bring his depth of reporting to the show.

Wright explains how he researches closed groups and violent movements without losing fairness. He shares stories from years of interviews with believers, spies, and officials. Rogan asks about faith, delusion, and why smart people join strange causes. The talk is a master class in patient journalism, told in a calm and careful voice.
proserpine-and-midas:
Mary Shelley wrote two short dramas on Greek myths that stayed unpublished in her lifetime and appear here with an introduction by their editor, A. Koszul. Koszul found the texts as early as 1905 and held them back for years, unsure of their worth.

The plays retell the stories of Proserpine, taken by the god of the dead, and of Midas, whose wishes turn to grief. Koszul notes that the dramas frame some of Percy Shelley's finest lyrics, long read apart from their setting. Readers get a rare view of Mary Shelley as a verse dramatist of the Romantic age.
protagoras:
Plato's dialogue on the teaching of virtue appears here in Benjamin Jowett's English version, with a long introduction by the translator. Socrates tells of a visit paid with the young Hippocrates to the house of Callias, where the famous teacher Protagoras was staying.

Protagoras claims he can make men better in private and public life, and Socrates presses him on whether such skill can truly be taught. Hippias, Prodicus, Alcibiades, and Critias join the talk, and Protagoras answers with a myth of Prometheus and Zeus. Readers get a lively contest over education, virtue, and the price of wisdom.
richard-wagner-composer-of-operas:
John F. Runciman wrote this life of Richard Wagner, composer of operas, for G. Bell and Sons of London in 1913. He dedicates the book to Harold Hodge. Its contents follow the composer from early life and boyhood through his juvenile works to Paris.

Chapters named for the operas mark the climb: Rienzi and The Flying Dutchman share one, then Dresden, Tannhäuser, and Lohengrin follow. Exile gets a chapter of its own. Tristan and Isolde and The Mastersingers of Nuremberg come next, then King Ludwig, whose aid changed Wagner's fortunes. The list shown ends with The Nibelung's Ring and The Valkyrie.
sacred-books-east-vol-11-buddhist-suttas:
T. W. Rhys Davids translated the Buddhist Suttas of Sacred Books of the East volume eleven, published in 1881. Rhys Davids was the leading British scholar of Pali in his day. The volume holds the discourses he judged most basic to the Buddha's message.

Chief among them is the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the long account of the Buddha's last days, his final teachings, and his death. The Dhamma-Kakka-Ppavattana Sutta follows: the first sermon, which set the wheel of the teaching rolling with the four noble truths. Other suttas treat signs of a great man and the rules of the order. The volume is a core shelf of early Buddhism.
story-of-aeneas:
M. Clarke, author of Story of Troy and Story of Caesar, retold the Story of Aeneas in 1898, with a map of the hero's wanderings across the sea from Troy toward Italy. Two opening chapters present Vergil, called the prince of poets, and the gods and goddesses of the tale.

The story proper follows Vergil's poem: the wooden horse, the flight from Troy, the harpies, and the giant Polyphemus; then the great storm, Carthage, and Dido's love. The Sibyl of Cumae and the golden bough come next. The regions of the dead follow. Then comes Latium and the shield Vulcan makes. The deaths of Pallas and Turnus end the war.
the-belted-seas:
Arthur Colton opened his sea book with verses about the hot belt of the earth, where seas laugh and thunder around still islands. Chapter one is set at Pemberton's, and chapter two names a ship, the Hebe Maitland. A hotel called Helen Mar appears and then ends.

Sadler moves through places named Portate and Saleratus in the headings. Captains, a Green Dragon pagoda, a King Julius, and a ship called Voodoo follow. The loss of a ship named Anaconda is tied to a captain who did not go back to Greenough, though another captain later returns there. Linked sea tales, rather than one straight voyage, shape the contents.
the-black-douglas:
S. R. Crockett published a Scottish novel with Doubleday and McClure in New York in 1899. Crockett is also named for The Raiders and The Stickit Minister. A frontispiece shows a figure sailing over seas to his own land.

Contents open with the Black Douglas riding home, then a fair lady and two riding together. A rose-red pavilion, a witch woman, and the prisoning of Malise the smith follow in the early headings. Romance, riding, and a smith in prison promise a tale of old Scotland in which a famed Douglas lord moves through love and danger rather than court record.
the-buccaneer-farmer-published-in-englan: Harold Bindloss wrote The Buccaneer Farmer, dated 1918. In England it ran under the title Askew's Victory. Part I, At Ashness, starts with The Lease and The Otter Hounds. A Council of Defense, The Peat Cutters, and Railton's Tally come next. Janet Meddles, Osborn's Pride Gets Hurt, and Osborn Interferes close the part. Part II, On the Caribbean, opens with The Old Buccaneer and The Presidio. The Gold Onza and The President's Ball follow, and the list stops there.
the-countess-of-escarbagnas:
Moliere's The Countess of Escarbagnas appears here in English prose translated by Charles Heron Wall, who adds short introductions and notes. A head note says the play was acted before the court at Saint-Germain-en-Laye on December 2, 1671. It played at the Palais Royal on July 8, 1672. It was first printed in 1682, after the author's death. The scene is set at Angouleme.

The cast shows the Countess with two suitors, the tax receiver Mr. Harpin and the councillor Mr. Thibaudier, while the Viscount loves Julia and Julia loves him back. Scene I opens on the pair at a meeting place. Julia scolds her lover, calling him Cleante, for coming last to their meeting. He pleads that an old bore of rank stopped him on the road, hungry to retail absurd court news.
the-cruise-of-the-kawa-wanderings-in-the: Walter E. Traprock's The Cruise of the Kawa, wanderings in the South Seas dated 1921, carries seventeen illustrations and a map, plus a frontispiece showing the author and his bride. A dedication names three girls, with name translations: Kippiputuona, daughter of pearl and coral; Lupoba-Tilaana, mist on the mountain; and Babai-Alova-Babai, essence of Alova. A publisher's note remarks on the spell the South Seas have cast on readers and the house's sole rights to Traprock's manuscript. Only the front matter and that note are present here.
the-death-wake-or-lunacy-a-necromaunt-in: Thomas T. Stoddart wrote The Death-Wake, or Lunacy, a necromaunt in three chimeras, printed in London by John Lane and in Chicago by Way and Williams in 1895, with an introduction by Andrew Lang. A motto from Shakespeare stands at the front. Lang contributes a poem headed Piscatori Piscator, hailing a fellow angler by the Tweed, by Elibank and Yair, whose boyhood found the waters clean and whose age deplored them foul with dye. Only the title page and Lang's poem are present here.
the-headless-horseman-a-strange-tale-of-:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote The Headless Horseman, subtitled a strange tale of Texas, dated 1865. The prologue opens at midnight on the prairie, where a stag of Texas is startled from sleep by the hoofstroke of a horse. Metal rings against stone, and the stag springs up and looks back at a rider in clear southern moonlight.

Reid holds the sight back step by step. The horse looks perfect, saddled and bridled, with nothing amiss. The rider, though, lacks something that fills the animal with fear and wonder. What is wanting is the head. The prologue sets a tale of dread on the open plains, told through the eyes of a watching animal.
the-life-of-stephen-a-douglas: William Gardner wrote his life of Stephen A. Douglas, the Illinois senator famous for debates with Abraham Lincoln. Only a Project Gutenberg header is present here, giving the book title, Gardner name, and an April 2001 electronic release note. The header also names the volunteer who prepared the text for release. The biography itself, covering Douglas rise, the Kansas Nebraska fight, and his 1860 presidential run, cannot be read in this record at all.
the-ned-m-keown-stories-traits-and-stori:
William Carleton's Traits and Stories of the Irish Peasantry fills volume 3 of his collected works, in an edition dated 1881. Its contents name five stories: Ned M'Keown, The Three Tasks, Shane Fadh's Wedding, Larry M'Farland's Wake, and The Battle of the Factions. The volume's introduction, written by Carleton himself, explains why such a book needs a word of preparation.

Carleton undertakes the task, he says, more for his country's sake than his own. English and Scotch readers especially need help understanding how the Irish peasantry think, feel, and live. He rejoices that demand for a new edition lets him attack the absurd prejudices held against his countrymen from time immemorial.
the-orations-of-lysias: The Orations of Lysias appear here in a literal English translation, in a series called Handy Literal Translations. No translator is named in the pages present. A contents list is present, and the speeches themselves are not. The list names the Funeral Oration and speeches For Callias, The Olive Tree, and speeches against Eratosthenes, Agoratus, and Alcibiades, plus The Grain Dealers and The Cripple. Lysias was an Athenian speech writer whose clients faced court cases and public charges.
the-pension-beaurepas:
An 1886 Macmillan edition presents The Pension Beaurepas, a tale of a Geneva boarding house. No author is named in the pages present. The narrator is a poor young man with a fancy for a literary career. He chose the cheap pension because a boarding house is a capital place to study human nature. Stendhal had given his sister the same advice.

The Pension Beaurepas stood in its own little garden near the lake, esteemed and sociable. Guests, though, entered through the kitchen smells. Madame Beaurepas was seventy-three and had kept lodgers for forty years. She was slightly deaf and fond of a surreptitious pinch of snuff. She asked only that guests pay their bills, use the door mat, and fold their napkins. Her house promises a study of characters.
the-princess-pocahontas: Virginia Watson's The Princess Pocahontas, drawn and decorated by George Wharton Edwards, opens with its title page and a contents list. The chapters promise The Return of the Warriors, Pocahontas and the Medicine Man, and Running the Gauntlet. Later entries name John Smith's Temptation, Pocahontas Defies Powhatan, and Pocahontas Visits Jamestown. Only these first leaves are present in the pages at hand; the tale's own first chapter does not appear.
the-spirit-of-christmas: Henry Van Dyke's Christmas book was published by Charles Scribner's Sons of New York, copyrighted in 1905 and issued again in 1911. The pages present here give the title page and contents only. They name a dream-story called The Christmas Angel. An essay on Christmas-giving and Christmas-living follows, with a short sermon on keeping Christmas. Two Christmas prayers, for the home and for lonely folk, close the list at the dream-story's heading, so the pieces themselves do not appear.
the-story-of-pocahontas:
Charles Dudley Warner tells Pocahontas's life plainly. The simple story, he argues, is romantic enough. It needs no extras from Captain Smith's vanity. It needs none from descendants proud of a rivulet of her blood. Witnesses of her time agree on her gifts, he says. She was a remarkably clever child. Early on she showed a tender regard for the English. She rendered them service, willing and unwilling.

Warner notes the London portrait. Simon de Passe engraved it in 1616. She was said to be twenty-one then. Warner traces her first mention to Smith's True Relation of 1608. There Powhatan sends his most esteemed child. She is a girl of ten. She brings a deer and bread as a present. The prisoners held by the English are afterwards given into her keeping. The gift honours her father's kindness.
the-witch-of-atlas:
Percy Bysshe Shelley opens The Witch of Atlas with a verse dedication to Mary. She had objected that the poem held no human interest. Shelley answers her in playful stanzas. He asks why a kitten must catch mice before it may leap and play. A young fly, he argues, deserves its brief hour too.

He tells how a winged vision came to Mary's feet. Its plumes faded as the sun went down and the shower fell. Shelley begs her not to grieve that passing beauty. The dedication sets a light, fanciful tone. Readers meet a poem that defends imagination for its own sake.
three-dramas:
Björnstjerne Björnson's Three Dramas collects The Editor, The Bankrupt, and The King. An introduction says these plays grew from years when Björnson's views changed drastically. Two were written during a three-year absence in southern Europe, and one just after it.

Earlier he had managed theatres and campaigned for truer equality between Sweden and Norway. Abroad he read Spencer, Darwin, Mill, Taine, and Max-Müller voraciously. The social philosopher replaced the poet, and prose drama gained a serious thesis. Readers get an account of Björnson reaching that form before Ibsen, with newly opened eyes and ears.
twas-the-night-before-christmas-a-visit-:
Clement C. Moore's A Visit from St. Nicholas appears in a Houghton Mifflin edition with pictures by Jessie Willcox Smith. An introduction tells how a New York company gathered at Moore's tomb one Christmas Eve. Standing together, they recited the poem aloud.

Moore, born near Chelsea Square in 1781, lived in the same great house all his life. He expected fame, if any, from his Hebrew dictionary, not from a children's poem. The introduction notes that he loved writing verse for his own children even more. Readers meet the famous night-before-Christmas verses with the poet's quiet scholarly life set out first.
typee-a-romance-of-the-south-seas:
Herman Melville's Typee, a romance of the South Seas, begins with a preface written after three years spent mostly at sea. Melville says sailors alone now see stirring adventure, and that his shipmates' warm response to his yarn persuaded him to publish. Fire-side readers, he hopes, will find the same interest.

He warns that he treats the islanders' obvious peculiarities without explaining the origin of their customs. Dates, too, will be vague, since he lost count of the days of the week among them. Polynesian words are spelled to carry their sound to a stranger's ear. The preface frames a sailor's captivity tale told plainly, with excuses made in advance.
uncle-silas:
Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu built this long tale of dread round a will and an heir in 1864. He was the Irish master of the ghost tale, and this is his great work of the sensation kind. The tale is told by Maud Ruthyn, a young heir in her teens, in her own words.

Maud's uncle Silas, a man with a dark past, gains charge of her life and her wealth. In his lone great house, plots close round her, and her friends can do no more than watch. Steeped in dread from first to last, it is the peak of its kind in its age.
weird-tales-from-northern-seas: Jonas Lie's Weird Tales from Northern Seas came from the Danish in R. Nisbet Bain's rendering of 1893, with twelve illustrations by Laurence Housman. Pages present here hold the title page and contents only, so the tales themselves are not shown. Contents promise eleven pieces. The Fisherman and the Draug, and Jack of Sjoholm and the Gan-Finn, lead. A tug of war, The Earth Draws, and the cormorants of Andvaer follow. Finn blood, and a homestead westward in the blue mountains, close the list.
white-shadows-in-the-south-seas: Frederick O'Brien's White Shadows in the South Seas is shown here through a detailed contents list, with no travel narrative present. Laurie printed the book in 1919, with many photographs. The contents open with a farewell to Papeete and a sea trip on the Morning Star. Darwin's theory of a sunken continent enters chapter one. Later chapters promise thirty-seven days at sea, sea birds, and a first sight of Fatu-hiva. A new governor's landing and a dance on a palace lawn follow in the list.
z-marcas:
Honore de Balzac wrote this tale, rendered into English by Clara Bell and others. The narrator opens by studying a striking stranger's face and name. Z. Marcas, he muses, sounds sinister and unfinished. The letter Z seems to carry an adverse fate. Marcas's first name was Zephirin, and he was a Breton. Names may shape destiny, the narrator half believes.

That brooding start frames a life of thwarted ambition. The tale is dedicated to Count William of Wurtemberg, with Balzac's gratitude. Readers get a short, intense character study. Political hope and ruin turn on one gifted man's failure to find his place.
